# 9.2 Market Structures

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four structures

Market structures are classified by three things: how many firms there are, whether their products are identical or differentiated, and whether new firms can enter.

| Structure | Number of firms | Product | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Perfect competition** | Many, all price-takers | Identical | Free entry and exit, no barriers |
| **Monopoly** | One | No close substitutes | Barriers to entry |
| **Oligopoly** | A small number of large firms | — | Barriers to entry |
| **Monopolistic competition** | Large numbers | Differentiated | Free entry and exit in the long run |

Every result in this topic follows from those three columns, so it is worth reading the table as a set of causes rather than a set of labels.

## Perfect competition

Firms in perfect competition are **price-takers**: they accept the market price rather than setting it. There is free entry and exit, and there are no barriers.

The reason firms are price-takers is that each one is too small to influence the market price on its own. That, and not any agreement or regulation, is what removes their pricing power — which is why a perfectly competitive firm producing identical output alongside many others has nothing to gain by charging more, since buyers can get the same good elsewhere.

*Which of the following is a characteristic of firms in a perfectly competitive industry? (A) Engaging in collusive behaviour (B) Facing significant barriers to entry (C) Setting the market price (D) Producing identical products (E) Earning long-run economic profit*

The answer is **(D)**. Each of the other four options contradicts one of the three defining columns: collusion and price-setting both require the market power that price-takers lack, barriers to entry contradict free entry, and long-run economic profit is competed away precisely because entry is free.

## Monopoly

A **monopoly** is an industry controlled by a monopolist, selling a good with no close substitutes. What keeps it a monopoly is that other firms cannot get in, and the guide gives four kinds of **barrier to entry**:

| Barrier | |
|---|---|
| Control of a scarce resource or input | The entrant cannot obtain what it would need to produce |
| Economies of scale | The incumbent's costs per unit fall with size, so a small entrant cannot match its prices |
| Technological superiority | The incumbent can do something the entrant cannot |
| Government created barriers | Entry is restricted by law |

## Oligopoly: interdependence and game theory

An **oligopoly** is a market with a small number of large firms. Its three characteristics are a few large firms, barriers to entry, and **interdependence** — each firm's best action depends on what the others do, because with only a handful of firms, one firm's price change is large enough to matter to the rest.

Interdependence is why oligopoly is often analysed with **game theory**, and it is the answer to the question of where game theory is useful:

*Game theory is most useful in describing outcomes in markets in which (A) firms are price takers (B) there is only one producer (C) there are many small producers (D) products are identical for all firms (E) there are interdependent firms*

The answer is **(E)**. Game theory analyses decisions that depend on other people's decisions. A price-taker among many small producers has nobody in particular to respond to, and a single producer has no rival at all; only interdependence gives the analysis something to work on.

The practice set names two ways oligopolists may compete with one another:

| Model | How firms compete |
|---|---|
| **Bertrand oligopoly** | Firms compete with each other by setting the price |
| **Cournot oligopoly** | Firms compete with each other by choosing the production quantity |

### The kinked demand curve

*The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly suggests that firms: (A) Ignore competitors' pricing decisions. (B) Match price cuts but not price increases, leading to price rigidity. (C) Always act as price takers. (D) Produce at minimum average total cost in the long run. (E) Are likely to become monopoly*

The answer is **(B)**. The model assumes each firm expects its rivals to follow a price cut but not a price rise. A firm that raises its price is therefore left alone at the higher price and loses customers to the rivals who stayed put; a firm that cuts its price finds the cut matched and gains little. Both moves look unattractive, so prices tend not to move at all — **price rigidity**. Note that (A) states the opposite of interdependence, and (C) belongs to perfect competition.

### Why collusion does not last

*Which of the following best explains why it is difficult to maintain lasting collusive agreements? (A) There is an unavoidable conflict in that a collusive agreement can increase the profits of some, but not all, firms in the industry. (B) There is little potential for gain from collusion unless there is a large number of consumers in the market. (C) Each firm in the industry views itself as facing a vertical demand curve, even though the market demand curve is downward sloping. (D) The firms in the industry have a common incentive to increase output to a more competitive level. (E) Each firm realises that its profits would increase if it were the only firm to violate the collusive agreement by increasing its production slightly.*

The answer is **(E)**, and it is a statement about incentives rather than about honesty. **Collusion** raises profits by restricting output between the firms, but the restriction is exactly what makes cheating attractive: with the price held up by everybody else's restraint, one firm selling a little more captures the gain while the others carry the cost. Every firm faces that calculation, which is why the agreement is unstable from the inside. (D) inverts the point — firms have a common incentive to *restrict* output, and an individual incentive to expand.

### Nash equilibrium in a symmetric game

The practice set also sets a rock-paper-scissors game and asks which statement about it is true, offering: that losing is just as hard as winning; that the game has one pure-strategy **Nash equilibrium**; that it has three such equilibria each with a payoff of (0 : 0); or that it has no equilibrium in pure or mixed strategies.

The answer key gives the first. A pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices that neither player would want to move away from, given what the other has chosen — and rock-paper-scissors has none, because whichever pair is named, the loser of that pair would rather have chosen differently. That disposes of the second and third options. The remaining claim is the symmetry of the game: each of the three choices beats one of the others and loses to one, so no strategy makes winning easier than losing.

The payoff table printed with the question did not survive into the extracted text, so the reasoning above rests on the structure of the game as the question names it.

## Monopolistic competition

**Monopolistic competition** combines large numbers of firms with **differentiated products** and free entry and exit in the long run. The differentiation gives each firm a little pricing power over its own version of the product; the free entry takes the profits away again.

*In the long run, firms in monopolistic competition typically earn (A) Economic profits due to barriers to entry. (B) Zero economic profits due to free entry and competition. (C) Losses because of excessive advertising costs. (D) Monopoly-level supernormal profits. (E) infinite profit*

The answer is **(B)**. Free entry is the operative feature. If firms in the market are earning economic profits, new firms enter and take a share of the demand, and entry continues until there is no economic profit left to attract anyone — the normal profit of the costs lesson, and the break-even condition of the previous lesson. (A) and (D) both assume barriers that this structure does not have.

*In monopolistic competition, advertising is primarily used to: (A) Lower production costs through economies of scale. (B) Make demand curves perfectly inelastic. (C) Create brand loyalty and perceived product differentiation. (D) Comply with government regulations. (E) Decrease profit*

The answer is **(C)**. Differentiation is what a firm in this structure competes on, and advertising is how differentiation is manufactured and maintained: it persuades buyers that this version is not interchangeable with the others. Note that (C) says *perceived* differentiation — the advertising need not change the product to change the demand for it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perfect competition** | A market of price-taking firms with free entry and exit and no barriers, producing identical products |
| **Price-taker** | A firm that accepts the market price rather than setting it, because it is too small to influence that price |
| **Monopoly** | An industry controlled by a monopolist, whose good has no close substitutes and which is protected by barriers to entry |
| **Barriers to entry** | Control of a scarce resource or input, economies of scale, technological superiority, and government created barriers |
| **Oligopoly** | A market with a small number of large firms, barriers to entry and interdependence |
| **Interdependence** | The condition in which each firm's best action depends on what the other firms do |
| **Bertrand oligopoly** | A market in which oligopolists compete with each other by setting the price |
| **Cournot oligopoly** | A market in which oligopolists compete with each other by choosing the production quantity |
| **Kinked demand curve model** | The oligopoly model in which firms match price cuts but not price increases, leading to price rigidity |
| **Collusion** | An agreement between firms to restrict output, unstable because each firm gains by violating it alone |
| **Nash equilibrium** | A combination of choices from which neither player would want to move, given the other's choice |
| **Monopolistic competition** | A market with large numbers of firms, differentiated products, and free entry and exit in the long run |

# 10.1 Industry Supply and Long-Run Equilibrium

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The industry supply curve

The **industry supply curve** shows the relationship between the price of goods and the total output of the industry as a whole. It is the market-level counterpart of the single firm's supply decision: each firm decides how much to produce at the going price, and the industry curve adds those decisions up.

**Short-run market equilibrium** is the price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, with the number of firms in the industry taken as given.

## The long-run industry supply curve

The **long-run industry supply curve** is the industry supply curve given sufficient time for entry into and exit from the industry. **Long-run market equilibrium** is again the price at which quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded — but now with the number of firms free to change.

The difference between the two is entry and exit, and it is what makes the long run behave differently from the short run. In the short run a price rise makes existing firms profitable and they stay profitable, because nobody else can get in yet. In the long run those profits are a signal, new firms act on it, and the industry's output rises by more than the existing firms alone could have raised it.

## Worked example: the sugar market adjusting to a rise in demand

The free-response question sets sugar in a perfectly competitive market, with inputs bought from perfectly competitive factor markets, and Frank Sugar Co. as a representative firm in it. The graphs it asks for are drawn side by side — the market on one, the firm on the other — and the parts below give the relationships those graphs have to show.

**(a) The firm is earning zero economic profit.** The market equilibrium price and quantity $P_M$ and $Q_M$ sit where the market's supply and demand curves cross. The firm is a price-taker, so the profit-maximising price for Frank Sugar Co. is not a separate decision: it is $P_M$. The firm's profit-maximising quantity $Q_F$ is the one at which its marginal cost equals that price, following the firm's optimal output rule. Zero economic profit adds one more condition, since the break-even price is the minimum of average total cost: the firm must be at the bottom of its ATC curve, with $P_M$ equal to minimum ATC.

**(b)(i) Demand for sugar increases.** The market demand curve shifts right, so the market price rises to $P_2$. Frank Sugar Co. still takes the price as given, and still produces where marginal cost equals it — but marginal cost rises with output, so the quantity that satisfies $MC = P_2$ is larger than $Q_F$. The firm's quantity $Q_N$ therefore exceeds $Q_F$.

**(b)(ii) What happens to the firm's short-run profit?** It rises. The firm was earning zero economic profit at a price equal to its minimum average total cost, and the price is now above that minimum, which is the profitable case of the break-even test. The firm earns a positive economic profit in the short run.

**(b)(iii) How will the long-run price compare to $P_2$?** It will be **lower than $P_2$**. Positive economic profits are what free entry responds to: sugar is a perfectly competitive market, so new firms enter, industry supply increases, and the price falls. Entry only stops when there is no economic profit left to attract it, which means when price has come back down to minimum average total cost. Sugar is stated to be a **constant-cost industry** — one whose costs per unit do not change as the industry expands — so that minimum is the same as it was before, and the long-run price returns to the original $P_M$.

The graphs cannot be reproduced here, since no figure from the practice set survived into the extracted text. Draw them from the relationships above, which is what the question is testing in any case: the firm's price is the market's price, its quantity is set by $MC = P$, and zero profit puts that intersection at the bottom of ATC.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Industry supply curve** | The curve showing the relationship between the price of goods and the total output of the industry as a whole |
| **Short-run market equilibrium** | The point at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, with the number of firms fixed |
| **Long-run industry supply curve** | The industry supply curve given sufficient time for entry into and exit from the industry |
| **Long-run market equilibrium** | The point at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded once entry and exit have run their course |
| **Constant-cost industry** | An industry whose costs per unit do not change as the industry expands |

# 10.2 Monopoly and Market Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The monopolist's demand curve

A monopolist is the industry, so the demand curve it faces is the market demand curve, and it slopes downward. Selling one more unit therefore has two consequences at once, and the guide separates them:

| Effect | What it does to total revenue |
|---|---|
| **Quantity effect** | One more unit is sold, increasing total revenue by the price at which that unit is sold |
| **Price effect** | To sell the last unit, the monopolist must cut the market price on all units sold, which decreases total revenue |

A firm with no market power has only the quantity effect to consider, because it can sell as much as it likes at the going price. The price effect is what market power costs the firm that holds it, and it is the source of every difference between monopoly and competition that follows.

Because the price effect subtracts from the quantity effect, the revenue gained from one more unit is less than the price that unit sells for. The firm stops producing when $MC = MR$ — the optimal output rule — and since marginal revenue is below the price, the price at that quantity is above marginal cost.

## Market power and efficiency

*The condition for allocative efficiency is violated when (A) firms are price makers (price searchers) (B) short-run profits exist in a competitive industry (C) price equals average total cost (D) the market demand curve is inelastic in a competitive industry (E) the market demand curve is elastic in a competitive industry*

The answer is **(A)**. Allocative efficiency requires the price of the last unit to equal the marginal cost of producing it, so that what buyers pay for one more unit matches what society gives up to make it. A price maker faces a downward-sloping demand curve and so faces the price effect, which puts marginal revenue below price; producing where $MC = MR$ therefore leaves price above marginal cost, and the condition fails. The elasticity of demand in a *competitive* industry, options (D) and (E), does not bear on the condition at all, since firms there set marginal cost equal to the price whatever the elasticity.

The same reasoning answers the question of what can be said about the quantity a producer with market power chooses:

*If a producer has market power (that is, with her actions she can influence the market price), what can we say about the quantity produced? (A) It is equitable (B) It is efficient (C) It maximises consumer surplus (D) None of the other answers is correct*

The answer is **(D)**. The quantity is not efficient, for the reason just given. It does not maximise consumer surplus either — consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the amount paid, and market power works by holding the price up and the quantity down, which cuts into both. And nothing about market power settles the question of equity one way or the other.

## Worked example: a per-unit tax on a monopolist

*A monopolist with a demand function $Q = 120 - P$ and total cost $TC = 2Q^2$ faces a per-unit tax of \$12. By how much will the consumer price increase?*

*(A) \$3 (B) \$6 (C) 2% (D) 10%*

The answer is **(C)**, and it is worth working in full because it shows how little of a per-unit tax may reach the consumer.

Write demand the way the firm sees it, as price in terms of quantity: $P = 120 - Q$. Total revenue is then

$$TR = PQ = 120Q - Q^2 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad MR = \frac{\Delta TR}{\Delta Q} = 120 - 2Q$$

Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as the demand curve, which is the price effect in algebra: each extra unit sold requires a price cut on everything already being sold.

From $TC = 2Q^2$, marginal cost is $MC = 4Q$. Before the tax, the monopolist produces where $MC = MR$:

$$120 - 2Q = 4Q \quad \Rightarrow \quad Q = 20, \qquad P = 120 - 20 = 100$$

A per-unit tax of \$12 adds \$12 to the cost of every unit, so marginal cost becomes $MC = 4Q + 12$:

$$120 - 2Q = 4Q + 12 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 6Q = 108 \quad \Rightarrow \quad Q = 18, \qquad P = 120 - 18 = 102$$

The consumer price rises from \$100 to \$102 — an increase of \$2, which is **2%**. The monopolist absorbs the rest of the \$12 in the form of a lower quantity and a smaller margin. The distractors \$3 and \$6 are there for students who assume the tax is split in some fixed proportion; the actual share passed on depends on the slopes of marginal revenue and marginal cost, which is what the algebra works out.

## A note on the diagram question

One further question shows the demand curve of a price-setting firm and asks at which of three labelled points a monopoly may find it optimal to produce; the answer key gives *points A or B only*. The figure did not survive into the extracted text, so the labelled points cannot be recovered and the reasoning cannot be reconstructed. Work it from the principle above: the monopolist's chosen quantity is the one where marginal cost meets marginal revenue, and marginal revenue lies below the price at every quantity because of the price effect.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quantity effect** | One more unit is sold, increasing total revenue by the price at which the unit is sold |
| **Price effect** | To sell the last unit, the monopolist must cut the market price on all units sold, which decreases total revenue |
| **Market power** | The ability of a producer to influence the market price by her own actions |
| **Allocative efficiency** | The condition, violated by price makers, that the price of the last unit equals its marginal cost |

# 11.1 The Labour Market: Competition and Monopsony

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two structures on the buying side

The labour market is analysed with the same tools as any other market, with one change of perspective: the firm is now the buyer and the worker is the seller. Two structures matter, and they differ in how much power the buyer has.

1. The **perfectly competitive labour market**
2. **Monopsony**

Two measures do the work in both:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Marginal factor cost (MFC)** | What it costs the firm to employ one more unit of the factor |
| **Marginal revenue product (MRP)** | The revenue the firm gains from employing one more unit of the factor |

## The perfectly competitive labour market

In perfect competition the labour market sets a price — the wage — and that price is the marginal factor cost for the individual firm. A firm hiring one more worker pays the going wage and nothing more, so the wage *is* the cost of the extra unit.

The demand for labour in an individual firm is its marginal revenue product, and it slopes downward. Firms here are price-takers in the labour market, and they hire the quantity at which the marginal revenue product meets the marginal factor cost — the optimal output rule again, applied to an input instead of an output: keep hiring while the next worker brings in more than they cost.

## Monopsony

In a **monopsony** the firm is the only firm in a labour market. Being the only buyer, it controls the wage rather than accepting one.

It employs the quantity at which marginal factor cost equals demand, which is the marginal revenue product — the same rule as before. But the wage it pays is not read off that intersection. The wage is the point on the **supply** curve at the quantity employed: having chosen how many workers to hire, the monopsonist pays only what it takes to attract that many.

The consequence is that a monopsonist's wage sits below the marginal revenue product of the workers it employs, and below the wage a competitive labour market would have produced.

## Worked example: when higher wages can raise total surplus

The practice set builds the question carefully. In perfectly competitive markets the equilibrium wage gives the most efficient outcome, so imposing a minimum wage reduces total social surplus, and labour unions negotiating a wage above what the employer wants to offer are a cause of deadweight loss. *However, when the markets are not perfectly competitive, higher wages may be beneficial for the economy.* Which market imperfection makes higher wages most likely to raise total social surplus: monopoly, monopsony, monopolistic competition, Bertrand oligopoly or Cournot oligopoly?

The answer is **monopsony**. It is the only option on the list that is an imperfection in the *labour* market; the other four describe a firm's power over the market for its product, which leaves the wage-setting story untouched.

The mechanism is the one described above. The monopsonist holds employment below the level a competitive market would reach, and pays a wage below the workers' marginal revenue product, because every extra worker it hires pushes the wage up along the supply curve. Fix the wage by law or by union agreement and that calculation disappears: the firm now faces a marginal factor cost equal to the fixed wage, exactly as a firm in a competitive labour market does, and it hires where the marginal revenue product meets it. A wage set above the monopsony wage can therefore raise employment as well as pay, and raise total surplus with it — the opposite of what the same policy does in a competitive labour market.

## Worked example: a lower wage and the substitution effect

*Catherine has just lost her job and found a new one right away, but at a lower wage rate. Based on the neoclassical theory of labour supply, the substitution effect of the lower wage will lead her to: (A) work fewer hours than before (B) work more hours than before (C) work the same hours as before (D) exit the labour market and thus supply zero hours of work*

The answer is **(A)**. The wage is the price of an hour of leisure, since an hour not worked is an hour of pay given up. When the wage falls, leisure becomes cheaper in exactly the sense the law of demand uses, and the **substitution effect** moves Catherine towards the thing that has become cheaper — more leisure, fewer hours of work.

## Worked example: derived demand

*The concept of derived demand is described by which of the following? (A) A decrease in the demand for theatre tickets will decrease the demand for actresses and actors. (B) If the salaries of basketball players increase, the quantity of basketball players demanded will decrease. (C) An increase in the income of consumers will increase the demand for opera tickets. (D) An increase in the demand for movie tickets will decrease the demand for video rentals. (E) A decrease in the price of movie tickets will increase the demand for movie tickets.*

The answer is **(A)**. **Derived demand** is the principle that demand for a factor of production comes from the demand for what it produces — which is precisely what the marginal revenue product says, since the revenue a worker generates depends on what the firm's output sells for. If audiences stop buying theatre tickets, the revenue an actor brings in falls, and the demand for actors falls with it.

The distractors are each a different idea in disguise: (B) is a movement along the demand curve for labour, (C) is an income effect, (D) is a relationship between substitute goods, and (E) is a movement along a demand curve for the good itself.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Marginal factor cost (MFC)** | The cost to the firm of employing one more unit of a factor; in a perfectly competitive labour market it equals the market wage |
| **Marginal revenue product (MRP)** | The revenue gained from employing one more unit of a factor; it is the individual firm's demand for labour and slopes downward |
| **Monopsony** | A labour market in which the firm is the only firm, and so controls the wage |
| **Derived demand** | Demand for a factor of production that comes from the demand for the good it produces |
| **Substitution effect (labour supply)** | The response to a change in the wage that comes from the change in the price of leisure — a lower wage leads to fewer hours worked |

# 12.1 Case Study: Protectionism and the Trade War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The case study

The final item in the practice set is a case study, *Is It Worth Breaking Out the World Trade War?* by Teresa Kamińska, written in August 2018, followed by three discussion questions. The answer key marks the case study "answer may vary", so what follows sets out what the article states and the approach each question calls for, rather than a single correct answer.

## The trade order the article describes

The **trade liberalisation** tenet has governed international economic relations since the Second World War, and has contributed to the urging of integration and globalisation. The United States used to play the role of main leader in the international organisations that created order in global trade — chiefly the United Nations, the World Bank and the World Trade Organization. Through never-ending negotiations aimed at gradually lowering duties, other fiscal and non-fiscal tariffs, and various barriers, it was roughly possible to solve, or at least mitigate, disputes between countries.

The mechanism there is worth noticing: the system worked by making trade disputes negotiable, so that a disagreement led to talks rather than to escalating charges.

## The turn in the late 2010s

The article describes a sudden reversal of that trade policy by the USA in the late 2010s. A new doctrine relying on the adage "America first" meant paralysing everything within the frames of the WTO that might be disadvantageous for the American economy or its world position.

To keep a powerful standing while negotiating new rules, the American government refused to talk with groups of countries — the European Union and NAFTA are the examples given — and insisted on bilateral debates. A country negotiating alone has less weight than the bloc it belongs to, which is what makes the choice between bilateral and group negotiation a bargaining decision rather than an administrative one.

## Steel, aluminium and the first round

The battle began with a significant import tariff on steel (25%) and aluminium (10%), to be applied unless the exporting countries voluntarily reduced their exports of those commodities to the USA. The tariff was therefore doing two jobs at once: raising the price of imports, and serving as the threat that made a voluntary reduction the lesser option.

Up to the time of writing (August 2018) this succeeded with three countries — South Korea, Brazil and particularly Mexico, although in recent years some steelworks had been moved there. Other meaningful American trade partners, namely Canada, the European Union and China, were not so submissive. They differ from each other regarding economic targets, which results in a lack of leadership among them; to be effective, the article argues, they should create an alliance.

## Retaliation and its reach

The EU, China and Canada prepared lists of retaliation charges. The effect was surprising, in the article's account, because American producers — Harley-Davidson is the example — threatened to move some of their production to their factories abroad, and the American government responded by threatening companies with extra taxes for such a move.

That sequence is the case study's central lesson about protectionism: a measure aimed at foreign producers changed the incentives facing domestic ones, and required a second measure to contain the response to the first.

## The German automobile industry

Regarding the EU, the article states that President Trump's policy was aimed mainly at the German automobile sector. A substantial increase in import tariffs on cars from BMW, Volkswagen and Daimler would make their prices soar in the American market, even though those firms already have their own factories there. Germany and the network of car component producers in other EU countries would lose, and the EU would implement severe retaliations.

The article's footnote gives the estimates: Germany might lose 0.2% of GDP and Poland 0.16% of GDP, while the EU's retaliations might increase unemployment in the USA by as much as about 4 million employees.

The Polish figure is the one that repays attention. Poland builds no cars under those three badges; it is in the estimate because of the component producers who supply them. A tariff on a finished good reaches back along the chain of suppliers who make its parts.

## The United States and China

American–Chinese clashes concern an immense trade surplus that has existed for decades, since investors — not only Americans — transformed China into the "world factory". Many of the American government's accusations against Chinese activities were aimed at reducing the increasing world power of the Chinese economy, covering joint ventures, illegal copying of new technologies and products, and investments in the IT sector.

The USA gradually raised tariffs on Chinese merchandise and China replied in the same way, its retaliation list appearing longer and including financial instruments and political actions weakening sanctions against North Korea. The article notes that the problem remains, since Chinese imports are still unsatisfactory from the American point of view.

Summing up, the article judges American policy not transparent because of discrepancies in its performance, such as breaking off negotiations to create the Trans-Atlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP). Trade partners such as the EU, Japan and Latin America do not want to follow the American lead, principally because they expect advantages from the American–Chinese trade conflicts.

## Question 1: the short-run and long-run results of protectionism

The question asks for a discussion of the possible short-run and long-run results of introducing protectionism into international trade. The article supplies both halves.

In the short run, a tariff raises the price of the imported good in the importing country, which is why the article expects German car prices to soar in the American market; it shifts demand towards domestic producers of the protected commodity; and it can extract concessions from exporters who prefer a voluntary reduction of exports to the tariff, as South Korea, Brazil and Mexico did.

In the longer run the article points to effects that run the other way: retaliation charges from the countries targeted; domestic producers relocating production abroad to escape the consequences, and further measures aimed at stopping them; measurable output losses in partner economies and their supplier networks; a rise in unemployment in the tariff-imposing country as retaliation bites; the paralysis of the institutions that previously made disputes negotiable; and a realignment of trade partners who expect to gain from the conflict rather than to join it.

## Question 2: illustrating the effects

The question asks for graphs of the impact of the steel and aluminium tariff increases on the US submarket for imported steel and aluminium, on heavy industry and on the labour market, and then on the export sectors and labour markets of China and the EU. No figures survived into the extracted text of the practice set and the key gives no model answer, so the diagrams have to be drawn from the relationships the earlier lessons supply.

The chain to represent is this. The tariff raises the price at which imported steel and aluminium can be sold in the United States, and by the law of demand the quantity imported falls. Buyers who switch to domestic supply raise the demand faced by American producers of those commodities, whose output rises. Because the demand for labour is a derived demand — the marginal revenue product of a worker depends on what that worker's output sells for — the change in each industry's output carries through to its labour market. In the exporting countries the sequence runs in reverse: the export sector sells less, so its derived demand for labour falls.

## Question 3: who would suffer from higher duties on German cars

If German automobile imports were burdened by duties of 25–30% instead of the present 2.5%, the article names the losers directly. Germany would lose, with an estimated 0.2% of GDP at stake. Other EU countries would lose through the network of car component producers supplying those manufacturers, Poland being the example given at 0.16% of GDP. And the United States would not escape: the cars would become far dearer in the American market, and the EU's retaliation is estimated to raise American unemployment by as much as about 4 million employees.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Trade liberalisation** | The tenet, governing international economic relations since the Second World War, of gradually lowering duties, tariffs and other barriers to trade |
| **Import tariff** | A charge imposed on an imported commodity, such as the 25% on steel and 10% on aluminium described in the case study |
| **Protectionism** | The use of tariffs and other barriers to restrict imports — the reversal of trade liberalisation |
| **Voluntary export reduction** | An exporting country's agreement to reduce its exports of a commodity, offered as the alternative to a tariff |
| **Retaliation charges** | Charges prepared by a targeted country against the imports of the country that imposed the original tariff |
| **Bilateral negotiation** | Negotiation between two countries individually, rather than with a group of countries such as the EU or NAFTA |
| **Trade surplus** | The excess of a country's exports over its imports in trade with a partner, as in the long-standing Chinese surplus with the USA |

markdown:
# 1 Themes in *The Things They Carried*

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The set text is ***The Things They Carried*** by **Tim O'Brien**. The guide sets
out nine themes, each with its examples and the purpose they serve.

## Verisimilitude and metafiction: storytelling as fact or fiction

**War resists simple truths.** By mixing truth and fiction, O'Brien reveals that
**the emotional core of a story can convey more reality than factual accuracy ever
could**. It emphasises the disorienting nature of trauma and the way memory
reshapes experience to protect or explain the self.

Stories are not used only to suggest and reflect a moral — **stories can keep the
dead alive** by giving them a new life and identity.

- **Shifting narration styles** in "How to Tell a True War Story" illustrate the
  instability of truth in storytelling and the need to question how war is
  remembered
- **O'Brien admitting he made up much of the story** in "Good Form" shows that
  emotional resonance can matter more than factual accuracy in conveying trauma
- **Repeated contradictions of detail**, such as how Curt Lemon died, highlight
  how memory is fragmented and unreliable under emotional stress — a key element
  of a war story
- **Layering stories within stories**, such as Linda's death mirroring other
  losses, underscores how storytelling becomes a coping mechanism, merging fact
  with feeling
- One should believe only **60–70% of Rat Kiley's stories** — exaggeration
  revealing emotional truths
- The **vignettes in "Speaking of Courage" and "Notes"** show multiple story angles
- **Using storytelling to revive Linda** shows how stories can keep the dead alive

Framing the war through emotional rather than literal facts allows the audience to
understand the **real implications of war**, beyond the death count and the major
events. It reflects the human side of things.

## War and love

O'Brien uses love to expose **emotional vulnerability** — not as romance, but as
something **almost sacred and irrational in the face of death**. It becomes a
tether to the world outside war.

- **Lt. Cross's obsession with Martha** interfering with his leadership reveals how
  emotional ties can conflict with responsibility and survival
- **Cross burning Martha's letters and photos** to commit to responsibility is
  conformity to wartime duty
- **O'Brien remembering Linda as his first love** to cope with death
- **Henry Dobbins wearing his girlfriend's stockings** around his neck

Love, or the idea of it, becomes **protective** — providing emotional security and
superstition amid chaos, a form of escapism and an anchor to home. **A war story
can also be a love story. They are not black and white.**

## The individual and the collective

The tension between self and group speaks to **how war is dehumanising despite the
efforts against it**. O'Brien and Cross resist this by emphasising that each
soldier carries unique memories, traumas and identities despite uniform
appearances.

- **Personal items symbolising each soldier's individuality**
- **Bowker unable to express his trauma to anyone post-war** — individual trauma
  and differing experiences causing isolation and invisibility
- **Men from different walks of life converging** to serve in the same platoon

## Social obligation

O'Brien suggests the war **was not driven by ideology so much as by shame,
pressure and conformity** — forces stronger than reason.

- **O'Brien deciding on the Rainy River to go to war just to avoid embarrassment**
  — societal pressure overriding moral objection
- The **war medals Bowker is expected to win, and finds pointless**. War is often
  meaningless
- The crude names — "Turncoat" and others — O'Brien imagines people calling him
  because he wants to escape the draft
- **Bowker feeling like a failure for not winning medals**, so that public
  validation becomes a false measure of self-worth
- **Pressure to avenge deaths even when unjustified**, which crosses into moral
  ambiguity

## Mortality and death

**Death in war is sudden, arbitrary and humiliating.** It does not matter who you
are, scholar or criminal: everyone is the same when faced with mortality, and who
lives and who dies is completely random.

- **Ted Lavender's sudden, meaningless death** — a lack of agency in the face of
  death, which becomes commonplace, with people waiting for their day to come
- **Kiowa's death in the shit field** — the grotesque and inescapable presence of
  mortality
- **Repeated storytelling about the Vietnamese soldier O'Brien killed**
- **Linda**, who connects a wider audience and makes the book more relatable by
  meshing wartime death with the universal experience of losing loved ones

## Morality and the moral ambiguity of the war

Characters make questionable decisions **not out of malice, but out of survival,
habit or emotional chaos**. O'Brien illustrates how traditional concepts of right
and wrong **dissolve** in Vietnam's landscape.

- **O'Brien wanting to hurt Jorgenson out of revenge** reveals how war distorts
  ethical boundaries
- **Kiley shooting a water buffalo to express pain**, with no one stopping him
- **Unclear blame for Kiowa's death** in the field — no single person can be held
  accountable in chaos
- **O'Brien's revenge prank on Jorgenson** — ethical erosion

## Fear of shame, masculinity and integrity

**Masculinity in the novel is tied closely to fear** — especially the fear of
appearing weak. The men carry not only weapons but **the immense burden of
reputation**. Their integrity often hinges on conforming to a masculine ideal, even
when it contradicts their inner truths. O'Brien critiques how **shame, not
patriotism, is what sends men to war and keeps them there**.

The soldiers are often tested on integrity — saying and doing things that are
correct but not popular. **Most of the time, however, soldiers choose the popular
side.**

- **Mary Anne's transformation** challenging male exclusivity in war subverts
  traditional gender roles and exposes insecurity
- **Lemon fainting at the dentist** is shame and embarrassment, succumbing to fear;
  **having a perfectly healthy tooth pulled** is bravery and a reintact reputation

## The allure of war

**War draws people to its adrenaline, clarity and mythic energy.** Mary Anne's
transformation and her recurring returns to violent memory suggest that war
awakens something primal — completely engulfed by Vietnam and by a consuming
fascination.

- **Mary Anne's transformation into a jungle warrior** — war seduces and changes
  people irreversibly
- **O'Brien enjoying moments of revenge and thrill**
- **Fascination with weapons and gear** — the appeal of control and power amid chaos

## The physical and emotional burdens of war

The soldiers carry physical loads — guns, supplies, tokens — but **their heaviest
burdens are emotional**: guilt, fear, loss and longing.

- The **literal inventory in "The Things They Carried"**, set against the invisible
  weight of fear, guilt and memory
- **Cross's emotional weight over Lavender's death**

## The effect of violence on humans

The weight of memory **outlasts the war itself**.

- **Bowker's guilt about Kiowa**
- **O'Brien's psychological weight from killing** — obsessing and rethinking details
- **Kiley's mental breakdown after Curt Lemon's death**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Verisimilitude** | The appearance of being true or real, which the novel unsettles by mixing truth and fiction |
| **Metafiction** | Fiction that draws attention to its own storytelling, as in O'Brien's admission that he invented much of a story |
| **Vignette** | A short scene showing one angle on a story, as in "Speaking of Courage" and "Notes" |
| **Moral ambiguity** | The dissolving of traditional right and wrong under the conditions of war |

# 2 Commonly Confused Literary Terms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Every pair here is grouped because the two terms are mistaken for one another.
Learn them in pairs rather than singly — the distinction is what gets tested.

## Synecdoche and metonymy

| Term | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Synecdoche** | When a **part represents the whole** | "wheels" for "car" |
| **Metonymy** | When something is referred to by something **closely associated** with it | "the crown" for "royalty" |

## Anthropomorphism and personification

**Anthropomorphism** gives human traits to animals or objects **literally**, and is
often used in fables — the talking animals in *Maus*, for example. It differs from
personification in that it **focuses on animals**, making animals figurative humans.

**Personification** gives human qualities or feelings to non-human things — "the
sun smiled". It is **more metaphorical**.

## Irony

**Irony** is a discrepancy between appearance and reality. There are three types:

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Verbal irony** | Not meaning what is said |
| **Situational irony** | A surprising ending |
| **Dramatic irony** | The readers know more than the characters |

## Paradox and oxymoron

| Term | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Paradox** | A statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth | "the more you know, the more you don't know" |
| **Oxymoron** | Two contradictory terms | "jumbo shrimp" |

Paradox is **often mistaken for oxymoron**. The difference is length and purpose: an
oxymoron is a pair of words, a paradox is a statement that resolves into an insight.

## Mood and atmosphere

**Mood** is the atmosphere the author constructs through **diction and details**. It
differs from atmosphere in that **mood is what the readers perceive and atmosphere
is what the author establishes**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Synecdoche** | When a part represents the whole |
| **Metonymy** | When something is referred to by something closely associated with it |
| **Anthropomorphism** | Giving human traits to animals or objects literally, making animals figurative humans |
| **Personification** | Giving human qualities or feelings to non-human things; more metaphorical |
| **Irony** | A discrepancy between appearance and reality |
| **Verbal irony** | Not meaning what is said |
| **Situational irony** | A surprising ending |
| **Dramatic irony** | When the readers know more than the characters |
| **Paradox** | A statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth |
| **Oxymoron** | Two contradictory terms |
| **Mood** | The atmosphere the author constructs through diction and details; what the readers perceive |
| **Atmosphere** | What the author establishes, as distinct from what the reader perceives |

# 3 Less Familiar but Still Important Literary Terms

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Schemes of repetition and word order

| Term | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Antimetabole** | Repetition of words in **reverse grammatical order** | "Eat to live, not live to eat" |
| **Anastrophe** | A synonym for **inversion**: inverted word order for emphasis or rhythm | "Powerful you have become" — it sounds like Yoda-speak |
| **Epistrophe** | Repetition **at the end** of phrases or clauses | "…by the people, for the people" |
| **Epanalepsis** | The **same word at the beginning and end** of a sentence | "Nothing is worse than doing nothing" |

**Epistrophe is the opposite of anaphora** — anaphora repeats at the beginning,
epistrophe at the end.

## Conjunctions in lists

| Term | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Asyndeton** | A list **without conjunctions** | "I came, I saw, I conquered" |
| **Polysyndeton** | A list **with many conjunctions** | "He ran and jumped and shouted and danced…" |

These two are **often confused with each other**, and the pairing is the point: the
same list, stripped of conjunctions or loaded with them, produces opposite
rhythms.

## Grammar terms that appear in analysis

**Apposition** is a noun phrase that explains, modifies or qualifies another noun —
"Ms. Sedlock, our teacher, …". It is a grammar term that comes up in literary
analysis.

**Apostrophe** is direct address to an absent, imaginary or dead person or thing —
"O Romeo…".

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Antimetabole** | Repetition of words in reverse grammatical order |
| **Anastrophe** | Inverted word order for emphasis or rhythm; a synonym for inversion |
| **Epistrophe** | Repetition at the end of phrases or clauses; the opposite of anaphora |
| **Anaphora** | Repetition at the beginning of phrases or clauses |
| **Epanalepsis** | The same word at the beginning and end of a sentence |
| **Asyndeton** | A list without conjunctions |
| **Polysyndeton** | A list with many conjunctions |
| **Apposition** | A noun phrase that explains, modifies or qualifies another noun |
| **Apostrophe** | Direct address to an absent, imaginary or dead person or thing |

title: Tips for Literary Analysis
summary: The five tips move from a lower to a higher level of analysis, each one raising what the previous one settles for. Insightful analysis is not just close reading — it is a form of argument. Rather than
markdown:
# 4 Tips for Literary Analysis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

> The guide states that this section was generated by ChatGPT, and repeats the
> note at the end of the section. It is reproduced here because it is part of the
> guide students revise from, but the guide's own attribution is worth keeping in
> view: unlike the rest of the guide, this advice was not written by the course's
> writer or editor.

The five tips move from a lower to a higher level of analysis, each one raising
what the previous one settles for.

## 1. Turn your analysis into argument

Insightful analysis is not just close reading — it is **a form of argument**.
Rather than simply observing literary devices, frame your analysis as a **claim
about human behaviour, ideology or emotional truth**.

- **Weaker:** O'Brien uses metafiction to show how storytelling helps him process
  trauma.
- **Stronger:** O'Brien's metafictional layers suggest that the line between
  fiction and truth dissolves under trauma — not because memory fails, but because
  reality itself becomes unlivable.

The difference: **one identifies a device; the other takes a stand.**

## 2. Layer interpretations, not just evidence

Go beyond "what this means" to **"what this also could mean"**. Look for
**interpretive friction** — places where one image or moment can mean several
things at once. **Tension is where the complexity lives.**

For example, Mary Anne's transformation into a feral killer is not just a loss of
innocence. It is a metaphor for war's erotic pull, the colonial fantasy of
Vietnam, and the collapse of Western femininity under foreign pressure.

Ask: **what is beneath the obvious? What is in conflict here?**

## 3. Collapse the distance between form and meaning

Do not treat literary devices as separate from content. Make your analysis show
that **the form is the content**.

- **Weaker:** The repetition emphasises the speaker's trauma.
- **Stronger:** The obsessive repetition *enacts* trauma — forcing the reader into
  the same loop of memory the speaker cannot escape.

This is more than pointing out techniques: it shows that **how something is
written is what it means**.

## 4. Make the text uncomfortable

Excellent analysis is unafraid to **question a narrator's reliability**,
**challenge what the author might be avoiding**, and **point out contradictions in
theme or tone**.

For example: O'Brien presents storytelling as healing, but his recursive grief over
Kiowa and the Vietnamese soldier suggests that no story can truly absolve him —
only numb him.

This shows you are **not just following the text, but wrestling with it**.

## 5. Elevate with thematic synthesis

The highest-level writing does not just explain parts of a text — it **braids
themes together into new insight**.

Taking **masculinity** and **memory** from *The Things They Carried*: the men's
silence around fear, framed as masculinity, is not just repression; it is a
collective reshaping of memory itself. Their manhood depends on **editing the
past**. In O'Brien's world, masculinity is not about truth, but about the stories
men allow each other to believe.

This is **synthesis** — not merely linking themes, but fusing them into a deeper
argument about identity, narrative and social structure.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Interpretive friction** | A place where one image or moment can mean several things at once, where complexity lives |
| **Thematic synthesis** | Braiding themes together into a new argument rather than merely linking them |

# 1 Kinematics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Kinematics** is the branch of physics that **describes the motion of objects
without considering the forces that cause the motion**. These equations form the
foundation for more complex physics concepts.

## The constant-acceleration equations

The following describe the relationships between **velocity, position,
acceleration and time** for objects moving with **constant acceleration**.

**Final velocity**, relating final velocity to the initial velocity plus the
product of acceleration and time:

$$v = v_0 + at$$

**Position**, giving the position of an object based on its initial position,
initial velocity, time and acceleration:

$$x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$$

**Velocity–displacement relationship**, relating final velocity to initial
velocity and displacement **without requiring time**:

$$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)$$

**Average velocity**, using the average of initial and final velocities to
calculate displacement:

$$x = x_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(v + v_0)t$$

## Where they apply

These equations are crucial for solving problems involving **motion in a straight
line** — free fall, projectile motion, and other scenarios where **acceleration is
constant**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kinematics** | The branch of physics describing motion without considering the forces causing it |
| **Constant acceleration** | The condition under which these four equations apply |

# 2 Dynamics: Forces and Newton's Laws

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Dynamics** is the study of **forces and their relationship to the motion of
objects**. Newton's laws of motion form the **cornerstone of classical mechanics**
and provide the framework for understanding how forces affect motion.

## Key formulas

**Newton's Second Law** — the net force acting on an object equals its mass
multiplied by its acceleration. The guide calls this **perhaps the most important
equation in classical mechanics**:

$$F_{\text{net}} = ma$$

**Weight** — the gravitational force exerted on an object by a massive body such
as Earth, equal to the product of mass and gravitational acceleration:

$$F_g = mg$$

**Friction** — the coefficient of friction multiplied by the normal force. This
applies to **both static and kinetic friction, though the coefficients differ**:

$$f = \mu N$$

## Other forces to understand conceptually

| Force | Description |
|---|---|
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Spring force** | The force exerted by a compressed or stretched spring |

## Method

When analysing physical systems it is crucial to **identify all forces acting on an
object**, **draw a free-body diagram**, and **apply Newton's Second Law** to
determine the resulting motion.

Remember that **forces are vector quantities**, having both magnitude and
direction — which is why the free-body diagram comes before the arithmetic.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dynamics** | The study of forces and their relationship to the motion of objects |
| **Newton's Second Law** | $F_{\text{net}} = ma$; the net force equals mass times acceleration |
| **Weight** | The gravitational force on an object, $F_g = mg$ |
| **Friction** | $f = \mu N$, the coefficient of friction times the normal force |
| **Tension** | Force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or wire |
| **Normal force** | The perpendicular force exerted by a surface |
| **Free-body diagram** | A diagram identifying all forces acting on an object |

# 3 Circular Motion and Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Circular motion** describes the movement of objects along a circular path, while
**gravitation** deals with the attractive force between masses. The two are closely
related, because **gravitational forces often cause circular orbital motions**.

## Centripetal force

When an object moves in a circular path it **constantly changes direction**, which
means it is **accelerating toward the centre of the circle**. That acceleration
requires a force — the **centripetal force**:

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_c$ | The centripetal force |
| $m$ | The mass of the object |
| $v$ | The **tangential** velocity of the object |
| $r$ | The radius of the circular path |

The reasoning matters as much as the formula: changing direction *is* acceleration,
even at constant speed, and acceleration requires a force.

## Gravitational force

**Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** states that **every mass attracts every
other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely
proportional to the square of the distance between them**:

$$F_g = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F_g$ | The gravitational force between the masses |
| $G$ | The gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |
| $m_1, m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the **centres** of the masses |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Centripetal force** | The force required to keep an object on a circular path, $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Tangential velocity** | The velocity of an object along its circular path |
| **Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation** | Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance |
| **Gravitational constant ($G$)** | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² |

# 4 Energy, Work and Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Energy** describes the **capacity to do work**. Understanding energy and its
various forms is crucial for analysing physical systems and their interactions.

## Kinetic energy

The energy an object possesses **due to its motion**:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$$

where $m$ is mass and $v$ is velocity. The equation shows that **kinetic energy
increases with the square of velocity**, making **speed much more significant than
mass** in determining an object's kinetic energy.

## Potential energy

**Potential energy** is **stored energy depending on an object's position or
configuration**. Two common forms:

**Gravitational potential energy** — the energy an object possesses due to its
height above a reference point:

$$PE = mgh$$

where $m$ is mass, $g$ gravitational acceleration and $h$ height.

**Elastic potential energy** — the energy stored in a stretched or compressed
spring:

$$PE_s = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$$

where $k$ is the spring constant and $x$ the displacement from equilibrium.

## Work and power

**Work** is the **energy transferred when a force moves an object**:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta$$

where $F$ is force, $d$ displacement, and $\theta$ the angle between the force and
displacement vectors.

**The work–energy theorem** — the net work done on an object equals its **change in
kinetic energy**:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$$

**Power** is the **rate at which work is done or energy is transferred**, measured
in **watts**:

$$P = \frac{W}{t} = Fv\cos\theta$$

Both forms of the power equation carry the same $\cos\theta$ as the work equation,
for the same reason: only the component of force along the motion does work.

## Conservation of energy

**Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to
another.** This principle is fundamental to solving many physics problems.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Energy** | The capacity to do work |
| **Kinetic energy** | Energy due to motion, $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Potential energy** | Stored energy depending on position or configuration |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgh$, from height above a reference point |
| **Elastic potential energy** | $PE_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, stored in a stretched or compressed spring |
| **Spring constant ($k$)** | The constant in the elastic potential energy formula |
| **Work** | Energy transferred when a force moves an object, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Work–energy theorem** | Net work equals the change in kinetic energy |
| **Power** | The rate at which work is done, measured in watts |
| **Conservation of energy** | Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed |

# 5 Momentum

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Momentum** is a **vector quantity** representing the **product of an object's mass
and velocity**. It is **conserved in closed systems**, which makes it a powerful
tool for analysing collisions and interactions.

## Linear momentum

$$p = mv$$

Since velocity is a vector, **momentum is also a vector quantity** with both
magnitude and direction.

## Impulse

**Impulse** represents the **change in momentum**, equal to the force applied
multiplied by the time interval over which it acts:

$$J = Ft = \Delta p$$

This relationship, the **impulse–momentum theorem**, is particularly useful for
analysing collisions and impacts. It shows that **a small force applied for a long
time can produce the same change in momentum as a large force applied for a short
time**.

## Conservation of momentum

In a **closed system where no external forces act**, the total momentum before an
interaction equals the total momentum after it:

$$m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = m_1v_1' + m_2v_2'$$

where the primed variables are the velocities after the interaction. This applies
to **collisions, explosions and other interactions** between objects.

Conservation of momentum **follows from Newton's laws of motion**, and it applies
**even where energy is not conserved** — as in **inelastic collisions**, where
kinetic energy is converted to other forms such as heat or sound.

That last point is what makes momentum more useful than energy for collision
problems: it holds in cases where an energy accounting would not close.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Momentum** | The vector product of an object's mass and velocity, $p = mv$ |
| **Impulse** | The change in momentum, $J = Ft = \Delta p$ |
| **Impulse–momentum theorem** | The relationship showing a small force over a long time equals a large force over a short time |
| **Conservation of momentum** | In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged by an interaction |
| **Inelastic collision** | A collision in which kinetic energy is converted to heat or sound, though momentum is still conserved |

markdown:
# 6 Rotational Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Rotational motion** deals with the movement of objects **around an axis**. Many
concepts from linear motion have **rotational analogues**, creating a parallel set
of equations and principles — which is the most efficient way to learn this topic.

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| Force $F$ | Torque $\tau$ |
| Mass $m$ | Rotational inertia $I$ |
| $F = ma$ | $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| Momentum $p = mv$ | Angular momentum $L = I\omega$ |

## Torque

**Torque** is the **rotational equivalent of force**, causing objects to rotate:

$$\tau = rF\sin\theta$$

where $r$ is the distance from the rotation axis to the point where the force is
applied, $F$ is the force, and $\theta$ the angle between the force vector and the
position vector.

**Torque is maximised when the force is perpendicular to the position vector** —
that is, when $\sin\theta = 1$.

## Rotational inertia

**Rotational inertia ($I$)** is the **rotational equivalent of mass**, representing
an object's **resistance to changes in rotational motion**. Its value **depends on
the object's mass distribution relative to the axis of rotation** — which is the one
place the analogy with mass breaks down, since mass alone does not depend on where
you put the axis.

## Newton's Second Law for rotation

$$\tau = I\alpha$$

where $\tau$ is net torque, $I$ rotational inertia and $\alpha$ angular
acceleration.

## Rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum

**Rotational kinetic energy** — the energy of a rotating object, where $\omega$ is
angular velocity:

$$KE_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$

**Angular momentum** — a **conserved quantity in systems with no external
torques**:

$$L = I\omega$$

## Why it matters

Rotational motion is essential for analysing **wheels, gears, motors and celestial
bodies**. Conservation of angular momentum explains phenomena **from figure skating
spins to the stability of gyroscopes**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Torque ($\tau$)** | The rotational equivalent of force, $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, maximised when force is perpendicular to the position vector |
| **Rotational inertia ($I$)** | The rotational equivalent of mass, depending on mass distribution relative to the axis |
| **Angular acceleration ($\alpha$)** | The rotational analogue of acceleration, in $\tau = I\alpha$ |
| **Rotational kinetic energy** | $KE_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of rotation |
| **Angular momentum ($L$)** | $L = I\omega$, conserved in systems with no external torques |

markdown:
# 7 Fluid Dynamics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Fluid dynamics** studies the **behaviour of liquids and gases in motion**, with
applications in engineering, meteorology, oceanography and biology.

## Density and pressure

**Density** — the mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

**Pressure** — force per unit area, measured in **pascals**. In fluids, **pressure
acts in all directions**:

$$P = \frac{F}{A}$$

**Pressure at a depth** — the pressure at depth $h$ in a fluid, where $P_0$ is
typically atmospheric pressure, $\rho$ the fluid density and $g$ gravitational
acceleration:

$$P = P_0 + \rho gh$$

## Pascal's and Archimedes' principles

**Pascal's Principle** — in hydraulic systems, **pressure is transmitted equally
throughout a confined fluid**, allowing **force multiplication through area
differences**:

$$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$

**Archimedes' Principle** — an object immersed in a fluid experiences an **upward
buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced**:

$$F_b = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$$

## Fluid flow

**The continuity equation** — for **incompressible fluids**, the product of
cross-sectional area and fluid velocity remains constant. This represents
**conservation of mass**:

$$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$$

**Bernoulli's equation** — representing **conservation of energy in fluid flow**:

$$P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$$

The two flow equations are the two conservation laws applied to a moving fluid:
continuity conserves mass, Bernoulli conserves energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Density ($\rho$)** | Mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m³ |
| **Pressure ($P$)** | Force per unit area, measured in pascals; in fluids it acts in all directions |
| **Pressure at depth** | $P = P_0 + \rho gh$ |
| **Pascal's Principle** | Pressure is transmitted equally through a confined fluid, allowing force multiplication |
| **Archimedes' Principle** | An immersed object experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced |
| **Buoyant force ($F_b$)** | $\rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ |
| **Continuity equation** | $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$, representing conservation of mass in incompressible flow |
| **Bernoulli's equation** | $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$, representing conservation of energy in fluid flow |

# 3.4 Linear Programming

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four parts of a linear program

**Linear programming** is a mathematical model consisting of a **linear function to
be optimised** — maximised or minimised — **and a set of inequalities representing
the restrictions on resources**.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised. It might represent amounts of money earned or spent, goods manufactured or delivered, or any of a variety of other quantities |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |

The central fact, and the reason the method works at all: **if a linear program has
a solution, it will occur at a vertex — a corner point — of the feasible region.**
If there are multiple solutions, **at least one of them will occur at a vertex**.

That is what turns an infinite search into a finite one. The feasible region
contains infinitely many points, but only its corners need to be tested.

## Method

1. **Solve the system of linear inequalities.** Determine the coordinates of the
   vertices of the feasible region — that is, solve the system of equations
   consisting of the lines whose intersection is the vertex
2. **Evaluate the objective function** to be optimised at each vertex
3. **Identify the maximum or minimum value** of the objective function

## When two vertices tie

If **two vertices of the feasible region are both solutions** to a linear program,
then **every point on the line segment connecting the two vertices is also a
solution**.

This follows from the objective function being linear: if it takes the same value
at both ends of a segment, it takes that value all along it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Linear programming** | A model consisting of a linear function to be optimised and a set of inequalities representing restrictions on resources |
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised in a linear program |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities of a linear program |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |
| **Vertex** | A corner point of the feasible region, where a solution will occur if one exists |

# 8.2 Sine and Cosine Curves

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three measurements of a sinusoid

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles the graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between the function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | Determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values of the function |

Amplitude and midline are the two halves of the same calculation: the **half
difference** of the extremes gives the amplitude, and their **average** gives the
midline. Together they fix the vertical position and reach of the curve, which is
why 8.3 uses them as the route from a graph back to an equation.

## The four transformations

| Transformation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal dilation** | $y = \sin(bx)$ and $y = \cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | $y = a\sin x$ and $y = a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | $y = \sin(x + c)$ and $y = \cos(x + c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | $y = \sin x + d$ and $y = \cos x + d$ |

The guide also lists **reflecting a trigonometric function** as part of this
section, without giving its form.

Each constant acts on one measurement above: $b$ changes the frequency, $a$ the
amplitude, $d$ the midline, and $c$ shifts the curve horizontally without altering
any of the three.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles a sinusoidal graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between a sinusoidal function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | The line determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values |
| **Horizontal dilation** | The transformation $y=\sin(bx)$ or $y=\cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | The transformation $y=a\sin x$ or $y=a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | The transformation $y=\sin(x+c)$ or $y=\cos(x+c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | The transformation $y=\sin x + d$ or $y=\cos x + d$ |

# 8.3 Modelling Periodic Behaviour

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Modelling runs in the opposite direction to 8.2: there, constants were given and
the curve followed; here the behaviour is observed and the constants must be
recovered from it.

## Recovering period and frequency

**The smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output
values start to repeat** can be used to determine or estimate the **period and
frequency** for a sinusoidal function model.

## Recovering amplitude and vertical shift

**The maximum and minimum output values** can be used to determine the
**amplitude and vertical shift** for a sinusoidal function model.

This is 8.2's amplitude and midline calculation used in reverse: the half
difference of the observed extremes gives the amplitude, and their average gives
the vertical shift.

## Choosing sine or cosine

**Flexibly select sine or cosine functions based on the situation**, making the
equation easier to calculate as well as promoting critical thinking.

The two curves differ only by a horizontal translation, so either can model the
same behaviour — but one will usually need a smaller phase shift than the other,
and that is the one worth choosing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Period** | Determined from the smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output values start to repeat |
| **Vertical shift** | Determined, with the amplitude, from the maximum and minimum output values |

# 10.4 Solving Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide carries the syllabus's own sub-codes here, which are given alongside each
statement below.

## Equations

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
equations.**

**Because trigonometric functions are periodic, there are often infinitely many
solutions to trigonometric equations** (10.4.A.3). This is the fact everything else
in the section responds to — every method below is a way of cutting an infinite
solution set down to the ones being asked for.

**Algebraic and graphical methods are used to solve trigonometric equations in a
finite interval, including the use of trigonometric identities and factorisation**
(10.4.A.4).

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving equations involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions.** An inverse returns one value where the equation has infinitely
many, so the others must be recovered by hand.

**In trigonometric equations arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.A.6).

## Inequalities

The same three points carry over.

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
inequalities.**

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving inequalities involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions** (10.4.B.2).

**In trigonometric inequalities arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.B.3).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equivalent trigonometric forms** | Rewritings of an expression that may make an equation or inequality solvable |
| **Domain restriction** | A limit on the input values, either from an inverse function or implied by the context, which reduces the number of solutions |
