# 11.1 Polar Coordinates and Graphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The polar coordinate system

The **polar coordinate system** is an alternative to the Cartesian system of
rectangular coordinates for locating points in a plane.

The polar coordinates of a point $P$ consist of an **ordered pair** $(r,\theta)$:

- $r$ is the **directed distance from the pole** to $P$
- $\theta$ is the **measure of the angle from the polar axis to** $OP$

The polar coordinates of the pole $O$ are $(0,\theta)$ — the distance is zero
whatever the angle, so the pole has infinitely many representations.

The angle $\theta$ can be measured in **degrees or radians**, and **both $r$ and
$\theta$ can be either positive or negative**. That last point is what the two
rules below exist to settle.

## The sign of the angle

| Sign of $\theta$ | How the polar angle is obtained |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | Rotating $OP$ **counterclockwise** from the polar axis |
| **Negative** | Rotating $OP$ **clockwise** from the polar axis |

## The sign of the distance

| Sign of $r$ | Where the polar distance is measured |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | From $O$ **along the terminal side** of the angle $\theta$ |
| **Negative** | From $O$ **on the ray opposite** the terminal side of the angle $\theta$ |

A negative $r$ therefore places the point on the far side of the pole from where
the angle points — which is why the same point has more than one set of polar
coordinates.

## Naming the plane

A plane is called an **$r\theta$-plane** when polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ are
used to identify its points.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polar coordinate system** | An alternative to the Cartesian system for locating points in a plane |
| **Polar coordinates** | The ordered pair $(r,\theta)$ giving a point's directed distance from the pole and the angle from the polar axis |
| **Pole** | The origin $O$ of the polar system, with coordinates $(0,\theta)$ |
| **Polar axis** | The reference ray from which the angle $\theta$ is measured |
| **Terminal side** | The side of the angle along which a positive polar distance is measured |
| **$r\theta$-plane** | A plane whose points are identified by polar coordinates |

# 8.1 Setting the Stage for the Cold War and Decolonisation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Governance.*

## Technological gains of the victorious allies

The **United States and the USSR** were the most important Allied powers.
Wartime government investment produced advances that all had **post-war
application and benefits**:

- **Nuclear energy** — the US created the atomic bomb in **1945**, the USSR in **1949**
- **Computing** — for example Colossus in the United Kingdom
- **Jet propulsion and rocketry**

## Economic gains

**The United States.** Significant government investment in wartime
manufacturing, the **arsenal of democracy**, expanded industrial capacity during
the war. The United States ended it as **50% of global GDP**.

**The USSR.** Despite a **10% population loss**, the five-year plans of
**1928–1941** and wartime industrial expansion, together with an **expansion of
resources and territory** through control of eastern Europe and eastern Germany.

The contrast matters for everything that follows: both powers emerged stronger
than they began, while the states between them did not.

## Shifts in the global power structure

The **destructiveness of the Second World War** exceeded that of the First. Japan
and Germany were in ruins, and there was widespread devastation in France, Britain
and other European nations.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arsenal of democracy** | The US wartime manufacturing effort that expanded its industrial capacity |
| **Five-year plans** | The Soviet economic programmes of 1928–1941 |

markdown:
# 8.2 The Cold War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Cultural developments and interactions.*

## Tensions at the end of the war

The **Yalta and Potsdam conferences of 1945** discussed ending the war and
post-war arrangements. Agreements were made on the **division of Germany into
allied occupation zones** and the **creation of the United Nations**.

But the goals for eastern Europe **diverged**:

- **The United States and Britain** wanted democratic governments with *free and
  fair* elections
- **Stalin** objected, aiming to establish **communist governments influenced by
  the USSR**, creating a **buffer against future invasions**

That disagreement is the origin of everything in this unit.

## The spread of communism in Europe

Communist governments were established after the war:

| Year | Country |
|---|---|
| **1947** | Poland |
| **1948** | Czechoslovakia |
| **1949** | Hungary |
| **1949** | East Germany, and others |

Europe divided into a **communist east under Soviet control** and a **capitalist
west influenced by the United States**.

## Rivalry for influence

**The Marshall Plan, 1948.** US financial aid to rebuild European economies after
the war. Its objectives were to **foster the development of rich capitalist
democracies** and to **secure gratitude and alignment with US ideology**. In the
long term it **exceeded expectations in effectiveness**, and recipients were often
enduring allies of the United States.

**COMECON, 1949** — the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, the Soviet
response. It focused on **resource and technology sharing among allies**, but
**often extracted more resources than it provided** in eastern Europe. The
economic disparity that followed is the direct result: **western European
economies prospered more than eastern bloc countries**.

## Foreign aid in Africa and Asia

The USSR gave **economic and military assistance to anti-colonial movements** —
Angola, Vietnam and others.

**Leaders of the newly independent world:**

- **Sukarno**, first president of **Indonesia**, faced the challenge of a
  **diverse and populous country of thousands of islands** and the difficulty of
  centralising control. His answer was **guided democracy**, balancing the power of
  diverse groups — communists, Islamists and the military
- **Kwame Nkrumah** led Ghana's independence movement and became its **first prime
  minister**. He advocated **pan-Africanism**, encouraging unity and cooperation
  among African nations with the goals of prosperity and stability across the
  continent, and **rejected the Cold War dichotomy**, dismissing both superpowers' ideas
- **Jawaharlal Nehru**, first prime minister of independent **India** and a leader
  of its independence movement, is distinguished from other leaders — many of whom
  were criticised for authoritarian rule — as an **advocate for multi-party
  democracy** with regular democratic elections

## Capitalism and communism compared

| Capitalism | Communism |
|---|---|
| Free market | State-owned resources |
| Free trade | State-controlled economy |
| Private property | Economic equality |
| Economic freedom | Strong authoritarian leadership |
| Liberal democracy | Stability and order |
| Competing political parties, regular elections | |

Each side presented itself to the newly independent world in the terms most likely
to appeal: **communism was portrayed as an anti-imperialist ideology**, while US
global assistance **aided both anti-imperialists and imperialists**.

## The Non-Aligned Movement

Many nations were **not willing to choose either side**. The movement was a
**diverse group of states with varied opinions**, mostly **newly independent from
colonial rule** — the exception being **Yugoslavia** under **Josip Broz Tito**, a
communist leader who **rejected Soviet control**.

Despite that diversity they agreed on core principles:

- **Mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty**
- **Mutual non-aggression and non-interference in domestic affairs**
- **Equality and mutual benefit**
- **Peaceful co-existence**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Yalta and Potsdam conferences** | The 1945 meetings on ending the war and post-war arrangements |
| **Marshall Plan** | 1948 US financial aid rebuilding European economies, securing alignment with US ideology |
| **COMECON** | The 1949 Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, the Soviet response to the Marshall Plan |
| **Guided democracy** | Sukarno's approach to balancing the power of Indonesia's diverse groups |
| **Pan-Africanism** | Nkrumah's advocacy of unity and cooperation among African nations |
| **Non-Aligned Movement** | Mostly newly independent states unwilling to choose either superpower |

markdown:
# 8.3 Effects of the Cold War

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Governance.*

## Containment

**Containment** was the US policy of **preventing the global spread of
communism**. In **1947 Harry Truman** presented the **Truman Doctrine**: the
United States would provide **military and financial aid to countries resisting
communism**, and **soldiers if necessary**.

## Alliances

| | **NATO, 1949** | **Warsaw Pact, 1955** |
|---|---|---|
| **Full name** | North Atlantic Treaty Organization | — |
| **Purpose** | *Collective security* against *communist aggression* | The eastern bloc equivalent |
| **Members** | USA, Canada, most western European nations | Eastern bloc |
| **Key article** | **Article 5**: an attack on one member is an attack on all | Article 4, structured the same way |
| **Led by** | The United States | The USSR |

## Nuclear proliferation

Atomic bombs came in **1945** and **1949**, and the **arms race** began. By
**1953 both had developed the hydrogen bomb**, a hundred times more powerful than
the earlier atomic bombs.

Advanced launch systems followed — **intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBM)**
and **submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBM)** — extending the range of
nuclear weapons and enabling **second-strike capabilities**.

That capability produces the logic of the whole period: **deterrence**, preventing
conflict through military strength. Cold War arsenals ran to **tens of thousands of
warheads**, and the result was **mutual assured destruction (MAD)** — in a nuclear
war there are **no winners, only apocalypse**.

## Proxy wars

A **proxy war** is an **indirect conflict via supported combatants**. In the Cold
War, the United States and the USSR **backed different sides of regional conflicts**
around the world, aiming to **spread influence without direct conflict**. Sometimes
neither was directly involved; sometimes only one was, with the opposing superpower
supporting its adversary.

### 1. The Korean War, 1950–53

In **1950 North Korea invaded South Korea** with Soviet weapons and funding, and
dominated early in the war, prompting **US and UN intervention**. From the US point
of view, Truman was **applying containment and the Truman Doctrine in Asia**.
**China**, communist since **1949**, was significantly involved, aiding North Korea.

The **1953 armistice** established a **demilitarised zone (DMZ)** near the original
**38th parallel**. It was one of the deadliest Cold War conflicts, with around
**3 million deaths, mostly civilians**, and it **never officially ended**.

> The guide gives the DMZ's position as the 28th parallel. Its own description —
> "near the original" parallel dividing Korea — points to the 38th, which is the
> line it elsewhere describes as the original division.

### 2. Vietnam

**Before the war:** French Indochina from **1887 to 1954**, occupied by Japan from
**1940 to 1945**. The **Viet Minh**, led by **Ho Chi Minh**, fought both Japanese
and French forces, and **declared independence in 1945**. The French sought to
regain the colony.

**The First Indochina War, 1946–54:** the USSR aided the Viet Minh while the United
States backed the French, on the grounds that they were fighting communists. The
**French withdrew in 1954**, and the country divided — **north** under Ho Chi Minh,
communist; **south** under **Ngo Dinh Diem**, anti-communist.

**The Second Indochina War, 1955–75 — the Vietnam War.** From **1955** the United
States ramped up military and financial support to the south to combat communism.
The motivation was the **domino theory**: fear of South East Asia falling under
communism, with potential spread to Thailand and Cambodia. **1963** saw significant
escalation, with **2.7 million US soldiers** participating. **1975** brought
communist victory and unification.

### 3. The Ogaden War, 1977–78 — Africa

**Somalia against Ethiopia.** Ethiopia was initially led by **Haile Selassie**,
initially part of the non-aligned movement but more tied with the United States and
anti-communist. In **1974 the Derg**, a communist military junta led by **Mengistu
Haile Mariam**, overthrew him, and Ethiopia became communist and allied with the USSR.

Somalia had been **closer to the Soviets**, receiving Soviet funding and military
aid, but increased US support over time. In **1977 Somalia attacked communist
Ethiopia**; the Soviet response was to **withdraw support from Somalia**, while the
United States **shifted toward** Somalia because of its anti-communist actions.
**Ethiopia won the war in 1987.**

The alignments swapped completely — which is the clearest illustration in the unit
that superpower support followed strategic advantage rather than ideology.

### 4. The Sandinista–Contra conflict, 1979–90 — Latin America

In **1979 the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN)** took power in
**Nicaragua**, establishing a socialist, nationalist government. Under the **Reagan
Doctrine** the United States supported anti-communist insurgents, viewing the regime
as a **Soviet-Cuban proxy despite minimal Soviet involvement**. The United States
**armed and trained the Contras**, aiming to disrupt the Sandinista government and
prevent the spread of communism. The impact on Nicaragua was **tens of thousands of
deaths and economic damage**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Containment** | The US policy of preventing the global spread of communism |
| **Truman Doctrine** | Truman's 1947 commitment of military and financial aid to countries resisting communism |
| **NATO** | The 1949 North Atlantic Treaty Organization, whose Article 5 makes an attack on one an attack on all |
| **Warsaw Pact** | The 1955 eastern bloc alliance led by the USSR |
| **ICBM / SLBM** | Intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles, extending nuclear range |
| **Second-strike capability** | The ability to retaliate after being attacked |
| **Deterrence** | Preventing conflict through military strength |
| **Mutual assured destruction (MAD)** | The condition in which nuclear war has no winners |
| **Proxy war** | Indirect conflict through supported combatants |
| **Demilitarised zone (DMZ)** | The zone established by the 1953 Korean armistice |
| **Domino theory** | The fear that one country falling to communism would bring its neighbours down |
| **Reagan Doctrine** | US support for anti-communist insurgents |

# 8.4 The Spread of Communism after 1900

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## China: internal tension and Japanese aggression

**1912** — the Qing dynasty ends and the Republic of China is created, with **Sun
Yat-sen** creating the nationalist party, the **KMT**. The **Communist Party of
China** forms in **1921**. In **1927** the KMT, led by **Chiang Kai-shek (蒋介石)**,
set out to **purge communism**, beginning the **Chinese Civil War (1927–37,
1945–49)**.

The Communist Party was **initially small**, but drew **large support from
peasants through land reforms** — the factor that decides the outcome. The
**Japanese invasion of 1937** produced a **temporary united front**.

## The civil war resumes, 1945–49

The United States provided **substantial money to the KMT**, aiming at containment
of communism. The communists, led by **Mao Zedong**, were **Soviet-assisted, but
less than the US assisted the KMT** — and their advantage was **more popular
support**. In **1949** communist victory established the **People's Republic of
China**.

## The PRC compared with the USSR

The parallels are explicit in the guide:

| PRC policy | Soviet parallel |
|---|---|
| **Land redistribution to peasants** | Like Lenin |
| **Five-year plans** | Like Stalin |
| **Collectivisation of agriculture** in the Great Leap Forward | Literally the same as Stalin |

**The first five-year plan (1953–57)** successfully established an industrial base
and increased agricultural output. **The second (1958–62)** saw a **rise in
industrial production** but a **decline in agricultural production**.

**The Great Leap Forward (大跃进)** combined **collectivisation of agriculture**
with a **reduction of the agricultural workforce in favour of industry**. Together
with **consecutive years of bad weather**, this produced **widespread famine**. The
government **ended the Great Leap Forward in 1961**.

## Land reform across the world

**Asia.** China redistributed land to peasants; **Vietnam** had similar goals under
**Ho Chi Minh's platform**, during the war of independence against France.

**Africa.** The **Ethiopian Derg**, a communist regime (1974–87) led by **Mengistu
Haile Mariam**, carried out **nationalisation of all agricultural land**, **granted
possessing rights** of land to peasants, and **seized land from the Ethiopian
church** — which the guide marks as a similarity with the **Russian Bolshevik
revolution of 1917**.

**Latin America.** In **Mexico**, **Lázaro Cárdenas (1934–40)** carried out
**Zapatista-inspired redistribution** to peasants. The **Sandinista government in
Nicaragua (1979–90)** aimed at **reversing inequality and exploitation**, and
established **cooperatives** with shared ownership and collectivisation.

## From the class notes on the Cold War

Stalin **ordered the communisation of occupied countries**, on the argument that
**the amount of loss suffered should determine the amount gained**:

| | Deaths | Cities |
|---|---|---|
| **USA** | 400,000 | Intact |
| **USSR** | 20 million | Destroyed |

Therefore, on this reasoning, the USSR should receive more territory.

The methods recorded are the **arrest of non-communist politicians accused of
terrorism**, the **slaughter of 20,000 in Bulgaria** — people opposed to his
electoral arrangements — the **imposition of communist dictatorship in Hungary**,
and the arrest of British and American nationals. The **Hungarian revolution** and
the **Prague Spring of 1968** are named.

**The two systems as the notes set them out:**

| USA | USSR |
|---|---|
| Mixed market economy | Command economy |
| Containment | |
| Nuclear fears | |
| HUAC, the Red Scare, McCarthyism | |

The flashpoints where it **heated up**: **Korea, the Cuban missile crisis, Vietnam
and Afghanistan**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **KMT** | The Chinese nationalist party created by Sun Yat-sen |
| **Chinese Civil War** | The 1927–37 and 1945–49 conflict between the KMT and the Communist Party |
| **People's Republic of China** | Established on communist victory in 1949 |
| **Great Leap Forward (大跃进)** | Collectivisation plus a shift of agricultural labour to industry, which with bad weather produced widespread famine |
| **The Derg** | The Ethiopian communist regime of 1974–87 under Mengistu Haile Mariam |
| **HUAC** | The House Un-American Activities Committee |
| **McCarthyism** | The US anti-communist campaign of the Red Scare |

# 8.5 Decolonisation after 1900

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Governance.*

**Nationalist leaders and parties sought autonomy**, and independence from European
imperialism was finally achieved — by **negotiation** or by **armed struggle**. The
cases below are grouped by which of those two routes they took.

## Armed struggle

**Ho Chi Minh in Vietnam.** A nationalist leader since the post-war era, whose
**Viet Minh** mounted armed resistance opposing French and Japanese imperialism.
Vietnam was also the location of **two Cold War proxy wars** (8.3): the **First
Indochina War (1946–54)** against the French and the **Second Indochina War
(1955–75)** against the United States.

**The Algerian War of Independence (1954–62).** Armed struggle against French
imperialism, led by the **Algerian National Liberation Front (FLN)**, achieving
independence in **1962**. It carried **proxy war elements**: the USSR gave
**financial support to the FLN**, aiming to **weaken NATO members like France**.

## Negotiated independence

**Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana**, under British control since **1821** through the Gold
Coast company. His political movement, the **Convention People's Party (1949)**,
sought independence through a philosophy of **positive action**: political
agitation, newspaper and educational campaigns, and non-violent struggle — strikes,
boycotts and non-cooperation. **Independence came in 1957** with Nkrumah as first
prime minister. He was also a leader of the non-aligned movement and an advocate of
pan-Africanism.

**The Indian National Congress** negotiated independence through **non-violent
resistance** led by **Mohandas Gandhi**, **Jawaharlal Nehru** and the Congress
itself. Nehru was a prominent figure in the non-aligned movement. **Indian
independence came in 1947.**

**Nasser in Egypt.** **Gamal Abdel Nasser** took power in **1952**. Egypt had been
independent since **1922**, but **King Farouk** was viewed as a **British puppet**.
Nasser acted to **eliminate foreign influence**, and in **1956 nationalised the
Suez Canal**.

## Challenges from new boundaries

The European division of Africa and Asia had been **driven by resource extraction,
trade and imperial rivalries**, with **disregard for local context** — ethnic and
religious diversity, and historical regional politics. The consequence of
decolonisation is that **independent states inherited numerous problems from
arbitrary borders**.

**The Biafran separatist movement in Nigeria.** Independence from Britain came in
**1960**, in a country whose ethnic composition included **Hausa, Fulani, Yoruba
and Igbo**. The **Igbo felt sidelined and under-represented**, and in **1967**
proclaimed the **Republic of Biafra**, resulting in civil war. **More than 3
million Igbo civilians died from famine.** The separatist movement failed, and
**ethnic tensions persist** in Nigerian society and politics.

**The Muslim League in British India.** The **All-India Muslim League**, founded in
**1906**, represented **Muslim minority interests** amid concern over Hindu
dominance in the Indian National Congress. In **1940 the Lahore Resolution**
proposed **independent states for Muslim-majority areas**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Viet Minh** | Ho Chi Minh's movement, mounting armed resistance against French and Japanese imperialism |
| **FLN** | The Algerian National Liberation Front, which led the independence struggle to 1962 |
| **Convention People's Party** | Nkrumah's 1949 movement for Ghanaian independence |
| **Positive action** | Nkrumah's philosophy of agitation, campaigns and non-violent struggle |
| **Republic of Biafra** | The state proclaimed by the Igbo in 1967, whose defeat cost over 3 million civilian lives |
| **All-India Muslim League** | The 1906 body representing Muslim minority interests in British India |
| **Lahore Resolution** | The 1940 proposal for independent states in Muslim-majority areas |

# 8.6 Newly Independent States

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Governance.*

## The partition of India

**Context.** The **Muslim League**, led by **Muhammad Ali Jinnah**, advocated an
**independent Muslim nation-state**. The **Hindu nationalist view** desired **Hindu
dominance** in the new country. **Gandhi and Nehru's vision** was to **unify the
nation on secular principles**. The decision was to **divide into two states** —
**India**, Hindu, and **Pakistan**, Muslim, split between the north-west and the
east, which is present-day Bangladesh.

**Independence and partition, 1947.** Hindu–Muslim tension escalated, and the
**British rushed for the exit to avoid blame**, producing a **hasty partition**.
**Mass migration** followed — **Sikhs and Hindus to India, Muslims to Pakistan** —
with consequences of **violence, displacement and family separation**. India and
Pakistan became **bitter rivals** in **frequent conflict**.

The haste is the cause the guide emphasises: a border drawn quickly, across
populations that then had to move.

## The creation of Israel

**Context.** **Zionism** is the **Jewish nationalism movement**. **Theodor Herzl**'s
*The Jewish State* (**1896**) advocated a **Jewish nation-state**, in response to
**minority status in Europe and the Ottoman Empire** and the risk of persecution.

In the First World War **Britain gained control of Palestine** under a **League of
Nations mandate**. The **Balfour Declaration of 1917** carried a **British promise
of a national Jewish home**, and **Jewish immigration to Palestine** followed.

**The Holocaust**, in which **6 million Jews were murdered**, increased
**international support for Zionism**.

With **UN approval, Israel was created in 1948**. The consequence for
**Palestinians** was **loss of home and displacement**. **Arab nations rejected
Israel**, producing the **1948 Arab–Israeli war** and an **Israeli victory** — with
**more Palestinian displacement, and more war**.

## States managing the economy

**Nasser in Egypt.** His policies were to **nationalise the Suez Canal (1956)**,
**promote industrialisation** and **form state-owned enterprises**. His economic
reforms carried out **land redistribution from the wealthy to peasants**, which was
**popular among peasants** and **reduced the power of traditional economic elites**.

Nasser appears in four separate places in this unit — as a **non-alignment leader**
(8.2), a **land reformer** (8.4), a **nationalist leader seeking autonomy** (8.5)
and a **state guiding economic life** (8.6). The guide notes he is therefore a
fairly important figure.

**Indira Gandhi in India**, third prime minister (**1966–77** and **1980–84**) and
daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru. Her government-led initiatives were the
**nationalisation of major banks (1969)** and **investment in the green
revolution**. The green revolution's impact was the **introduction of genetically
modified crops** and **higher yields of rice and wheat**, increasing food supply.

## Decolonisation and migration to former metropoles

After decolonisation, **political ties were cut** but **cultural and economic ties
remained** — cultural influences in language, religion and custom.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Partition** | The 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan |
| **Zionism** | The Jewish nationalism movement advocating a Jewish nation-state |
| **Balfour Declaration** | Britain's 1917 promise of a national Jewish home in Palestine |
| **Green revolution** | The introduction of genetically modified crops giving higher rice and wheat yields |
| **Metropole** | The former imperial home country to which post-colonial migration flowed |

# 8.7 Global Resistance to Established Power Structures after 1900

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

*Cultural developments and interactions.*

The twentieth century saw many conflicts — **the two world wars, mass atrocities,
proxy wars and armed resistance**. Against that background the guide sets
non-violent resistance.

## Mohandas Gandhi

Gandhi was **leader of the Indian National Congress** and a prominent figure in
India's independence movement after the First World War.

He led a resistance movement based on **firmly holding to truth** — **non-violence
in thought, word and deed**. The guide notes this principle is important in Indian
religion: **Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism**. Alongside it stands
**self-sufficiency**.

## The non-cooperation movement, 1919–22

Its methods were **boycotts of imported British goods** and **homemade clothing
using handlooms**, a **pre-industrial method**. The intent was **economic
disruption to British imperialism**.

This was **symbolic of the swadeshi principle**, advocating **Indian self-reliance**
and opposing **British colonial dependency**. The two halves work together: refusing
British goods only becomes sustainable if the alternative is made at home, which is
why the handloom is the movement's emblem rather than merely its method.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Non-violence** | Gandhi's principle of firmly holding to truth in thought, word and deed |
| **Non-cooperation movement** | The 1919–22 campaign of boycotts and homemade cloth aimed at disrupting British imperialism economically |
| **Swadeshi** | The principle of Indian self-reliance, opposing colonial dependency |

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The role of DNA

Whatever molecule turns out to carry inheritance has three jobs to do, and the
experiments in this section are all attempts to find the molecule that does them.

- **Storing information** — the genetic material stores the information needed by
  every living cell: ion transport, movement, cell growth and respiration.
- **Copying information** — before a cell divides, its genetic information must be
  copied.
- **Transmitting information** — when a cell divides, each daughter cell must get a
  **complete** copy of the genetic information.

## Griffith's experiments on bacterial transformation

Frederick Griffith worked with **two different strains of pneumonia bacteria**,
testing each on mice.

| Strain | Behaviour | Colonies |
|---|---|---|
| **Smooth strain (S strain)** | Disease-causing | Grow into smooth colonies |
| **Rough strain (R strain)** | Harmless | Grow into colonies with rough edges |

The four injections and their outcomes:

1. **Living S strain** → the mouse **dies of pneumonia**.
2. **Living R strain** → the mouse **lives**.
3. **Heat-killed S strain** → the mouse **lives**. This rules out a poison: the
   **cause of pneumonia was not a toxin** from the disease-causing bacteria, because
   dead S strain carries any such toxin and yet does no harm.
4. **Heat-killed S strain mixed with living R strain** → the mouse **dies of
   pneumonia**, and **living, disease-causing S strain bacteria were found in the
   mouse's blood**.

Step 3 is what makes step 4 decisive. Neither ingredient of the mixture kills on its
own, so something must have passed out of the dead S strain and changed the harmless
R strain into the disease-causing form.

**Transformation** is the process in which one strain of bacteria is changed
permanently by **a gene or genes of another strain** of bacteria.

## Avery's experiment on the molecular cause of transformation

Griffith showed that *something* was transferred. Oswald Avery identified it by
elimination, removing the lipids, carbohydrates, protein, RNA and DNA from a
solution of heat-killed S strain in turn.

1. Add the enzymes that remove **RNA (ribonuclease)**, lipids, carbohydrates and
   **protein (proteinase)** → no RNA, lipids, carbohydrates or protein left in the
   sample → add R strain → **transformation still occurs**.
2. Add the enzyme that removes **DNA (deoxyribonuclease)** → no DNA left in the
   sample → add R strain → **S strain does not appear**.

Transformation survives the loss of every molecule except one, and fails the moment
that one is destroyed.

**Conclusion:** **DNA is the molecule that stores and transmits genetic information
from one generation of an organism to the next.**

## The Hershey–Chase experiment on bacteriophages

**Bacteriophages** are **viruses that infect bacteria**. Each consists of a **protein
coat** and a **DNA or RNA core**, so a phage is made of exactly the two candidate
molecules the question is between.

How a phage attacks a bacterium:

1. The bacteriophage **latches onto** the bacterium.
2. **Bacteriophage DNA is injected into the cell**, taking over the bacterium's
   functions.
3. The **host bacterium begins producing new virus parts**.
4. **Viruses are assembled**, filling the bacterium.
5. The bacterium **explodes and releases the new viruses**.

Hershey and Chase used **radioactive markers (isotopes)**, each chosen to label only
one of the two molecules:

| Marker | What it labels |
|---|---|
| **³⁵S (sulfur)** | **Protein only** |
| **³²P (phosphorus)** | **DNA only** |

1. **³⁵S on the protein coat** → the phages infect the bacteria with their genetic
   material → **no radioactivity enters** the cell.
2. **³²P on the DNA** → the phages infect the bacteria with their genetic material →
   **radioactivity enters the cell**.

**Conclusion:** the genetic material of the bacteriophage was **DNA, not protein**.
DNA is the genetic material found in genes **not just in viruses and bacteria but in
all living cells** — which confirmed Avery's result.

## Worked examples

**Which of these would cause mice to die: heat-killed S strain; heat-killed S strain
and living R strain; living R strain; heat-killed R strain?**
Only the **mixture of heat-killed S strain and living R strain**. Each of the others
is one of Griffith's harmless outcomes — heat-killed S alone, living R alone, and R
strain, which is harmless whether alive or dead. Transformation needs both a source
of the gene (the dead S strain) and a living strain to receive it.

**Avery proved DNA is the genetic material because transformation failed in the test
tube treated with which enzyme?**
**Deoxyribonuclease.** Proteinase and ribonuclease left transformation working, so
they eliminated protein and RNA as candidates; only the removal of DNA stopped it.

**If Hershey and Chase had found only ³⁵S radioactivity inside the bacteria, what
would it have meant?**
That **protein entered the bacteria** — since ³⁵S labels protein alone, radioactivity
inside the cell would show that the protein coat, not the DNA, had been injected, and
the conclusion of the experiment would have been reversed.

**In the ³²P version of the experiment, where was the radioactivity primarily
detected?**
**Inside the bacterial cells.** ³²P labels the DNA, and the DNA is what the phage
injects; the empty protein coats stay outside.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transformation** | The process where one strain of bacteria is changed permanently by a gene or genes of another strain of bacteria |
| **S strain (smooth)** | The disease-causing pneumonia strain, which grows into smooth colonies |
| **R strain (rough)** | The harmless pneumonia strain, which grows into colonies with rough edges |
| **Ribonuclease** | The enzyme that removes RNA |
| **Proteinase** | The enzyme that removes protein |
| **Deoxyribonuclease** | The enzyme that removes DNA |
| **Bacteriophage** | A virus that infects bacteria, consisting of a protein coat and a DNA or RNA core |
| **³⁵S (sulfur)** | The radioactive marker that labels protein only |
| **³²P (phosphorus)** | The radioactive marker that labels DNA only |

# 12.2 Structure of DNA

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Components of DNA

DNA is built from **nucleotides**, and each nucleotide has three parts:

- A **5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose)**
- A **phosphate group**
- A **nitrogen base** — **adenine**, **thymine**, **cytosine** or **guanine**

Nucleotides are **joined together by covalent bonds between the 5-carbon sugar of one
nucleotide and the phosphate group of another**, and they may be joined **in any
order**.

The consequence of that construction is the whole reason DNA can carry information.
The **deoxyribose and phosphate group form the backbone** of the DNA chain, identical
all the way along, while the **nitrogen bases sit in between the two strands**. Since
the backbone never varies and the bases may come in any order, the base sequence is
the only thing that can differ from one stretch of DNA to the next.

## Chargaff's rule

**The amount of adenine (A) equals the amount of thymine (T), and the amount of
guanine (G) equals the amount of cytosine (C).**

## Franklin's X-rays (Photo 51)

**Rosalind Franklin** used **X-rays to take photographs of DNA molecules** after
extracting them.

**Conclusion:** the strands of DNA are **twisted around each other — a helical
structure**; the **angle of the X pattern** in the photograph shows there are **two
strands**; and the **nitrogenous bases lie near the centre** of the molecule.

## Watson and Crick's work

Watson and Crick built the **double helix model** — two strands wound around each
other — **with the help of Franklin's X-ray work**.

## The double helix

- The **two strands are twisted** around one another.
- The strands are **antiparallel**: they **run in opposite directions**.
- **Hydrogen bonds form between the nitrogen bases** and hold the two strands
  together.
- The **complementary base pairing rule**: **A pairs with T, G pairs with C**.

Chargaff's rule and the base pairing rule are two views of the same fact. If every A
in the molecule is bonded to a T on the opposite strand, the two must occur in equal
amounts, and likewise for G and C.

## Worked examples

**What do Chargaff's rules show about DNA?**
That **A = T and G = C**. The looser statement A + G = T + C is true as an arithmetic
consequence, but it is not what Chargaff measured — his finding pairs each base with
one specific partner, not purines with pyrimidines in bulk.

**What did Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction reveal?**
The **double helix with the bases near the centre**. Diffraction gives the shape and
dimensions of the molecule, not the order of its bases, so it could not reveal a
nucleotide sequence.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Nucleotide** | The unit of DNA: a 5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and a nitrogen base |
| **Deoxyribose** | The 5-carbon sugar of DNA |
| **Backbone** | The chain of deoxyribose and phosphate groups running along a DNA strand |
| **Chargaff's rule** | The amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine |
| **Photo 51** | Franklin's X-ray photograph of extracted DNA molecules, showing a helical structure of two strands with the bases near the centre |
| **Double helix** | Watson and Crick's model of DNA: two strands wound around each other |
| **Antiparallel** | Running in opposite directions, as the two strands of DNA do |
| **Complementary base pairing rule** | A pairs with T, and G pairs with C |

# 12.3 DNA Replication

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## When replication happens, and why it works

DNA replication takes place in the **S phase of interphase**. Copying **ensures each
cell will have a complete set of DNA**.

What makes copying possible is that **the two DNA strands are complementary**. Each
strand of the double helix therefore **has all the information needed to reconstruct
the other half by base pairing**, and the **base pairing rules (A with T, G with C)
help reconstruct the sequence of the new strand**. A single strand is not half the
information — it is all of it, written once.

## The steps

Replication is led by various **enzymes**, whose names end in *-ase*.

1. **Unzipping by helicase.** Helicase **unwinds the double helix**, **breaking the
   hydrogen bonds between base pairs** so that the DNA unwinds and the two strands
   separate.
2. **Building the new strands.** With the strands separated, **free nucleotides can
   stick on**. Each strand serves as a **template** to produce two new complementary
   strands, following the base pairing rules. This proceeds **in two directions**,
   carried out by **DNA polymerase**, with complementary bases attaching to the
   template.
3. **Two identical DNA molecules are formed**, each made of **one old strand and one
   new strand**.

**DNA polymerase** is the enzyme that **joins individual nucleotides together to
produce a new strand of DNA**.

Because each product keeps one of the original strands, DNA replication is
**semi-conservative replication** — **at least one strand of the original DNA is
conserved**.

The review guide tells you to ignore the leading and lagging strands when learning
these steps; the practice set does ask about them, and they are covered under the
worked examples below.

## The enzymes

**Enzymes** are **biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions by lowering
activation energy**.

| Enzyme | Role in replication |
|---|---|
| **Helicase** | Unzips the two strands of DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, forming the **replication fork** |
| **DNA polymerase** | Joins individual nucleotides together to produce a new strand of DNA |
| **Topoisomerase** | Relieves the **overwinding strain** created as the helix is unwound |
| **DNA polymerase I** | Replaces the primers with DNA sequence |
| **DNA ligase** | Joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand together |
| **Telomerase** | Adds short repeated DNA to telomeres |

The **replication fork** is the **Y-shaped region where the double strands are
unwound and DNA is replicated**.

## Telomeres and telomerase

**Telomeres** are a structure of DNA: **short, repeated DNA sequences at the ends of
eukaryotic chromosomes**. The **ends of DNA are hard to replicate**, and the telomere
**prevents genes from being damaged or lost during replication** — the repeated
sequence is expendable, so any shortening eats into it rather than into a gene.

**Telomerase** is the enzyme that **adds short repeated DNA to telomeres to make up
for the loss when chromosomes are replicated**, and so **prevents DNA from being
damaged or lost during replication**.

Telomerase is **often switched off in adults**, and **may be activated again in
cancer cells**. That single fact explains the difference between an ordinary body
cell and a cancer cell's capacity to divide:

| Cell type | Telomerase | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Somatic cells** | **Inactive** | Telomeres shorten → **limited cell division** (stem cells and fast-growing cells are the exception) |
| **Cancer cells** | **Highly active** | Telomere shortening is prevented → **unlimited division** |

## Prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA

| | **Prokaryotic DNA** | **Eukaryotic DNA** |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | The **cytoplasm** | The **cell nucleus** |
| **Form** | **Single, circular** DNA — still a double helix | **Multiple, linear** chromosomes |
| **Amount** | — | **1000 times more base pairs** |
| **Packing** | Usually **not packed by proteins** | **Wrapped around histones** |
| **Telomeres** | **None** | **Telomeres protect the ends from shortening** |

Eukaryotic DNA has to be packed because there is so much more of it. DNA and
**histones** together form **nucleosomes** — **beadlike structures formed by DNA and
histones** — and the nucleosome chain coils further into **supercoiled chromatin**,
**chromatin** being **coiled DNA fibres with histones**.

The presence or absence of telomeres follows from the shape. A circular chromosome
has no ends, so nothing erodes at a terminus; only a linear chromosome needs a
protective cap.

## Worked examples

**Contrast two structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA.**
Prokaryotic DNA is a **single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm** and has **no
telomeres**. Eukaryotic DNA is **multiple linear chromosomes in the nucleus**, and
**telomeres protect the ends from shortening**.

**Explain why the lagging strand requires discontinuous synthesis.**
**DNA polymerase synthesises only in the 5′→3′ direction**, but the **lagging strand
runs 3′→5′**. Because the lagging strand is **replicated away from the replication
fork**, it cannot be built as one continuous piece and must instead be made as short
**Okazaki fragments**. **DNA polymerase I** then replaces the primers with DNA
sequence, and **DNA ligase joins the fragments** into a single strand.

**Describe one consequence if DNA polymerase loses its proofreading function.**
**Increased mutations**, because errors go uncorrected — and those accumulated
errors lead to diseases such as cancer. This is why DNA polymerase III without
proofreading produces more mutations rather than simply faster replication.

**How does topoisomerase prevent problems during replication?**
By **relieving overwinding strain**. Separating the double helix is helicase's job;
topoisomerase deals with the twisting that unwinding creates ahead of the fork.

**What does telomerase inactivity in somatic cells cause?**
**Limited cell division.** With no telomerase to replace what is lost, telomeres
shorten with each replication until the cell can no longer divide.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **DNA replication** | The copying of DNA in the S phase of interphase, ensuring each cell has a complete set |
| **Semi-conservative replication** | Replication in which at least one strand of the original DNA is conserved in each product |
| **Enzyme** | A biological catalyst that speeds up a chemical reaction by lowering activation energy |
| **Helicase** | The enzyme that unzips the two strands of DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs |
| **Replication fork** | The Y-shaped region where the double strands are unwound and DNA is replicated |
| **DNA polymerase** | An enzyme that joins individual nucleotides to produce a new strand of DNA |
| **Topoisomerase** | The enzyme that relieves overwinding strain during replication |
| **Okazaki fragments** | The short pieces in which the lagging strand is synthesised, because it is replicated away from the replication fork |
| **DNA ligase** | The enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments together |
| **Telomere** | Short, repeated DNA sequences at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes that prevent genes from being damaged or lost during replication |
| **Telomerase** | The enzyme that adds short repeated DNA to telomeres to make up for the loss when chromosomes are replicated |
| **Histones** | The proteins that eukaryotic DNA wraps around |
| **Nucleosome** | The beadlike structure formed by DNA and histones |
| **Chromatin** | Coiled DNA fibres with histones |

# 13.1 RNA

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What RNA is

**RNA** is a **nucleic acid made up of nucleotides**. It **contains the decoded
genetic instructions from DNA**, and that information **controls the assembly of
amino acids into protein**.

An RNA nucleotide has three parts:

- A **phosphate group**
- A **5-carbon sugar — ribose**
- A **nitrogenous base**

## RNA compared with DNA

| | **RNA** | **DNA** |
|---|---|---|
| **Nitrogen bases** | A, **U**, G, C | A, **T**, G, C |
| **How many strands** | **Single** strand | **Double** strand |
| **5-carbon sugar** | **Ribose** | **Deoxyribose** |
| **Where it is found** | Nucleus **and** cytoplasm | Nucleus |

The base swap is the one to hold onto: RNA carries **uracil (U)** wherever DNA would
carry thymine. The guide's comparison table prints the last row's two entries the
wrong way round; go by the rest of the guide, which is consistent that DNA stays in
the nucleus while RNA is made there and then works in the cytoplasm.

## The three types of RNA

| Type | Function |
|---|---|
| **Messenger RNA (mRNA)** | Carries the instructions from DNA to other parts of the cell |
| **Transfer RNA (tRNA)** | Brings each amino acid to the ribosome according to the message in the mRNA |
| **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)** | Ribosomes are made up of rRNA and proteins |

## Transcription

**Segments of DNA — genes — act as a template to produce complementary RNA
molecules**: a segment of DNA is copied into RNA by **matching opposite bases**.

Where it happens depends on whether the cell has a nucleus:

- **Prokaryotes** — transcription **and** protein synthesis both happen in the
  **cytoplasm**.
- **Eukaryotes** — transcription in the **nucleus**, protein synthesis in the
  **cytoplasm**.

Transcription **requires RNA polymerase**, which **separates the two DNA strands and
builds up the RNA**.

It **starts at the promoter**, a **specific base sequence** which is **where RNA
polymerase binds** and which **signals where to start making RNA**. It **ends at the
terminator**, which carries **signals similar to the promoter's, telling
transcription to stop**.

### The steps

1. **RNA polymerase binds to the promoter** and **unzips the DNA double helix by
   breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.**
2. **RNA polymerase builds the RNA by base pairing RNA nucleotides to one strand of
   the DNA**, which acts as the template.
3. **RNA polymerase reaches the end of the gene** and the **pre-RNA is released.**

Summarised as the enzyme's own two jobs: RNA polymerase **separates the DNA molecule
by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases**, then **moves along one of the DNA
strands and links RNA nucleotides together**.

## RNA editing

The **pre-cut mRNA** released at the end of transcription is not yet usable. Editing
turns it into **mature RNA**:

1. **Cut out the introns** — the **segments that do not code for proteins**.
2. **Join the exons back together** — this is **splicing**.
3. **Add the cap and the tail.**

Some genes can **combine their exons in different ways, producing different versions
of mRNA**. This is **alternative splicing**, and it is how a single gene yields more
than one protein.

## Worked examples

**What does alternative RNA splicing enable?**
**The production of multiple proteins from one gene.** If the same set of exons can be
assembled in more than one order or combination, one gene's transcript becomes
several different mRNAs, each translated into a different protein.

**RNA splicing keeps all of the following except which one: exons, introns, poly-A
tails, 5′ caps?**
**Introns.** Splicing exists precisely to remove them; the exons are rejoined, and
the cap and tail are added, not taken away.

**Why does prokaryotic transcription overlap with translation?**
Because of **the lack of a nucleus**. In a eukaryote the nuclear membrane forces
transcription to finish and the mRNA to travel to the cytoplasm before a ribosome can
read it; a prokaryote does both in the same compartment, so the two can run at once.

**How does eukaryotic RNA polymerase bind to promoters?**
**Via transcription factors.**

**Why do eukaryotes process mRNA — cap, tail and splicing — before translation?**
The **5′ cap and 3′ poly-A tail protect the mRNA from degradation and enable ribosome
binding**. **Splicing removes the non-coding introns and joins the exons**, which
allows more than one functional protein to be produced from a single DNA sequence.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **RNA** | A nucleic acid made of nucleotides, containing the decoded genetic instructions from DNA that control the assembly of amino acids into protein |
| **Ribose** | The 5-carbon sugar of RNA |
| **Uracil (U)** | The RNA base that takes the place of DNA's thymine |
| **Messenger RNA (mRNA)** | RNA that carries the instructions from DNA to other parts of the cell |
| **Transfer RNA (tRNA)** | RNA that brings each amino acid to the ribosome according to the message in the mRNA |
| **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)** | The RNA that, with proteins, makes up ribosomes |
| **Transcription** | The copying of a segment of DNA into a complementary RNA molecule by matching opposite bases |
| **RNA polymerase** | The enzyme that separates the DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds, then moves along one strand linking RNA nucleotides together |
| **Promoter** | A specific base sequence where RNA polymerase binds, signalling where to start making RNA |
| **Terminator** | The signal, similar to a promoter, at which transcription stops |
| **Transcription factors** | The proteins through which eukaryotic RNA polymerase binds a promoter |
| **Intron** | A segment that does not code for protein, cut out during RNA editing |
| **Exon** | The segments joined back together after the introns are removed |
| **Splicing** | The joining of exons after introns have been cut out |
| **Alternative splicing** | Combining exons in different ways to produce different versions of mRNA from one gene |

# 13.2 Ribosomes and Protein Synthesis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Translation

**Translation** **makes a polypeptide chain using the genetic code on the mRNA**. It
is carried out **by the ribosome, in the cytoplasm**.

## Proteins

A **polypeptide** is a **long chain of amino acids**, containing a combination of
**only 20 amino acids**. The **sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide determines
the properties, shape and function of the protein** — which is why translating the
mRNA in the right order matters so much, and why changing a single amino acid can
change what the protein does.

Proteins have **four levels of organisation**:

| Level | What it is |
|---|---|
| **1** | The **sequence** of amino acids in the chain |
| **2** | The **folding or coiling** of the chain |
| **3** | The complete **3D arrangement** — held by ionic bonds, covalent bonds, van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonds |
| **4** | **More than one chain** together |

## The genetic code

A **codon** is **three consecutive nucleotide bases on the mRNA** — a triplet — and it
**codes for a single amino acid**.

- **Start codon:** **AUG**, which codes for **methionine**
- **Stop codons:** **UAA**, **UAG**, **UGA**

Some amino acids are **universal** and **can be coded for by more than one codon**.

## The steps of translation

**1. mRNA.** The mRNA is **transcribed in the nucleus and enters the cytoplasm**, and
the **ribosome attaches to the mRNA in the cytoplasm**.

**2. tRNA.** **Translation begins at the start codon, AUG.** **tRNA brings the proper
amino acids into the ribosome**, and the **ribosome attaches those amino acids to the
growing chain**.

**3. The polypeptide "assembly line".** The **bond between an amino acid and its RNA
is unbound**, the **amino acids are joined together by peptide bonds**, and the
**ribosome moves along, binding new tRNA and amino acids**.

**4. Completing the polypeptide.** The ribosome comes to a **stop codon (UAA, UAG or
UGA)** and **releases the newly formed polypeptide and the mRNA**. **Translation
ends.**

## The role of rRNA

The rRNA in the ribosome **helps hold the ribosomal proteins in place** and **helps
locate the beginning of the mRNA message**, and it **may even carry out the chemical
reaction that joins the amino acids together**.

## The molecular basis of heredity

The **central dogma of molecular biology** is that **genetic information is
transferred from DNA to RNA to protein**.

**Genes contain the instructions for making proteins**, and proteins are what a cell
actually runs on:

- **Enzymes catalyse and regulate chemical reactions**
- Proteins **build and operate living cells**

This is what ties the whole unit together. DNA is the store, RNA is the working copy,
protein is the product — and because protein does the work of the cell, a change
anywhere along that path shows up as a change in the organism.

## Worked examples

**Transcribe the DNA template 3′-TAC GTA CTT GCA-5′ into mRNA and translate it,
given AUG = methionine, CAU = histidine, GAA = glutamic acid, CGU = arginine.**

Transcription matches opposite bases, with **U in place of T**:

| DNA template | 3′- | TAC | GTA | CTT | GCA | -5′ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **mRNA** | 5′- | **AUG** | **CAU** | **GAA** | **CGU** | -3′ |
| **Amino acid** | | Methionine | Histidine | Glutamic acid | Arginine | |

The chain is **methionine – histidine – glutamic acid – arginine**. Note that it opens
with AUG, the start codon, which is where translation begins.

**Which mRNA codon does a tRNA with the anticodon AUU pair with?**
**None.** Matching opposite bases gives UAA, and UAA is a **stop codon** — it codes
for no amino acid, so no tRNA carries one for it. The other options can be ruled out
faster still: ATG contains thymine, which does not occur in mRNA.

**How do retroviruses violate the central dogma?**
By going **RNA → DNA**, the reverse of the DNA → RNA step the central dogma sets out.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Translation** | Making a polypeptide chain using the genetic code on mRNA, carried out by the ribosome in the cytoplasm |
| **Polypeptide** | A long chain of amino acids, containing a combination of only 20 amino acids |
| **Codon** | Three consecutive nucleotide bases on mRNA, coding for a single amino acid |
| **Start codon** | AUG, which codes for methionine and is where translation begins |
| **Stop codon** | UAA, UAG or UGA, at which the polypeptide and mRNA are released and translation ends |
| **Peptide bond** | The bond by which amino acids are joined together in the growing chain |
| **Central dogma of molecular biology** | Genetic information is transferred from DNA to RNA to protein |

# 13.3 Mutations

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Mutations and mutagens

**Mutations** are **heritable changes in genetic information**. Because they are
heritable, they are changes to the DNA itself rather than damage to a protein — the
alteration is copied on to every descendant cell.

**Mutagens** are **chemical or physical agents in the environment that cause
mutations**: **pesticides, tobacco smoke, pollutants, X-rays and UV light**.

## The two types

| Type | Scale of the change |
|---|---|
| **Gene mutation** | Changes in **one gene** |
| **Chromosomal mutation** | Changes in a **whole chromosome** |

## Gene mutations

A **point mutation** is a **change in one nucleotide**, and there are three kinds:

1. **Single base substitution** — one nucleotide base is **replaced** with another
2. **Single base insertion** — one nucleotide base is **added**
3. **Single base deletion** — one nucleotide is **removed**

Their consequences are not equally serious, and the reason is the triplet code.

- A **single base substitution affects no more than one amino acid.** Changing one
  base changes at most the one codon it sits in, so the rest of the chain is read
  exactly as before.
- A **single base insertion or deletion is more dramatic**: it **changes every amino
  acid following the mutation point**. Adding or removing a base shifts where every
  subsequent triplet begins, so the **altered protein is unable to perform its normal
  functions**. This is the case the practice set calls a **frameshift**.

The practice set also names two kinds of substitution by their effect on the protein:

| Name | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Missense** | The substituted base changes one amino acid into a different one |
| **Nonsense** | The substituted base creates a **stop codon**, cutting the chain short and leaving a **non-functional protein** |

## Chromosomal mutations

### Changes of structure

| Mutation | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Duplication** | Produces **extra copies** of parts of a chromosome |
| **Inversion** | **Reverses the direction** of part of a chromosome |
| **Translocation** | Part of a chromosome **breaks off and attaches to another** |
| **Deletion** | **Loss of part or all** of a chromosome |

### Changes of number

**Aneuploidy** is having **one fewer or one extra chromosome (2n + 1, 2n − 1)**.
**Down syndrome** is the example: **47 chromosomes**, **trisomy 21** — three copies of
chromosome 21.

**Polyploidy** is having **three or more sets of each type of chromosome** —
**triploid (3n)**, **tetraploid (4n)**. It arises when **chromosomes fail to separate
in meiosis**. **Polyploid plants are usually larger and stronger than diploid
plants.**

## The effects of mutations

**Many mutations are neutral** — they have **little or no effect on gene expression**,
which is to say on protein function.

**Beneficial mutations** **produce proteins with new activities useful to the
organism**. **Insects resisting pesticides** and **bacteria resisting antibiotics**
are the examples, and this is the reason mutation matters beyond disease: it is the
**source of the genetic variation** on which evolution works.

**Harmful mutations** include:

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **Progeria** | Causes children to age quickly |
| **Sickle cell disease** | A **point mutation** |
| **Marfan syndrome** | |
| **Albinism** | |
| **Red-green colour blindness** | |
| **Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)** | Causes the nerves that control muscle to stop working |

## Worked examples

**Sickle cell anaemia's Glu → Val mutation is which type?**
**Missense.** One amino acid has been replaced by another and the rest of the chain is
intact, which is the signature of a single base substitution — not a frameshift,
which would have altered every amino acid after the mutation point, and not a
nonsense mutation, which would have produced a stop codon instead of valine.

**A mutation changes the DNA of 3′-TAC GTA CTT GCA-5′ to 3′-TAC GTA CTT CCA-5′.
Identify the mutation type and compare the original and mutated amino acid
sequences.**
The mutation type is a **substitution** — one base has been swapped, with none added
or removed. Only the **fourth codon** is affected: the first three amino acids stay
**methionine – histidine – glutamic acid**, and the fourth changes from **arginine
(CGU)** to **proline (CCA)**. The answer key reads the mutated codon CCA straight off
the DNA strand rather than transcribing it as part (a) does, but either way the
examinable point holds: one substituted base changes one amino acid and leaves the
rest of the chain untouched.

**How does a translocation cause chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML)?**
By **activating a gene that drives uncontrolled cell division**. The chromosome
material is moved rather than lost, so the damage comes from a gene switched on in
the wrong place, not from deletion.

**How does polyploidy benefit plants, and how does its impact differ in animals?**
In **plants** it is **beneficial** — polyploid plants are **larger and stronger**. In
**animals** it is **lethal**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Mutation** | A heritable change in genetic information |
| **Mutagen** | A chemical or physical agent in the environment that causes mutations |
| **Gene mutation** | A change in one gene |
| **Chromosomal mutation** | A change in a whole chromosome |
| **Point mutation** | A change in one nucleotide |
| **Single base substitution** | One nucleotide base replaced with another; affects no more than one amino acid |
| **Single base insertion** | One nucleotide base added |
| **Single base deletion** | One nucleotide removed |
| **Frameshift** | An insertion or deletion that changes every amino acid following the mutation point |
| **Missense mutation** | A substitution that changes one amino acid into a different one |
| **Nonsense mutation** | A substitution that creates a stop codon, giving a non-functional protein |
| **Duplication** | A chromosomal mutation producing extra copies of parts of a chromosome |
| **Inversion** | A chromosomal mutation reversing the direction of part of a chromosome |
| **Translocation** | A chromosomal mutation in which part of a chromosome breaks off and attaches to another |
| **Deletion (chromosomal)** | Loss of part or all of a chromosome |
| **Aneuploidy** | Having one fewer or one extra chromosome (2n + 1, 2n − 1) |
| **Trisomy 21** | Down syndrome: 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 |
| **Polyploidy** | Having three or more sets of each type of chromosome, such as triploid (3n) or tetraploid (4n), arising when chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis |
| **Neutral mutation** | A mutation with little or no effect on gene expression |
| **Beneficial mutation** | A mutation producing proteins with new activities useful to the organism, and a source of genetic variation |

# 13.4 Gene Regulation and Expression

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Prokaryotic gene regulation

In prokaryotes, **DNA binding proteins regulate genes by controlling transcription**
— the switch is thrown before any RNA is made at all.

The genes themselves are organised into **operons**: **groups of genes that are
regulated together**. The example is the **lac operon in *E. coli***, which
**contains three lactose genes**. Those three genes **need to be expressed together**
so that the proteins they code for are all present and the bacterium can **digest
lactose as food** — there is no use in producing one enzyme of a pathway without the
others, which is precisely why they share a single switch.

### Operon structure

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Promoter** | The **RNA polymerase binding site** |
| **Operator** | The **repressor protein binding site** |
| **Genes** | A **cluster of functionally related genes** — for instance the lactose metabolism genes in *E. coli* |

## Eukaryotic gene regulation

### RNA interference (RNAi)

The mechanism runs as follows:

1. **Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs / miRNAs) form hairpin loops.**
2. These are **diced by the Dicer enzyme into 20-base-pair fragments.**
3. The fragments **load into a silencing complex**, which **binds complementary
   mRNA** and **blocks translation or degrades the mRNA.**

Note where in the sequence this acts: the mRNA has already been transcribed, so RNAi
regulates a gene after the fact rather than at the promoter.

**Discovery (Fire and Mello, 1998).** **Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) injections caused
gene silencing** — the ***unc-22* gene in *C. elegans***, whose silencing made the
worms twitch. **Single-stranded RNA had no effect**, which is what identified
double-strandedness as the trigger.

**Significance.** RNAi is a **universal regulatory tool across life forms**, and it
has **medical potential**: **silencing viral or cancer genes** using RNAi technology.

## Cell specialisation and differentiation

**Differentiation** is the process by which **cells become specialised** — a liver
cell as against a nerve cell — **via selective gene expression**.

**The challenge this answers:** **all cells share identical DNA.** Since the
instruction set is the same everywhere, the difference between one cell type and
another cannot lie in the genes present; it is **regulation that enables the
diversity**.

## Genetic control of development

### Homeotic genes

**Homeotic genes** are **master switches determining body part identity** — whether a
fruit fly structure develops as a leg or as an antenna.

**When they mutate**, the result is **body part misplacement**: a leg growing from
the head.

### Homeobox and Hox genes

The **homeobox** is a **180-base-pair DNA sequence coding for transcription factors
that activate developmental genes**.

**Hox genes** are a **subgroup of homeobox genes**, **arranged in clusters** whose
**order correlates with the body axis, head to tail**. Their **role** is to **define
segment identity** — a Hox mutation alters the position of an organ.

**Evolutionary conservation:** **identical clusters appear in fruit flies, mice and
humans**, controlling, for example, limb and fin development.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Operon** | A group of genes that are regulated together |
| **lac operon** | The operon in *E. coli* containing three lactose genes, expressed together so the bacterium can digest lactose as food |
| **Promoter (operon)** | The RNA polymerase binding site |
| **Operator** | The repressor protein binding site |
| **RNA interference (RNAi)** | Regulation in which small RNAs are diced into fragments that load into a silencing complex and bind complementary mRNA, blocking translation or degrading the mRNA |
| **siRNA / miRNA** | Small interfering RNAs that form hairpin loops and are diced into 20-base-pair fragments |
| **Dicer** | The enzyme that dices small RNAs into 20-base-pair fragments |
| **Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** | The form of RNA whose injection caused gene silencing in Fire and Mello's 1998 experiment; single-stranded RNA had no effect |
| **Differentiation** | Cells becoming specialised via selective gene expression |
| **Homeotic genes** | Master switches determining body part identity; mutation causes body part misplacement |
| **Homeobox** | A 180-base-pair DNA sequence coding for transcription factors that activate developmental genes |
| **Hox genes** | A subgroup of homeobox genes, arranged in clusters whose order correlates with the body axis from head to tail, defining segment identity |

# 2.2 Properties of Water

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Polarity

Water's **polarity** means there is a **greater probability of finding its shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom**.

**Polar molecules have unevenly distributed charges** — **oxygen is slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive**.

## Hydrogen bonding

A **hydrogen bond** is a **weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another**.

## Cohesion, adhesion, and capillary action

| Property | Definition | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the **same** substance | Causes **surface tension** |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of **different** substances | Causes **menisci** to form |

**Capillary action** works by both at once: **cohesion holds the continuous column of water together as adhesion causes it to rise**. This is what **draws water out of roots into stems**.

## Solutions

Water's polarity lets it **dissolve ionic compounds and other polar molecules**.

- **Solute** — the substance that is dissolved
- **Solvent** — the substance in which the solute dissolves

## The pH scale

The **pH scale** measures the **concentration of H⁺ ions** in a solution, ranging from **0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic)**.

| pH | Condition | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| **< 7** | Acidic | [H⁺] > [OH⁻] |
| **= 7** | Neutral | [H⁺] = [OH⁻] |
| **> 7** | Basic | [H⁺] < [OH⁻] |

$$\text{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^+}], \qquad [\mathrm{H^+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$$

Because the scale is **logarithmic**, each whole step is a **tenfold** change in H⁺ concentration — pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5, not slightly more.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polarity** | The greater probability of finding water's shared electrons closer to its oxygen atom |
| **Polar molecule** | A molecule with unevenly distributed charges |
| **Hydrogen bond** | A weak intermolecular attraction between hydrogen on one molecule and oxygen on another |
| **Cohesion** | Attraction between molecules of the same substance, causing surface tension |
| **Adhesion** | Attraction between molecules of different substances, causing menisci |
| **Capillary action** | Cohesion holding a water column together while adhesion causes it to rise |
| **Solute** | The substance that is dissolved |
| **Solvent** | The substance in which the solute dissolves |
| **pH scale** | A logarithmic measure of H⁺ concentration, from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very basic) |

# 3.1 What Is Ecology?

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basics

The **biosphere** consists of **all life and all parts of the Earth with life**.

**Ecology** is the **scientific study of interactions among organisms, and between organisms and their physical environment**.

The Greek root is **oikos**, meaning *house*:

- **Ecology** — the study of nature's "houses" and the inhabitants of those houses
- **Economics** — the study of human "houses" and interactions involving money and trade

The shared root is not a coincidence, and it is a useful reminder of what ecology studies: not organisms alone but the **household they run**.

## Levels of organisation

From least to most inclusive:

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1. Individual organism** | A single living thing |
| **2. Population** | A group of individuals of **one species** living in the **same area**. A **species** is a group of similar organisms that can produce **fertile offspring** |
| **3. Community** | **All the different populations** that live together in an area |
| **4. Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area **together with their physical environment** |
| **5. Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing **similar climates and organisms** |
| **6. Biosphere** | Our entire planet |

## Environmental factors

The **environment** is **all the conditions and factors surrounding an organism**.

| Factor | Nature | Definition | Example (for a bullfrog) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Biotic** | Biological | Any **living** part of the environment an organism might interact with | Insects and herons |
| **Abiotic** | Physical | Any **nonliving** part of the environment | Water availability and temperature |

**Both types of factor can influence the other**, shaping an environment with their dynamic mix.

## Ecological methods

- **Observation**
- **Experimentation** — can be used to **test hypotheses**
- **Modelling** — helps understand events that happen over **long periods of time or large distances**, using **formulas based on data from observation and experimentation**

Note why modelling exists as a third method: some ecological questions span centuries or continents, where neither watching nor experimenting is possible.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Biosphere** | All life and all parts of the Earth with life |
| **Ecology** | The scientific study of interactions among organisms and with their physical environment |
| **Population** | A group of individuals of one species living in the same area |
| **Species** | Similar organisms that can produce fertile offspring |
| **Community** | All the different populations living together in an area |
| **Ecosystem** | All organisms in an area together with their physical environment |
| **Biome** | A group of ecosystems sharing similar climates and organisms |
| **Environment** | All conditions and factors surrounding an organism |
| **Biotic factor** | Any living part of the environment an organism might interact with |
| **Abiotic factor** | Any nonliving part of the environment |
| **Modelling** | Using formulas based on observational and experimental data to understand events over long times or distances |

markdown:
# 3.2 Energy, Producers, and Consumers

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Producers

**Autotrophs** are organisms that **use solar or chemical energy to produce "food" (glucose)**.

They are also called **primary producers**, because they are the **first producers of energy-rich compounds** later used by other organisms, and they are **essential to energy flow in the biosphere**.

The Greek roots are **auto** (by itself) and **trophikos** (to feed).

### Photosynthesis

A process in which **light energy powers reactions to produce carbohydrates**, converting **carbon dioxide and water into oxygen and energy-rich sugars and starches**.

Performed by:

- **Plants**, on land
- **Algae**, in freshwater and the upper layers of the ocean
- **Bacteria** (commonly **cyanobacteria**), in tidal flats and salt marshes

### Chemosynthesis

A process in which **chemical energy is used to produce carbohydrates**. **Chemosynthetic bacteria power ecosystems** at deep-sea volcanic vents, hot springs, and coastal tidal marshes.

## Consumers

**Heterotrophs** must **acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms**.

| Type | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Carnivores** | Kill and eat other animals | Snakes, dogs, cats |
| **Herbivores** | Eat plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits | Cows, caterpillars, deer |
| **Omnivores** | Diets include both plants and animals | Humans, bears, pigs |
| **Scavengers** | Consume carcasses of animals killed by other predators or dead by other means | Vultures, flies |
| **Decomposers (saprotrophs)** | Release digestive enzymes to break down organic matter **externally**, producing **detritus** | Fungi, bacteria |
| **Detritivores** | Feed on **detritus particles**, chewing and grinding them into smaller pieces; commonly digest the decomposers living on or in those particles | Mites, snails, shrimp, crabs |

**Detritus** is small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains.

Note the trade-off in carnivory: **catching and killing prey requires energy**, but meat is generally **rich in nutrients and energy and easily digested**.

## Beyond the consumer categories

**Strict categories do not represent the full complexity.**

- **Plant leaves are much less nutritious and harder to digest than seeds or fruits**, so herbivores that eat different parts differ in how they obtain and digest food. **Most birds do not have the digestive systems to digest leaves**
- **Hyenas**, though classified as carnivores, **will scavenge**
- **Aquatic animals** eat a mixture of algae, bits of animal carcasses, and detritus
- **Carnivorous plants and euglenoids are mixotrophic** — both heterotrophic and autotrophic

This is the section's real point: the categories are a useful first pass, and almost every organism examined closely violates them somewhere.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Autotroph** | An organism using solar or chemical energy to produce food (glucose) |
| **Primary producer** | Another name for an autotroph — the first producer of energy-rich compounds |
| **Photosynthesis** | Light energy powering reactions that convert CO₂ and water into oxygen and sugars |
| **Chemosynthesis** | Chemical energy being used to produce carbohydrates |
| **Heterotroph** | An organism that must acquire energy and nutrients from other organisms |
| **Carnivore** | A consumer that kills and eats other animals |
| **Herbivore** | A consumer that eats plant leaves, roots, seeds, or fruits |
| **Omnivore** | A consumer whose diet includes both plants and animals |
| **Scavenger** | A consumer of carcasses killed by others or dead by other means |
| **Decomposer (saprotroph)** | An organism releasing digestive enzymes to break down organic matter externally |
| **Detritus** | Small pieces of dead and decaying plant and animal remains |
| **Detritivore** | An organism feeding on detritus particles, grinding them smaller |
| **Mixotroph** | An organism that is both heterotrophic and autotrophic |
