summary: One column is selected by name; several are selected by passing a list of names, which is why the double square brackets appear. A row can be reached either by its name or by its position: This is the
markdown:
# 5.4 Selecting Data in Pandas

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Selecting columns

One column is selected by name; several are selected by passing a list of names, which is why the double square brackets appear.

```python
df['colname']
df[['col1', 'col2', 'col3']]
```

## Selecting rows

A row can be reached either by its name or by its position:

```python
df.loc['rowname']    # by row name
df.iloc[index]       # by position
```

This is the distinction that runs through the whole of this lesson. `loc` works with names, `iloc` works with index numbers.

A specific row can also be picked out by a condition on one of its columns:

```python
df.loc[df['col'] == value]
```

## Selecting rows and columns together

With `iloc`, both arguments are positions:

```python
df.iloc[[row index], [column index]]
df.iloc[starting index:ending index + 1, starting index:ending index + 1]
```

With `loc`, both arguments are names:

```python
df.loc[[row name], [column name]]
df.loc[starting name:ending name, starting name:ending name]
```

Compare the two range forms carefully. The `iloc` version needs `ending index + 1` because a positional range excludes its end, exactly as ordinary Python slicing does; the `loc` version needs no such adjustment because a range of labels includes the end name.

## Slicing

Slicing with `loc` takes row labels:

```python
df.loc[rowStartLabel:rowEndLabel]
```

Slicing with `iloc` takes row and column positions:

```python
df.iloc[rowStartId:rowEndId, colStartId:colEndId]
```

## Selection with a condition

Comparing a column against a value does not immediately return rows — it returns a **Boolean Series**, which has `True` at each position where the comparison holds. Passing that Series back to the DataFrame is what selects the elements with `True` at the corresponding value.

```python
Selected_data = df['column name'] == values in the column
```

```python
boolSeries = data['age'] == 14
```

Multiple conditions are combined with `&` for "and" and `|` for "or". Each condition must be wrapped in its own brackets:

```python
boolSeries = (data['age'] >= 14) & (data['country'] == 'USA')
```

The whole thing can be put on one line by writing the condition inside the selection brackets:

```python
Data = df[df['column name'] == values in the column]
data = df[(df['column name'] == values in the column) & (df['column name'] == values in the column)]
```

## Extracting data

Combining a condition with a list of columns extracts a specific block — some rows, some columns. There are two equivalent ways of writing it:

```python
Df1 = df.loc[df['col'] == 'condition', ['col1', 'col2']]
Df2 = df.loc[df['col'] == 'condition'][['col1', 'col2']]
```

The first passes the row condition and the column list as the two arguments of a single `loc`; the second selects the rows first and then indexes the columns of the result.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **`loc`** | Selects rows and columns by name or label |
| **`iloc`** | Selects rows and columns by index position |
| **Boolean Series** | The selected part produced by a condition; selects elements with `True` at the corresponding value |
| **`&` (pandas)** | Combines multiple conditions as "and" |
| **Vertical bar (pandas)** | Combines multiple conditions as "or" |

# 5.5 Modifying Data and File Formats

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Adding or modifying a column

Assigning to a column name both adds a new column and overwrites an existing one. The data is usually a list whose number of elements equals the number of rows in the DataFrame — it has to line up with the rows already there.

```python
df[colname] = data
df['col'] = [value1, value2]
df.loc[:, 'col'] = [value1, value2]
```

The colon in `df.loc[:, 'col']` means "all rows", so the two forms do the same job.

## Adding or modifying a row

```python
df.loc[rowname] = data
df.iloc[rowindex] = data
```

To add one row of data at the end, give it a row label one past the current length, or append a one-row DataFrame:

```python
df.loc[str(len(df))] = [value1, value2]
df = df._append(pd.DataFrame([[value1, value2]], columns=df.columns))
```

Using `str(len(df))` works because a DataFrame of $n$ rows has no row labelled $n$ yet, so assigning to that label creates a new row rather than overwriting one.

## Modifying a specific cell

```python
df.loc['row', 'col']
df.iloc[rowind, colind]
```

## Modifying by condition

A condition can stand in place of a row label, so the same assignment syntax updates every row that matches:

```python
df.loc[<condition>] = [val1, val2]
df.loc[<condition>, ['col1', 'col2']] = [val1, val2]
df.iloc['row_idx'] = [val1, val2]
```

```python
df.loc[df['col'] == 'condition', 'col'] = value
df.loc[df['col'] == 'condition', ['col1', 'col2']] = [value1, value2]
```

## Deleting rows and columns

A column can be deleted by name, or by looking its name up from its position:

```python
del df[col_name]
del df[df.columns[col_index]]
```

`drop()` handles both rows and columns, and the `axis` argument decides which:

```python
df = df.drop([row_label1, row_label2])
df = df.drop([col_name1, col_name2], axis=1)
```

| `axis` | Effect |
|---|---|
| `axis = 1` | Drops a column |
| `axis = 0` | Drops a row |
| No `axis` given | Assume `axis = 0`, so a row is dropped |

Rows can also be dropped by row label number:

```python
df = df.drop([row_label_num])
df = df.drop([row_label_num1, row_label_num2])
```

Data can also be removed by keeping everything that does not match a condition — the `!=` here is what turns a selection into a removal:

```python
Df = df.loc[df['col'] != 'condition', :]
```

## Data in different formats

| Format | Read | Write |
|---|---|---|
| Excel | `data = pd.read_excel('filename.xlsx')` | `df.to_excel('filename.xlsx', 'Sheet1', index=False)` |
| CSV | `data = pd.read_csv('filename.csv')` | `data.to_csv('filename.csv', index=False)` |

## Other useful operations

`dropna()` is used to remove all the rows of which the content is NULL, while `fillna(val)` is used to replace the NULL values with a specified value — two different answers to the same problem of missing data.

```python
df.dropna()
df.fillna(val)
```

Sorting takes the column to sort by and a direction:

```python
df2 = df1.sort_values(by='score', ascending=True)
```

If `ascending == True` the result is in ascending order; if `ascending == False` it is in descending order.

Resetting the index tidies up the row labels after rows have been sorted or removed:

```python
df2 = df2.reset_index(drop=True)
df2.index = range(len(df2))
```

If `drop == True` the indexes are reset. If `drop == False`, the old index becomes a new column and new indexes are added alongside it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **`drop()`** | Deletes rows or columns; `axis = 1` drops a column, `axis = 0` (the default) drops a row |
| **`read_excel()` / `to_excel()`** | Read from and write to an Excel file |
| **`read_csv()` / `to_csv()`** | Read from and write to a CSV file |
| **`dropna()`** | Removes all the rows of which the content is NULL |
| **`fillna(val)`** | Replaces the NULL values with a specified value |
| **`sort_values()`** | Sorts by a given column; `ascending=True` for ascending order, `ascending=False` for descending |
| **`reset_index()`** | Resets the row indexes; `drop=True` discards the old index, `drop=False` keeps it as a new column |

# 6.1 Plotting with Matplotlib

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Matplotlib** is a comprehensive library for creating static, animated and interactive visualisations in Python.

## Installation and import

```bash
python -m pip install matplotlib
```

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

## Basic grammar

An empty figure is created with:

```python
fig = plt.figure()
```

## Line plots

```python
plt.plot(x, y, color='', linestyle='', mfc='', marker='', label='')
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x`, `y` | The values of the x and y axes, in lists |
| `color` | Colour of the line, bar or sections |
| `label` | Labels the name of the line |
| `linestyle` | The style of the line in the line plot; the default setting is solid |
| `mfc` | Colour of the dot |
| `marker` | Shape used to display the points in the line plot |

```python
plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
```

## Scatter plots

A scatter plot shows the points without joining them, so it takes `marker` but not `linestyle`.

```python
plt.scatter(x, y, color='', marker='')
plt.scatter([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
```

## Bar charts

```python
plt.bar(x, y, color='', width=)
plt.bar(['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], [20, 35, 30, 25])
```

`width` sets the width of the bar. The horizontal version is `barh`:

```python
plt.barh(x, y, color='', width=)
plt.barh(['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], [20, 35, 30, 25])
```

### Multiple bar charts

To place several bars side by side at each category, a Series can be used to customise the location of the bars quickly. Build a Series of evenly spaced positions, then shift copies of it left and right by a fraction of the bar width `w`:

```python
x = pd.Series(list(range(1, len(df) + 1)))
x1, x2 = x - w/2, x + w/2        # 2 bars
x1, x2, x3 = x - w, x, x + w     # 3 bars
```

With two bars the offsets are half a width either side of centre; with three the middle bar sits on the centre and the outer two move a full width out, which keeps each group symmetrical about its tick.

## Histograms

```python
plt.hist(np.random.randn(1000), bins=20)
```

`bins` sets how many intervals the data is divided into.

## Pie charts

```python
plt.pie(values, color='', labels=[], autopct='')
plt.pie([15, 30, 45, 10], labels=['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `labels` | Labels each section of the pie chart |
| `autopct` | Format for the percentage shown on each slice, for example `'%.1f%%'` |
| `startangle` | Sets the starting angle of the first slice |
| `explode` | Represents the fraction of the radius by which a specific slice is pushed out |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Matplotlib** | A comprehensive library for creating static, animated and interactive visualisations in Python |
| **`plt.figure()`** | Creates an empty figure |
| **`plt.plot()`** | Draws a line plot |
| **`plt.scatter()`** | Draws a scatter plot |
| **`plt.bar()` / `plt.barh()`** | Draw a vertical and a horizontal bar chart |
| **`plt.hist()`** | Draws a histogram |
| **`plt.pie()`** | Draws a pie chart |
| **`linestyle`** | The style of the line in a line plot; solid by default |
| **`mfc`** | Colour of the dot |
| **`marker`** | Shape used to display the points in the line plot |
| **`autopct`** | Format of the percentage labels on a pie chart |
| **`explode`** | The fraction of the radius by which a specific pie slice is offset |

# 6.2 Customising and Arranging Plots

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## rcParams

`plt.rcParams` sets defaults that apply to the whole figure, so they are written once rather than repeated on every call.

```python
plt.rcParams['font.family'] = 'Times New Roman'
plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 14
plt.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2
```

## Labels

`plt.legend()` displays the labels given to each plotted series, and `loc` places the legend box:

```python
plt.legend(loc='position')
```

The available positions are `'best'`, `'upper right'`, `'upper left'`, `'lower left'`, `'lower right'`, `'right'`, `'center left'`, `'center right'`, `'lower center'`, `'upper center'` and `'center'`.

Axis names and a figure title are set with:

```python
plt.xlabel('name of x axis')
plt.ylabel('name of y axis')
plt.title('name of the graph')
```

## Axis customisation

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `plt.xticks()`, `plt.yticks()` | Set the tick marks on each axis |
| `plt.xlim()`, `plt.ylim()` | Set the range shown on each axis |

A grid is added with:

```python
plt.grid(axis='x', linestyle='')
```

where `axis` is `'x'` or `'y'`.

## Figure size and twin axes

The size of the plot is customised when the figure is created:

```python
plt.figure(figsize=(width, height))
```

`plt.twinx()` creates a second y-axis sharing the same x-axis. Directly after using this function, write the code for the other twin graph — the order matters, since everything plotted after the call belongs to the new axis.

```python
plt.twinx()
```

## Subplots

Several plots can be arranged in a grid:

```python
plt.subplot(rows, cols, index)
```

`GridSpec` customises the grid structure when a plain grid of equal cells is not enough.

## The zip() function

`zip()` combines the data series, colours and labels into tuples, and `for a, b in zip(...)` iterates over those tuples. This is what lets one loop step through several parallel lists at the same time — plotting each series in its own colour with its own label, for instance.

```python
list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = ['a', 'b', 'c']
zipped = zip(list1, list2)
```

Output:

```text
[(1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c')]
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **`rcParams`** | Settings that control figure-wide defaults such as font family, font size and line width |
| **`plt.legend(loc=)`** | Displays the legend and sets its position |
| **`plt.xlabel()` / `plt.ylabel()`** | Name the x and y axes |
| **`plt.title()`** | Names the graph |
| **`plt.xticks()` / `plt.yticks()`** | Set the tick marks on the axes |
| **`plt.xlim()` / `plt.ylim()`** | Set the displayed range of the axes |
| **`plt.grid()`** | Draws a grid on a chosen axis with a chosen line style |
| **`figsize`** | Customises the size of the plot |
| **`plt.twinx()`** | Adds a twin graph; the code for the twin is written directly after the call |
| **`plt.subplot(rows, cols, index)`** | Places a plot within a grid of subplots |
| **`GridSpec`** | Customises the grid structure |
| **`zip()`** | Combines the data series, colours and labels into tuples for iteration |

Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy. ## HTML and CSS **HTML** (HyperText Markup Language) and **CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) are the fundamental technologies for building web pages. HTML is used to structure the content of a webpage, while CSS is used to style and visually format that content. HTML is the foundation of all web pages: it uses **tags** to structure content and define its meaning within a document. ## The basic document structure Every HTML document begins with a basic structure, and understanding it is crucial for writing valid HTML. ```html Page Title

``` | Part | Purpose | |---|---| | `` | Declares the document type and version of HTML. Always the first line. | | `` | The root element of an HTML page. `lang="en"` specifies the language as English. | | `` | Contains meta-information about the HTML document, not displayed on the page itself | | `` | Configures the viewport for responsive design | | `` | Contains the visible page content | The split between `` and `` is the organising idea: anything the browser needs to know but the reader never sees goes in the head, and everything the reader does see goes in the body. ## Headings Headings define the hierarchy of content, with `

` being the most important and `

``` ## Paragraphs Paragraphs are used for blocks of text. Browsers automatically add space before and after paragraphs, so no extra markup is needed to separate them. ```html

This is the first paragraph. It contains sentences that form a coherent block of text.

This is another paragraph. Each paragraph should represent a distinct block of information or thought.

``` ## Line breaks and horizontal rules The `

# 7.3 Links, Images, Lists and Tables > Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy. ## Hyperlinks Hyperlinks, or links, connect web pages and resources. The `` (anchor) tag creates hyperlinks. ```html Visit Indexademics Website Go to Another Page on this Site Jump to Section 2 on This Page Email Indexademics Call Us ``` The `href` attribute specifies the link's destination. An **absolute URL** is a full web address to an external site, for example `https://indexademics.com/`. The examples above show that `href` is not restricted to web pages: a `#` prefix jumps within the current page, and `mailto:` and `tel:` hand the link to another application. The `rel` attribute specifies the relationship between the current document and the linked resource. Common values are: | Value | Purpose | |---|---| | `noopener` | For security when opening links in new tabs. Prevents the new page from accessing the opener page via JavaScript. Often used with `target="_blank"`. | | `nofollow` | Tells search engine crawlers not to follow the link. Used for links to untrusted content or in user-generated content areas. | ## Images The `` tag embeds images into a web page. ```html ``` | Attribute | Purpose | |---|---| | `src` | Path to the image file | | `alt` | Alternative text for the image, for accessibility and if the image fails to load. Crucial for SEO. | | `width` and `height` | Specify image dimensions in pixels. Best practice is to control sizing with CSS. | Two loading behaviours are available. `lazy` defers loading the image until it is about to enter the viewport, which is good for performance, especially for long pages with many images. `eager` loads the image immediately, regardless of whether it is in the viewport, and is the default behaviour. The `srcset` and `sizes` attributes are for responsive images, allowing the browser to choose the most appropriate image source based on screen size and resolution. This is a more advanced topic for responsive image handling. ## Lists HTML supports unordered and ordered lists. Both use `
  • ` for their items; the difference is only in the container, `
      ` for unordered and `
        ` for ordered. ```html
        • Item 1
        • Item 2
        • Item 3
        1. First Step
        2. Second Step

        ``` A list nests by placing a whole new list inside a list item, not between items: ```html
        • Coffee
        • Tea
          • Black tea
          • Green tea
        • Milk
        ``` ## Tables Tables display data in rows and columns. `` defines the table container, `` a row, ``, `` and `` group the rows into a header, a body and a footer. `
        ` a header cell and `` a data cell. ```html
        Example Data Table
        Column 1 Header Column 2 Header
        Row 1, Data 1 Row 1, Data 2

# 7.9 Network Basics and Protocols

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Network types

Networks are classified by the physical distance they cover.

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Local Area Network (LAN)** | Connects devices over a relatively short distance, for example in an office building or a school |
| **Wide Area Network (WAN)** | Spans a large physical distance. The Internet is the largest WAN, connecting millions of devices worldwide. |

## IP addresses

**IP addresses** are numerical labels assigned to devices on a network.

**IPv4** addresses are 32-bit numbers, usually represented in dot-decimal notation, for example `192.168.1.1`. IPv4 has a limited address space and is being phased out — with only 32 bits to work with, there are not enough distinct labels for the number of devices now connected.

IPv4 addresses are classified into different classes: A, B, C, D and E. Classes A, B and C are commonly used, with each class having a specific address range and being suitable for different-sized networks.

## Network protocols and commands

The **Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)** is used to automatically assign IP addresses to network devices, eliminating the need for manual IP configuration.

Two network commands are worth knowing. Each has a second name used on other systems, meaning MacOS.

| Command | Alternative | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ipconfig` | `ifconfig` | Used to view a computer's IP address information |
| `tracert` | `traceroute` | Shows the route that a data packet takes from the source to the destination |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Local Area Network (LAN)** | Connects devices over a relatively short distance, e.g. in an office building or a school |
| **Wide Area Network (WAN)** | Spans a large physical distance; the Internet is the largest WAN |
| **IP address** | A numerical label assigned to a device on a network |
| **IPv4** | A 32-bit address, usually represented in dot-decimal notation; it has a limited address space and is being phased out |
| **Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)** | Automatically assigns IP addresses to network devices, eliminating the need for manual IP configuration |
| **`ipconfig` / `ifconfig`** | Command used to view a computer's IP address information |
| **`tracert` / `traceroute`** | Command that shows the route a data packet takes from the source to the destination |

# 8.1 Web Scraping: Concepts and Ethics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What web scraping is

**Web scraping** is extracting data from websites in an automated manner. It collects the unstructured data from the websites and stores it in a structured form — turning a page written for a human reader into rows and columns a program can work with.

## Features of a well-behaved crawler

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Implicit politeness** | Avoid hitting any site too often, as this may lead to denial of service |
| **Explicit politeness** | Use the `robots.txt` file to indicate which parts of the site should not be accessed by web crawlers; a crawler must always adhere to it |
| **Robustness** | The crawler should be immune to malicious behaviours of web servers |

The two forms of politeness address different things. Implicit politeness is about rate — how hard you hit the server — while explicit politeness is about permission, and is stated by the site itself.

## The Robots Exclusion Protocol

The **Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP)** is a standard that regulates web robot behaviour and tells whether a website allows web scraping or not. You find a website's rules by appending `/robots.txt` to the URL, for example `https://example.com/robots.txt`. Checking it is the basic requirement of ethical scraping.

## The process of web scraping

1. Send an HTTP request to get a response
2. Parse the web data
3. Extract the data
4. Store the data
5. Visualisation

## Networking vocabulary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Domain name** | Identifies a particular computer on the Internet. Computers convert the domain name to an IP address for it to be readable. |
| **IP address** | Internet Protocol address; a number used to indicate the location of a computer on a network |
| **Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)** | Establishes a connection between sender and receiver and ensures data is delivered accurately and in order |
| **Internet Protocol (IP)** | Defines how data is addressed and routed between devices on a network |
| **Domain Name System (DNS)** | Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses, which computers use to locate and communicate with each other |

TCP and IP divide the work between them: IP is concerned with where the data goes, and TCP with whether it all arrives, in the right order.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Web scraping** | Extracting data from websites in an automated manner; collects unstructured data from websites and stores it in a structured form |
| **Implicit politeness** | Avoiding hitting any site too often, which may lead to denial of service |
| **Explicit politeness** | Using the `robots.txt` file to indicate which parts of the site should not be accessed by web crawlers |
| **Robustness** | The crawler should be immune to malicious behaviours of web servers |
| **Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP)** | A standard that regulates web robot behaviour and tells whether a website allows web scraping or not |
| **`robots.txt`** | The file, found by appending `/robots.txt` to a URL, that states a site's crawling rules |
| **Domain name** | Identifies a particular computer on the Internet |
| **IP address** | A number used to indicate the location of a computer on a network |
| **Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)** | Establishes a connection between sender and receiver and ensures data is delivered accurately and in order |
| **Internet Protocol (IP)** | Defines how data is addressed and routed between devices on a network |
| **Domain Name System (DNS)** | Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses |

# 8.2 Requests and Beautiful Soup > Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy. ## Making a request The `requests` library performs the first step of scraping — sending the HTTP request and receiving the response. ```python res = requests.get(url, headers=headers) ``` | Attribute | Meaning | |---|---| | `res.status_code` | An integer showing whether the page is accessible. `200` means the request has succeeded. | | `res.text` | String data | | `res.content` | Binary data | | `res.encoding` | Returns the webpage encoding | The distinction between `res.text` and `res.content` matters in practice: HTML is parsed from the string form, whereas an image or a video has to be written out from the binary form. A POST request is made in the same way: ```python res = requests.post(url, json=json, headers=headers) ``` ## Beautiful Soup Beautiful Soup performs the second step, parsing the web data into a structure that can be searched. ```python soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser') ``` `'html.parser'` is a built-in parser. An alternative parser is `lxml`, which has to be installed first: ```python soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'lxml') # pip install lxml ``` The **Document Object Model (DOM)** defines the logical tree structure of the website, and it is that tree the selectors below navigate. ## CSS selectors in Beautiful Soup | Selector | Selects | |---|---| | `soup.select('div')` | All elements named `
` | | `soup.select('div#author')` | All elements named `
` that use an `id` attribute named `author` | | `soup.select('div.notice')` | All elements named `
` that use a `class` attribute named `notice` | | `soup.select('div span')` | All elements named `` that are within an element named `
` | | `soup.select('div > span')` | All elements named `` that are directly within an element named `
`, with no other element in between | | `soup.select('input[name]')` | All elements named `` that have a `name` attribute with any value | | `soup.select('input[type="button"]')` | All elements named `` that have an attribute named `type` with the value `button` | `select()` always returns a list, which is why the examples index into it with `[0]`: ```python soup.select('tag[attr="val"]')[0].getText() # inner text of the first matching element soup.select('tag[attr="val"]')[0].get('href') # value of the href attribute of that element ``` Three ways of getting a specific attribute are available, and they are equivalent: ```python soup.select('a')[0]['href'] soup.select('a')[0].get('href') soup.select('a')[0].attrs['href'] ``` Two ways of getting the text value are equivalent as well: ```python soup.select('a')[0].getText() soup.select('a')[0].text ``` ## An example page The code examples below all refer to this HTML structure: ```html Sample Page

Welcome to Example.com

First paragraph of text.

Second paragraph with a link.

Page 1 Page 2
1 2 3
``` ## 1. Retrieve text from HTML ```python import requests import bs4 url = "https://example.com" res = requests.get(url) soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser') # Extract all paragraphs with class text text_elements = soup.select('p.text') for p in text_elements: print(p.getText()) ``` ## 2. Extract links ```python # Extract all links (anchor tags) links = soup.select('a') for link in links: link_url = link.get('href') link_text = link.getText() print(f"Link Text: {link_text}, URL: {link_url}") ``` Each anchor gives up two different things: `get('href')` reads an attribute, while `getText()` reads the visible content between the tags. ## 3. Download images ```python import os # Create directory for images if not os.path.exists if not os.path.exists('images'): os.makedirs('images') # Download all images i = 0 images = soup.select('img') for img in images: img_url = img['src'] res_img = requests.get(img_url) with open(f'images/image_{i}.jpg', 'wb') as f: f.write(res_img.content) print(f"Downloaded: {img_url}") i += 1 ``` Note the `'wb'` mode and the use of `res_img.content`: an image is binary data, so it is written in binary rather than as text. ## 4. Handle videos ```python # Extract video URL from script tag video_script = soup.select('script[name="video"]')[0] video_url = video_script['src'] # Download video res_video = requests.get(video_url) with open('video.mp4', 'wb') as f: f.write(res_video.content) print("Video downloaded!") ``` ## 5. Scrape multiple pages ```python base_url = "https://example.com/page" # Scrape pages 1-3 for page in range(1, 4): url = f"{base_url}{page}" res = requests.get(url) soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser') print(f"Scraping {url}...") # Add your extraction logic here titles = soup.select('h1') for title in titles: print(title.getText()) ``` The whole fetch-and-parse pair sits inside the loop, so `soup` is rebuilt for each page before anything is extracted from it. ## Keywords | Term | Definition | |---|---| | **`requests.get()`** | Fetches HTML content by sending an HTTP request | | **`res.status_code`** | An integer showing whether the page is accessible; `200` means the request has succeeded | | **`res.text`** | String data from the response | | **`res.content`** | Binary data from the response | | **`res.encoding`** | Returns the webpage encoding | | **Beautiful Soup** | The library that parses web data; `bs4.BeautifulSoup(res.text, 'html.parser')` | | **`'html.parser'`** | The built-in parser used by Beautiful Soup | | **`lxml`** | An alternative parser, installed with `pip install lxml` | | **Document Object Model (DOM)** | Defines the logical tree structure of the website | | **`soup.select()`** | Selects elements from the parsed page using CSS selectors | | **`getText()` / `.text`** | Get the inner text of an element |

# 8.3 Dynamic Pages, APIs and JSON

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Dynamic webpage loading

**Dynamic webpage loading** is what happens when you browse a website and, as you continue to scroll down the page, it refreshes with new content — but the URL on the browser has not changed. That unchanged URL is the difficulty for a scraper: requesting the same address again will not produce the extra content, because the content never came from a new page load.

**JavaScript** is used in this kind of dynamic loading page. It interacts with HTML elements or nodes, manipulating them in response to user inputs, triggering visual feedback and dynamically updating content. In short, it deals with user interaction.

## APIs

**Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)** allow developers to create complex functionality more easily. Their benefit for the user is that page updates are a lot quicker and you do not have to wait for the page to refresh, meaning that the site feels faster and more responsive.

## JSON

**JSON** stands for JavaScript Object Notation. The page makes an HTTP request to a server to retrieve specific resources, and the data requested is often JSON, which is a good format for transferring structured data. In Python, JSON data is usually represented as a string.

In the early days this dynamic loading technique was known as **Asynchronous JavaScript and XML (Ajax)**, because it tended to request XML data. This is normally not the case these days — the data requested now is usually JSON.

## Getting JSON data

There are two ways to turn a response into usable JSON data:

```python
json_data = res.json()
json_data = json.loads(res.text)
```

The first asks the response object to do the decoding itself; the second takes the response's string form and hands it to the `json` module, which is the same operation written out in two steps.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dynamic webpage loading** | When scrolling down a page refreshes it with new content, but the URL on the browser has not changed |
| **JavaScript** | Interacts with HTML elements or nodes, manipulating them in response to user inputs, triggering visual feedback and dynamically updating content; deals with user interaction |
| **Application Programming Interface (API)** | Allows developers to create complex functionality more easily |
| **JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)** | A good format for transferring structured data; in Python it is usually represented as a string |
| **Ajax (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML)** | The early name for the dynamic loading technique, from when it tended to request XML data |
| **`res.json()` / `json.loads(res.text)`** | The two ways of obtaining JSON data from a response |

# 9.1 Artificial Intelligence

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What AI is

**AI (artificial intelligence)** is the technology that enables computers and machines to simulate human intelligence and problem-solving capabilities. It can be modelled after the decision-making processes of the human brain, and it can "learn" from available data and make increasingly more accurate classifications or predictions over time.

## Strong and weak AI

| Type | Also known as | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Strong AI** | General AI, superintelligence | A theoretical form of AI, where it has the same intelligence as humans and will surpass the ability of the human brain. It possesses self-awareness and consciousness, and is able to solve problems, learn and plan for the future. |
| **Weak AI** | Narrow AI | AI trained to perform specific tasks. Examples: Apple's Siri, self-driving vehicles. |

The word "theoretical" is doing the important work in that table: strong AI does not exist, whereas every AI system you can actually name — Siri, a self-driving car — is weak AI, tied to the particular task it was trained for.

## History of AI

| Year | Development |
|---|---|
| **1950** | Alan Turing asks the question: can machines think? He offers a test, now famously known as the **Turing Test**, where a human interrogator would try to distinguish between a computer and a human text response. |
| **1956** | John McCarthy coined the term "artificial intelligence", at the first-ever AI conference at Dartmouth College |
| **1967** | Frank Rosenblatt built the **Mark 1 Perceptron**, the first computer based on a neural network that "learned" through trial and error |
| **1980s** | Neural networks which use a **back-propagation** algorithm to train themselves become widely used in AI applications |
| **1995** | Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig published the first textbook about AI, "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach". It delved into four potential goals or definitions of AI, which differentiate computer systems on the basis of rationality and thinking versus acting. |
| **1997** | IBM's Deep Blue defeats chess champion Garry Kasparov |
| **2016** | DeepMind's AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol in Go |
| **2023** | Rise of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **AI (artificial intelligence)** | The technology that enables computers and machines to simulate human intelligence and problem-solving capabilities |
| **Strong AI** | Also general AI or superintelligence; a theoretical form of AI with the same intelligence as humans, surpassing the human brain, possessing self-awareness and consciousness |
| **Weak AI** | Also narrow AI; AI trained to perform specific tasks, such as Apple's Siri or self-driving vehicles |
| **Turing Test** | Alan Turing's 1950 test, where a human interrogator would try to distinguish between a computer and a human text response |
| **Mark 1 Perceptron** | Built by Frank Rosenblatt in 1967; the first computer based on a neural network that "learned" through trial and error |
| **Back-propagation** | The algorithm by which neural networks train themselves, widely used from the 1980s |
| **Large language models (LLMs)** | Models such as ChatGPT, which rose to prominence in 2023 |

# 9.2 Machine Learning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Machine learning and deep learning

**Machine learning** uses an input layer, one or two "hidden" layers, and an output layer. It needs more feature engineering by human experts to help with feature extraction, and it uses supervised learning: the data needs to be structured or labelled to enable the algorithm to extract features from the data.

It uses neural networks with a lot of layers to "learn" from huge amounts of data. These neural networks are programmatic structures modelled after the decision-making processes of the human brain, and contain layers of interconnected nodes to extract features from data and make predictions.

**Deep learning** has an input layer, three or more — but usually hundreds of — hidden layers, and an output layer. It costs much more data than before, but labelled datasets are limited, which is why it turns to unsupervised learning: deep learning models automate the extraction of features from large, unlabelled and unstructured data sets, saving human intervention.

| | Machine learning | Deep learning |
|---|---|---|
| Hidden layers | One or two | Three or more, usually hundreds |
| Feature extraction | Needs feature engineering by human experts | Automated |
| Learning type | Supervised; data must be structured or labelled | Unsupervised; works on unlabelled, unstructured data |

## The three types of learning

| Type | Definition | Algorithm |
|---|---|---|
| **Supervised Learning** | Labels datasets to train models to classify data or predict outcomes as intended | **K-nearest-neighbour (KNN)**: find the k nearest neighbours to determine which category the point belongs to |
| **Unsupervised Learning** | Learns from the input data itself, identifying patterns and structures in the data without the explicit labels or outcomes | **K-Means Clustering**: repeatedly assigning points to clusters and updating those clusters' centres, until it can reach the centre of clusters |
| **Reinforcement Learning** | Learns to perform a task by trial and error | |

## Data types

| Type | Data |
|---|---|
| **Classification** | Discrete categories |
| **Regression** | Continuous values |

## Distance between points

Both KNN and K-Means depend on measuring how far apart two points are, so a distance metric has to be chosen. Taking $x$ and $y$ as two points, with $x_i$ and $y_i$ the coordinates in each axis:

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Euclidean Distance** | Measures a straight line between the query point and the other point being measured |
| **Manhattan Distance** | Measures the absolute value between two points |
| **Minkowski Distance** | The generalised form of Euclidean and Manhattan distance metrics |
| **Hamming Distance** | Identifies the points where the vectors do not match |

| **Deep learning** | Uses an input layer, three or more (usually hundreds of) hidden layers, and an output layer; automates the extraction of features from large, unlabelled and unstructured data sets |
| **Supervised Learning** | Labels datasets to train models to classify data or predict outcomes as intended |

# 9.3 Neural Networks and CNNs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a neural network is

A **neural network** is a type of machine learning modelled after the human brain, using interconnected nodes to learn through trial and error.

Its structure is built from **nodes**, the basic processing units, which form layers that process different levels of detail in data.

## Example 1: a college acceptance model

The inputs are grades and class activities. The hidden layers each take on a level of detail — the first layer focuses on grades, for example English and Maths grades.

Each node processes a specific aspect within its layer, with dense connections to all nodes in the next layer. The "dense" connection is what lets a later layer combine every aspect the previous layer worked out, rather than following a single chain.

## Example 2: a temperature conversion model

The simple case is a linear conversion from °C to °F, with one input (°C) and one output (°F). The model computes:

$$\text{Output} = \text{Weight} \times \text{Input} + \text{Bias}$$

Training is a matter of correcting the weight and bias. Initial, incorrect weights might give:

$$F = 5.67 \times C + 12.5$$

and the refined weights:

$$F = 1.828 \times C + 28.54$$

**Complexity warning:** using more nodes — for example cubic equations — can overcomplicate simple linear problems. This connects directly to the model fitting parameters: the number of nodes increases model complexity, and more complexity is not automatically better.

## The convolution operation

**Convolution** is a mathematical operation combining two functions, for example input data and a kernel, to generate an output. It is widely used in signal processing and computer vision.

A **kernel**, for example a $3 \times 3$ matrix, slides over the input data, performing element-wise multiplication and summation to produce a new feature matrix.

## Convolutional Neural Networks

**Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)** are feed-forward neural networks that learn feature engineering via filter (kernel) optimisation. In other words, the kernels are not designed by hand — the network works out what they should be.

A key layer is the **convolution layer**, which applies kernels to extract features.

## CNNs in computer vision

Digital photos are represented as pixel arrays, with RGB values from 0 to 255. That numeric representation is what makes convolution possible on an image at all.

One application of convolution is **blurring**, where the kernel replaces pixels with the mean of their neighbours.

A cat classification pipeline runs:

```text
Input → [Conv → ReLU → MaxPool] → [Conv → ReLU → MaxPool] → Fully Connected → Output
```

The convolution-and-pooling block appears twice, each repetition working on the features the previous one extracted, and the fully connected layer at the end turns those features into the final output.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Neural network** | A type of machine learning modelled after the human brain, using interconnected nodes to learn through trial and error |
| **Node** | The basic processing unit of a neural network; nodes form layers that process different levels of detail in data |
| **Weight and bias** | The parameters in $\text{Output} = \text{Weight} \times \text{Input} + \text{Bias}$, adjusted as the model is refined |
| **Convolution** | A mathematical operation combining two functions, such as input data and a kernel, to generate an output |
| **Kernel** | The matrix that slides over input data, performing element-wise multiplication and summation to produce a new feature matrix |
| **Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)** | A feed-forward neural network that learns feature engineering via filter (kernel) optimisation |
| **Convolution layer** | Applies kernels to extract features |
| **Blurring** | A convolution application in which the kernel replaces pixels with the mean of their neighbours |

# 1 Computer Category and Programming Language

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two categories of computer

Every computer falls into one of two categories, and the dividing line is how much of its behaviour is fixed in advance.

A **special-purpose computer** is a computer designed for a particular function. It executes the same stored set of instructions whenever it is requested to run, so it does one job and does not need to be told how to do anything else. Microwave ovens, washing machines and medical diagnostic equipment all contain special-purpose computers.

A **general-purpose computer** is used for solving many different types of problems. It is available in various sizes and has a wide range of capabilities. Because it is not tied to a single stored routine, the same machine can be given a new set of instructions and made to do something new — which is exactly what programming is for.

## Classes of general-purpose computer

General-purpose computers are classified by size and by the scale of work they are built to handle.

| Class | Description | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Microcomputers** | Sometimes referred to as personal computers (PCs) | Individual and general use |
| **Laptop (notebook) computers** | The smallest microcomputers | Portable personal use |
| **Desktop computers** | Compact microcomputer systems that fit on a desk, designed for individual use | Individual use |
| **Workstations** | The largest type of microcomputer | Scientific and engineering applications |
| **Mainframe computers** | The largest computer; massive memory and extremely rapid processing power | Large-scale business, military and scientific fields |
| **Supercomputers** | Built for tasks requiring rapid and complex calculations involving numerous variables | Scientific research, weather prediction, aircraft design, nuclear weapons |

Mainframes are described as handling massive amounts of data or complex processes, which is why they belong in large-scale business, military and scientific settings rather than on a desk. Supercomputers are distinguished not by the volume of data but by the speed and complexity of the calculation, which is why the examples are all problems with numerous interacting variables.

## Machine language

**Machine language** is the natural language of the computer. It is the only language that can be directly used by a computer, so it does not need translation and is executed immediately. Every instruction is a binary string of 1s and 0s.

The advantage follows from that directness: machine language runs fast and efficiently, because nothing stands between the instruction and the hardware. The disadvantages follow from it too. Programs written in binary strings are difficult to write and debug, and each computer has its own machine language, so machine language is **not portable** — a program written for one type of computer cannot be run on another type.

## Assembly language

**Assembly language** consists of English-like abbreviations in place of raw binary. This makes it far easier to read than machine language, but the trade-off is that assembly programs cannot be directly processed by the computer. They must be translated first.

An **assembler** is a language translator that converts assembly language into machine code. The full path is:

```text
Assembly Language --> Assembler + Linker --> Machine Language
```

Because of variations in assembly languages between machines, programs written using them are also not portable. Assembly language is useful for implementing system hardware and for small embedded system applications. Its advantages are that the programmer is in control of the hardware, and that the resulting code is space and time efficient.

## High-level languages

**High-level languages** — Basic, Java and FORTRAN, for example — are **machine independent**. Programmers do not need to know anything about the internal structure of the computer, and they deal with high-level coding rather than with hardware detail.

High-level languages enable programmers to write instructions using English words and familiar mathematical symbols and expressions. As with assembly, the price of readability is translation:

```text
High-Level Language --> Compiler or Interpreter --> Machine Code --> Hardware
```

Notice the pattern across all three levels. The closer a language sits to the hardware, the faster and more controlled it is but the harder it is to write and the less portable it becomes; the further from the hardware, the more readable and portable, but the more translation the machine must do first.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Special-purpose computer** | A computer designed for a particular function, which executes the same stored set of instructions when requested |
| **General-purpose computer** | A computer used for solving many different types of problems, available in various sizes and with a wide range of capabilities |
| **Microcomputer** | A general-purpose computer sometimes referred to as a personal computer (PC) |
| **Laptop (notebook) computer** | The smallest microcomputer |
| **Desktop computer** | A compact microcomputer system that fits on a desk, designed for individual use |
| **Workstation** | The largest type of microcomputer, used in scientific and engineering applications |
| **Mainframe computer** | The largest computer, with massive memory and extremely rapid processing power, used to handle massive amounts of data or complex processes |
| **Supercomputer** | A computer used for tasks requiring rapid and complex calculations involving numerous variables |
| **Machine language** | The natural language of the computer; the only language that can be directly used by a computer, written as binary strings of 1s and 0s |
| **Assembly language** | A language consisting of English-like abbreviations, which cannot be directly processed by the computer |
| **Assembler** | A language translator that converts assembly language to machine code |
| **High-level language** | A machine-independent language, such as Basic, Java or FORTRAN, written using English words and familiar mathematical symbols and expressions |
| **Portability** | The property of a program being able to run on a type of computer other than the one it was written for |

# 2 Programming Intro

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Hardware, software and the user

A computer system can be pictured as three layers:

```text
User --> Software --> Hardware
```

**Hardware** only understands the binary system, which is machine language. That is hard for humans to understand and use directly, so something has to sit in between.

**Software** is that interface between humans and hardware. It is a set of step-by-step instructions for hardware operations. Its job runs in both directions: it translates human intention into a form computers can understand, and it turns feedback from the hardware into a form humans can understand.

## Programming

**Computer programming** is the process of writing, testing, debugging and maintaining the source code of computer programs. Programming is done through software development, and through programming we create software. The point of it is practical: we use programming to solve hard or large-scale problems that would not be tractable by hand.

## Computational thinking

**Computational thinking** involves the ability to:

- think procedurally — to break a task into ordered steps;
- think logically — to reason about conditions and outcomes;
- think ahead — to anticipate what the program will need.

## Two ways to run code

There are two ways to run Python code, and they suit different situations.

| | Interactive mode | Script mode |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt | Has the `>>>` prompt | Does not have the `>>>` prompt |
| Getting a result | Result returned immediately after pressing enter | File must be created and saved before executing the code to get results |
| Editing | No direct method to edit code | A direct way of editing your code |
| File | — | Uses a `.py` file |

Interactive mode starts with `>>>` and answers straight away, which makes it good for trying a single expression. Script mode stores the code in a file, which is what makes editing possible — the code still exists after it has run.

## Indentation

**Indentation** is space at the beginning of a code line. What it means depends on the language, and this is a genuine difference rather than a matter of taste:

- In **Python**, indentation marks out a block of code. It is part of the syntax.
- In **other programming languages**, indentation is for readability only and carries no specific meaning.

## The print() function

The `print()` function is used to print values to the screen. When Python calls the `print()` function, a value is passed to the function. A value passed to a function call is called an **argument**.

```python
print('Hello, world!')
```

The keyword `end` defines something to be printed automatically at the end of the output. It defaults to the newline character `\n`, which is why each `print()` normally starts a fresh line.

```python
print('Hello', end='')
print('world')
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hardware** | The physical layer of a computer, which only understands the binary system (machine language) |
| **Software** | The interface between humans and hardware: step-by-step instructions for hardware operations, translating human intention into a form computers can understand and hardware feedback into a form humans can understand |
| **Computer programming** | The process of writing, testing, debugging and maintaining the source code of computer programs |
| **Computational thinking** | The ability to think procedurally, think logically and think ahead |
| **Interactive mode** | A way of running code with the `>>>` prompt, in which the result is returned immediately after pressing enter |
| **Script mode** | A way of running code using a `.py` file, in which the file must be created and saved before executing the code to get results |
| **Indentation** | Space at the beginning of a code line; in Python it marks a block of code, in other languages it only aids readability |
| **Argument** | A value passed to a function call |
| **end** | A keyword of `print()` that defines something to be printed automatically at the end of the output; it defaults to the newline `\n` |

# 3 Variables and Data Types

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## String concatenation

The **concatenation operator** `+` is used to join two strings together as the operation.

```python
>>> 'hello' + ' python'
'hello python'
```

## The input() function

The `input()` function reads a string from standard input. Whatever the user types, `input()` returns it as the **string** type — so a number typed at the keyboard arrives as text, not as a number, until it is converted.

```python
name = input('What is your name? ')
```

## Variables

**Variables** are containers for storing data values. You store a numerical or data value into a variable temporarily and get the value from the variable later when you need it. A variable is created at the moment you assign a value to it.

Variables are worth using for four reasons:

- they make code more readable;
- they let you avoid typing a value repeatedly;
- they make code easier to modify and debug, because a value appears in one place rather than many;
- they let programs run faster, since a stored value does not have to be recomputed.

## Naming rules

A variable name must obey these rules:

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| Contains only letters, numbers and underscores (`_`) | No other characters |
| Does not start with a number | `8piece` is invalid |
| No spaces | — |
| Case sensitive | `AGE`, `age` and `Age` are three different variables |
| Does not use reserved keywords | See the list below |

The **reserved keywords** cannot be used as variable names:

```python
['False', 'None', 'True', 'and', 'as', 'assert', 'async', 'await',
 'break', 'class', 'continue', 'def', 'del', 'elif', 'else', 'except',
 'finally', 'for', 'from', 'global', 'if', 'import', 'in', 'is',
 'lambda', 'nonlocal', 'not', 'or', 'pass', 'raise', 'return', 'try',
 'while', 'with', 'yield']
```

Beyond the rules, names should be short and descriptive. **Camel case naming** makes compound names more readable: `myOneMethod` is easier to read than `myonemethod`.

## Assigning variables

The equal operator `=` is used to assign a value to a variable. Python also allows **multiple assignment**, assigning in a single statement.

Assigning a single value to multiple variables:

```python
>>> x = y = z = 50
```

Assigning multiple values to multiple variables:

```python
>>> a, b, c = 5, 10, 15
```

## Data types

| Type | Holds | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Integer** | Whole numbers | `0`, `-2`, `29` |
| **Float** | Floating point numbers | `1.0`, `9.902`, `1e10`, `44e-2` |
| **String** | Textual values | `'the'`, `'1'`, `'num of line'` |

Note that `'1'` is a string, not an integer. The quotation marks, not the character inside them, decide the type — which is why input read with `input()` has to be converted before it can be used in arithmetic.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concatenation operator (`+`)** | The operator used to concatenate two strings as the operation |
| **input()** | A function that reads a string from standard input and returns the string type |
| **Variable** | A container for storing data values, created when you assign a value to it |
| **Camel case naming** | A naming style that makes compound names more readable, such as `myOneMethod` |
| **Multiple assignment** | Assigning a value to multiple variables in a single statement |
| **Integer** | A data type for whole numbers such as `0`, `-2`, `29` |
| **Float** | A data type for floating point numbers such as `1.0`, `9.902`, `1e10`, `44e-2` |
| **String** | A data type for textual values such as `'the'`, `'1'`, `'num of line'` |

# 4 Expressions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What an expression is

An **expression** consists of values (such as `4`) and operators (such as `*`). The defining property of an expression is that it always evaluates down to a single value.

```python
>>> 2 + 3 * 4
14
```

That single-value rule is what lets expressions be nested inside one another: because every expression collapses to one value, an expression can stand anywhere a value can.

## Built-in functions

All Python programs can call a basic set of functions called the **built-in functions**, which include `print()` and `input()`. These need nothing to be set up first — they are always available.

## Importing modules

Python also comes with a set of modules called the **standard library**. Each **module** contains a related group of functions that can be embedded in your programs.

A module is brought in with the `import` statement:

```python
>>> import math
```

After you import a module, you can use all the functions of that module. The `math` module, imported above, is the standard library module for mathematical functions.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Expression** | A combination of values (such as `4`) and operators (such as `*`) that always evaluates down to a single value |
| **Built-in functions** | The basic set of functions all Python programs can call, including `print()` and `input()` |
| **Standard library** | The set of modules that comes with Python |
| **Module** | A file containing a related group of functions that can be embedded in your programs |
| **import statement** | The statement used to bring a module into a program, after which all functions of that module can be used |

# 5 Lists

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a list is

A **list** is a collection of items in a particular order. Square brackets `[]` indicate a list, and the individual elements are separated by commas.

```python
numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

The phrase "in a particular order" is what makes the rest of this lesson work: because the order is fixed, each element has a permanent position that can be used to reach it.

## Index

You can access any element in a list by telling Python the position, or **index**, of the desired item. Access an element by writing the name of the list followed by the index of the item enclosed in square brackets.

The first item's index is `0`.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList[0]
0
>>> numList[2]
2
```

## The len() function

The `len()` function returns the number of elements in a list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> len(numList)
6
```

Because indexing starts at 0, a list of length 6 has indexes 0 to 5 — the last valid index is always one less than the length.

## Adding elements to a list

The `append()` method adds the new element to the end of the list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList.append(12)
>>> numList
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12]
```

You can add a new element at any position in your list by using the `insert()` method. The first argument is the index at which the new element should sit; everything from that position onwards shifts along.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> numList.insert(2, 12)
>>> numList
[0, 1, 12, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

## Removing elements from a list

Which tool you use depends on what you know about the item.

Use the `del` statement when you know the **position** of the item you want to remove from a list.

```python
>>> numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> del numList[2]
>>> numList
[0, 1, 3, 4, 5]
```

Use the `remove()` method if you only know the **value** of the item you want to remove. It deletes only the first occurrence of the value you specify — a point worth remembering when a value appears more than once:

```python
>>> numList = [1, 5, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3]
>>> numList.remove(3)
>>> numList
[1, 5, 4, 2, 0, 3]
```

The second `3` survives, because only the first occurrence was removed.

## Finding the index of an element

`lst.index(value)` returns the first occurrence of the value.

```python
>>> numList = [1, 5, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3]
>>> numList.index(3)
4
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **List** | A collection of items in a particular order, written with square brackets `[]` and elements separated by commas |
| **Index** | The position of an element in a list, used to access it; the first item's index is 0 |
| **len()** | A function that returns the number of elements in a list |
| **append()** | A method that adds a new element to the end of the list |
| **insert()** | A method that adds a new element at any position in a list |
| **del** | A statement used to remove an item from a list when you know its position |
| **remove()** | A method used to remove an item when you only know its value; it deletes only the first occurrence |
| **index()** | A method that returns the first occurrence of a value in a list |

# 6 For-loop

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Purpose

A **for loop** is used to iterate a block of statements several times. Rather than writing the same statements once for each item you want to handle, you write them once and let the loop present each item in turn.

## Syntax

```python
for variable in someList:
    statements
```

The loop variable takes the value of each element of the list in order, and the indented statements run once for each of those values. The indentation is what marks out the block that belongs to the loop.

```python
numList = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
for n in numList:
    print(n)
```

## Converting each element

A list read in from input holds strings, so the loop body is the natural place to convert each element to `int` or `float` before using it in arithmetic.

```python
for item in someList:
    value = int(item)
    print(value * 2)
```

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **For loop** | A loop used to iterate a block of statements several times, taking each element of a list in turn |

# 7 For-Range

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The range() function

`range()` is used to generate a sequence of numbers. It gives a for loop something to iterate over when there is no existing list — when what you want is simply to repeat something a set number of times, or to count.

## Syntax

```python
for variable in range(start, stop, step):
    statements
```

The three parts are the value the sequence starts from, the value it stops at, and the size of the step between successive values.

```python
for i in range(10):
    print(i)
```

## Random numbers

The module `random` contains functions that generate random numbers in a variety of ways. Like any module, it must be imported before its functions can be used.

The function `randint(a, b)` returns an integer in the range $[a, b]$. Both endpoints are included in that range, which is what the square brackets indicate.

```python
import random

for i in range(10):
    print(random.randint(1, 6))
```

This is a for-range loop and a random function working together: `range(10)` fixes how many numbers are produced, and `randint(1, 6)` decides what each one is. The result is ten independent rolls of a six-sided die.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **range()** | A function used to generate a sequence of numbers, taking a start, a stop and a step |
| **random** | A module containing functions that generate random numbers in a variety of ways |
| **randint(a, b)** | A function of the `random` module that returns an integer in the range $[a, b]$ |

# 8 If Statement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Boolean values

**Boolean values** have only two possible values: `True` or `False`. Every condition a program tests eventually reduces to one of these two.

```python
'5' + '6' == '56'   # evaluates to True
1 != '1'            # evaluates to True
8 >= 8              # evaluates to True
```

In the first example the `+` concatenates the two strings into `'56'`, and that result is then compared with `'56'`, so the whole expression is `True`. The arithmetic-looking part happens before the comparison.

The second example is worth pausing on: the integer `1` and the string `'1'` are not equal, so `!=` gives `True`. A comparison looks at type as well as at the characters on the page.

## Relational operators

**Relational operators** compare two values and produce a Boolean.

| Operator | Description | Example | Evaluates to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<` | Less than | `2**3 < 9` | `True` |
| `>` | Greater than | `0 > 1` | `False` |
| `<=` | Less than or equal to | `4 <= 5` | `True` |
| `>=` | Greater than or equal to | `9**0.5 >= 3` | `True` |
| `==` | Equal to | `1 == 2` | `False` |
| `!=` | Not equal to | `'B' != 'B'` | `False` |

Note the distinction between `=` and `==`. A single `=` assigns a value to a variable; a double `==` asks whether two values are equal.

## The if statement

```python
if condition:
    statements
```

The statements run only when the condition evaluates to `True`. The colon and the indentation together mark out the block that the condition guards.

```python
ph = float(input('Enter the pH level: '))
if ph < 7.0:
    print(str(ph), 'is acidic.')
if ph > 7.0:
    print(str(ph), 'is alkaline.')
```

Here two independent `if` statements are used. Each is tested on its own, and a pH of exactly 7.0 satisfies neither, so nothing is printed.

## The if … else … statement

```python
if condition:
    statements1
else:
    statements2
```

`else` catches everything the condition did not, so exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

```python
n = int(input())
line = 'Today, I ate ' + str(n) + ' apple'
if n > 1:
    line += 's.'
else:
    line += '.'
print(line)
```

The example shows the pattern at its most useful: a sentence is assembled up to the point where it depends on the data, and the branch supplies only the part that differs.

## The if … elif … else … statement

```python
if condition1:
    statements1
elif condition2:
    statements2
else:
    statements3
```

`elif` is tested only if the condition above it was `False`, so the conditions are checked in order and the first one that succeeds wins.

```python
age = int(input('What is your age? '))
if age < 11:
    print('You are a kid.')
elif age < 20:
    print('You are a teenager.')
else:
    print('You are an adult.')
```

The second condition is written as `age < 20`, not as a range between 11 and 20, precisely because it is only reached when `age < 11` has already failed. The order of the branches is doing part of the work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Boolean value** | A value with only two possibilities: `True` or `False` |
| **Relational operator** | An operator that compares two values and evaluates to a Boolean: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` |
| **if statement** | A statement that runs its block of statements when a condition is true |
| **else** | The clause that runs when the `if` condition is false |
| **elif** | A further condition tested only when the conditions above it are false |

# 9 Boolean Operators

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three Boolean operators

Relational operators produce Boolean values; **Boolean operators** combine them. There are three types: `not`, `and`, `or`.

A **truth table** shows all possible results of a Boolean operator. Since each Boolean input has only two values, the tables are short and can be memorised outright.

## Truth table of the and operator

The `and` operator evaluates an expression to `True` if both Boolean values are `True`; otherwise it evaluates to `False`.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `True and True` | `True` |
| `True and False` | `False` |
| `False and True` | `False` |
| `False and False` | `False` |

## Truth table of the or operator

The `or` operator evaluates an expression to `True` if either of the two Boolean values is `True`; otherwise it evaluates to `False`.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `True or True` | `True` |
| `True or False` | `True` |
| `False or True` | `True` |
| `False or False` | `False` |

## Truth table of the not operator

The `not` operator evaluates to the opposite Boolean value.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| `not True` | `False` |
| `not False` | `True` |

## Precedence

Operator precedence among the Boolean operators follows this order:

```text
() > not > and > or
```

Brackets are evaluated first, then `not`, then `and`, then `or`. This is why an expression such as `False and True or True` is `True`: the `and` binds tighter, so it is read as `(False and True) or True`.

A longer illustration, with the grouping made explicit by brackets:

```python
(a > b and c > d) or (a > b and a != c) or (not b == c)
```

Each bracketed group settles to a single Boolean, and the two `or` operators then combine those three results.

## Worked Boolean expressions

These expressions evaluate to `True`:

```python
2 >= 2 and 1 < 3
1 <= 2 or 1 != 1
not 'A' == 'a'
```

These expressions evaluate to `False`:

```python
not 1 == 1
'a' == 'A' or 'b' == 'B'
3 > 4 and 3 < 5
```

The last one is a common trap: `3 < 5` is perfectly true, but `and` requires both sides, and `3 > 4` is false.

## Remainder

The remainder operator `%` returns the remainder after dividing the first operand by the second operand.

```python
22 % 5                      # 2
math.floor(123 / 10) % 10   # 2
```

The second example is a digit-extraction idiom: dividing by 10 and taking the floor throws away the last digit, and `% 10` then keeps the last digit of what remains — here, the tens digit of 123.

## Integer division

Integer division `//` returns the floor value of the quotient produced by dividing the two operands.

```python
(1234 // 100) % 10          # 2
```

Because the result is the **floor**, negative operands do not simply truncate towards zero. Consider `-14 // 3`: the quotient is $-4.\overline{6}$, and the floor of that is $-5$, not $-4$.

The same reasoning settles `-13 % 3`. Since `-13 // 3` is $-5$, the remainder must be $-13 - 3 \times (-5) = 2$. The remainder is positive even though the dividend is negative, because the floor was taken downwards.

## Precedence of common operators

| Operator | Description |
|---|---|
| `**` | Exponentiation (raise to the power) |
| `*` `/` `%` `//` | Multiply, divide, modulo, and integer division |
| `+` `-` | Addition and subtraction |
| `<=` `<` `>` `>=` `!=` `==` | Relational operators |
| `not` `and` `or` | Boolean operators |

The table is ordered from highest precedence at the top to lowest at the bottom. Arithmetic happens before comparison, and comparison happens before the Boolean operators — which is why `2 + 2 == 4` needs no brackets to work as intended.

## Exercise

Evaluate the following Boolean expressions.

```python
'T' == 't' or 4 > 1
13 % 5 > 3 and not 3 == 2
(3 * 5) % (12 / 2) >= 9 ** (1 / 2)
9 > 3 * 3 or not 11 - 5 < 6 and 2 + 5 >= 7
2 + 2 == 4 and not 2 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2
not 2 > 1 and 3 < 4 or 5 > 5 and 2 > 1 and 3 >= 3
```

Working through them using the precedence table:

| Expression | Reasoning | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `'T' == 't' or 4 > 1` | `False or True` | `True` |
| `13 % 5 > 3 and not 3 == 2` | `13 % 5` is 3, so `3 > 3` is `False`; `False and True` | `False` |
| `(3 * 5) % (12 / 2) >= 9 ** (1 / 2)` | `15 % 6.0` is `3.0`; `9 ** 0.5` is `3.0`; `3.0 >= 3.0` | `True` |
| `9 > 3 * 3 or not 11 - 5 < 6 and 2 + 5 >= 7` | `9 > 9` is `False`; `6 < 6` is `False` so `not` gives `True`; `7 >= 7` is `True`; `False or (True and True)` | `True` |
| `2 + 2 == 4 and not 2 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 2 == 2 + 2` | All three parts are `True` | `True` |
| `not 2 > 1 and 3 < 4 or 5 > 5 and 2 > 1 and 3 >= 3` | `not True` is `False`, so the first `and` group is `False`; `5 > 5` is `False`, so the second group is `False`; `False or False` | `False` |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Boolean operator** | One of the three operators `not`, `and`, `or` that combine Boolean values |
| **Truth table** | A table showing all possible results of a Boolean operator |
| **and** | Evaluates an expression to `True` if both Boolean values are `True`; otherwise `False` |
| **or** | Evaluates an expression to `True` if either of the two Boolean values is `True`; otherwise `False` |
| **not** | Evaluates to the opposite Boolean value |
| **Remainder (`%`)** | Returns the remainder after dividing the first operand by the second operand |
| **Integer division (`//`)** | Returns the floor value of the quotient produced by dividing the two operands |
