markdown:
# 15.2 Spanish and Portuguese Colonies in the Americas

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ruling the Spanish empire

Spain claimed a vast empire stretching from **California to South America**, divided into **four provinces**, including **New Spain** and **Peru**.

### Governing the provinces

Spain was determined to maintain strict control over its empire, and the machinery reflects that determination at every level.

| Body or office | Role |
|---|---|
| **Council of the Indies** | Set up by the king to pass laws for the colonies, and to monitor colonial officials closely so they did not assume too much authority |
| **Viceroys** | Representatives appointed to rule in the king's name in each province |
| **Audiencias** | Advisory councils of Spanish settlers, who with lesser officials helped the viceroy rule |

The Council's watch over its own officials is the telling detail: the danger Spain guarded against was not only rebellion by the colonised but independence by the colonisers.

### Spreading Christianity

To Spain, **winning souls for Christianity was as important as gaining land**. The Catholic Church worked with the government to convert Native Americans, and Church leaders often served as royal officials, helping to regulate the activities of Spanish settlers. As Spain's American empire expanded, Church authority expanded with it.

**Missionaries** baptised thousands of Native Americans and built mission churches, working to turn new converts into loyal subjects of the Catholic king of Spain. They introduced European clothing, the Spanish language, and new crafts such as carpentry and locksmithing — **forcibly imposing European culture over Native American culture**.

### Controlling trade

Trade was controlled to make the empire profitable. The most valuable resources shipped from Spanish America to Spain were **silver and gold**.

Colonists could export raw materials only to Spain and could buy only Spanish-manufactured goods. Laws forbade them from trading with other European nations, or even with other Spanish colonies.

**Sugarcane** became profitable. It had to be grown on **plantations** — large estates run by an owner or the owner's overseer — and plantations needed large numbers of workers to be profitable. That last requirement drives the two sections that follow.

## Encomienda: a system of forced labour

Spanish monarchs granted the conquistadors **encomiendas**: the right to demand labour and tribute from Native Americans in a particular area.

The conquistadors used the system to force Native Americans to work under the most brutal conditions, and those who resisted were hunted down and killed. Disease, starvation, and cruel treatment caused drastic declines in the Native American population.

The system was used in the mines as well as on the plantations. Tons of silver from the **Potosí** region of Peru and Bolivia filled Spanish treasure ships, and Native Americans were forced to extract the rich ore from dangerous shafts deep inside the Andes Mountains. Thousands of Indians died from the terrible conditions.

### A Spanish priest speaks out

**Bartolomé de Las Casas** condemned the evils of the encomienda system. He detailed the horrors that Spanish rule had brought to Native Americans and pleaded with the king to end the abuse.

In **1542** Spain passed the **New Laws of the Indies**, which forbade the enslavement and abuse of Native Americans.

The relief was limited. Many Native Americans were instead forced to become **peons** — workers forced to labour for a landlord in order to pay off a debt. Landlords advanced workers food, tools, or seed, creating debts that workers could never pay off in their lifetime.

### Bringing workers from Africa

Las Casas urged colonists to import workers from Africa, believing that Africans were immune to tropical diseases and had skills in farming, mining, and metalworking. This furthered the brutal African slave trade — the same man's protest producing both the New Laws and this.

As demand for sugar products skyrocketed, millions of Africans were imported. They were forced to work as field hands, miners, or servants, and also became artists, artisans, and mechanics. Some Africans earned enough money to buy their freedom; some rebelled or ran away.

## Colonial society and culture

### Cultural blending

Influence moved in every direction.

| Group | What they contributed |
|---|---|
| **Native Americans** | Settlers learned Native American styles of building, ate American food, travelled in Indian-style canoes, and were influenced by Indian artistic styles |
| **Europeans** | Taught their religion to Native Americans and introduced animals, which transformed the lives of many Native Americans |
| **Africans** | Introduced their farming methods, cooking styles, crops, drama, dance, and songs |

### A layered society

| Rank | Group | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| Top | **Peninsulares** | People born in Spain — the term refers to the Iberian Peninsula; they filled the highest positions in both colonial governments and the Catholic Church |
| | **Creoles** | American-born descendants of Spanish settlers; they owned most of the plantations, ranches, and mines |
| | **Mestizos** | People of Native American and European descent |
| | **Mulattoes** | People of African and European descent |
| Bottom | American and African descendants | The lowest social classes |

Birthplace, not wealth, sets the top of this hierarchy: a creole might own the mines and still rank below a peninsular.

### Lively towns and cities

Spanish settlers generally lived in towns and cities. Mexico City's population grew so quickly that it became the **largest Spanish-speaking city by the 1550s**.

Colonial cities were centres of government, commerce, and European culture. Around the central plaza stood government buildings and a Spanish-style church, and broad avenues and public monuments symbolised European power and wealth. They were also centres of intellectual and cultural life, where architecture, painting, poetry, and the exchange of ideas flourished.

### Emphasising education

The colonies built universities; the **University of Mexico** was established as early as **1551**.

A woman wishing for an education might enter a convent. **Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz** was refused admission to the University of Mexico because she was a girl, so she entered a convent and devoted herself to study and to the writing of poetry, earning a reputation as one of the greatest poets ever to write in the Spanish language.

## The Portuguese colony in Brazil

### Settling Brazil

The **Tupian Indians** were the Native Americans who lived in Brazil, and they were largely wiped out by disease.

Portugal issued grants of land to Portuguese nobles, who agreed to develop the land and share the profits with the crown. Landowners sent settlers to build towns, plantations, and churches.

Brazil offered no instant wealth from silver or gold, so early settlers cut and exported **brazilwood**, and the Portuguese forced Indians and Africans to clear land for plantations.

### Challenging Portugal and Spain

The wealth of the Americas helped make Spain the most powerful country in Europe. The English and Dutch were jealous, and shared the resentment the French king Francis I expressed when he declared that he should like to see Adam's will, in which the Earth was divided between Spain and Portugal.

To get around the strict control those countries kept over colonial trade, **smugglers** traded illegally with Portuguese and Spanish colonists. In the Caribbean and elsewhere, Dutch, English, and French **pirates** preyed on treasure ships from the Americas. Some pirates, called **privateers**, even operated with the approval of European governments.

Other European explorers continued to sail the coasts of the Americas, hunting for gold and other treasure as well as for a northwest passage to Asia.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Council of the Indies** | The body set up by the king to pass laws for the colonies and monitor colonial officials |
| **Viceroys** | Representatives who ruled in the king's name in each province |
| **Audiencias** | Advisory councils of Spanish settlers who helped the viceroy rule |
| **Plantations** | Large estates run by an owner or the owner's overseer, needing large numbers of workers to be profitable |
| **Encomiendas** | The right, granted to conquistadors, to demand labour and tribute from Native Americans in a particular area |
| **Bartolomé de Las Casas** | The Spanish priest who condemned the encomienda system and pleaded with the king to end the abuse |
| **New Laws of the Indies** | The laws passed by Spain in 1542 forbidding the enslavement and abuse of Native Americans |
| **Peons** | Workers forced to labour for a landlord in order to pay off a debt they could never clear |
| **Peninsulares** | People born in Spain, at the top of the social classes, filling the highest positions in colonial government and the Church |
| **Creoles** | American-born descendants of Spanish settlers, who owned most of the plantations, ranches, and mines |
| **Mestizos** | People of Native American and European descent |
| **Mulattoes** | People of African and European descent |
| **Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz** | Refused admission to the University of Mexico because she was a girl, she entered a convent and became one of the greatest poets ever to write in Spanish |
| **Tupian Indians** | The Native Americans who lived in Brazil, largely wiped out by disease |
| **Privateers** | Pirates who operated with the approval of European governments |

# 15.3 Effects of Global Contact

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The Columbian Exchange

After Christopher Columbus first reached the Americas, he initiated trade between Western Europe — the **Old World** — and the Americas — the **New World**. This exchange process was later called the **Columbian Exchange**.

### New foods and animals

The traffic ran in both directions.

| Direction | What moved |
|---|---|
| Americas to Europe | **Tomatoes** and **corn**, which met the food needs of a highly populated Europe; they then spread further and became important crops worldwide |
| Europe to the Americas | **Grapes** and **wheat** |
| Africa and Asia to the Americas | **Bananas** and **sugar cane** |
| Europe to the Americas (animals) | **Cattle, pigs, goats, and chickens**, which gave local Americans a better diet; **horses and donkeys**, which allowed them to transport goods and hunt more easily |

### The global population explodes

American crops allowed the **European population to increase by the 1700s** — the direct consequence of new, productive foods reaching a crowded continent.

The Columbian Exchange also moved people. Millions migrated from Europe to the Americas by boat, and the **Atlantic slave trade** forcibly brought millions of Africans to the Americas.

The Native American population, by contrast, **decreased**, because they had no immunity to European diseases such as **smallpox** and **measles**.

## A commercial revolution

### The price revolution strikes

During the **1500s** prices in European markets began to rise. Too much money was in circulation, which caused severe **inflation**.

The trigger was the enormous amount of **silver and gold flowing into Europe from the Americas** by the mid-1500s. This period is known as the **price revolution**. The mechanism is worth stating plainly: treasure taken from the Americas increased the money supply without increasing the goods available to buy, so prices rose.

### Capitalism emerges

Expanded trade allowed the growth of European **capitalism**. **Entrepreneurs** are critical to the success of capitalism.

### Exploring new business methods

**Banks** increased in importance, allowing wealthy merchants to lend money at interest.

### Bypassing the guilds

Capitalists bypassed the guilds using the **"putting-out" system**. It was first used to produce textiles, but later spread to other industries.

Two things make it significant. It **separated capital and labour for the first time**, and it divided the work from raw material to finished product into different phases in different factories.

## Mercantilism arises

**Mercantilism** aimed to strengthen national economies. It held that a nation's real wealth was measured in its **gold and silver treasure**, and that a nation must **export more goods than it imported**.

### The role of colonies

Because mercantilism aimed to gain benefits from the colonies, European powers passed strict laws regulating trade with them. Colonists could not set up their own industries to manufacture goods — a rule that follows straight from the doctrine, since a colony that manufactures for itself stops buying from the mother country.

### Increasing national wealth

**Tariffs** are taxes on imported goods, designed to protect local industries from foreign competition by increasing the price of imported goods.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Old World / New World** | Western Europe and the Americas, the two sides of the trade Columbus initiated |
| **Columbian Exchange** | The exchange process between the Old World and the New World that followed Columbus's arrival in the Americas |
| **Price revolution** | The period during the 1500s when severe inflation struck European markets, triggered by silver and gold flowing in from the Americas |
| **Capitalism** | The economic system whose growth in Europe was allowed by expanded trade, and to whose success entrepreneurs are critical |
| **"Putting-out" system** | The method by which capitalists bypassed the guilds, separating capital and labour for the first time and dividing production into phases in different factories |
| **Mercantilism** | The doctrine that a nation's real wealth is measured in gold and silver treasure, and that a nation must export more than it imports |
| **Tariffs** | Taxes on imported goods, designed to protect local industries from foreign competition by raising the price of imports |

# 7 Measurement of Angles, Sectors of Circles and Trigonometric Functions

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide sets the range of the paper as chapters 9, 10 and 13 mostly, together with chapters 7 and 8. Chapter 7 is therefore examinable, but the guide treats it as a list of things you must already be able to do rather than as worked theory, and this lesson keeps that shape — the chapter's own checklist, organised into the three blocks it uses. The guide also carries one warning worth stating once for the whole course: the review guide, the review practices and the practice set are unofficial references, and they neither contain nor hint at the questions on the actual exam.

## Measurement of angles

Three definitions carry this block: the **radian**, **standard position** and **coterminal angles**. Alongside them the guide asks you to memorise the **special angles**.

That memorisation instruction pays off twice over inside this same guide. The special angles are what the sine and cosine calculations at the end of this chapter are performed on, and they are what makes the chapter 10 examples workable at all — there, $\cos 105^\circ$ is evaluated without a calculator by splitting it as $\cos(45^\circ + 60^\circ)$, and $\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}$ by splitting it as $\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$. Every angle in those decompositions is a special angle. If they are not memorised, the addition formulas have nothing to land on.

## Sectors of circles

Three items: the **area of a sector** of a circle, taken in the two cases the guide separates — the angle given in degrees, and the angle given in radians — then **apparent size**, then **angular velocity and linear velocity**.

The guide gives the two area formulas in its chapter 9 material:

$$A = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 \qquad (\theta \text{ in degrees})$$

$$A = \frac{1}{2}\theta r^2 \qquad (\theta \text{ in radians})$$

The degree form is written so that its structure is visible: $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ is the fraction of a full turn the sector occupies, and $\pi r^2$ is the area of the whole circle. The radian form is the same quantity with the fraction absorbed into the angle measure, which is the reason the guide insists on knowing which measure the angle is in before the formula is chosen.

## Sine, cosine and the unit circle

The definitions of the **sine** and **cosine** functions, taken together with the **unit circle**, and then **reference angles** and the use of them to find the sines and cosines of the special angles.

## The six trigonometric functions

Definitions, graphs and calculations for all six: sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant.

The guide names the standard question on this material outright: you are given one trigonometric value together with a domain, and asked to find the values of the other five functions. The domain is part of the given data, not decoration — the guide states it as one of the two things the question hands you.

## Inverse trigonometric functions

The chapter closes with the definitions and the graphs of the inverse trigonometric functions.

# 8 Solving Trigonometric Functions, Shifting and Dilation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Chapter 8 is the second of the two chapters the guide places outside the main weight of the paper — the range is chapters 9, 10 and 13 mostly, with chapters 7 and 8 alongside — and like chapter 7 it arrives as a checklist rather than as worked theory. What follows is that checklist in the three blocks the guide uses, with the one piece of working the guide supplies elsewhere brought in where it belongs.

## Solving trigonometric functions

Three items: **general solutions**, **inclination and slope**, and **solving trigonometric inequalities**.

Inclination and slope is the one item in this chapter whose working the guide does print, though it prints it in chapter 10. There, the angle between two intersecting lines is found from their inclinations, and the guide states the link explicitly: a line $l_1$ with slope $m_1$ has **inclination** $\alpha$ satisfying

$$\tan\alpha = m_1$$

so the tangent of the inclination is the slope. That is the whole of the connection this chapter asks for, and chapter 10 then builds the angle-between-two-lines formula on top of it.

## Shifting and dilation

**Vertical dilation** (stretch and shrink) and **horizontal dilation** (stretch and shrink) head the block, and the guide places **finding period and amplitude** directly beneath the two of them — period and amplitude are the numbers you read off once you know what the dilations have done.

The block then moves to **solving trigonometric equations after a shrink or a stretch**. That ordering is the point of the block: the dilations are not examined for their own sake but through equations set on the dilated function, so the equation-solving from the first block has to survive a change of period and amplitude.

Last comes **modelling periodic behaviour**, under which the guide lists **transformation** and **solving application problems** — the applied end of the same machinery.

## Relationships among the functions

Three families of identity: **reciprocal ratio identities**, **Pythagorean relationships** and **cofunction relationships**.

The guide singles out the Pythagorean relationships. It repeats the bullet marker and adds an arrow pointing back at them, and it does that for no other item in the chapter — read it as the identity family to have cold.

The block closes with **proving questions**. The identities are examined by being used: you are asked to prove results with them rather than merely to quote them. Chapter 10's own review list repeats the same instruction, telling you to know how to prove the formulas there too, so proof technique is being tested across both chapters rather than in one.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inclination** | The angle $\alpha$ of a line, related to the line's slope $m$ by $\tan\alpha = m$ (the guide sets this out in its chapter 10 work on the angle between two lines) |

# 9 Solving Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Chapter 9 is one of the three chapters the guide says the paper draws on mostly, and unlike chapters 7 and 8 it is written out in full. It is the chapter where a triangle is handed to you part-specified and you are expected to recover the rest of it.

## Notation

A capitalised letter such as $A$ is an angle; the matching lowercase letter $a$ is the side that corresponds to that angle. Every formula in the chapter is written in that convention, and the law of cosines below only reads correctly if $a$ is understood as the side opposite $A$.

## Solving right triangles

The guide lists the configurations you are expected to handle:

- The lengths of the **diagonals** of a rhombus, square, rectangle and so on, including the measure of the angle between the diagonals.
- **Similar triangles** and the ratios between them.
- The **circumscribed circle** and the **inscribed circle**. For the circumscribed circle the guide gives the extended form of the sine rule, in which the common ratio is not merely constant but is the diameter itself:

$$\frac{c}{\sin C} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A} = \text{diameter of the circumscribed circle}$$

- **Tangent lines** to the circle.
- **Polygons**, handled by cutting them into congruent triangles from the centre. The **central angle** is

$$\text{central angle} = \frac{360}{n} \quad \text{for } n \text{ sides}$$

and the area follows by taking the triangle area formula $n$ times:

$$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C \times n \text{ sides}$$

- The **properties of an isosceles triangle**.
- The **area of a segment**, which the guide gives as a subtraction: sector minus triangle.

## Areas of sectors, triangles and segments

The area of a sector depends on which measure the angle is in:

$$A = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 \quad (\text{degrees}) \qquad A = \frac{1}{2}\theta r^2 \quad (\text{radians})$$

The area of a triangle is half of one side, times the other side, times the sine of the included angle:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{one side} \times \text{other side} \times \sin(\text{included angle}) = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Those two together give the segment. A segment is what is left of a sector once the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord is taken away, which is exactly the guide's "sector $-$ triangle", and it is also why the polygon area above is a triangle area repeated $n$ times.

## Law of Sines

In $\triangle ABC$:

$$\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}$$

The guide notes it may equally be written the reciprocal way round, as $\dfrac{a}{\sin A}$ and so on; that is the form that matches the circumscribed-diameter statement above.

## The ambiguous case

The SSA situation — two sides and a non-included angle — is called the **ambiguous case**, because the data do not always pick out one triangle. The guide gives the test with angle $B$ given, side $b$ opposite angle $B$, and side $a$ adjacent:

| Condition | Number of triangles |
|---|---|
| $a\sin B < b < a$ | 2 solutions |
| $b \geq a$ | 1 solution |
| $b = a\sin B$ | 1 solution |
| $b < a\sin B$ | 0 solutions |

The guide prints $b > a\sin B$ on its own as the test for 2 solutions; that is an error — two triangles need $b < a$ as well, and when $b \geq a$ there is exactly one.

The quantity $a\sin B$ is the benchmark in every line, so it is the thing to compute first.

## Law of Cosines

In $\triangle ABC$, to solve for a side:

$$a^2 = c^2 + b^2 - 2cb\cos A$$
$$b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac\cos B$$
$$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$$

All three are one statement in different letters, which the guide spells out in words:

$$(\text{side opposite angle})^2 = (\text{side adjacent})^2 + (\text{other side adjacent})^2 - 2(\text{one adjacent side})(\text{other adjacent side})\cos(\text{angle})$$

Rearranged to solve for an angle instead:

$$\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} \qquad \cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2ac} \qquad \cos A = \frac{c^2 + b^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$

which in words is

$$\cos(\text{angle}) = \frac{(\text{adjacent})^2 + (\text{adjacent})^2 - (\text{opposite})^2}{2(\text{adjacent})(\text{adjacent})}$$

The guide prints the numerator of $\cos B$ as $a^2 + c^2 - c^2$; take it from the worded form directly beneath it, where the subtracted square is always the side opposite the angle, giving $a^2 + c^2 - b^2$.

## Choosing which law to use

The guide's decision table, which is the fastest route through any "solve the triangle" question:

| Given | Use | To find |
|---|---|---|
| Side, angle, side | Cos law | The third side, and then one of the remaining angles |
| Side, side, side | Cos law | Any two angles |
| Angle, side, angle / Angle, angle, side | Sin law | The remaining sides |
| Side, side, angle | Sin law | An angle opposite a given side, and then the third side (note that 0, 1 or 2 triangles are possible) |

The last row is the ambiguous case again, and the parenthesis is the guide's own reminder that the answer may not be a single triangle.

## Navigation and surveying

The **course** of a ship or plane is the angle measured in degrees from the north direction to the direction of the ship or plane, measured *clockwise*.

The **compass bearing** of one location from another is measured in the same way. It is usually given as an acute angle from the north–south line toward the east–west direction.

The guide's worked example, with bearings written to three digits:

- bearing of $B$ from $A = 060^\circ$
- bearing of $A$ from $B = 240^\circ$

The two readings are the same line taken in opposite directions, and they differ by $180^\circ$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of Sines** | In $\triangle ABC$, $\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}$, or the reciprocal form $\frac{a}{\sin A}$; the reciprocal ratio equals the diameter of the circumscribed circle |
| **Law of Cosines** | $(\text{side opposite angle})^2 = (\text{side adjacent})^2 + (\text{other side adjacent})^2 - 2(\text{one adjacent side})(\text{other adjacent side})\cos(\text{angle})$ |
| **Ambiguous case** | The SSA situation, in which 0, 1 or 2 triangles are possible; tested against $a\sin B$ |
| **Central angle** | For a polygon of $n$ sides, $\frac{360}{n}$ |
| **Area of a segment** | Sector minus triangle |
| **Course** | The angle measured in degrees from the north direction to the direction of the ship or plane, clockwise |
| **Compass bearing** | The bearing of one location from another, measured the same way as a course; usually given as an acute angle from the north–south line toward the east–west direction |

# 10 Sum, Difference, Double- and Half-Angle Formulas

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Chapter 10 is one of the three the guide says the paper draws on mostly, and it is the chapter of identities: formulas that break a compound angle into the special angles you were told to memorise in chapter 7, so that values such as $\cos 105^\circ$ can be produced without a calculator.

## Cosine of a sum and a difference

The guide attaches a mnemonic to each pair. For cosine it is *coscos sinsin, sign different*:

$$\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta$$
$$\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$$

The mnemonic reads off both halves of the structure. The two products are cosine-with-cosine and sine-with-sine, and the sign joining them is the *opposite* of the sign inside the bracket — a sum inside gives a minus outside, a difference inside gives a plus.

### Worked example: $\cos(105^\circ)$ without a calculator

$105^\circ$ splits into two special angles, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$:

$$\cos(105^\circ) = \cos(45^\circ + 60^\circ) = \cos 45^\circ \cos 60^\circ - \sin 45^\circ \sin 60^\circ$$

## Sine of a sum and a difference

For sine the mnemonic is *sincos cossin, sign same*:

$$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta$$
$$\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta$$

Here both products mix the two functions — sine of one angle with cosine of the other — and the sign outside matches the sign inside the bracket, which is the contrast with the cosine pair. The guide's printed formulas put the wrong angle under two of the four cosines, and repeat that slip in the worked example below; the versions here are the ones its own *sincos cossin* rule describes.

### Worked example: $\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)$ without a calculator

The angle is rewritten as a difference of special angles, $\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{9\pi}{6} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{8\pi}{6} = \frac{4\pi}{3}$:

$$\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\cos\frac{\pi}{6} - \cos\frac{3\pi}{2}\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$$

## Tangent of a sum and a difference

The tangent formulas are a fraction, and the guide's rule for the signs is *sign same in the numerator, different in the denominator*:

$$\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha + \tan\beta}{1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$$
$$\tan(\alpha - \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha - \tan\beta}{1 + \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$$

### Worked example: evaluate $\tan(195^\circ)$ without a calculator

Take the reference angle first, $\tan(195^\circ) = \tan(15^\circ)$, then split $15^\circ$ into special angles:

$$\tan(15^\circ) = \tan(60^\circ - 45^\circ) = \frac{\tan 60^\circ - \tan 45^\circ}{1 + (\tan 60^\circ \times \tan 45^\circ)}$$

## The angle between two lines

The difference formula for tangent is what lets you find the angle between two intersecting lines, and this is where chapter 8's "inclination and slope" item is cashed out.

Consider the angle $\theta$ between lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ with slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$. The **inclination** $\alpha$ of $l_1$ satisfies $\tan\alpha = m_1$, and the inclination $\beta$ of $l_2$ satisfies $\tan\beta = m_2$. Since $\theta$ is the difference of the two inclinations, the difference formula applies directly, and the two tangents can be replaced by the two slopes:

$$\tan\theta = \tan(\alpha - \beta) = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2}$$

so the angle between the lines is computable from the slopes alone, with no need to find either inclination.

## Double-angle formulas

Each double-angle formula is the corresponding sum formula with $\beta$ set equal to $\alpha$, and the guide derives them that way in the writing:

$$\sin 2\alpha = \sin(\alpha + \alpha) = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$$

$$\tan 2\alpha = \tan(\alpha + \alpha) = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - (\tan\alpha)^2}$$

$$\cos 2\alpha = \cos(\alpha + \alpha) = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha$$

Cosine has two further forms:

$$\cos 2\alpha = 2\cos^2\alpha - 1 \qquad \text{or} \qquad \cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha$$

Both of these, the guide notes, are got from the trigonometric identity. Which of the three forms to reach for is decided by what the rest of the question is written in: the second is the one to use when only cosines are wanted, the third when only sines are.

## Half-angle formulas

$$\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{2}}$$

$$\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos\alpha}{2}}$$

$$\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha}}$$

The tangent half-angle has two alternative forms that carry no $\pm$ and no radical:

$$\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = \frac{\sin\alpha}{1 + \cos\alpha} \qquad \text{or} \qquad \tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}$$

## What to review for this chapter

The guide closes the chapter with its own list of what will be asked:

1. **Trigonometric equations**, solved by
   a) the double- and half-angle formulas,
   b) the sum and difference formulas,
   c) the quadratic formula.
2. **Trigonometric inequalities**.
3. **Knowing how to prove the formulas** — not only using them.
4. **Finding the supplementary angles formed by two lines**.

Item 1(c) is the reason the double-angle forms of $\cos 2\alpha$ matter so much: writing an equation in a single function, all sines or all cosines, is what turns it into a quadratic the formula can finish.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inclination** | The angle $\alpha$ of a line whose slope is $m$, with $\tan\alpha = m$ |
| **Angle between two lines** | For lines of slopes $m_1$ and $m_2$, the angle $\theta$ with $\tan\theta = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{1 + m_1 m_2}$ |

# 13 Sequences, Series and Mathematical Induction

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Chapter 13 is the third of the chapters the guide says the paper draws on mostly, and it is the longest piece of written-out material in the guide. It moves in one direction throughout: from a list of terms, to the sum of that list, to what happens to the sum when the list never ends.

## Sequences and terms

A **sequence** is a function whose domain is the set of positive integers, or a subset of the positive integers that consists of the $n$ integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$. Because it is a function of position, every term has an address, and the notation uses that address:

- $a_1$ = the first term in the sequence
- $a_n$ = the $n$th term in the sequence

A **term** is each number in the sequence.

## Arithmetic sequences

A sequence is an **arithmetic sequence** if there is a constant difference $d$ for which

$$a_n = a_{n-1} + d \qquad \text{for all integers } n > 1$$

The condition is $n > 1$, matching the geometric definition below — a term can only be defined from its predecessor once a predecessor exists.

**General (explicit) formula.** This gives any term straight from its position:

$$a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d$$

**Recursive formula.** This gives a term from the one before it, and needs two parts:

1. $a_1$, an initial condition that tells where the sequence starts.
2. $a_n - a_{n-1} = d$, a formula that tells how each term in the sequence is related to the preceding term.

The initial condition is not optional: the difference alone fixes the shape of the sequence but not its position, so without $a_1$ there is nothing for the recursion to start from.

**Arithmetic mean.** For two numbers $a$ and $b$:

$$\text{arithmetic mean} = \frac{a+b}{2}$$

## Geometric sequences

A sequence is a **geometric sequence** when there is a constant ratio $r$ for which

$$a_n = a_{n-1} \times r \qquad \text{for all integers } n > 1$$

**General (explicit) formula:**

$$a_n = a_1 r^{\,n-1}$$

**Recursive formula:**

$$r = \frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}$$

a formula that tells how each term in the sequence is related to the preceding term.

**Geometric mean.** For two numbers $a$ and $b$:

$$\text{geometric mean} = \sqrt{ab}$$

The two definitions run in parallel throughout: where the arithmetic sequence adds a constant, the geometric sequence multiplies by one, and the same swap turns the arithmetic mean into the geometric mean.

## Series and sigma notation

A **series** is the indicated sum of the terms of a sequence. A series may be written using **sigma notation**, in which the sum runs over an index; the letter $k$ is called the **index of summation**, as in $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}$.

For the geometric series formula, the guide records the condition $r \neq 1$.

## Limits of infinite sequences

A sequence that does not have a last term is called **infinite**.

- A **convergent series** is one where the sum approaches a finite value as more terms are added.
- A **divergent series** is one in which the sum grows without bound or does not converge to a single value.

For the powers of the ratio $r$ the guide gives the test:

| Ratio | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| $\lvert r \rvert < 1$ | $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} r^n = 0$ |
| $r = 1$ | $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} r^n = 1$, since every term is $1$ |
| $\lvert r \rvert > 1$ or $r = -1$ | Divergent, with no limits |

The guide prints $\lvert r \rvert > 1$ or $r = \pm 1$ as divergent with no limits here; that is an error for the sequence — at $r = 1$ the sequence is constant, so it converges to $1$.

## Sums of infinite series

The sum of an infinite series of numbers is defined to be the limit of its associated sequence of partial sums $S_n$ as the number of the sequence's terms increases without bound.

- For any infinite series, if the sequence of partial sums has a finite limit $S$, then the infinite series is said to **converge** to the sum $S$.
- If the sequence of partial sums approaches infinity or has no finite limit, the infinite series is said to **diverge**.

That definition is what makes the ratio test above matter. The sum is not computed by adding forever; it is computed by watching the partial sums, and it is the behaviour of $r^n$ that decides whether they settle.

For a geometric series only:

| Ratio | Sum |
|---|---|
| $\lvert r \rvert < 1$ | $\displaystyle S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1-r}$ |
| $\lvert r \rvert > 1$ or $r = \pm 1$ | Divergent, with no limits |

## Repeating decimals

The infinite geometric sum is the tool that turns a repeating decimal into a fraction, because the repeating part is a geometric series.

### Worked example: write $1.64134134134\ldots$ as a fraction

Split the number into its non-repeating head and the repeating tail, then write the tail as a series:

$$1.64134134134\ldots = 1.64 + 0.00134 + 0.00000134 + 0.00000000134 + \cdots$$

The tail is geometric: each term is the one before it shifted three decimal places, because the repeating block "134" is three digits long.

$$a_1 = 0.00134 \qquad r = 0.001$$

$$S = \frac{a_1}{1-r} = \frac{0.00134}{1 - 0.001} = \frac{0.00134}{0.999}$$

Then add the head back on:

$$\frac{0.00134}{0.999} + \frac{164}{100} = \text{fraction for this repeating decimal}$$

## Mathematical induction

**The principle of mathematical induction.** Let $P_n$ be a statement involving the positive integer $n$. The statement is true for every $n$ greater than or equal to 1 if the following two conditions hold:

1. The statement is true for $n = 1$; that is, $P_1$ is true.
2. For any positive integer $k$, whenever $P_k$ is true, then $P_{k+1}$ is true.

The two conditions do different jobs and both are needed. The first supplies a case that is known to be true outright; the second supplies a rule for passing truth from any case to the next one. Applied to the first, the rule reaches the second case, then the third, and so on through every positive integer.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sequence** | A function whose domain is the set of positive integers, or a subset of the positive integers that consists of the $n$ integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$ |
| **Term** | Each number in the sequence |
| **Arithmetic sequence** | A sequence with a constant difference $d$ for which $a_n = a_{n-1} + d$ for all integers $n > 1$ |
| **General (explicit) formula** | A formula giving a term from its position: $a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d$ for an arithmetic sequence, $a_n = a_1 r^{\,n-1}$ for a geometric one |
| **Recursive formula** | An initial condition telling where the sequence starts, plus a formula telling how each term is related to the preceding term |
| **Arithmetic mean** | $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ |
| **Geometric sequence** | A sequence with a constant ratio $r$ for which $a_n = a_{n-1} \times r$ for all integers $n > 1$ |
| **Geometric mean** | $\sqrt{ab}$ |
| **Series** | The indicated sum of the terms of a sequence |
| **Index of summation** | The letter $k$ in sigma notation |
| **Infinite sequence** | A sequence that does not have a last term |
| **Convergent series** | One where the sum approaches a finite value as more terms are added |
| **Divergent series** | One in which the sum grows without bound or does not converge to a single value |
| **Sum of an infinite series** | The limit of its associated sequence of partial sums $S_n$ as the number of terms increases without bound |
| **Principle of mathematical induction** | $P_n$ is true for every $n \geq 1$ if $P_1$ is true and, for any positive integer $k$, $P_k$ true implies $P_{k+1}$ true |

# 1.1 Sets and Venn Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a set is

A **set** is a collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right. The objects that make up a set are its **elements**, also called its **members**. A set that does not contain any elements is the **empty set**, or **null set**, written $\emptyset$.

Because a set is itself an object, sets can be compared, combined and taken apart, and that is what the rest of this lesson is about.

## Membership, subsets and size

| Symbol | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x \in A$ | Element | $x$ is an element of $A$ |
| $x \notin A$ | Not an element | $x$ is not an element of $A$ |
| $A \subset B$, $A \subseteq B$ | Subset | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $B \supset A$, $B \supseteq A$ | Superset | Every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| $\lvert A \rvert$ | Cardinality | The number of elements in the set $A$ |

The two subset symbols are not interchangeable. $A \subset B$ means $A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$ — $B$ has elements that are not in $A$. $A \subseteq B$ can also mean that $A$ equals $B$.

A **superset** is simply the other side of the same relation: $B \supset A$ says that the second set named is a subset of the first, and not the other way around.

## Operations on sets

The **intersection** $A \cap B$ is the set containing the elements common to both $A$ and $B$. The **union** $A \cup B$ is the set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$.

The **complement** of $A$, denoted $A'$, is the set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$. Textbooks usually print this as a bar over the name of the set, $\overline{A}$; the prime is the same thing written in a form a computer can type.

The **difference** of $A$ and $B$, denoted $A - B$, is the set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$. Written as a condition on membership, $C = A - B$ when for every $n \in C$ we have $n \in A$ and $n \notin B$, that is

$$C = \{\, n \mid n \in A,\ n \notin B \,\}$$

## The laws of sets

For sets $A$, $B$ and $C$ inside a universal set $U$:

| # | Law | Union form | Intersection form |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Commutative | $A \cup B = B \cup A$ | $A \cap B = B \cap A$ |
| 2 | Associative | $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ | $(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$ |
| 3 | Distributive | $A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$ | $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$ |
| 4 | Identity | $A \cup \emptyset = A$ | $A \cap U = A$ |
| 5 | Complement | $A \cup A' = U$ | $A \cap A' = \emptyset$ |
| 6 | Idempotent | $A \cup A = A$ | $A \cap A = A$ |
| 7 | Null | $A \cup U = U$ | $A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset$ |
| 8 | Absorption | $A \cup (A \cap B) = A$ | $A \cap (A \cup B) = A$ |
| 9 | Difference | $A - B = A \cap B'$ | |
| 10 | De Morgan | $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ | $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$ |

The names carry the reasoning. The empty set is the identity element for union, because adding nothing changes nothing; the universal set is the identity for intersection, because everything is already inside it. Correspondingly, a union with the universal set is the universal set, and an intersection with the empty set is empty.

Law 9 restates difference in terms of the two basic operations: taking $A$ but not $B$ is the same as taking what is both in $A$ and outside $B$.

**De Morgan's laws are the ones to know cold.** They say that complementing a union turns it into an intersection of complements, and complementing an intersection turns it into a union of complements — the operation flips when the bar goes on.

## Venn diagrams

A **Venn diagram** is a diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets. Each set is represented by a **circle**, usually drawn inside a rectangular field which stands for the universal set. Regions of overlap are exactly the intersections, so a Venn diagram turns the laws above into pictures.

## Counting with Venn diagrams

Two counting formulas follow from the picture:

$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

$$n(A') = n(U) - n(A)$$

The subtraction in the first is necessary because the elements lying in both sets sit in the overlap and are therefore counted once in $n(A)$ and again in $n(B)$; removing $n(A \cap B)$ corrects the double count. The second says the number of elements not in $A$ is everything in the universal set minus what is in $A$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Set** | A collection of distinct objects, considered as an object in its own right |
| **Element (member)** | An object that makes up the set |
| **Empty set (null set)** | A set that does not contain any elements |
| **Intersection $\cap$** | $A \cap B$ is the set containing elements common to both set $A$ and set $B$ |
| **Union $\cup$** | $A \cup B$ is the set containing all elements of $A$ and $B$ |
| **Cardinality $\lvert A \rvert$** | Number of elements in the set $A$ |
| **Element of $\in$** | If set $A$ contains a certain element, it is symbolised $x \in A$, read "$x$ is an element of $A$" |
| **Not an element $\notin$** | If set $A$ does not contain a certain element, it is symbolised $x \notin A$ |
| **Subset $\subset$, $\subseteq$** | A set $A$ is a subset of set $B$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Proper subset** | $A \subset B$: $A$ is a subset of $B$ and $B$ has elements not in $A$ |
| **Superset $\supset$, $\supseteq$** | A set $B$ is a superset of set $A$ if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ |
| **Complement $A'$** | The set of elements in the universal set that are not in $A$ |
| **Difference $A - B$** | The set of all elements which are in $A$ but not in $B$ |
| **Venn diagram** | A diagram that shows all possible logical relations between a finite collection of different sets |
| **Circle** | Each set is represented by a circle, usually inside a rectangular field (the universal set) |

# 1.2 Inductive and Deductive Reasoning

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two directions of argument

Mathematical arguments run in one of two directions, and the difference is which end you start from.

**Inductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents you have experienced, observations you have made, or facts you know to be true or false. It works upwards: several particular cases suggest a rule that covers them all.

**Deductive reasoning** is a type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions. It works downwards: an accepted rule is applied to a particular case.

## Comparing the two

| | Inductive reasoning | Deductive reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Specific incidents, observations, or known facts | A general fact, rule, or premise |
| Direction | From particular cases to a generalisation | From the general rule to specific details |
| Result | A generalisation | A conclusion inferred about the particular case |

Because inductive reasoning generalises from cases you happen to have seen, its conclusion goes beyond the evidence used to reach it. Deductive reasoning does not: the specific conclusion is already contained in the general premise you started from, and drawing it out is what "deduce" means.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Inductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking that involves forming generalisations based on specific incidents you've experienced, observations you've made, or facts you know to be true or false |
| **Deductive reasoning** | A type of logical thinking where you start with a general fact, rule, or premise and then deduce or infer certain specific details or conclusions |

# 1.3 Logic Statements

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Propositions

A **proposition**, also known as a statement, is a declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both. That restriction is what makes a proposition usable in logic: every proposition has exactly one truth value to work with.

A **compound proposition** is a combination of two or more propositions using logical operators. The operators are conjunction, disjunction, implication and biconditional, and each has its own rule for when the compound comes out true.

## The logical operators

- **Conjunction** — a compound proposition that uses the logical operator AND. For the conjunction $p \wedge q$ to be true, both $p$ and $q$ must be true.
- **Disjunction** — a compound proposition that uses the logical operator OR. For the disjunction $p \vee q$, it is enough for either $p$ or $q$ to be true for the entire disjunction to be true.
- **Negation** — the negation of a proposition $p$ is "not $p$", denoted $\sim p$ or $\neg p$. If $p$ is true, then $\sim p$ is false, and vice versa.
- **Conditional statement (implication)** — a compound proposition of the form "if $p$ then $q$", represented as $p \to q$. It is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false; otherwise it is true.
- **Biconditional statement** — a statement of the form "$p$ if and only if $q$", true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values and false when they are different. It is represented as $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$.

Setting those rules side by side gives the truth values of every compound:

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \wedge q$ | $p \vee q$ | $p \to q$ | $p \leftrightarrow q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | F | F | T | T |

The conditional row worth pausing on is the third: $p$ false, $q$ true still gives a true implication, because the only way to break "if $p$ then $q$" is to have the hypothesis hold and the conclusion fail.

## Contradiction and contingency

A **contradiction** is a compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of the individual propositions that constitute it. A **contingency** is a compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions.

## Sufficient and necessary

These two words describe the two roles in a conditional.

- **Sufficient**: when given $A$, we can know $B$; then $A$ is sufficient for $B$.
- **Necessary**: when given $A$, we can know $B$; then $B$ is necessary for $A$.

The same single implication supports both readings — the hypothesis is the sufficient condition, the conclusion is the necessary one.

## Converse, inverse and contrapositive

In a conditional statement of the form "if $p$ then $q$", also written $p \to q$, different forms are created by switching or negating the hypothesis and the conclusion.

| Form | Statement | Symbols | Built by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original | if $p$ then $q$ | $p \to q$ | — |
| **Converse** | if $q$ then $p$ | $q \to p$ | Switching the hypothesis and the conclusion |
| **Inverse** | if not $p$ then not $q$ | $\neg p \to \neg q$ | Negating both the hypothesis and the conclusion |
| **Contrapositive** | if not $q$ then not $p$ | $\neg q \to \neg p$ | Both switching and negating the hypothesis and the conclusion |

## Logical equivalence

In terms of truth values, certain relationships always hold:

- A statement and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent**. This means they are both either true or false. If "if $p$ then $q$" is true, then "if not $q$ then not $p$" is also true, and vice versa.
- Similarly, a converse and an inverse are logically equivalent. If "if $q$ then $p$" is true, then "if not $p$ then not $q$" is also true, and vice versa.

Notice what these pairings do *not* say. The original and its converse are not paired, and the original and its inverse are not paired; proving $p \to q$ therefore tells you nothing about whether $q \to p$ holds.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Proposition** | A declarative sentence that is either true or false but not both |
| **Compound proposition** | A combination of two or more propositions using logical operators |
| **Conjunction** | A compound proposition using AND; $p \wedge q$ is true only when both $p$ and $q$ are true |
| **Disjunction** | A compound proposition using OR; $p \vee q$ is true when either $p$ or $q$ is true |
| **Negation** | "Not $p$", denoted $\sim p$ or $\neg p$; false when $p$ is true and true when $p$ is false |
| **Conditional statement (implication)** | "If $p$ then $q$", written $p \to q$; false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false |
| **Biconditional statement** | "$p$ if and only if $q$", written $p \leftrightarrow q$ or $p \equiv q$; true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth values |
| **Contradiction** | A compound proposition that is always false regardless of the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Contingency** | A compound proposition that could be either true or false depending on the truth values of its constituent propositions |
| **Sufficient** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $A$ is sufficient for $B$ |
| **Necessary** | When given $A$ we can know $B$, then $B$ is necessary for $A$ |
| **Converse** | The converse of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if $q$ then $p$" |
| **Inverse** | The inverse of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if not $p$ then not $q$" |
| **Contrapositive** | The contrapositive of "if $p$ then $q$" is "if not $q$ then not $p$" |

# 1.4 Geometric Theorems and Postulates

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Postulates that set up measurement

Before anything can be proved about a figure, the figure has to be measurable. Two postulates do that work.

The **Ruler Postulate** states that the points on a line can be paired with the real numbers in such a way that any given point can always be paired with zero and any other with a positive number. This is what licenses talking about the length of a segment at all: once points carry numbers, distance is a difference of numbers.

The **Protractor Postulate** states that, taking $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ to be opposite rays in a plane, we can measure angles $\angle AOB$ for every rotation about point $O$. It is the angular counterpart of the Ruler Postulate.

## Adding angles

The **Angle Addition Postulate**: if point $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then

$$m\angle AOB + m\angle BOC = m\angle AOC$$

The condition matters — $B$ must lie *in the interior* of the angle, otherwise the two smaller angles do not partition the larger one.

## The Parallel Postulate

In Euclidean geometry, the **Parallel Postulate** states that given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point that is parallel to the given line. "Exactly one" is doing two jobs: at least one such line exists, and no second one does.

## Angle relationships

| Name | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary (their sum is $180°$) |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |

The last two are the working tools for any diagram containing a transversal: knowing the lines are parallel turns a pair of angles in different places into a pair of equal measures.

## A triangle theorem

The **Isosceles Triangle Theorem**: if two sides of a triangle are congruent — that is, the triangle is isosceles — then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ruler Postulate** | The points on a line can be paired with the real numbers so that any given point can be paired with zero and any other with a positive number |
| **Protractor Postulate** | With $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ opposite rays in a plane, angles $\angle AOB$ can be measured for every rotation about point $O$ |
| **Angle Addition Postulate** | If point $B$ lies in the interior of $\angle AOC$, then $\angle AOB + \angle BOC = \angle AOC$ |
| **Parallel Postulate** | Given a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point parallel to the given line |
| **Linear Pair Postulate** | If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary (their sum is $180°$) |
| **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the alternate interior angles are congruent |
| **Corresponding Angles Postulate** | If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then the pairs of corresponding angles are congruent |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |

# 2.1 Isosceles Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The parts of an isosceles triangle

An isosceles triangle has two congruent sides, and its parts are named around that fact.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leg** | Either of the congruent sides of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angle** | Either of the other two angles |

So a leg is a side, the base is the odd side out, the vertex angle sits between the legs, and the base angles sit at the ends of the base.

## The Isosceles Triangle Theorem and its converse

**Isosceles Triangle Theorem:** if two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

$$\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC} \implies \angle B \cong \angle C$$

**Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem:** if two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent.

$$\angle B \cong \angle C \implies \overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$$

Because both directions hold, congruent legs and congruent base angles are interchangeable pieces of evidence: in a triangle, whichever you are given, you may conclude the other.

## The bisector of the vertex angle

The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is the perpendicular bisector of the base.

This is a strong statement, because one line is doing three jobs at once. Drawn from the vertex angle, it bisects that angle, it meets the base at right angles, and it cuts the base into two congruent halves.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Leg** | The congruent sides of an isosceles triangle |
| **Base** | The third side of an isosceles triangle |
| **Vertex angle** | The angle formed by the two congruent sides |
| **Base angle** | Either of the two angles other than the vertex angle |
| **Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent |
| **Converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem** | If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite the angles are congruent |

# 2.2 Equilateral Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## From equilateral to equiangular

If a triangle is equilateral, then the triangle is **equiangular**.

The reason is already available from the isosceles case. An equilateral triangle has three congruent sides, so it is isosceles in three different ways at once — any pair of its sides can be taken as the legs. Applying the Isosceles Triangle Theorem to one pair gives one pair of congruent angles; applying it to a second pair gives another. Between them, all three angles are forced to be congruent, which is what equiangular means.

$$\overline{AB} \cong \overline{BC} \cong \overline{CA} \implies \angle A \cong \angle B \cong \angle C$$

## Working with the result

Because an equilateral triangle is isosceles on every side, everything established for isosceles triangles applies to it from any vertex. In particular, the bisector of the angle at any vertex is the perpendicular bisector of the opposite side, since that vertex angle is the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle whose base is that opposite side.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equilateral triangle** | A triangle whose sides are all congruent |
| **Equiangular** | Having all angles congruent; if a triangle is equilateral, then the triangle is equiangular |

# 2.3 Inequalities in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The exterior angle inequality

The measure of an **exterior angle** of a triangle is greater than the measure of each of its **remote interior angles**. Labelling the exterior angle $\angle 1$ and the two remote interior angles $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$:

$$m\angle 1 > m\angle 2 \quad \text{and} \quad m\angle 1 > m\angle 3$$

Note that the comparison is with *each* remote interior angle separately, not with their sum.

## Sides against angles

The next two theorems are converses of one another, and they are the reason a triangle's shape can be read off from either its sides or its angles.

| Theorem | Statement | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| **Theorem 5-10** | If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side | 大边对大角 |
| **Theorem 5-11** | If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle | 大角对大边 |

Read together: in any triangle, longest side and largest angle face each other, and shortest side and smallest angle face each other. Given the three side lengths you can rank the angles without measuring any of them, and given the three angles you can rank the sides.

## The Triangle Inequality

**Theorem 5-12:** the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side.

$$a + b > c, \qquad b + c > a, \qquad a + c > b$$

The word *any* means all three comparisons have to hold, so testing whether three given lengths can form a triangle means checking each pair in turn.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Exterior angle** | An angle of a triangle whose measure is greater than the measure of each of its remote interior angles |
| **Theorem 5-10** | If two sides of a triangle are not congruent, then the larger angle lies opposite the longer side |
| **Theorem 5-11** | If two angles of a triangle are not congruent, then the longer side lies opposite the larger angle |
| **Theorem 5-12 (Triangle Inequality)** | The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the length of the third side |

# 2.4 Bisectors in Triangles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The perpendicular bisector

The **perpendicular bisector** of a segment is the line perpendicular to it at its midpoint. Both conditions are part of the definition: right angles alone are not enough, and cutting the segment in half is not enough either.

**Perpendicular Bisector Theorem:** if a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment.

**Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem:** if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Taken together the two statements say that the perpendicular bisector *is* the set of points equidistant from the two endpoints — nothing else qualifies, and nothing that qualifies is left out.

$$P \text{ on the perpendicular bisector of } \overline{AB} \iff PA = PB$$

## The angle bisector

**Angle Bisector Theorem:** if a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle.

**Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem:** if a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector.

The converse carries an extra condition the forward theorem does not need: the point must lie *in the interior* of the angle.

Note also what "distance from a side" means here. The sides of an angle are lines, so the distance meant is the perpendicular distance to each side, and the theorem says the bisector is where those two perpendicular distances are equal.

## The pattern

Both pairs follow the same shape. A bisector is characterised by an equal-distance property, and the property runs in both directions, so it can be used either to deduce equal distances from a known bisector or to prove a point lies on a bisector from known equal distances.

| Bisector | Equidistant from | Forward direction | Converse direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Perpendicular bisector of a segment | The endpoints of the segment | On the bisector $\Rightarrow$ equidistant | Equidistant $\Rightarrow$ on the bisector |
| Bisector of an angle | The sides of the angle | On the bisector $\Rightarrow$ equidistant | Equidistant and in the interior $\Rightarrow$ on the bisector |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perpendicular bisector** | A line that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint |
| **Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the perpendicular bisector of a segment, then it is equidistant from the endpoints of the segment |
| **Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem** | If a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment |
| **Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point is on the bisector of an angle, then the point is equidistant from the sides of the angle |
| **Converse of the Angle Bisector Theorem** | If a point in the interior of an angle is equidistant from the sides of the angle, then the point is on the angle bisector |

# 2.5 Concurrent Lines, Medians, and Altitudes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Concurrency

When three or more lines intersect in one point, they are **concurrent**. The point at which they intersect is the **point of concurrency**.

Three arbitrary lines in a plane will normally meet in three different points, so concurrency is a special condition. The theorems below say that four different sets of lines built from a triangle are concurrent every time.

## Four sets of lines in a triangle

| Lines | Point of concurrency | Theorem |
|---|---|---|
| Perpendicular bisectors of the sides | **Circumcentre** | Theorem 5-6 |
| Bisectors of the angles | **Incentre** | Theorem 5-7 |
| Medians | — | Theorem 5-8 |
| Lines containing the altitudes | **Orthocentre** | Theorem 5-9 |

A **median** of a triangle is a segment whose endpoints are a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side. An **altitude** of a triangle is the perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side.

## The theorems

**Theorem 5-6:** the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices. That point is the circumcentre.

**Theorem 5-7:** the bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the sides. That point is the incentre.

The distance properties in these two are not coincidental. A point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, so a point on all three perpendicular bisectors is equidistant from all three vertices. Likewise a point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from that angle's two sides, so a point on all three angle bisectors is equidistant from all three sides.

**Theorem 5-8:** the medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is two thirds the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. If the median from vertex $A$ meets the opposite side at midpoint $M$, and the point of concurrency is $P$, then

$$AP = \tfrac{2}{3}\,AM$$

**Theorem 5-9:** the lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent. Their point of concurrency is the orthocentre.

## A caution about altitudes

Unlike angle bisectors and medians, an altitude of a triangle can be a side of the triangle, or it may lie outside the triangle. This is why Theorem 5-9 is phrased in terms of the *lines containing* the altitudes rather than the altitude segments themselves — in an obtuse triangle the segments themselves need not meet inside the figure at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concurrent** | Three or more lines that intersect in one point |
| **Point of concurrency** | The point at which concurrent lines intersect |
| **Circumcentre** | The point of concurrency of the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle |
| **Incentre** | The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle |
| **Median** | A segment whose endpoints are a vertex of a triangle and the midpoint of the opposite side |
| **Altitude** | The perpendicular segment from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side |
| **Orthocentre** | The point of concurrency of the lines containing the altitudes of a triangle |
| **Theorem 5-6** | The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the vertices |
| **Theorem 5-7** | The bisectors of the angles of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the sides |
| **Theorem 5-8** | The medians of a triangle are concurrent at a point that is two thirds the distance from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side |
| **Theorem 5-9** | The lines that contain the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent |

title: Isometries
summary: A transformation of a geometric figure is a change in its position, shape, or size. The original figure is the preimage; the resulting figure is the image, and the preimage and image must be similar.
markdown:
# 5.1 Isometries

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Transformations, preimages and images

A **transformation** of a geometric figure is a change in its position, shape, or size. The original figure is the **preimage**; the resulting figure is the **image**, and the preimage and image must be similar.

An **isometry** is a transformation in which the preimage and image are congruent. Isometries are therefore the transformations that move a figure without altering it: position may change, size and shape may not.

## Notation

A transformation maps a figure onto its image and may be described with arrow notation, $\triangle ABC \longrightarrow \triangle A'B'C'$. Prime notation is sometimes used to identify image points, so the image of $A$ is written $A'$.

Notice that you list corresponding points of the preimage and image in the same order, as you do for corresponding points of congruent or similar figures. Getting that order right is what makes the statement say which point went where.

## Translations

A **translation**, or slide, is an isometry that maps all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction. Both conditions are required — every point moves, and every point moves identically.

A **composition** of translations is a combination of two or more transformations. In a composition, each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation, so the order in which they are carried out is part of the description.

## Reflections

A **reflection**, or flip, is an isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientations. This is why a reflected image in a mirror appears "backwards".

You can use the following two rules to reflect a figure across a line $r$:

- If a point $A$ is on line $r$, then the image of $A$ is $A$ itself, that is $A' = A$.
- If a point $B$ is not on line $r$, then $r$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BB'}$.

The second rule is the working construction: drop a perpendicular from $B$ to $r$ and continue the same distance beyond it.

## Rotations

To describe a rotation you need to know three things: the **centre of rotation** (a point), the **angle of rotation** (a positive number of degrees), and whether the rotation is clockwise or counterclockwise. Unless stated otherwise, rotations here are counterclockwise.

You can use the following two rules to rotate a figure through $x°$ about a point $R$:

- The image of $R$ is itself, that is $R' = R$.
- For any point $V$, $RV' = RV$ and $m\angle VRV' = x$.

The first rule identifies the one fixed point; the second says every other point keeps its distance from the centre and turns through the same angle.

## Rotating regular polygons

A regular polygon has a centre that is equidistant from its vertices. Segments that connect the centre to the vertices divide the polygon into congruent triangles, and this fact can be used to find rotation images of regular polygons: rotating by the angle that carries one of those congruent triangles onto the next carries the whole polygon onto itself.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transformation** | A change in the position, shape, or size of a geometric figure |
| **Preimage** | The original figure |
| **Image** | The resulting figure |
| **Isometry** | A transformation in which the preimage and image are congruent |
| **Translation (slide)** | An isometry that maps all points of a figure the same distance in the same direction |
| **Composition** | A combination of two or more transformations, each performed on the image of the preceding transformation |
| **Reflection (flip)** | An isometry in which a figure and its image have opposite orientations |
| **Centre of rotation** | The point about which a rotation turns a figure |
| **Angle of rotation** | The positive number of degrees through which a rotation turns a figure |

markdown:
# 5.2 Compositions of Reflections

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a composition is

A **composition** is a combination of two or more transformations. In a composition, each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation — the output of one becomes the input of the next.

Because reflections are isometries, any composition of reflections is again a transformation that preserves congruence: each step leaves the figure congruent to what it received, so the final image is congruent to the original preimage.

## Glide reflections

If two figures are congruent and have opposite orientations, but are not simply reflections of each other, then there is a slide and a reflection that will map one onto the other. That combination of a translation with a reflection is a **glide reflection**.

The description tells you when to reach for one. Opposite orientations rule out a translation or a rotation on its own, since those preserve orientation. But if a single reflection does not do the job either — the figures are turned the right way round yet displaced along the mirror line — then the missing ingredient is the slide, and the pair of moves together completes the map.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Composition** | A combination of two or more transformations, in which each transformation is performed on the image of the preceding transformation |
| **Glide reflection** | The slide and reflection that map one figure onto another when the two are congruent with opposite orientations but are not simply reflections of each other |

# 5.3 Symmetry

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Symmetry as self-mapping

A figure has **symmetry** if there is an isometry that maps the figure onto itself. The definition is worth reading carefully: symmetry is not a property of how a figure looks but a statement that some motion leaves it apparently unchanged.

## Reflectional symmetry

**Reflectional symmetry** is the case where the isometry that maps the figure onto itself is a reflection. The line of that reflection is a line across which the figure matches itself point for point.

## Rotational symmetry

A figure that has **rotational symmetry** is its own image for some rotation of $180°$ or less.

A square has $90°$ and $180°$ rotational symmetry with the centre of rotation at the centre of the square. Because it has $180°$ rotational symmetry, a square also has **point symmetry**.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Symmetry** | A figure has symmetry if there is an isometry that maps the figure onto itself |
| **Reflectional symmetry** | Symmetry in which the isometry mapping the figure onto itself is a reflection |
| **Rotational symmetry** | A figure has rotational symmetry if it is its own image for some rotation of $180°$ or less |
| **Point symmetry** | The symmetry a figure has when it is its own image under a $180°$ rotation |
