# 11.2 Surface Areas of Prisms and Cylinders

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Prisms

A **prism** is a polyhedron with at least two congruent parallel faces, called the **bases**. The other faces are the **lateral faces**. A prism is named by the shape of its base — a triangular prism has triangular bases, a hexagonal prism hexagonal ones.

An **altitude** of a prism is a perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases, and the **height** $h$ of the prism is the length of an altitude. Because the bases are parallel, every altitude has the same length, so the height is well defined.

## Lateral area and surface area

The **lateral area** of a prism is the sum of the areas of the lateral faces. The **surface area** is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases.

Keeping the two apart matters, because a question asking how much material wraps *around* a solid wants the lateral area, while one asking for the total outside surface wants the surface area.

**Theorem 11-1 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Prism):** The lateral area of a right prism is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. The surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the bases.

$$L.A. = Ch, \qquad S.A. = Ch + 2B$$

Here $C$ is the distance round the base and $B$ is the area of one base — hence the factor of $2$, since a prism has two.

## Cylinders

A **cylinder** has two congruent parallel bases, which are circles.

Unrolling the curved face results in a rectangle. That rectangle's height is the height of the cylinder, and its width is the distance around the base, so its area is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. This is why the cylinder obeys the same formula as the prism.

**Theorem 11-2 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Cylinder):** The lateral area of a right cylinder is the product of the circumference of the base and the height. The surface area is the sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases.

$$L.A. = Ch, \qquad S.A. = Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$$

The final form simply substitutes the area of a circle for $B$.

An **altitude** of a cylinder, as for a prism, is a perpendicular segment joining the planes of the bases, and the **height** is its length.

| Solid | Lateral area | Surface area |
|---|---|---|
| Right prism | $Ch$ | $Ch + 2B$ |
| Right cylinder | $Ch$ | $Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$ |

The identical structure is not a coincidence. Both solids are a base swept straight upwards through a height, and unrolling the side of either gives a rectangle of width $C$ and height $h$.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prism** | A polyhedron with at least two congruent parallel faces, called the bases; the other faces are the lateral faces. Named by the shape of its base |
| **Lateral area** | The sum of the areas of the lateral faces |
| **Surface area** | The sum of the lateral area and the area of the two bases |
| **Cylinder** | A solid with two congruent parallel bases, which are circles |
| **Altitude** | A perpendicular segment that joins the planes of the bases |
| **Height ($h$)** | The length of an altitude |
| **Theorem 11-1** | For a right prism, $L.A. = Ch$ and $S.A. = Ch + 2B$ |
| **Theorem 11-2** | For a right cylinder, $L.A. = Ch$ and $S.A. = Ch + 2B = Ch + 2\pi r^2$ |

markdown:
# 11.3 Surface Areas of Pyramids and Cones

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Pyramids

A **pyramid** is a polyhedron in which one face, the base, can be any polygon, and the other faces — the **lateral faces** — are the triangular sides that meet at a common vertex, the **vertex of the pyramid**. As with a prism, a pyramid is named by the shape of its base.

Two different lengths have to be kept apart.

The **altitude** is the perpendicular segment from the vertex of the pyramid to the plane of the base, and the length of the altitude is the **height** $h$. The **slant height** $\ell$ is the length of the altitude of a lateral face.

So the height runs through the inside of the solid, and the slant height runs along the surface of a triangular face. The slant height is always the longer of the two, and confusing them is the most common error in these problems.

A **regular pyramid** is a pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles. That condition is what makes a single slant height meaningful — in an irregular pyramid, each face would have its own.

## Cones

The base of a **cone** is a circle. In a right cone, the altitude is a perpendicular segment from the vertex to the center of the base, and the **height** $h$ is the length of the altitude. The **slant height** $\ell$ is the distance from the vertex to a point on the circumference of the base.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-3 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Regular Pyramid):**

$$L.A. = \tfrac{1}{2}C\ell, \qquad S.A. = L.A. + B$$

**Theorem 11-4 (Lateral and Surface Areas of a Cone):**

$$L.A. = \pi r\ell, \qquad S.A. = L.A. + \pi r^2$$

The two agree with each other. A cone's base has circumference $C = 2\pi r$, so $\tfrac{1}{2}C\ell = \tfrac{1}{2}(2\pi r)\ell = \pi r\ell$ — the cone formula is the pyramid formula with a circular base. Likewise $B = \pi r^2$ turns the pyramid's $S.A. = L.A. + B$ into the cone's.

| Solid | Lateral area | Surface area |
|---|---|---|
| Regular pyramid | $\tfrac12 C\ell$ | $\tfrac12 C\ell + B$ |
| Cone | $\pi r \ell$ | $\pi r\ell + \pi r^2$ |

Note that only **one** base area is added here, against the two of 11.2. A pyramid or cone has a single base; the rest of it tapers to a point.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Pyramid** | A polyhedron in which one face (the base) can be any polygon and the other faces (the lateral faces) are triangular sides that meet at a common vertex |
| **Vertex of the pyramid** | The common point at which the lateral faces meet |
| **Altitude (pyramid)** | The perpendicular segment from the vertex of the pyramid to the plane of the base |
| **Height ($h$)** | The length of the altitude |
| **Slant height ($\ell$)** | For a pyramid, the length of the altitude of a lateral face; for a cone, the distance from the vertex to a point on the circumference of the base |
| **Regular pyramid** | A pyramid whose base is a regular polygon and whose lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles |
| **Cone** | A solid whose base is a circle; in a right cone the altitude runs from the vertex to the center of the base |
| **Theorem 11-3** | For a regular pyramid, $L.A. = \tfrac12 C\ell$ and $S.A. = L.A. + B$ |
| **Theorem 11-4** | For a cone, $L.A. = \pi r\ell$ and $S.A. = L.A. + \pi r^2$ |

markdown:
# 11.4 Volumes of Prisms and Cylinders

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Volume

**Volume** is the measure of the amount of 3-dimensional space occupied by a solid object, expressed in cubic units such as $\text{cm}^3$, $\text{m}^3$ or $\text{in}^3$. It quantifies the capacity of the object, or how much a container can hold.

The cubic units are the immediate contrast with 11.2 and 11.3, where surface area was measured in square units. Checking the units of an answer is the quickest way to catch a volume formula used where a surface-area formula was wanted.

## Cavalieri's principle

**Theorem 11-5 (Cavalieri's Principle):** If two space figures have the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level, then they have the same volume.

This is the theorem that makes the rest of the chapter's volume formulas possible. It says volume depends only on how much cross section there is at each level, not on where that cross section sits. A prism sheared over so that it leans has the same base area at every height as the upright one, and therefore the same volume — so the formulas below hold whether the solid is upright or oblique.

The two conditions must both be met. Equal heights alone, or equal cross sections at a single level, prove nothing.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-6 (Volume of a Prism):**

$$V = Bh$$

**Theorem 11-7 (Volume of a Cylinder):**

$$V = Bh = \pi r^2 h$$

$B$ is the area of the base and $h$ is the height. Both formulas are the same statement — stack the base straight up through a height $h$ and every level contributes the same area $B$ — and the cylinder version simply substitutes $\pi r^2$ for the area of its circular base.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Volume** | The measure of the amount of 3-dimensional space occupied by a solid object, expressed in cubic units; it quantifies capacity, or how much a container can hold |
| **Cavalieri's Principle (Th 11-5)** | If two space figures have the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level, then they have the same volume |
| **Volume of a Prism (Th 11-6)** | $V = Bh$ |
| **Volume of a Cylinder (Th 11-7)** | $V = Bh = \pi r^2 h$ |

markdown:
# 11.5 Volumes of Pyramids and Cones

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The formulas

**Theorem 11-8 (Volume of a Pyramid):**

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}Bh$$

**Theorem 11-9 (Volume of a Cone):**

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}Bh$$

The two theorems give the same expression, exactly as the surface-area theorems of 11.3 did. What differs is the base area $B$ substituted into it: any polygon for a pyramid, and a circle for a cone, so that a cone's volume works out as $\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$.

## The factor of one third

Set these against the prism and cylinder of 11.4:

| Solid | Volume |
|---|---|
| Prism | $Bh$ |
| Cylinder | $Bh$ |
| Pyramid | $\tfrac13 Bh$ |
| Cone | $\tfrac13 Bh$ |

A pyramid or a cone occupies one third of the prism or cylinder built on the same base with the same height. The reason is visible in the shape: a prism holds its full cross-sectional area $B$ all the way up, whereas a pyramid's cross section shrinks from $B$ at the base to nothing at the vertex.

The height $h$ is still the length of the altitude — the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the plane of the base, as defined in 11.3. It is not the slant height, and substituting $\ell$ for $h$ here is the standard error.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Volume of a Pyramid (Th 11-8)** | $V = \tfrac13 Bh$ |
| **Volume of a Cone (Th 11-9)** | $V = \tfrac13 Bh$ |

markdown:
# 11.6 Surface Areas and Volumes of Spheres

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The sphere and its parts

A **sphere** is the set of all points in three-dimensional space equidistant from a fixed point called the **center**.

This is the three-dimensional counterpart of a circle, and the vocabulary carries across unchanged. A **radius** is a segment that has one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the sphere. A **diameter** is a segment passing through the center with endpoints on the sphere.

A **great circle** is the largest possible circle of the sphere, and it contains the center of the sphere. A great circle divides a sphere into two hemispheres.

The great circle is the largest because any other plane cutting the sphere misses the centre and so slices off a smaller circle. Its radius is the sphere's own radius $r$, which is why $\pi r^2$ keeps appearing in the formulas below.

## Surface area

**Theorem 11-10 (Surface Area of a Sphere):**

$$S.A. = 4\pi r^2 = \pi d^2$$

The two forms are equal because $d = 2r$, so $\pi d^2 = \pi(2r)^2 = 4\pi r^2$.

Read the first form as four great circles: the surface of a sphere has the same area as four circles of radius $r$.

## Volume

**Theorem 11-11 (Volume of a Sphere):**

$$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

As always, surface area goes as $r^2$ and volume as $r^3$. Doubling a sphere's radius multiplies its surface area by $4$ and its volume by $8$ — the special case of the similar-solids result in 11.7.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Sphere** | The set of all points in three-dimensional space equidistant from a fixed point called the center |
| **Radius** | A segment that has one endpoint at the center and the other endpoint on the sphere |
| **Diameter** | A segment passing through the center with endpoints on the sphere |
| **Great circle** | The largest possible circle of the sphere, containing the center; it divides a sphere into two hemispheres |
| **Surface Area of a Sphere (Th 11-10)** | $S.A. = 4\pi r^2 = \pi d^2$ |
| **Volume of a Sphere (Th 11-11)** | $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$ |

markdown:
# 11.7 Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The theorem

**Theorem 11-12 (Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids):** If the similarity ratio of two similar solids is $a : b$, then

$$\frac{SA_1}{SA_2} = \frac{a^2}{b^2}, \qquad \frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{a^3}{b^3}$$

## Reading the exponents

The similarity ratio $a : b$ is a ratio of *lengths* — corresponding edges, radii, heights, slant heights. The exponents record how many lengths are multiplied together to produce each quantity.

| Quantity | Built from | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Length | One dimension | $a : b$ |
| Surface area | Two dimensions | $a^2 : b^2$ |
| Volume | Three dimensions | $a^3 : b^3$ |

Every surface-area formula in this chapter is a product of two lengths — $Ch$, $\pi r\ell$, $4\pi r^2$ — so scaling all lengths by a factor multiplies the area by that factor twice over. Every volume formula is a product of three — $Bh$, $\tfrac13 Bh$, $\tfrac43\pi r^3$ — so the factor applies three times.

## Using it

The direction of the calculation is what catches people out. Going from a length ratio to an area or volume ratio means squaring or cubing; going the other way, from a known volume ratio back to the scale of the solids, means taking a cube root.

So two similar solids in the ratio $2 : 1$ do not have twice the surface area — they have four times, and eight times the volume.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Similarity ratio** | The ratio $a : b$ of corresponding lengths in two similar solids |
| **Areas and Volumes of Similar Solids (Th 11-12)** | If the similarity ratio of two similar solids is $a:b$, then $\dfrac{SA_1}{SA_2}=\dfrac{a^2}{b^2}$ and $\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}=\dfrac{a^3}{b^3}$ |

# 12 Coordinate Geometry: Points, Lines, and Circles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Coordinate geometry basics

The **rectangular** or **Cartesian coordinate system** locates every point in the plane by a pair of numbers. The **x-axis** is a horizontal number line, and the y-axis the vertical one crossing it.

Points are written as **ordered pairs** $(x, y)$. The x-coordinate, also called the **abscissa**, is the distance from the y-axis; the y-coordinate is the distance from the x-axis.

Any set $S$ of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ can therefore be represented by points in the plane, which is what allows a geometric figure to be described by an equation and an equation to be drawn as a figure.

## Forms of linear equations

A straight line can be written in four ways, and choosing the right one for the information given saves most of the algebra.

| Form | Equation | Use it when you know |
|---|---|---|
| **General form** | $Ax + By = C$ | Any line, including vertical ones |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + k$ | The slope $m$ and the y-intercept $k$ |
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ | The slope and any one point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line |
| **Intercept form** | $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$ | The x-intercept $a$ and the y-intercept $b$ |

## Finding intercepts

An intercept is where the line crosses an axis, and on each axis the other coordinate is zero. That single observation is the whole method.

**Example.** For $2x + 3y = 15$:

y-intercept — set $x = 0$:

$$3y = 15 \implies y = 5$$

So the y-intercept is $(0, 5)$.

x-intercept — set $y = 0$:

$$2x = 15 \implies x = 7.5$$

So the x-intercept is $(7.5, 0)$.

## Distance and midpoint

For points $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$:

$$AB = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$$

$$M = \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$$

The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem of 8.1 applied to the right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical gaps between the two points. The midpoint formula averages the coordinates separately, because the midpoint is halfway across in each direction independently.

## Slopes of lines

For points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$:

$$m = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$$

Horizontal lines have slope $m = 0$: the y-coordinates are equal, so the numerator vanishes. Vertical lines have no defined slope, because the denominator vanishes instead — which is why a vertical line cannot be written as $y = mx + k$ and must be given as $x = \text{constant}$.

**Parallel lines** have the same slope, $m_1 = m_2$. **Perpendicular lines** have slopes whose product is $-1$, that is $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

## Circles in the coordinate plane

A circle with center $(h, k)$ and radius $r$ has the standard equation

$$(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$$

This is the distance formula in disguise: the left-hand side is the squared distance from $(x, y)$ to the centre, and setting it equal to $r^2$ says exactly that the point lies $r$ from the centre.

A line is **tangent** to a circle if it intersects it at exactly one point.

## Proofs using coordinate geometry

Placing a figure on axes turns a geometric claim into an algebraic one, provable with the distance, midpoint and slope formulas above.

**Midsegment Theorem (Trapezoid):** The midsegment of a trapezoid is parallel to the bases and its length is the average of the lengths of the bases.

$$\text{midsegment} = \frac{b_1 + b_2}{2}$$

The two conclusions are proved by two different tools: parallelism by the slope formula, and length by the distance formula.

## Practice questions

**1. The line with x-intercept $-3$ and y-intercept $8$.**

Intercept form with $a = -3$ and $b = 8$:

$$\frac{x}{-3} + \frac{y}{8} = 1$$

**2. The line with x-intercept $-2$ and through $(3, 7)$.**

An x-intercept of $-2$ is the point $(-2, 0)$, so

$$m = \frac{7-0}{3-(-2)} = \frac{7}{5}$$

Point-slope form through $(3,7)$:

$$y - 7 = \frac{7}{5}(x-3)$$

**3. The line through $(8, 5)$ and perpendicular to $y = 4$.**

$y = 4$ is horizontal, so a perpendicular line is vertical, and every point on it shares the x-coordinate of $(8,5)$:

$$x = 8$$

**4. The line through $(9, 2)$ and the origin.**

$$m = \frac{2-0}{9-0} = \frac{2}{9}$$

The line passes through the origin, so its y-intercept is $0$:

$$y = \frac{2x}{9}$$

**5. A quadrilateral has vertices $(-4,4)$, $(-6,0)$, $(-4,-4)$, $(-2,0)$. Name the type of quadrilateral and find its area.**

Each side, by the distance formula, has length $\sqrt{2^2+4^2} = \sqrt{20}$, so all four sides are equal and the quadrilateral is a **rhombus**.

Its diagonals run from $(-4,4)$ to $(-4,-4)$, of length $8$, and from $(-6,0)$ to $(-2,0)$, of length $4$. Using the rhombus area formula of 8.6:

$$A = \tfrac{1}{2}d_1 d_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(8)(4) = 16$$

**6. $ABCD$ is a square with vertices $A(0,0)$ and $B(5,3)$. Find the coordinates of $C$ and $D$.**

Side $AB$ is the displacement $(5, 3)$. Side $AD$ must be perpendicular to it and the same length, so it is $(-3, 5)$ or $(3, -5)$, and there are two squares.

Taking $(-3,5)$: $D = (-3, 5)$ and $C = B + (-3,5) = (5-3,\ 3+5) = (2, 8)$.

Taking $(3,-5)$: $D = (3, -5)$ and $C = B + (3,-5) = (8, -2)$.

**7. $\triangle ABC$ has vertices $A(-2,-1)$, $B(0,7)$ and $C(8,3)$. Find the circumcenter $Q$.**

The circumcentre is the point equidistant from all three vertices, so write $Q = (x, y)$ and set the squared distances equal using the distance formula.

From $QA^2 = QB^2$:

$$(x+2)^2 + (y+1)^2 = x^2 + (y-7)^2$$
$$4x + 2y + 5 = -14y + 49 \implies x + 4y = 11$$

From $QB^2 = QC^2$:

$$x^2 + (y-7)^2 = (x-8)^2 + (y-3)^2$$
$$-14y + 49 = -16x - 6y + 73 \implies 2x - y = 3$$

Substituting $y = 2x - 3$ into $x + 4y = 11$ gives $9x = 23$, so

$$Q = \left(\frac{23}{9},\ \frac{19}{9}\right)$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular (Cartesian) coordinate system** | The system locating points by an ordered pair of distances from two perpendicular number lines |
| **x-axis** | The horizontal number line |
| **Ordered pair** | A point written as $(x, y)$ |
| **Abscissa** | The x-coordinate; the distance from the y-axis |
| **General form** | $Ax + By = C$ |
| **Slope-intercept form** | $y = mx + k$, where $m$ is the slope |
| **Point-slope form** | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, where $(x_1, y_1)$ is a point on the line |
| **Intercept form** | $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} = 1$, where $a$ is the x-intercept and $b$ is the y-intercept |
| **Distance formula** | $AB = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$ |
| **Midpoint formula** | $M = \left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$ |
| **Slope formula** | $m = \dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$; horizontal lines have $m = 0$ |
| **Parallel lines** | Lines with the same slope, $m_1 = m_2$ |
| **Perpendicular lines** | Lines whose slopes satisfy $m_1m_2 = -1$ |
| **Standard equation of a circle** | $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$, with center $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ |
| **Tangent to a circle** | A line that intersects the circle at exactly one point |
| **Midsegment Theorem (Trapezoid)** | The midsegment of a trapezoid is parallel to the bases and its length is the average of the lengths of the bases |

# 13 Statistics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Structured and unstructured data

**Unstructured data** are easy to read and contain great information, but they are usually given in natural language. They can vary greatly in length, style, and content, which makes them difficult to analyse. This is the kind of data most common in daily life.

**Structured data** are any data that are organised in a predefined manner, typically in a table format with rows and columns — a **data table**.

The contrast explains why the rest of this lesson is about tables. Analysis needs values that can be counted and compared, and a predefined structure is what guarantees that the same kind of information appears in the same place for every case. Unstructured data have to be turned into structured data before any of the displays below can be built.

## Variables

**Variables** are the characteristics recorded about each individual. In a data table, each row is an individual and each column is a variable.

Two types are distinguished, and the type decides which displays and summaries are legitimate.

| Type | What it records |
|---|---|
| **Categorical variables** | Related to the category of what is measured |
| **Quantitative variables** | Related to the quantity of what is measured |

Gender, for instance, is categorical: it sorts individuals into groups rather than measuring an amount.

## How to display data

A **frequency table** lists the categories of a variable together with the count in each. A **relative frequency table** does the same but displays percentages instead of the actual numbers, which makes groups of different sizes comparable.

A **bar chart** displays the distribution of a categorical variable, showing the counts for each category.

A **pie chart** shows the whole group of cases as a circle, where each slice is proportional to the fraction of the whole in that category. The choice between the two follows from what the reader is meant to see: a bar chart compares categories against each other, a pie chart shows each category as a share of the whole.

The **area principle** governs both: the area occupied by a part of the graph should correspond to the magnitude of the value it represents. This is the rule that a display is judged against, because the eye reads area rather than any label. A bar drawn twice as wide as its neighbour, or a picture scaled in two dimensions to show a doubling, breaks the principle and misleads even when its numbers are correct.

## Analysing two variables together

A **contingency table**, also called a **crosstabulation**, shows how the individuals are distributed along each variable, contingent on the value of the other variable.

Three terms describe its parts:

- A **cell** gives the count for a combination of values of the two variables.
- In the margins of a contingency table, the frequency distribution of one of the variables is called its **marginal distribution**.
- **Conditional distributions** show the distribution of one variable for just those cases that satisfy a condition on another variable.

The marginal distribution ignores the second variable altogether, while a conditional distribution restricts attention to one of its values. Comparing conditional distributions with each other, or with the marginal distribution, is how a relationship between the two variables is detected: if the conditional distributions all look alike, knowing one variable tells you nothing about the other.

A **segmented bar chart** displays exactly that comparison. Each bar is a whole and divides proportionally into segments corresponding to the percentage in each group, so the bars stand for conditional distributions and can be read against one another at a glance.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unstructured data** | Data that are easy to read and contain great information but are usually given in natural language, varying greatly in length, style and content, which makes them difficult to analyse |
| **Structured data** | Any data that are organised in a predefined manner, typically in a table format with rows and columns |
| **Data table** | A table of structured data |
| **Variables** | The characteristics recorded about each individual |
| **Categorical variables** | Variables related to the category of what is measured |
| **Quantitative variables** | Variables related to the quantity of what is measured |
| **Frequency table** | A table giving the count in each category |
| **Relative frequency table** | A table displaying percentages instead of the actual numbers |
| **Bar chart** | A display of the distribution of a categorical variable, showing the counts for each category |
| **Pie chart** | A display of the whole group of cases as a circle, where each slice is proportional to the fraction of the whole in the category |
| **Area principle** | The area occupied by a part of the graph should correspond to the magnitude of the value it represents |
| **Contingency table (crosstabulation)** | A table showing how the individuals are distributed along each variable, contingent on the value of the other variable |
| **Cell** | The count for a combination of values of the two variables |
| **Marginal distribution** | The frequency distribution of one of the variables, given in the margins of a contingency table |
| **Conditional distribution** | The distribution of one variable for just those cases that satisfy a condition on another variable |
| **Segmented bar chart** | A chart in which each bar is a whole, divided proportionally into segments corresponding to the percentage in each group |

# 1 Historical Periods of Music

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide organises every period the same way: a **key word**, the historical
context, the characteristic style, the forms and genres, the composers to know,
and a listening focus. The key word is the shortest possible summary of the
period — learn those first and the rest of each period hangs off them.

Read the periods as a sequence rather than as five separate lists. The texture
alone tells a story: one line in the Middle Ages, several equal lines through the
Renaissance and Baroque, then a single tune with accompaniment from the Classical
period onwards.

## Middle Ages (c. 500–1400)

**Key word: dark.**

**Context.** The period is dominated by the Church, and music served religious
ritual. The practice set sums the whole period up as religious and sacred, built
on church modes and written in the new notation.

**Style.**

- **Monophony** — a single melodic line, as in Gregorian chant.
- **Neumes** — early notation, developed as the notation for Gregorian chant.

**Forms and genres.** **Plainchant**, also called Gregorian chant: sacred songs
in Latin. The practice answers add that it was the official music of the Roman
Catholic Church, which is the reason the guide gives for it being the period's
one central genre.

**Key composer.** **Hildegard of Bingen** — a mystic nun and a prolific composer.

**Listening focus.** A chant-like quality; **modal scales** (Ionian, Dorian,
Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian); and a lack of steady beat.

## Renaissance (c. 1400–1600)

**Key word: humanism.**

**Context.** The rise of secularism, and the invention of the printing press. The
practice answers describe the period as more secular but still mostly sacred and
still modal, with harmony beginning to develop — and place it alongside realism
and linear perspective in the visual arts of the same moment.

**Style.**

- **Polyphony** — interweaving independent lines.
- **Word painting** — the music literally illustrates the lyrics. The guide's
  example is a setting of "rise rise rise rise" in which each "rise" is one
  semitone higher than the last; the practice answers give the same idea as
  "ascending" set to rising pitch.

**Genres.**

| Genre | Sacred or secular | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Mass** | Sacred | Polyphonic (many voices simultaneously) or plainchant |
| **Motet** | Sacred | A choral composition and a standalone piece, polyphonic, freer than the Mass and not always for worship |
| **Madrigal** | Secular | Vocal secular music |

**Key composers.** **Josquin des Prez**, who wrote motets, and **Palestrina**, who
wrote masses. The practice set adds **Weelkes** to the same list.

**Listening focus.**

- **Clarity of text.**
- **Imitative texture** — a polyphonic texture in which one voice or part imitates
  the melody of another voice or part, usually at a slightly later time.
- **Modal harmony** — no structural harmony such as V–I, but still a tonal centre,
  namely the mode.

Clarity of text and word painting belong together: both are ways of making the
music serve the words, which is what the period's humanism amounts to in
practice.

## Baroque (1600–1750)

**Key word: absolutism.**

**Context.** The dramatic arts, with their drastic contrasts of colour and their
characters in bloody motion; Versailles as the centre of music; and the
Counter-Reformation.

**Style.**

- **Unity of mood** — maintaining a constant emotional atmosphere.
- **Rhythmic drive** — a strong sense of momentum, usually maintained by drums or
  bass.
- **Basso continuo** — a continuous bassline played by one instrument, which can
  change and vary.
- **Terraced dynamics** — abrupt shifts between loud and soft.

**Key forms and genres.**

| Form | Description |
|---|---|
| **Fugue** | A musical structure: counterpoint with subject, answer, exposition, development and coda |
| **Concerto grosso** | Dialogue between the soloists (**concertino**) and the orchestra (**ripieno**) |
| **Opera** | A dramatic work or story, mostly sung, with orchestral accompaniment |
| **Oratorio** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra, choir and soloists |
| **Cantata** | A vocal composition with instrumental accompaniment, sacred or secular |
| **Toccata** | Free-flowing and improvisational, for organ or harpsichord |

The practice set lists **ritornello** alongside opera, oratorio, cantata and
toccata as a Baroque form. Neither the review guide nor the practice answers
define it, so learn it as a name on that list.

**Key composers.** **J.S. Bach**, famous for fugues; **G.F. Handel**, for the
"Hallelujah" chorus from *Messiah*; **Vivaldi**, for *The Four Seasons*;
**Monteverdi**; and **Pachelbel**, for *Canon in D*.

**Listening focus.**

- **Harpsichord** — a piano, except that the strings are plucked.
- **Ornamentation** — additional decorative elements, such as trills.
- **Continuous melody** — an uninterrupted flow.
- **Contrapuntal complexity** — elaborate use of counterpoint, meaning two or more
  melodic lines at the same time.

## Classical (1750–1820)

**Key word: enlightenment.**

**Context.** Enlightenment ideals — balance, clarity, form.

**Style.**

- **Homophony** — melody with accompaniment, that is, with harmony.
- **Balanced phrases** — a structure of two or more **phrases** (musical sentences
  that convey ideas) of equal length and similar tension.
- **Simple harmony** — two or more notes played together pleasingly, for example
  triads.
- **Clear cadences** — cadences with a clear conclusion: **authentic** (V–I) and
  **plagal** (IV–I).

Balance, clarity and form are exactly what those four features deliver, so the key
word is not decoration here: it names the thing the style was built to produce.

**Key forms and genres.**

| Form | Description |
|---|---|
| **Sonata form** | Exposition – Development – Recapitulation |
| **Symphony** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra; fast–slow–dance–fast |
| **Concerto** | A musical composition for one solo instrument |
| **String quartet** | Two violins, a viola and a cello |
| **Zu 2** | Two instruments play in unison |

**Key composers.** **Haydn**, the father of the string quartet and of the
symphony; **Mozart**, a prodigy, famous for his forty-one or so symphonies; and
**early Beethoven**. The practice answers call these the three giants: Haydn,
Mozart and Beethoven. The guide prints "nine symphonies" for Mozart here; that
is an error — nine is Beethoven's number, and Mozart wrote around forty-one.

## Romantic (1820–1900)

**Key word: individualism.**

**Context.** Nationalism and the Industrial Revolution.

**Themes.** Love, death, nature, the supernatural, exoticism.

**Musical features.**

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Program music** | Music that tells a story — for example *Symphonie fantastique* |
| **Rubato** | Speeding up and slowing down, with the overall duration left intact |
| **Expanded orchestration** | Increasing the size of the orchestra and the types of instrument in it |
| **Virtuosity** | Extreme technical skill — Paganini and Liszt |
| **Self-expression** | Composers tried to express their inner feelings through the music they created |

Program music and self-expression are the two features that follow directly from
the key word: both make the individual — a story, or the composer's own feeling —
the subject of the piece.

### Key composers

**Beethoven (late)** lost his hearing and became much more Romantic, expressing
his frustration through his music. He is the one composer the guide lists twice,
early under Classical and late under Romantic.

**Chopin** was Polish and physically weak, and wrote **nocturnes** — quiet, calm,
beautiful pieces. He is known as the poet of the piano.

**Liszt** was a pianist with big hands, a handsome womaniser who played difficult
pieces for fun.

**Berlioz** wrote unconventional music. He fell in love and wrote *Symphonie
fantastique*, in which the protagonist kills the woman he loves, goes to hell, and
meets her there.

**Brahms** was conservative and German, and was close friends with Clara Schumann.

**Tchaikovsky** was the Russian master of ballet — *The Nutcracker*, *Swan Lake* —
and was gay.

**Mendelssohn** was a devoted admirer of Bach, took advice from his sister Fanny,
and died at 38 from overwork.

**Schubert** was a hard-working admirer of Beethoven who wrote **Lieder** — art
songs, settings of a poem to music, such as *Erlking*.

**Richard Wagner** was German, hated Jews, and was a favourite of Hitler. He
used the **leitmotif**: a musical theme that suggests a person, an idea or an
event. The guide prints "Hungarian" here; that is an error — Wagner was German.

**Puccini** was Italian and worked in **verismo**, operas that portrayed real
people. *La Bohème* shows the real, difficult life of musicians, philosophers and
playwrights, and has soaring melodies.

**Listening focus.** Rich harmonies, dynamic contrasts, expressive melodies, and
experimenting with dissonance.

## The Modern era and the "isms" (1900–present)

**Context.** Two world wars, technology, global influence, and philosophical
shifts.

Where the earlier periods each have one dominant style, the modern era splits into
parallel movements, and the guide expects you to tell them apart by a single
distinguishing trait each.

### Impressionism

**Inspiration.** Claude Monet's painting *Impression: Sunrise*.

**Musical traits.**

- Whole-tone, pentatonic and modal scales.
- Colour and texture valued over clear form.
- Extended chords (9ths, 13ths) and floating rhythms.

**Key composers.** **Claude Debussy** (*Clair de Lune*) and **Maurice Ravel**.

### Primitivism

**Inspiration.** Folk art, tribal rhythms, prehistoric themes.

**Traits.**

- Savage rhythms.
- **Ostinatos** — short, repetitive musical phrases, typically at the same pitch
  or in the same rhythm.
- **Polytonality** — two or more keys or tonal centres used simultaneously.
- **Harsh dissonance** — exactly what it sounds like.
- **Simple motives** — short, recognisable ideas, such as the *Mission Impossible*
  theme.

**Key work.** Stravinsky's *The Rite of Spring*.

### Expressionism

**Themes.** Inner anxiety, nightmares, alienation. The practice set describes the
result as music that is often anxiety-inducing and spooky.

**Traits.** **Atonality**, extreme dissonance, and **Sprechstimme** — spoken
singing.

**Technique.** The **twelve-tone system**: serialism using tone rows. The practice
answers pair the twelve-tone system directly with atonality, which is how the two
terms relate — the system is the method, atonality the result.

**Key composers.** Schoenberg, Berg, Webern.

### Minimalism

**Traits.** Repetition, gradual change, and a steady pulse.

**Composers.** **Steve Reich** (*Clapping Music*) and **Philip Glass**.

### Electronic and chance (aleatoric, indeterminate) music

**Traits.** Synthesizers, tape loops, ambient textures, and **chance** — luck and
randomness as part of the composition.

**Figures.**

- **John Cage** (*4′33″*) — a music professor; his work asks what music is.
- **Varèse** (*Poème électronique*) — a pioneer of electronic music.
- **Kraftwerk** — pioneers of electric-synth, techno and electronic dance music.

### Telling the isms apart

The practice set is a matching exercise, and its answers amount to a checklist of
the one clue that identifies each movement.

| Clue | Movement |
|---|---|
| Repetition with gradual changes | Minimalism |
| An example would be Steve Reich's *Clapping Music* | Minimalism |
| Pentatonic, modal and whole-tone scales | Impressionism |
| Key figure: Claude Debussy | Impressionism |
| Some elements determined by chance | Electronic and chance music |
| Tape loops and synthesizers | Electronic and chance music |
| Prehistoric themes and tribal rhythms | Primitivism |
| Polytonality | Primitivism |
| The 12-tone system (atonality) | Expressionism |
| Often anxiety-inducing and spooky | Expressionism |

The practice answers mark polytonality as expressionism, but the review guide
lists polytonality among the traits of primitivism and does not give it to
expressionism at all; the table above follows the review guide.

## The periods side by side

The practice set opens with this table as a fill-in-the-blank exercise, so it is
worth being able to reproduce from memory.

| Period | Starts | Prominent texture | Key word |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | ~500 | Monophonic | Dark |
| **Renaissance** | ~1400 | Polyphonic | Humanism |
| **Baroque** | ~1600 | Mostly polyphonic | Absolutism |
| **Classical** | ~1750 | Homophonic | Enlightenment |
| **Romantic** | ~1820 | Homophonic (mostly) | Individualism |

| Period | Composers to name | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | Hildegard of Bingen | Religious, sacred; neumes as early notation; church modes |
| **Renaissance** | Josquin des Prez, Palestrina, Weelkes | More secular but mostly sacred, and modal; harmony development; realism and linear perspective in art; word painting |
| **Baroque** | J.S. Bach, Handel, Vivaldi, Monteverdi, Pachelbel (*Canon in D*) | Terraced dynamics, basso continuo, unity of mood, rhythmic drive, dramatic art |
| **Classical** | The three giants: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven | Balanced phrases, simple harmony, clear cadences |
| **Romantic** | Chopin, Liszt, Berlioz, Brahms, Tchaikovsky | Love, death, nature, the supernatural, exoticism |

| Period | Forms to name |
|---|---|
| **Middle Ages** | Plainchant (Gregorian chant) |
| **Renaissance** | Mass (sacred), motet (sacred), madrigal (secular) |
| **Baroque** | Fugue, concerto grosso, opera, oratorio, cantata, toccata, ritornello |
| **Classical** | Sonata form, symphony, concerto, string quartet |
| **Romantic** | Program music, rubato, expanded orchestration, virtuosity |

## A note on the listening material

Each period in the guide ends with a **listening focus** rather than a named
recording, so everything the guide asks you to recognise is described in words and
is reproduced above. Where a specific piece is named — *Symphonie fantastique*,
*Clair de Lune*, *The Rite of Spring*, *Clapping Music*, *4′33″* — the guide gives
the title and nothing more, so learn the title and the trait it illustrates rather
than expecting a description of the sound.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Monophony** | A single melodic line, as in Gregorian chant |
| **Neumes** | Early notation, the notation used for Gregorian chant |
| **Plainchant (Gregorian chant)** | Sacred songs in Latin; the official music of the Roman Catholic Church |
| **Modal scales** | Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian |
| **Polyphony** | Interweaving independent lines |
| **Word painting** | Music that literally illustrates the lyrics |
| **Mass** | A sacred genre; polyphonic (many voices simultaneously) or plainchant |
| **Motet** | A sacred choral composition; a standalone piece, polyphonic, freer than the Mass and not always for worship |
| **Madrigal** | Vocal secular music |
| **Imitative texture** | A polyphonic texture in which one voice or part imitates the melody of another, usually at a slightly later time |
| **Modal harmony** | Harmony with no structural progressions such as V–I, but still with a tonal centre — the mode |
| **Unity of mood** | Maintaining a constant emotional atmosphere |
| **Rhythmic drive** | A strong sense of momentum, usually maintained by drums or bass |
| **Basso continuo** | A continuous bassline played by one instrument, which can change and vary |
| **Terraced dynamics** | Abrupt shifts between loud and soft dynamics |
| **Fugue** | A musical structure: counterpoint with subject, answer, exposition, development and coda |
| **Concerto grosso** | Dialogue between soloists and orchestra |
| **Concertino** | The group of soloists in a concerto grosso |
| **Ripieno** | The orchestra in a concerto grosso |
| **Opera** | A dramatic work or story, mostly sung, with orchestral accompaniment |
| **Oratorio** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra, choir and soloists |
| **Cantata** | A vocal composition with instrumental accompaniment, sacred or secular |
| **Toccata** | A free-flowing, improvisational piece for organ or harpsichord |
| **Harpsichord** | A piano, except that the strings are plucked |
| **Ornamentation** | Additional, decorative elements such as trills |
| **Continuous melody** | An uninterrupted flow of melody |
| **Counterpoint** | Two or more melodic lines at the same time |
| **Contrapuntal complexity** | Elaborate use of counterpoint |
| **Homophony** | Melody with accompaniment, that is, with harmony |
| **Phrase** | A musical sentence that conveys an idea |
| **Balanced phrases** | A structure of two or more phrases of equal length and similar tension |
| **Simple harmony** | Two or more notes played together pleasingly, for example triads |
| **Authentic cadence** | A cadence with a clear conclusion: V–I |
| **Plagal cadence** | A cadence with a clear conclusion: IV–I |
| **Sonata form** | Exposition – Development – Recapitulation |
| **Symphony** | A large-scale musical composition for orchestra; fast–slow–dance–fast |
| **Concerto** | A musical composition for one solo instrument |

# 2 Instruments and the Orchestra

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Instrument families

The practice set asks for **four instrument families** and answers **string,
woodwind, brass and percussion**. The same practice set then asks you to sort
individual instruments into six labels — the four families plus **keyboard** and
**electronic** — and the review guide lists all six groups together. Learn four as
the answer to "how many families", and six as the set of labels you sort
instruments into.

### Strings

Violin, viola, cello (violoncello), double bass, harp.

Played with a bow (**arco**) or plucked (**pizzicato**).

### Woodwinds

Flute (*flauto*), oboe (*oboi*), clarinet (in B♭), bassoon (*fagotti*),
contrabassoon.

Tone is produced via a **vibrating air column**.

### Brass

Trumpet (in B♭), French horn (in F, written as C, *corni*), trombone
(*tromboni*), tuba (in C or B♭). The guide glosses the trombone as *trombe*
here; that is an error — *trombe* is the Italian for trumpets, and *tromboni* is
the Italian for trombones.

The lips buzz into a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

### Percussion

- **Pitched:** timpani, xylophone.
- **Unpitched:** snare drum, cymbals.

### Keyboards

Piano (strings struck), organ, harpsichord.

The guide's own description of the harpsichord in the Baroque period is the
distinction to hold onto here: it is a piano except that the strings are plucked
rather than struck.

### Electronic

Synthesizers, samplers.

### Sorting practice

The practice set gives eighteen instruments to label. Its answers are worth
reading straight through, because most of the labelling is settled by the family
descriptions above rather than by memory.

| Instrument | Family | Instrument | Family |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trumpet | Brass | Piano | Keyboard |
| Harpsichord | Keyboard | Double bass | String |
| Flute | Woodwind | French horn | Brass |
| Organ | Keyboard | Tuba | Brass |
| Bassoon | Woodwind | Cello | String |
| Violin | String | Synthesizer | Electronic |
| Trombone | Brass | Harp | String |
| Clarinet | Woodwind | Viola | String |
| Oboe | Woodwind | Sampler | Electronic |

## The orchestra

**Seating.** Strings at the front, woodwinds in the centre, brass at the back,
percussion at the rear. The practice set asks these four as separate questions —
front, centre, back, rear — so the four positions have to be kept in that order.

Modern orchestras often include over 90 musicians.

## How the orchestra changed

| Period | The orchestra |
|---|---|
| **Baroque** | Small, harpsichord-centred ensembles |
| **Classical** | Balanced, with winds used in pairs, and less bass |
| **Romantic** | Larger, with added instruments (tuba, cymbals, harp) and an expanded size of the existing parts of the orchestra |
| **Modern** | Expanded percussion, exotic instruments, electronics |

The Romantic line here is the same fact as **expanded orchestration** in the list
of Romantic features: the period's taste for a bigger sound and its bigger
orchestra are one development described twice.

**Examples.** The guide names one work per stage:

- Haydn's Symphony No. 31 — Classical
- Wagner's *Ride of the Valkyries* — Romantic
- Stravinsky's *The Rite of Spring* — Modern

These are listening examples. The guide prints the titles and the period label
only, with no description of what to listen for in each, so treat them as three
titles to match to three stages of the orchestra's growth.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Arco** | Playing a string instrument with the bow |
| **Pizzicato** | Plucking a string instrument |
| **Strings** | Violin, viola, cello, double bass, harp; played with a bow or plucked |
| **Woodwinds** | Flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, contrabassoon; tone produced by a vibrating air column |
| **Brass** | Trumpet, French horn, trombone, tuba; the lips buzz into a cup-shaped mouthpiece |
| **Percussion** | Pitched (timpani, xylophone) and unpitched (snare drum, cymbals) instruments |
| **Keyboards** | Piano (strings struck), organ, harpsichord (strings plucked) |
| **Electronic** | Synthesizers and samplers |

# 3 Transposing

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **transposing instrument** does not sound the note that is written for it. The
guide's clearest statement of the problem is the clarinet, trumpet and cornet:
when the player sees a C on the score, it is actually a B♭ that comes out when
they blow it. Transposing is the four-step procedure for getting from one to the
other.

## The procedure

1. **Understand the key of the instrument.** This is the note that sounds when the
   instrument plays a written C, and it is what the tables below record.
2. **Find the interval between that key and concert pitch (C).**
3. **Move all the notes in the piece by that interval.**
4. **Adjust the key signature** to match your new transposed key.

Steps 2 and 3 are why step 1 matters: the instrument's key is not a label to
memorise on its own, it is the thing you measure the interval from.

## Keys of the instruments

The guide groups the instruments by their key and gives an interval for some of
them. Where the interval column is empty, the guide names the instrument in that
key but does not print the interval.

| Key | Instruments | Interval the guide gives |
|---|---|---|
| **B♭** | Clarinet, trumpet, cornet | — (a written C sounds as B♭) |
| **F** | French horn, English horn, alto clarinet | English horn: a perfect fifth (P5) lower |
| **E♭** | Alto saxophone, baritone saxophone, E♭ clarinet | Alto saxophone: a major sixth (M6) lower. Baritone saxophone: a major sixth plus an octave (M6 + P8) lower. E♭ clarinet: a minor third (m3) higher |
| **G** | Alto flute | A perfect fourth (P4) lower |

Two of these run in the less obvious direction and are worth marking: the **E♭
clarinet sounds higher** than written, not lower, and the **baritone saxophone**
is the only instrument given an interval larger than an octave.

## Degrees of the scale

The practice set also asks for the names of the degrees of the scale, filling in
the gaps in a printed sequence. Its answer key gives them in this order:

| Degree | Name |
|---|---|
| 1 | Tonic |
| 2 | Supertonic |
| 3 | Mediant |
| 4 | Subdominant |
| 5 | Dominant |
| 6 | *(the answer key prints "subdominant" a second time)* |
| 7 | Leading tone |

The answer key repeats "subdominant" for both the fourth and the sixth degree;
since it names the fourth degree the subdominant in the sequence itself, go by the
positions and treat the sixth as the one name the guide does not supply.

## What the guide does not print

Steps 3 and 4 describe operations on a piece of notation — moving every note,
then rewriting the key signature — but the guide sets out the procedure without a
worked transposition and without a notated example to work it on. Practise the
steps on music you already have in front of you; there is no exercise supplied
here to check yourself against.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Transposing** | Moving all the notes of a piece by an interval and adjusting the key signature to the new key |
| **Key of an instrument** | The pitch that actually sounds when the instrument plays a written C — B♭ for the clarinet, trumpet and cornet, F for the French horn, and so on |
| **Concert pitch** | C; the reference the instrument's key is measured against |

# 18.1 The Electric Battery

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Galvani, Volta and the argument that produced the battery

In the 1780s **Luigi Galvani** carried out a series of experiments on the contraction of a frog's leg muscles using electricity produced by static electricity. He concluded that the source of the electric charge lay in the frog's muscle or nerve itself, and that the metal merely transmitted the charge to the proper points. He named this charge *animal electricity*.

**Alessandro Volta** disagreed. He believed the source of the electricity was the contact between the two dissimilar metals — that is, a chemical reaction of oxidation and reduction — rather than anything in the animal.

To test this he placed a piece of cloth soaked in salt solution or dilute acid between a disc of zinc and one of silver, and piled up a "battery" of such couplings. When strips of metal connected to the two ends of the pile were brought close together, a spark was produced. On this basis he designed and built the first electric battery; he published the discovery in 1800. The guide prints 1900 here; that is an error — Volta's pile dates to 1800, immediately after Galvani's experiments of the 1780s.

The word *battery* still carries Volta's meaning: a pile of separate couplings acting together.

## Cells and batteries

A **battery** produces electricity by transforming chemical energy into electrical energy. It is made of several electric cells connected together.

An electric cell has three parts:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Electrodes** | Two plates or rods made of dissimilar metals. The positive $(+)$ electrode is the **cathode** — for example carbon, copper or silver. The negative $(-)$ electrode is the **anode** — for example zinc or aluminium. |
| **Electrolyte** | The solution the electrodes are immersed in (wet batteries), or a paste (dry batteries). Sulfuric acid is a wet example. |
| **Terminal** | The part of each electrode that lies outside the solution. |

Dry cells are the ones normally used, because wet cells are easy to spill or leak, which is neither safe nor convenient.

## How an electric cell works

Take sulfuric acid as the electrolyte, zinc as the anode and copper as the cathode.

**1. The acid dissolves the anode.**

$$\mathrm{H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2H^+ + SO_4^{2-}} \qquad \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

**2. Two electrons stay behind, making the anode negative.** The positive $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ ion enters the sulfuric acid and makes the acid positive:

$$\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow ZnSO_4}$$

so the acid is now $\mathrm{ZnSO_4}$ together with $\mathrm{2H^+}$.

**3. Electrons are pulled off the copper cathode.**

$$\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

**4. The positive $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion stays behind, making the cathode positive.** The two electrons enter the acid and make it neutral again:

$$\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow 2H}$$

The opposite charges now sitting on the two electrodes create a potential difference, and so chemical energy is made available as electrical energy.

(The guide names the electrode in step 3 as the carbon cathode, but the example it sets up uses copper and its own equation is written for $\mathrm{Cu}$; read it as the copper cathode.)

## Why a disconnected cell does not run down

Whether the cell keeps reacting depends entirely on whether the terminals are joined:

- **Terminals not connected.** Only a small amount of zinc dissolves. As the zinc anode becomes increasingly negative, new positive zinc ions produced at it are attracted straight back to the anode, so the reaction stalls and a voltage is simply maintained.
- **Terminals connected.** Charge is now allowed to flow between the terminals, so far more zinc can dissolve. One electrode is used up after a time and the cell goes "dead".

This is why an unconnected cell simply holds its voltage, while a cell left joined into a circuit is eventually used up.

## What sets the voltage

The voltage a cell produces depends on the material of the electrodes and on their relative ability to be dissolved or to give up electrons.

It does **not** depend on the size of the cell. Smaller cells contain fewer reactants and therefore produce less electrical energy in total, but the voltage does not change.

## Cells in series

When two or more cells are connected with the positive terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the next, they are connected **in series**, and their voltages add:

$$\mathrm{EMF_{battery}} = n(\text{cells}) \times \mathrm{EMF_{cell}}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battery** | A device that produces electricity by transforming chemical energy into electrical energy; several electric cells connected together |
| **Electrodes** | Plates or rods made of dissimilar metals, one positive and one negative, immersed in the electrolyte |
| **Cathode** | The positive $(+)$ electrode, e.g. carbon, copper, silver |
| **Anode** | The negative $(-)$ electrode, e.g. zinc, aluminium |
| **Electrolyte** | The solution (wet batteries) or paste (dry batteries) in which the electrodes are immersed |
| **Terminal** | The part of each electrode outside the solution |
| **Connected in series (cells)** | Positive terminal of one cell joined to the negative terminal of another, so that the voltages add |

# 18.2 Electric Current

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The circuit

An **electric circuit** is a continuous conducting path connected between the terminals of a battery — so there is a potential difference across it. Its elements are the battery, a device run by electrical energy (the resistance), conducting wires, and a switch.

Three kinds of circuit are distinguished:

| Circuit | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Complete circuit** | A continuous conducting path |
| **Open circuit** | There is a break in the circuit, so no current flows |
| **Short circuit** | Two wires that should not have touched have touched, so the current is shortened |

In many real circuits the wires are connected to a common conductor, called the **ground**, to provide continuity.

## What a current is

The purpose of a battery is to produce a potential difference, and a potential difference is what makes charges move. Potential difference is the same thing as voltage, so voltage provides the force that pushes charge through a circuit. When a complete circuit is formed, any flow of charge through the wires is called an electric current.

**Electric current** is the net amount of charge that passes through the wire's full cross-section at any point, per unit time:

$$I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$$

where $I$ is the electric current in amperes (A), $\Delta Q$ is the amount of charge that passes through in coulombs (C), and $\Delta t$ is the time interval in seconds (s).

The unit is the **ampere (A)**, named after André Ampère:

$$1\ \mathrm{A} = 1\ \mathrm{C/s} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{mA} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} \qquad 1\ \mu\mathrm{A} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{A}$$

Current is a **scalar**. Its direction along a given wire is constant, but it is not a vector quantity.

## Conventional current and electron current

Two directions have to be kept apart:

- **Conventional current** is the direction in which positive charge would flow: from high potential to low potential. This convention was fixed before the electron was discovered, and it is still the one used today.
- **Electron current** is the direction electrons actually flow: from low potential to high potential.

Nothing is lost by keeping the old convention, because positive charges flowing in one direction is exactly equivalent to negative charges flowing in the opposite direction.

## Conservation of electric charge

Charge does not disappear. A steady current is, at any instant, the same at one point of the circuit as at any other point. A battery does not create or destroy charge, and a lightbulb does not destroy or create charge either — the battery supplies the potential difference and the bulb converts energy, but the quantity of charge passing per second is the same all the way round.

## Measuring current

An **ammeter** is a device that measures electric current. Because the whole current must pass through it, it is connected **in series**. Its own resistance $R_{\text{ammeter}} \approx 0$, so it can be treated as a piece of wire and does not change the circuit it is measuring.

Its measurement ranges are $0$–$3\ \mathrm{A}$ and $0$–$0.6\ \mathrm{A}$. Use the larger range first to prevent damage to the instrument, then change to the smaller range once you know the current is safe.

A **galvanometer** measures smaller currents.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electric circuit** | A continuous conducting path connected between the terminals of a battery |
| **Complete circuit** | A continuous conducting path |
| **Open circuit** | A circuit with a break in it, so no current flows |
| **Short circuit** | A circuit in which two wires that should not have touched have touched |
| **Ground** | A common conductor to which wires are connected to provide continuity |
| **Electric current** | The net amount of charge that passes through the wire's full cross-section at any point per unit time, $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$ |
| **Ampere (A)** | The unit of current; $1\ \mathrm{A} = 1\ \mathrm{C/s}$ |
| **Conventional current** | The direction positive charge would flow, from high potential to low potential |
| **Electron current** | The direction of electron flow, from low potential to high potential |
| **Conservation of electric charge** | Charge does not disappear; a steady current is the same at every point of a circuit at any instant |
| **Ammeter** | A device that measures electric current, connected in series, with $R \approx 0$ |
| **Galvanometer** | A device that measures smaller currents |

# 18.3 Ohm's Law: Resistance and Resistors

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Potential difference and the energy it carries

The higher the voltage, the more energy there is to push electrons out, and so the greater the flow of current. The energy carried by a charge moved through a potential difference is

$$E = QV$$

where $E$ is energy in joules (J), $Q$ is charge in coulombs (C) and $V$ is the potential difference in volts (V).

A **voltmeter** measures potential difference. Because a potential difference is a difference *across* something, the voltmeter is connected **in parallel** with the component whose voltage is wanted. Its measurement ranges are $0$–$15\ \mathrm{V}$ and $0$–$3\ \mathrm{V}$.

## Ohm's law

**Georg Simon Ohm** established that the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the potential difference applied to its two ends:

$$I \propto V$$

Written with the constant of proportionality made explicit, this is **Ohm's law**:

$$V = IR$$

with $V$ the voltage in volts (V), $I$ the current in amperes (A) and $R$ the electrical resistance in ohms ($\Omega$).

**Electrical resistance** is the ratio of the potential difference across a resistor to the current through it.

## Resistors

**Resistors** are used to control the amount of current. Their values range from under $1\ \Omega$ to over $10^{6}\ \Omega$. The two main types are:

- **Wire-wound** resistors, which consist of a coil of fine wire.
- **Composition** resistors, usually made of carbon, and thin carbon or metal films.

## Ohmic and non-ohmic materials

Ohm's law is not a fundamental law. It is a description of a certain class of materials — metal conductors. Its precondition is that $R$ is a constant independent of $V$. Materials whose $R$ is not constant are said to be **non-ohmic**; semiconductor diodes and filament lamps are the examples the guide gives.

This has a direct consequence for graphs. On an $I$–$V$ graph the slope is $\dfrac{1}{R}$, so the shape of the curve reads off how the resistance behaves:

| Component | How $R$ behaves | Shape of the $I$–$V$ graph |
|---|---|---|
| Conductor (metal) | $R$ is constant | Straight line — a linear relationship |
| Semiconductor diode | $R$ decreases as $V$ increases | Concave up |
| Filament lamp | $R$ increases as $V$ increases | Concave down |

A rising slope means a falling $R$, and a falling slope means a rising $R$ — which is why the diode's curve bends upwards and the lamp's bends downwards.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Voltmeter** | A device that measures potential differences, connected in parallel |
| **Ohm's law** | $V = IR$: the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the potential difference applied to its two ends |
| **Electrical resistance** | The ratio of the potential difference across a resistor to the current through it, measured in ohms ($\Omega$) |
| **Resistor** | A component used to control the amount of current; wire-wound (a coil of fine wire) or composition (carbon, or thin carbon or metal films) |
| **Non-ohmic** | Describes a material whose resistance is not constant and independent of $V$, e.g. semiconductor diodes and filament lamps |

# 18.4 Resistivity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The law of resistance

The resistance $R$ of any wire is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area:

$$R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$$

- $R$: resistance ($\Omega$)
- $\rho$: resistivity ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$)
- $L$: length (m)
- $A$: cross-sectional area ($\mathrm{m^2}$)

**Resistivity** is the constant of proportionality in that relationship. Unlike $R$ itself it does not describe a particular piece of wire but the material the wire is made of. It also depends somewhat on purity, heat treatment, temperature and other factors.

## Choosing a material for wires

Resistivity alone does not decide which metal gets used:

| Metal | Property | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Silver | Lowest resistivity, but very expensive | Not used for ordinary wiring |
| Copper | Resistivity close to silver's, and much less expensive | Most wires |
| Aluminium | Higher resistivity, but less dense | Preferable for transmission lines |

Aluminium is the case worth noticing: resistivity is not the only criterion, and here the lower density is what decides.

## Temperature dependence

**For metal conductors, resistance increases with temperature.** As $T$ rises the atoms move more rapidly and are arranged in a less orderly fashion, so they interfere more with the flow of electrons and make them harder to move past.

Provided the temperature change is not too great, resistivity increases nearly linearly with temperature:

$$\rho_T = \rho_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]$$

- $\rho_T$: resistivity at temperature $T$ ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$)
- $\rho_0$: resistivity at the reference temperature $T_0$, usually taken as $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- $\alpha$: temperature coefficient ($1/^\circ\mathrm{C}$)

Because $R = \rho L/A$, multiplying both sides by $L/A$ turns the same statement into one about resistance:

$$R_T = R_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]$$

**For semiconductors the effect runs the other way**: resistance and resistivity *decrease* as temperature increases. As $T$ rises, some electrons that were normally not free become free and can contribute to the current flow. The temperature coefficient for a semiconductor can therefore be negative.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of resistance** | The resistance of any wire is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, $R = \rho L/A$ |
| **Resistivity ($\rho$)** | The constant of proportionality in $R = \rho L/A$; depends on the material used, and somewhat on purity, heat treatment and temperature ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$) |
| **Temperature coefficient ($\alpha$)** | The constant in $\rho_T = \rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$, in $1/^\circ\mathrm{C}$; can be negative for semiconductors |

# 18.5 Electric Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where the energy goes

Electrical devices convert electrical energy into other forms — mechanical, thermal and so on. In an ordinary lightbulb only a few percent of the energy is transformed into visible light; the remaining more than 90 per cent becomes thermal energy.

The chain of events inside the filament explains why:

1. Many collisions occur between the moving electrons and the atoms of the wire.
2. In each collision part of the electron's kinetic energy is transferred to the atom.
3. The kinetic energy of the atoms increases, and hence the temperature of the wire increases.
4. This increased thermal energy can then be transferred as heat by conduction, convection or radiation, or as light.

## Power

**Power** is the rate at which energy is transformed. Starting from $E = QV$ and $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{QV}{t} = IV$$

Substituting Ohm's law gives the two other forms, which matter because in practice you rarely know all three of $I$, $V$ and $R$ at once:

$$P = IV = I(IR) = I^2R \qquad\qquad P = IV = \left(\frac{V}{R}\right)V = \frac{V^2}{R}$$

The unit is the **watt (W)**:

$$1\ \mathrm{W} = 1\ \mathrm{J/s} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{kW} = 1000\ \mathrm{W} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{hp} = 746\ \mathrm{W}$$

## Ratings and actual power

Three related terms must be kept apart:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Voltage rating** | The designed voltage of the device |
| **Power rating** | The power when the device is supplied with its designed voltage |
| **Power dissipated** | The actual power the device is using |

It is the power dissipated, not the power rating, that determines how a bulb behaves: the greater the actual power used by a lightbulb, the brighter it is.

## Energy

$$E = Pt$$

with $E$ in joules. Electricity is billed in kilowatt-hours rather than joules:

$$1\ \mathrm{kWh} = (1000\ \mathrm{W})(3600\ \mathrm{s}) = 3.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Power** | The rate of energy transformed, $P = E/t = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$ |
| **Watt (W)** | The unit of power; $1\ \mathrm{W} = 1\ \mathrm{J/s}$ |
| **Voltage rating** | The designed voltage of a device |
| **Power rating** | The power of a device when supplied with its designed voltage |
| **Power dissipated** | The actual power used by a device |

# 18.6 Power in Household Circuits

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Overloading, and the two devices that guard against it

A wire is **overloaded** when it carries more current than is safe. Two devices break the circuit before that happens.

A **fuse** is a length of wire designed to melt, and so break the circuit, when the current passing through it goes above a certain level. It is simple and cheap, and its material should have a low melting point and high conductivity. The thicker the fuse wire, the greater the current required to make it melt. Its **rating current** is the labelled maximum effective current it is designed to allow: when

$$I_{\text{effective}} > I_{\text{rating}}$$

the fuse melts and burns. Once a fuse has burnt out it cannot be used again.

A **circuit breaker** is a safety device that uses an electromagnet or a bimetallic strip to shut off the circuit when the current goes above a certain value. Circuit breakers act more quickly than fuses, and can be reset using the outside switch instead of being replaced.

| Type | How it operates |
|---|---|
| **Bimetallic strip circuit breaker** | Heating of the strip causes it to bend so far to one side that the notch in the spring-loaded metal strip drops down over the end |
| **Electromagnet circuit breaker** | Too much current causes the electromagnet to produce a magnetic field strong enough to open the switch |

If a circuit repeatedly burns out a fuse or opens a circuit breaker, there are two possibilities: too many devices are drawing current in that circuit, or there is a short circuit, in which the resistance is very small and so the current is very large.

## Why household circuits are wired in parallel

Household circuits are parallel circuits. There are several paths for the current to take, and the voltage across each component is the same.

- **Advantages.** If one light goes out, the others burn brightly without change. As lights are added, the current flowing through each light does not change.
- **Disadvantage.** Parallel circuits are more difficult to design and build.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Overloaded** | Describes a wire carrying more current than is safe |
| **Fuse** | A length of wire designed to melt, and so break a circuit, when the current through it goes above a certain level |
| **Rating current** | The labelled maximum effective current a fuse is designed to allow |
| **Circuit breaker** | A safety device using an electromagnet or bimetallic strip to shut off the circuit when the current goes above a certain value |

markdown:
# 18.7 Alternating Current

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two kinds of current

**Direct current (dc)** moves steadily in one direction. Thomas Alva Edison championed and commercialised it, and a battery is the everyday example.

**Alternating current (ac)** reverses direction many times per second and is commonly sinusoidal. Nikola Tesla developed and championed it, and electric generators are the everyday example. The guide prints that dc was "first found by" Edison and ac "first found by" Tesla; that is an error — neither man discovered a kind of current, and each promoted one side of the late-nineteenth-century dispute over how electricity should be distributed.

## Voltage and current in an ac circuit

The voltage of an ac supply is

$$V = V_0\sin 2\pi f t = V_0\sin\omega t$$

- $V$: the potential, which oscillates between $+V_0$ and $-V_0$ (V)
- $V_0$: peak voltage (V)
- $f$: frequency — the number of complete oscillations made per second ($1/\mathrm{s}$)
- $\omega$: angular frequency, $\omega = 2\pi f$ ($\mathrm{rad/s}$)

Applying Ohm's law to that voltage gives the current:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t = I_0\sin\omega t$$

where $I_0$ is the peak current (A). The current is counted positive when electrons flow in one direction and negative when they flow in the opposite direction, so the **average current is zero**.

## Power, and why it is not zero

$$P = I^2R = I_0^2R\sin^2\omega t$$

Although the average current is zero, the average power is not, because the current is squared: $P$ is always positive. This is why an ac supply delivers energy at all, despite the average current cancelling to nothing.

Taking the average of $\sin^2\omega t$ over a cycle gives

$$\bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2R = \tfrac{1}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{R}$$

where $\bar P$ is the average power (W).

## Root-mean-square values

The same factor of $\tfrac12$ appears in the mean square current and voltage:

$$\overline{I^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2 \qquad\qquad \overline{V^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_0^2$$

Taking the square root of each defines the **rms (root-mean-square)** values, sometimes called the **effective values**:

$$I_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{I^2}} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,I_0 \qquad\qquad V_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{V^2}} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,V_0$$

Written with these, the average power takes exactly the form the dc power equations had:

$$\bar P = I_{\mathrm{rms}}V_{\mathrm{rms}} \qquad \bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2R = I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R \qquad \bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{R}$$

That is the point of defining them: a direct current whose values of $I$ and $V$ equal the rms values of $I$ and $V$ for an alternating current will produce the same power.

One consequence of the squaring is worth remembering for graphs: the period of the power is half the period of the voltage and the current.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Direct current (dc)** | Current that moves steadily in one direction |
| **Alternating current (ac)** | Current that reverses direction many times per second, commonly sinusoidal |
| **Peak voltage ($V_0$)** | The maximum value of the oscillating potential, between $+V_0$ and $-V_0$ |
| **Peak current ($I_0$)** | The maximum value of the oscillating current |
| **Frequency ($f$)** | The number of complete oscillations made per second ($1/\mathrm{s}$) |
| **Angular frequency ($\omega$)** | $\omega = 2\pi f$, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$ |
| **Average power ($\bar P$)** | $\bar P = \tfrac12 I_0^2R = I_{\mathrm{rms}}V_{\mathrm{rms}}$ |
| **rms (root-mean-square) values** | $I_{\mathrm{rms}} = I_0/\sqrt2$ and $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$; also called the effective values |

title: EMF and Terminal Voltage
