markdown:
# 19.1 EMF and Terminal Voltage

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Electromotive force

**Electromotive force (emf)** is the potential difference between the terminals of a source when no current flows to an external circuit. A source of emf transforms one type of energy — chemical, mechanical, light and so on — into electrical energy. A battery and an electric generator are both sources of emf.

The qualification "when no current flows" is the whole content of this section, because as soon as current *does* flow the terminals no longer read the emf.

## Internal resistance and terminal voltage

**Internal resistance** is the resistance of the battery itself. It is usually small, but it increases as the battery ages.

**Terminal voltage** is the voltage actually measured between the two terminals $a$ and $b$:

$$V_{ab} = V_a - V_b$$

Two cases follow:

| Condition | Terminal voltage |
|---|---|
| No current is drawn from the battery | $V_{ab} = \varepsilon$ |
| A current flows from the battery | $V_{ab} = \varepsilon - Ir$ |

where $V_{ab}$ is the terminal voltage (V), $\varepsilon$ is the emf (V) and $Ir$ is the internal voltage drop (V). The drop $Ir$ is why a battery under load reads lower than the same battery sitting unconnected — the current has to be pushed through the battery's own resistance before it reaches the terminals.

## The circuit equation

Since $V_{ab} = IR$ for the external resistance $R$:

$$IR = \varepsilon - Ir \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \varepsilon = I(R + r)$$

This is a better exemplification of Ohm's law than $V = IR$ alone, because it accounts for every resistance the current meets, inside the source as well as outside it.

The same split applies to power:

$$P_T = P_R + P_r = I^2R + I^2r = I^2(R + r)$$

Some of the energy the source supplies is dissipated inside the source itself, and only $I^2R$ reaches the external circuit.

## Worked example: finding the internal resistance from two voltage readings

*Two resistors are placed in series with a battery of potential $V$. Resistance $R_2$ has the value $1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega$. A voltmeter shows the potential across $R_1$ to be $3.00\ \mathrm{V}$ and an ammeter shows the current through $R_2$ to be $5.00\ \mathrm{mA}$.*

**Connecting the meters.** The voltmeter goes across $R_1$, in parallel with it, and no existing wire has to be disconnected to do that. The ammeter must carry the current itself, so it goes in series with $R_2$: the wire on one side of $R_2$ is broken and the ammeter inserted into the gap.

**(c) The value of $R_1$.** The resistors are in series, so the ammeter reading is also the current through $R_1$:

$$R_1 = \frac{V_1}{I} = \frac{3.00\ \mathrm{V}}{5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}} = 6.00\times10^{2}\ \Omega$$

**(d) The power dissipated by $R_2$.** Current and resistance are the two quantities known for $R_2$, so use $P = I^2R$:

$$P_2 = I^2R_2 = (5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A})^2(1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega) = 2.50\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{W}$$

**(e) The terminal voltage $V$ of the battery.** In series the voltages add, and

$$V_2 = IR_2 = (5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A})(1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega) = 5.00\ \mathrm{V}$$

$$V_{ab} = V_1 + V_2 = 3.00 + 5.00 = 8.00\ \mathrm{V}$$

**(f) The internal resistance.** With the battery disconnected no current is drawn, so the $8.20\ \mathrm{V}$ measured then is the emf itself. The difference between emf and terminal voltage is the internal drop:

$$\varepsilon - V_{ab} = Ir \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r = \frac{\varepsilon - V_{ab}}{I} = \frac{8.20 - 8.00}{5.00\times10^{-3}} = 40\ \Omega$$

The $0.20\ \mathrm{V}$ that appears to have gone missing between parts (e) and (f) is exactly the voltage lost inside the battery.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electromotive force (emf, $\varepsilon$)** | The potential difference between the terminals of a source when no current flows to an external circuit |
| **Internal resistance ($r$)** | The resistance of the battery itself; usually small, but it increases as the battery ages |
| **Terminal voltage ($V_{ab}$)** | The actual voltage measured between the two terminals, $V_{ab} = V_a - V_b$; equal to $\varepsilon$ with no current drawn and to $\varepsilon - Ir$ when a current flows |

# 19.2 Resistors in Series and in Parallel

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Series circuits

Two or more resistors are **connected in series** when they are joined end to end along a single path. There is only one path, so if one device is disconnected the current stops in all the others.

**The same current passes through each resistor.**

$$I = I_1 = I_2 = I_3$$

This follows from conservation of charge: any charge that passes through $R_1$ must also pass through the others, so the same $Q$ passes each resistor in the same time and $I$ is the same.

**The total voltage is the sum of the voltages across each resistor**, by conservation of energy:

$$V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$$

Applying Ohm's law to each term:

$$V = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3 = I(R_1 + R_2 + R_3) = IR_{eq}$$

$$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$$

The **equivalent resistance** $R_{eq}$ is a single resistor whose resistance is the same as the total resistance of the circuit — here, the sum of the separate resistors. Since the current is common, the voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances:

$$V_1 : V_2 : V_3 = R_1 : R_2 : R_3$$

Power behaves the same way:

$$P_T = I^2R_T = I^2(R_1 + R_2 + R_3) = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 \qquad P_1 : P_2 : P_3 = R_1 : R_2 : R_3$$

so in a series circuit the **larger resistance gives the brighter lightbulb**.

**Advantage:** simple to design and build. **Disadvantages:** if one light goes out, all the lights go out; and the lightbulbs become dimmer as more bulbs are added.

## Parallel circuits

Resistors are **connected in parallel** when the current from the source splits into separate branches or paths.

**The same voltage is across each resistor:**

$$V = V_1 = V_2 = V_3$$

**The total current is the sum of the currents flowing through each resistor:**

$$I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3$$

Applying Ohm's law, $I = V/R_{eq}$, and

$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} \qquad I_1 : I_2 : I_3 = \frac{1}{R_1} : \frac{1}{R_2} : \frac{1}{R_3}$$

Because the voltage is now the common quantity, the ratios invert: the *smallest* resistance takes the largest share of the current.

$$P_T = I_TV = (I_1 + I_2 + I_3)V = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 \qquad P_1 : P_2 : P_3 = \frac{1}{R_1} : \frac{1}{R_2} : \frac{1}{R_3}$$

**Advantages:** if there is a break in one branch, current can still move through the other branches; and the brightness of the original lightbulbs does not change when more are added (ignoring $r$). **Disadvantages:** more difficult to design and build; and adding too many appliances will increase the current too much, which might heat up the wire and cause a fire.

## Worked example: adding a lamp in parallel

*A lamp, a voltmeter $V$, an ammeter $A$ and a battery with zero internal resistance are connected together. A second lamp is then connected in parallel with the first.*

**How does the ammeter's reading change?** *It increases, because the net resistance of the circuit decreases.* Adding a resistance in parallel always lowers $R_{eq}$ — the reciprocals add, so $1/R_{eq}$ grows and $R_{eq}$ shrinks. The ammeter sits where the whole current passes, so with the same voltage across a smaller $R_{eq}$ it reads a larger $I = V/R_{eq}$. The tempting answer, that the current "splits to feed both branches" and so falls, confuses the current in one branch with the current through the ammeter.

**How does the voltmeter's reading change?** *It remains the same, because the voltmeter is connected to the two ends of the battery.* The voltmeter reads the terminal voltage, and with zero internal resistance $V_{ab} = \varepsilon - Ir = \varepsilon$ no matter how much current is drawn. The second branch therefore changes the current without changing the voltage — which is exactly the property that makes parallel wiring usable in houses.

## 19.2(2) Combined circuits

A **combined circuit** is a circuit which includes both series and parallel branches — a parallel-series or a series-parallel arrangement. The guide flags this as one of the two focuses of the final.

The problem-solving strategy is fixed:

1. Figure out the series or parallel relationships between the resistors in the circuit.
2. Get $R_{eq}$.
3. Get $I_{\text{total}}$ and $V_{\text{total}}$.
4. Find the individual $V$, $I$ and $P$.

*Worked example.* A circuit contains a $2\ \Omega$ resistor and two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors, with a switch that changes how they are connected. Begin by settling the relationships for the switch position in question. With the switch off, the two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel with each other and that combination is in series with the $2\ \Omega$ resistor.

**Step 2.** The parallel pair first:

$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{4.0} + \frac{1}{4.0} = \frac{1}{2.0} \qquad R_{eq} = 2.0\ \Omega$$

then the total, since this pair is in series with the $2\ \Omega$ resistor:

$$R_{\text{total}} = 2\ \Omega + 2.0\ \Omega = 4.0\ \Omega$$

**Step 3.**

$$I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{R_{\text{total}}}$$

**Step 4.** Work outwards from what each element shares with the rest of the circuit.

- The $2\ \Omega$ resistor is in series with everything else, so it carries the whole current: $I_{2\Omega} = I_{\text{total}}$, and its voltage is its share of the total,

$$V_{2\Omega} = V_{\text{total}}\times\frac{2\ \Omega}{R_{\text{total}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{total}}$$

- The two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel, so their currents *sum* to $I_{\text{total}}$ while their voltages are equal to each other:

$$V_{4.0\Omega} = V_{\text{total}}\times\frac{R_{eq}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{total}}$$

The two halves add back to $V_{\text{total}}$, which is the check worth doing at the end of any combined-circuit problem.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Connected in series** | Two or more resistors connected end to end along a single path |
| **Connected in parallel** | Resistors arranged so that the current from the source splits into separate branches or paths |
| **Equivalent resistance ($R_{eq}$)** | A single resistor with the resistance that is the same as the total resistance of the circuit |
| **Combined circuit** | A circuit which includes both series and parallel branches |

markdown:
# 20.1 Magnets and Magnetic Fields

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## History of magnetism

The ancient Greeks and Chinese discovered that lodestone could attract iron objects and other lodestone. Chinese sailors employed magnets as navigation compasses approximately 900 years ago.

## Magnets and magnetic poles

A **magnet** is an object surrounded by a magnetic field which has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials — iron, nickel and cobalt. A compass needle is simply a bar magnet supported at its centre of gravity so that it can rotate freely.

The **magnetic poles** are the areas of a magnet where the magnetic effect is strongest. Every magnet is **polarised**: it has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). The N pole is the north-seeking pole and the S pole is the south-seeking pole — the names describe which way the pole turns when the magnet is free to rotate.

Between magnets, **like poles repel and unlike poles attract**.

Magnetic poles always appear in pairs. Monopoles of magnets do not exist.

## Magnetism and magnetic domains

**Ferromagnetism** is the strong magnetic effect shown by iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys.

Its source lies inside the atoms and then in how the atoms group together:

- The spinning and orbiting motion of the electrons makes each atom a tiny magnet.
- A cluster of billions of atoms whose magnetic fields are all lined up in the same way forms a **magnetic domain**. Each domain is itself like a tiny magnet.

**Magnetisation** is then a question of how the domains are arranged. An unmagnetised piece of iron is made up of domains that are randomly arranged, so their fields cancel. In a magnet the domains are aligned in one direction, and the magnetisation process may also alter their size.

## Induced magnetism and making a magnet

Both the N and the S pole of a magnet attract metals such as iron and steel. This is because unmagnetised materials such as steel and iron acquire two opposite magnetic poles when placed in the neighbourhood of a magnet — the material becomes a magnet itself, oriented so as to be attracted. That is how **induced magnetism** arises.

Two ways of making a magnet follow:

- Place the unmagnetised material near a magnet. This gains only weak magnetism.
- Use an **electromagnet**: pass a direct current through a coil of wire placed outside the material.

## Hard and soft magnetic materials

Magnetic materials are classified by how well they keep their magnetism.

| | Hard magnetic materials | Soft magnetic materials |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour | Difficult to magnetise, but do not readily lose their magnetism | Relatively easy to magnetise, but their magnetism is only temporary |
| Used for | Permanent magnets | Temporary magnets — the cores of electromagnets and transformers, because their magnetic effect can be switched on or off or reversed easily |
| Examples | Steel, and the alloys Alnico, Alcomax and Magnadur | Iron (soft iron) and Mumetal |

**Non-magnetic materials** include the metals brass, copper, zinc, tin and aluminium, as well as non-metals.

## Demagnetising a magnet

Both methods work by destroying the alignment of the domains:

- Drop a magnet on the floor or strike it with a hammer. The principle is to jar the domains into randomness, and the magnet loses some or all of its magnetism.
- Heat a permanent magnet. Raising the temperature increases the random thermal motion of the atoms, which tends to randomise the domains. Above a certain temperature the material loses the property of ferromagnetism altogether.

## The magnetic field and its field lines

The **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where the magnetic force is exerted.

It can be investigated in two ways. A small compass can be used: the direction of the magnetic field $B$ at any point is the same as the direction the compass indicates. Alternatively the field can be mapped out with iron filings, which line up along it. In both cases the field $B$ is strong where the lines are dense and weak where they are sparse.

**Magnetic field lines** are imaginary lines used to map out the magnetic field around a magnet. They are three-dimensional. The field direction is defined as the direction in which the force on an N pole would act. This definition fixes the arrows:

- Outside the magnet, the lines run from N to S.
- Inside the magnet, they run from S to N.
- A compass placed at any point lies tangent to the line of force passing through that point.
- The density of the lines represents how strong the magnetic field is.

Where two magnets sit near one another their fields superpose into a single combined field.

Bringing other materials into a field has different effects depending on the material. Glass produces no reaction. In a ferromagnetic material the field lines become concentrated within the material, and the material is magnetised by induction: the end closest to the N pole of the magnet becomes the S pole of the material, and the end closest to the S pole of the magnet becomes the N pole.

Between two wide poles of a magnet the magnetic field is nearly **uniform**, except near the edges.

## Earth as a magnet

Earth's magnetism is due to the circulation of the molten metal within Earth's core. The Earth is a large weak magnet with its magnetic S pole — the south-seeking pole — under a point in Canada.

Two angles describe how a compass behaves at a given place:

- **Magnetic declination** is the angular difference between the direction of a compass needle, which points along the magnetic field lines, and true (geographical) north at that location.
- **The angle of dip**, or angle of inclination, is the angle that the Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point. It is not zero because the Earth's magnetic field at most locations is not tangent to the Earth's surface.

The field is not fixed. Magnetic poles reverse themselves periodically, and Earth's north magnetic pole has been moving over time, on the order of 10 km per year in recent decades. Magnetism in rocks solidified at various times in the past — their ages determined by radioactive dating — suggests that the poles reversed direction 400 times over the last 330 million years.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Magnet** | An object surrounded by a magnetic field which has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) |
| **Magnetic poles** | The areas of a magnet where the magnetic effect is strongest |
| **Ferromagnetism** | The strong magnetic effect shown by iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys |
| **Magnetic domain** | A cluster of billions of atoms whose magnetic fields are all lined up in the same way; each domain is like a tiny magnet |
| **Magnetisation** | The process by which randomly arranged domains become aligned in one direction, their size possibly being altered too |
| **Induced magnetism** | The magnetism acquired by an unmagnetised material such as iron or steel, which gains two opposite poles when placed near a magnet |
| **Electromagnet** | A magnet made by passing direct current through a coil of wire placed outside the material |
| **Hard magnetic materials** | Materials difficult to magnetise that do not readily lose their magnetism; used for permanent magnets |
| **Soft magnetic materials** | Materials relatively easy to magnetise whose magnetism is only temporary; used for temporary magnets and the cores of electromagnets and transformers |
| **Magnetic field** | The region around a magnet where the magnetic force is exerted |
| **Magnetic field lines** | Imaginary three-dimensional lines mapping out the magnetic field, directed as the force on an N pole would act |
| **Magnetic declination** | The angular difference between the direction of a compass needle at any location and true (geographical) north |
| **Angle of dip (angle of inclination)** | The angle that the Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point |

title: Electric Currents Produce Magnetic Fields
summary: Hans Christian Oersted (1777–1851) made the discovery in 1820 that magnetism and electricity are related. - The compass needle deflects if, and only if, the wire carries an electric current. - Wheneve
markdown:
# 20.2 Electric Currents Produce Magnetic Fields

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Oersted's experiment

Hans Christian Oersted (1777–1851) made the discovery in 1820 that magnetism and electricity are related.

- The compass needle deflects if, and only if, the wire carries an electric current.
- Whenever he turned on the electricity, the compass needles lined up in a circle around the wire.
- Iron filings also align along the direction of the magnetic field lines near a straight current-carrying wire.

The "if and only if" is the important half: a wire with no current does nothing, so it is the current, not the metal, that produces the field.

## The magnetic field around a wire

If an electric current is passed through a wire, a weak magnetic field is produced. It has three features:

- The magnetic field lines are circles.
- The field is strongest close to the wire.
- Increasing the current increases the strength of the field.

The direction of the current $I$ determines the direction of the magnetic field $B$. Use the **1st right-hand rule**: grip the wire with the right hand so that the thumb points along the conventional current, and the fingers curl in the direction of the field lines.

*Worked example.* A long straight wire conductor carries a constant, stable conventional current towards the north. A compass is placed directly above the wire. When a large conventional current flows, which way does the N pole of the compass point?

Point the right thumb north along the current. The fingers curl over the top of the wire towards the east, so at a point directly above the wire the field runs east. A compass needle lies along the field, so its **N pole points east**.

## Magnetic field due to a long straight wire (section 20.5)

$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$

where $\mu_0$ is the **permeability of free space**,

$$\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$$

and $r$ is the distance from the wire. The standard unit of magnetic field $B$ is the **tesla (T)**. The $1/r$ in the formula is the quantitative form of "the field is strongest close to the wire", and the $I$ on top is "increasing the current increases the field".

## Combining the fields of two wires

When two wires are present, both the magnitude and the direction of $B$ must be found for each wire separately and then combined. Two cases recur.

**Where do the fields cancel?** *Two very long current-carrying wires are shown end on. The wire on the left carries $4\ \mathrm{A}$ into the plane of the paper and the wire on the right carries $3\ \mathrm{A}$ out of the paper. Disregarding $x\to\infty$, in which region of the $x$-axis could the two fields add to zero?*

Because the currents are in opposite directions, the two fields point the *same* way in the region between the wires, so they can never cancel there. Outside the pair they oppose, and cancellation requires

$$\frac{\mu_0(4\ \mathrm{A})}{2\pi d_1} = \frac{\mu_0(3\ \mathrm{A})}{2\pi d_2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{d_1}{d_2} = \frac{4}{3}$$

so the point must be further from the $4\ \mathrm{A}$ wire than from the $3\ \mathrm{A}$ wire. That is only possible on the far side of the weaker wire — the region beyond the $3\ \mathrm{A}$ wire, region III, and no other.

**What is the resultant at a given point?** *A long pair of insulated wires conducts $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$ of dc current to and from an instrument. The wires are of negligible diameter and are $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. What is the magnetic field $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from their midpoint, in their plane? Compare it with the magnetic field of the Earth.*

"To and from" means the two currents are equal and opposite. Each wire lies $1.4\ \mathrm{mm}$ from the midpoint, so the field point is at

$$r_1 = 0.100 - 0.0014 = 0.0986\ \mathrm{m} \qquad r_2 = 0.100 + 0.0014 = 0.1014\ \mathrm{m}$$

At a point in the plane of the wires and outside the pair, the two fields are antiparallel, so they subtract:

$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right) = (2\times10^{-7})(24.5)\left(\frac{1}{0.0986} - \frac{1}{0.1014}\right)$$

$$B = (4.9\times10^{-6})(10.142 - 9.862) = 1.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{T}$$

The nearer wire wins, so the resultant takes its direction, which in the figure is into the page. Comparing with the Earth's field of $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$:

$$\frac{1.4\times10^{-6}}{5\times10^{-5}} \approx 0.03$$

so $B$ is about **3 per cent of $B_E$**. Notice how much the near-cancellation costs: each wire on its own would give about $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$ at this point, and together they give a field more than thirty times smaller. Two nearly cancelling fields is what makes this pair of leads worth comparing with the Earth's field at all.

## Magnetic field for coils (section 20.7, solenoids)

A **solenoid** is a current-carrying coil of wire with many loops.

- The magnetic field lines are bunched up inside the loop.
- Increasing the number of loops increases the field.

A solenoid acts like a magnet: one end can be considered the north pole and the other the south pole. Increasing the current increases the strength of the field. Unlike a bar magnet, the field is temporary — it is turned on and off by switching the current on and off — and the north and south poles change with the direction of the current.

To find the poles of the solenoid, use the **2nd right-hand rule**, which also works in reverse to find the direction of the current in the wires:

- Grip the coil with your right hand.
- Your fingers point in the conventional current direction.
- Your thumb points towards the N pole of the coil.

Two consequences worth stating as true-or-false drill: the right-hand rule *can* be used to determine the direction of the magnetic field inside a solenoid when the current direction is known, since the rule relates current direction to field in exactly that way. But the claim that the field strength inside a solenoid *increases* if the number of turns per unit length decreases is false — more loops means a stronger field, so fewer turns per unit length gives a weaker one.

## Electromagnets

If a piece of iron is placed inside a solenoid, the magnetic field is increased greatly, because the iron itself becomes a magnet. The resulting magnetic field is the sum of the field due to the current and the field due to the iron, and can be hundreds or thousands of times the field due to the current alone.

The properties of electromagnets are basically those of solenoids, with the iron core added as a fourth:

- Can be switched on and off freely.
- $I$ increases, $B$ increases.
- Number of loops increases, $B$ increases.
- Soft iron core added, $B$ increases.

Applications include the electromagnetic crane, magnetic circuit breakers, the doorbell, and the magnetisation and demagnetisation of magnets:

- **To magnetise** a magnet, insert the material into the solenoid.
- **To demagnetise** a magnet, slowly pull it out of a solenoid through which an alternating current is passing. The ac produces a magnetic field which changes direction very rapidly and throws the atoms in the magnet out of line.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1st right-hand rule** | The rule giving the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire from the direction of the conventional current |
| **Permeability of free space ($\mu_0$)** | The constant $4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$ appearing in $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi r$ |
| **Tesla (T)** | The standard unit of magnetic field $B$ |
| **Solenoid** | A current-carrying coil of wire with many loops |
| **2nd right-hand rule** | Grip the coil with the right hand, fingers in the conventional current direction; the thumb points towards the N pole of the coil |
| **Electromagnet** | A solenoid with a piece of iron placed inside it, whose field is the sum of the field due to the current and the field due to the iron |

markdown:
# 20.3 Force on an Electric Current in a Magnetic Field

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ampère's force

Section 20.2 showed that a current produces a magnetic field. The converse also holds: a magnet exerts a force on a current-carrying wire. This is **Ampère's force**.

$$F = Il_\perp B = IlB\sin\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the current direction and the magnetic field, and $l_\perp$ is the component of the wire's length perpendicular to $B$. The two extremes follow immediately from the sine:

$$F_{\max} = IlB \quad \text{when } \theta = 90^\circ\ (\text{wire} \perp \text{magnetic field})$$

$$F_{\min} = 0 \quad \text{when } \theta = 0^\circ\ (\text{wire} \parallel \text{magnetic field})$$

So the statement that the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is zero if the wire is parallel to the magnetic field is **true** — $\sin 0^\circ = 0$ removes the force entirely.

The standard unit of $B$, the **tesla (T)**, is derived from this formula:

$$1\ \mathrm{T} = 1\ \mathrm{N/(A\cdot m)}$$

## How big are real magnetic fields?

| Field | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| Earth's magnetic field | $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T} = 0.5$ gauss |
| Strongest permanent magnets | near $2\ \mathrm{T}$ |
| Superconducting electromagnets | $10\ \mathrm{T}$ or more |

with $1\ \text{gauss} = 1\ \mathrm{G} = 1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}$.

## Direction of the force

To find the direction of the force — or, given the force, of the current or the field — use the **3rd right-hand rule (RHR)**.

## Force between two parallel wires (section 20.6)

Each wire produces a magnetic field at the position of the other, and each therefore sits in a field and feels Ampère's force. The result depends only on the relative direction of the two currents:

- **Currents in the same direction — attraction.**
- **Currents in opposite directions — repulsion.**

*Worked example.* Two light conductor wires are hung vertically, with the electrical current in both wires directed upwards. What happens? The currents are in the same direction, so **the wires experience a force of attraction**. The forces do not cancel — they are an action-reaction pair pulling the two wires together, not two forces on one object.

The magnitude, derived from Ampère's law, is a force per unit length:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$

where $d$ is the centre-to-centre separation of the wires. The structure of the expression is the field of one wire, $\mu_0I_1/2\pi d$, multiplied by $I_2l$ from $F = IlB$.

*Worked example.* *A long pair of insulated wires carries $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$ to and from an instrument, the two wires being $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. A third wire is placed in the plane of the two, parallel and just to the right, carrying $25.0\ \mathrm{A}$ upward, $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ from the nearest wire centre to centre. What force per metre of length does it exert on each of the other two wires?*

Both other wires carry $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$, so only the separations and the current directions differ. The common factor is

$$\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi} = (2\times10^{-7})(25.0)(24.5) = 1.225\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N}$$

**The nearer wire**, at $d = 2.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{1.225\times10^{-4}}{2.8\times10^{-3}} = 4.4\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N/m}$$

Its current runs the same way as the third wire's, so this force is **attractive**.

**The further wire**, at $d = 2.8 + 2.8 = 5.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{1.225\times10^{-4}}{5.6\times10^{-3}} = 2.2\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N/m}$$

It carries the return current, in the opposite direction, so this force is **repulsive**. Doubling the separation has halved the force, as the $1/d$ requires, and because one force is attractive and the other repulsive the two partly cancel on the third wire.

## Applications

Applications of the force on a current in a magnetic field include the galvanometer, the motor and the loudspeaker.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ampère's force** | The force a magnet exerts on a current-carrying wire, $F = Il_\perp B = IlB\sin\theta$ |
| **Tesla (T)** | The standard unit of magnetic field, $1\ \mathrm{T} = 1\ \mathrm{N/(A\cdot m)}$ |
| **Gauss (G)** | A smaller unit of magnetic field, $1\ \mathrm{G} = 1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}$ |
| **3rd right-hand rule** | The rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field, or of the current or field given the other two |

title: Force on an Electric Charge Moving in a Magnetic Field
summary: The guide covers Part A of this section only. The Lorentz force is the force that free moving charged particles experience when they pass through a magnetic field. Its magnitude is F = qvB\sin\theta w
markdown:
# 20.4 Force on an Electric Charge Moving in a Magnetic Field

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide covers Part A of this section only.

## The Lorentz force

The **Lorentz force** is the force that free moving charged particles experience when they pass through a magnetic field. Its magnitude is

$$F = qvB\sin\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of $v$ and $B$.

This is not a new law but the same Ampère force written for one particle. If $N$ particles of charge $q$ pass a given point in time $t$, they constitute a current

$$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{Nq}{t}, \qquad \frac{l}{t} = v$$

so that

$$F = IlB\sin\theta = \frac{Nq\,l\,B\sin\theta}{t} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F = qvB\sin\theta$$

The extremes follow from the sine, exactly as in 20.3:

$$F_{\max} = qvB \quad \text{when } \theta = 90^\circ\ (\text{charge moves} \perp \text{magnetic field})$$

$$F_{\min} = 0 \quad \text{when } \theta = 0^\circ\ (\text{charge moves} \parallel \text{magnetic field})$$

(The guide labels the $\theta = 0^\circ$ line $F_{\max}$; it is the minimum, as the same guide's 20.3 states for the parallel case.)

The direction of the force is given by the **3rd right-hand rule**, almost the same rule used to find the direction of the Ampère force.

Two immediate consequences are worth stating outright. A charged particle entering a uniform field *parallel* to its velocity **experiences no change in velocity**, since $\sin 0^\circ = 0$ and there is no force at all. And a charged particle **at rest** in a uniform magnetic field experiences **no** magnetic force, because $v = 0$ makes $F = qvB\sin\theta$ vanish however strong the field.

## Worked example: the force on a proton approaching a current-carrying wire

*The conventional current $I$ in a long straight wire flows upward. At the instant a proton of charge $+e$ is a distance $R$ from the wire and heading directly towards it, what is the force on the proton?*

Two steps: get $B$ at the proton, then apply the Lorentz force.

The wire's field at distance $R$ has magnitude $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi R$, and the 1st right-hand rule puts it into the page on one side of the wire and out of the page on the other. Applying the 3rd right-hand rule with $v$ pointing at the wire gives a force **downward — opposite to the direction of $I$**. The answer is the same whichever side of the wire the proton is on, because moving to the other side reverses both $v$ and $B$, and reversing both leaves the force unchanged.

The magnitude combines the two formulas:

$$F = evB = ev\cdot\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 evI}{2\pi R}$$

## Worked example: crossed fields

*A positively charged particle moves to the right into a region where an electric field is directed up the plane of the paper. In which direction must the magnetic field point so that the particle maintains a constant velocity?*

Constant velocity means zero net force. The electric field pushes the positive charge up the page, so the magnetic force must be equal in size and directed down the page. With $v$ to the right, the 3rd right-hand rule gives a downward force on a positive charge when the magnetic field points **out of the plane of the page**.

## The circular path

If a charged particle is moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, its path will be a **circle**. The reason is that the force is always perpendicular to the motion: it changes the direction of $v$ without ever changing its magnitude, which is precisely the condition for uniform circular motion.

Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force,

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_C = F_B \qquad \frac{mv^2}{r} = qvB \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r = \frac{mv}{qB} \qquad r \propto v$$

The period follows:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$$

and the striking feature is that **$T$ is not related to $v$**: the $v$ in the numerator of $2\pi r$ cancels the $v$ hidden in $r$. A fast particle travels a proportionately larger circle in the same time.

The reciprocal of the period is the **cyclotron frequency**, the frequency at which particles revolve in a cyclotron:

$$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$

## Charge separation in a moving wire

A wire moved through a magnetic field experiences an induced charge separation. The mechanism is the Lorentz force again: the free charges inside the wire are carried along at the wire's velocity, so each of them feels $F = qvB\sin\theta$, and that force drives them along the wire towards one end. One end becomes positive and the other negative.

The 3rd right-hand rule, applied to the wire's velocity and the field, gives the direction the positive charge is pushed — so given any two of the velocity, the field and the observed separation of charge, the third can be deduced.

## The aurora

Charged ions approach the Earth from the Sun — the "solar wind" — and enter the atmosphere mainly near the poles, ionising the air; as the electrons recombine with the atoms, light is emitted.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lorentz force** | The force that free moving charged particles experience when they pass through a magnetic field, $F = qvB\sin\theta$ |
| **Cyclotron frequency** | The frequency at which particles revolve in a cyclotron, $f = 1/T = qB/2\pi m$ |
| **Aurora** | Light emitted when charged ions from the solar wind enter the atmosphere near the poles, ionise the air, and the electrons then recombine with atoms |

# 1.4-1.7 Measurement and Estimating

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A **measurement** is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard. Everything that follows in this section is a consequence of that: because a measurement is a comparison made with a real instrument, it is never exact, and the notation we use has to carry the size of that inexactness along with the number.

## Significant digits

**Significant digits** are the valid, reliable digits in a measurement. The **last digit in a measurement is an estimated, uncertain digit** — it is the one you read off between the marks on the instrument. Every rule below follows from that idea: a digit is significant if it carries information about the measurement, and not significant if it is only there to position the decimal point.

Counting significant digits:

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| All non-zero digits count, and so do any zeros contained between non-zero digits | 6 s.f. in 300042 |
| **Exact numbers and constants have infinite significant digits** | a counted number, or a defined constant |
| Trailing zeros count if there is a decimal point | 3 s.f. in 200. |
| Trailing zeros do not count unless scientific notation is explicitly used | 3 s.f. in 2990, but 4 s.f. in $2.990 \times 10^{3}$ |

The last row is where marks are lost. Writing 2990 leaves the reader unable to tell whether that final zero was measured or is a placeholder, so the convention treats it as a placeholder. Scientific notation removes the ambiguity, because everything written in the mantissa is there deliberately.

## Calculating with significant digits

A result may not claim more precision than the weakest measurement that went into it. The two rules differ because addition and multiplication degrade precision in different ways.

- **Addition and subtraction:** round the result to have as many **decimal places** as the measured number with the smallest number of decimal places.
- **Multiplication and division:** round the result to have as many **significant figures** as the measured number with the smallest number of significant figures.

## Uncertainty and the two kinds of error

**Uncertainty** is the variation in measured data. It comes from two distinct sources, and telling them apart determines whether repeating the experiment will help.

| | **Systematic error** | **Random error** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | A consistent or reproducible error that affects the **accuracy** of a measurement | An unpredictable variation in measurements |
| Caused by | Instrument, environment, or methodology | Human or environmental fluctuations |

Because systematic error is reproducible, repeating the measurement reproduces the error too; only a change of instrument or method removes it.

## Accuracy, precision, and instrument limits

- **Accuracy** is how close a measurement is to the accepted value.
- **Precision** is the repeatability of the measurement using a given instrument — which is what the number of significant figures records.
- **Instrument Limit of Error (ILE)** is the maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value. It is generally taken as **half of the instrument's least count**.
- **Deviation** is the amount by which a single value differs from the average.

Accuracy and precision are independent. A systematically mis-calibrated instrument can be highly precise — reading the same wrong value every time — and still be inaccurate.

## Representing an experimental result

- **Absolute uncertainty (absolute error)** is the uncertainty stated in the same units as the measurement, quoted as $x \pm \Delta x$.
- **Relative uncertainty** is the absolute uncertainty compared with the measurement itself:

$$\text{relative uncertainty} = \frac{\Delta x}{x}$$

- **Relative error** compares the result with the value it should have had:

$$\text{relative error} = \frac{\text{measured value} - \text{expected value}}{\text{expected value}}$$

- **Percentage uncertainty (percentage error)** is the relative uncertainty expressed as a percentage.

## Error propagation

When measurements are combined, their uncertainties combine too, and the rule depends on the operation.

| Operation | How the uncertainty propagates |
|---|---|
| Addition and subtraction | Add the **absolute** uncertainties |
| Multiplication and division | Add the **relative** uncertainties |
| Multiplication by an exact number | Multiply the uncertainty by that same exact number |
| Powers | For a quantity raised to the power $n$, multiply the relative uncertainty by $n$ |

Note that subtraction adds absolute uncertainties rather than cancelling them — subtracting two close measurements leaves a small result carrying the full uncertainty of both, which is why such differences are unreliable.

## Graphing data

Data is plotted to show a relationship, so the plot must be set up so the relationship, not the drawing, is what the reader sees.

- Identify the **independent** and **dependent variable** before plotting.
- **Choose simple scales.**
- **Plot the points neatly.**
- **Draw a best fit line** through the data if the points form a straight line; **draw a best fit curve** if they form a curve.
- **Check anomalous data** — either investigate it or ignore it.
- **Draw error bars** for the data, so the uncertainty in each point is visible on the graph.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Measurement** | A comparison between an unknown quantity and a standard |
| **Significant digits** | The valid, reliable digits in a measurement; the last one is estimated |
| **Uncertainty** | The variation in measured data |
| **Systematic error** | A consistent or reproducible error that affects the accuracy of a measurement; caused by instrument, environment, or methodology |
| **Random error** | An unpredictable variation in measurements, caused by human or environmental fluctuations |
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the accepted value |
| **Precision** | The repeatability of a measurement using a given instrument (its number of significant figures) |
| **Instrument Limit of Error (ILE)** | The maximum amount by which a measurement made by an instrument can deviate from the true value; generally half the least count |
| **Deviation** | The amount by which a single value differs from the average |
| **Absolute uncertainty** | The uncertainty of a measurement expressed in the units of the measurement |
| **Relative uncertainty** | The absolute uncertainty divided by the measurement |
| **Relative error** | (measured value − expected value) / expected value |
| **Percentage uncertainty** | The relative uncertainty expressed as a percentage |

title: 2.5-2.7 Motion at Constant Acceleration and Falling Objects
summary: Uniformly accelerated motion is motion with constant acceleration. In the cases treated here the acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction, and the motion is along a straight line. Beca
markdown:
# 2.5-2.7 Motion at Constant Acceleration and Falling Objects

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Uniformly accelerated motion

**Uniformly accelerated motion** is motion with constant acceleration. In the cases treated here the acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction, and the motion is along a straight line.

Because $a$ does not change, a single set of formulas describes the whole motion — there is no need to break the journey into pieces.

## The motion formulas

Four equations relate the initial velocity $v_0$, the final velocity $v$, the acceleration $a$, the displacement $x - x_0$, and the time $t$:

$$v = v_0 + at$$

$$x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^{2}$$

$$v^{2} = v_0^{2} + 2a(x - x_0)$$

$$\bar{v} = \frac{v + v_0}{2}$$

Each equation omits one of the five quantities. Choosing an equation is therefore a matter of asking which quantity you neither know nor want, and picking the equation that leaves it out.

## Free fall

**Free fall** is the motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the only force acting is gravity — the motion of a falling object when the action can be considered due to gravity alone.

**Galileo's hypothesis:** at a given location on Earth, and in the absence of air resistance, **all objects fall with the same constant acceleration**. The mass of the object does not enter into it.

The **acceleration due to gravity** on Earth is

$$g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}$$

directed **towards the Earth's centre**.

## Working free-fall problems

Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion with $a = g$, so **the same four equations solve every scenario** — whether the object is dropped from rest, thrown downwards, or thrown upwards. An initial upward or downward velocity changes only the value of $v_0$ you substitute; it does not change which equations apply, and it does not change the acceleration, which points downwards throughout, including at the top of an upward throw.

The one habit that prevents most errors: **it is important to define the direction of gravity before doing the question**. Either fix your sign convention at the start, or state the direction explicitly in the final answer. Whether $g$ enters your equations as $+9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ or $-9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ depends entirely on which direction you chose to call positive, and mixing conventions midway through is the usual source of a sign error.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniformly accelerated motion** | Motion with constant acceleration |
| **Free fall** | The motion of a falling object when air resistance is negligible and the only force acting is gravity |
| **Galileo's hypothesis** | At a given location on Earth, without air resistance, all objects fall with the same constant acceleration |
| **Acceleration due to gravity ($g$)** | $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, directed towards the Earth's centre |

# 2.8 Graphical Analysis of Linear Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A graph of motion carries more than the quantity on its vertical axis. The **slope** and the **area** each mean something physical, and knowing which is which turns a graph into a complete description of the motion.

## The position-time graph

On a position–time graph the vertical axis gives position and the slope gives velocity.

**No motion** appears as a **horizontal straight line** — the position is not changing, so the slope is zero.

**Uniform motion** appears as a **slanted straight line**:

- The **$y$-intercept is the initial position**.
- The **average velocity is the slope of the line**.
- Because the line is straight, the **instantaneous velocity equals the average velocity** everywhere on it.
- An **intersection of two lines means the two objects meet** — at that instant they are at the same position at the same time.

**Many straight lines** joined together represent **many different velocities**, one for each segment. On each segment, **velocity = slope**.

**A curve** means the velocity is changing continuously, and the two kinds of velocity now differ:

- **Average velocity** between two points is the **slope of the straight line connecting those two points** on the curve.
- **Instantaneous velocity** at a point is the **slope of the line tangential to the curve** at that point.

## The velocity-time graph

On a velocity–time graph the vertical axis gives the velocity of an object. Here the slope gives acceleration and the area gives displacement.

**A horizontal line** means the **velocity is constant**.

**The area under the graph line is the displacement.** This gives a second way to spot two objects meeting: **they meet when the area is the same**.

**Uniformly accelerated motion** appears as a **slanted straight line**:

- The **slope is the average acceleration**.
- A **rising** line means $a > 0$; a **falling** line means $a < 0$.
- **The steeper the slope, the larger the magnitude of $a$.**

**Motion with changing acceleration** appears as a curve, and the **instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent to the curve**.

## The acceleration-time graph

The third graph in the set plots acceleration against time.

## What slope and area mean

Reading these graphs is a matter of remembering two chains. Differentiating downwards, the slope of position–time gives velocity and the slope of velocity–time gives acceleration. Going the other way, the area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement. This is why the same shape means different things on different axes: a horizontal line means *no motion* on a position–time graph but *constant velocity* on a velocity–time graph, and a slanted straight line means *uniform motion* on the first and *uniform acceleration* on the second. Always check the axis label before interpreting the shape.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Average velocity (on a graph)** | The slope of the line joining two points on a position–time graph |
| **Instantaneous velocity (on a graph)** | The slope of the tangent to a position–time curve at a point |
| **Instantaneous acceleration (on a graph)** | The slope of the tangent to a velocity–time curve at a point |
| **Area under a velocity–time graph** | The displacement of the object |

# 3.1 Vectors and Scalars

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

A **vector** has both **magnitude and direction**. A **scalar** has **magnitude only, no direction**.

The distinction matters because the two kinds of quantity obey different arithmetic. Two scalars are combined by ordinary addition; two vectors are not, because their directions must be accounted for as well.

## Representing a vector

A vector is drawn as **a line and an arrow**:

- The **length** of the line represents the **magnitude**.
- The **direction** of the arrow represents the **direction** of the vector.

**Drawing to scale.** Use a ruler and a compass to draw out vectors accurately. For large vectors, make a **scale bar** and follow that scale consistently throughout the diagram — a scale is only useful if every vector in the drawing obeys it.

## Stating a direction

The single most common source of a lost mark is a magnitude given without a direction. **Either define your directions before you start solving, or include the direction in the final answer.**

For motion along one line, signs are enough:

| Direction | Sign |
|---|---|
| Up | $+$ |
| Down | $-$ |
| Right | $+$ |
| Left | $-$ |

In two dimensions, **rectangular coordinates** are used — a direction such as *40 degrees North of East*.

## The same direction, named different ways

One direction can be described in more than one correct way, depending on which axis you measure from. For instance, **30 degrees West of South is the same direction as 60 degrees South of West**: the two descriptions measure the same angle from perpendicular reference lines, so they are complementary. Similarly, an angle given as so many degrees West of North can equally be stated as an angle measured from the vertical axis.

Being able to convert between these forms is what lets you recognise that two differently worded problems are the same problem.

**If the question provides you with any compass directions, it is best to use them** in your answer — matching the question's own convention avoids conversion errors.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vector** | A quantity with both magnitude and direction |
| **Scalar** | A quantity with magnitude only, and no direction |
| **Rectangular coordinates** | A way of stating a direction as an angle from a reference direction, e.g. 40 degrees North of East |
| **Scale bar** | A drawn reference length used so that large vectors can be represented proportionally on a diagram |

markdown:
# 3.2 Addition of Vectors – Graphical Methods

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **resultant**, or **net vector**, is the sum of two or more vectors. Vector addition is **commutative**: the order in which the vectors are added does not change the result.

## The tail-to-tip method

To find the resultant of several vectors:

1. **Move the tail of one vector to the head of another**, without changing its magnitude or its direction. Sliding a vector is allowed; rotating or rescaling it is not.
2. Repeat until all the vectors are joined head to tail.
3. **The resultant points from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.**

Two consequences follow directly:

- **If three or more vectors form a closed polygon, there is no resultant.** The head of the last vector has arrived back at the tail of the first, so the displacement between them is zero.
- **It does not matter which order you do this in** — this is the commutative property drawn out.

A practical point for the awkward case: **if the vectors lie along one straight line, draw them on close parallel lines** so that the diagram remains readable and the head-to-tail construction is clear.

## The parallelogram method

An alternative construction for two vectors:

1. **Place the two vectors tail-to-tail.**
2. **Construct a parallelogram** with the two vectors as its sides.
3. **The diagonal drawn from the common origin is the resultant vector.**

The two methods give the same answer; the parallelogram method simply keeps both vectors starting from the same point, which is often more natural when the vectors represent forces acting at one point.

## Calculating the resultant

The **Pythagorean theorem** can be used to calculate not only the magnitude of the resultant but also its angle:

$$R = \sqrt{A^{2} + B^{2}} \qquad \theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$$

**These apply only if the angle between the vectors is 90 degrees.** This is the restriction that is most often forgotten. For vectors that are not perpendicular, the component method of section 3.4 is required.

## Practice

1. Draw the resultant vector and calculate the net displacement to scale for a person who walks 8 km east and then 6 km north.
2. True or false: the magnitude of a vector sum is always greater than the magnitude of either contributing vector.
3. True or false: can the magnitude of a vector ever (a) be equal to one of its components, or (b) be less than one of its components?
4. Forces of 30 N due north and 40 N due east act on a mass. What is the net, or resultant, force on the mass?

Questions 2 and 3 are answered by the constructions above rather than by calculation. Question 2 should be tested against the case where two vectors point in opposite directions; question 3 against the Pythagorean relation between a resultant and its components.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resultant (net vector)** | The sum of two or more vectors |
| **Tail-to-tip method** | Joining vectors head to tail; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last |
| **Parallelogram method** | Placing two vectors tail-to-tail and taking the diagonal of the resulting parallelogram from the common origin as the resultant |

markdown:
# 3.3 Subtraction of Vectors, and Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Negative vectors

Two vectors are **negatives** of one another if they have the **same magnitude but opposite directions**. Writing $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ says exactly that: the same length, reversed.

## Subtracting vectors

There is no separate construction for subtraction. **Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its negative:**

$$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$$

So to subtract graphically, reverse the second vector and then use the tail-to-tip or parallelogram method exactly as before. Every rule for addition carries over unchanged.

## Multiplying a vector by a scalar

A vector $\vec{A}$ can be multiplied by a scalar $c$. The scalar changes the length of the vector, and its sign decides whether the direction survives:

| Sign of $c$ | Direction of the product | Magnitude of the product |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ positive | The **same** direction as $\vec{A}$ | $cA$ |
| $c$ negative | The **opposite** direction to $\vec{A}$ | $\lvert c \rvert A$ |

Multiplying by $-1$ is therefore the operation that produces the negative vector used in subtraction — the special case that ties the two halves of this section together.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Negative vectors** | Two vectors with the same magnitude but opposite directions |
| **Vector subtraction** | Adding the negative of a vector: $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$ |
| **Scalar multiplication of a vector** | Multiplying a vector by a scalar $c$; the product has magnitude $\lvert c \rvert A$ and keeps the original direction if $c$ is positive, reverses it if $c$ is negative |

markdown:
# 3.4 Adding Vectors by Components

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The graphical methods of section 3.2 work only for perpendicular vectors if you want a number out of them. The component method removes that restriction, and it is the general technique.

## Vector components and resolution

Once a vector is placed in a coordinate plane, it can be broken down into an **$x$ component** and a **$y$ component**. This process is called **vector resolution**.

The components are the two perpendicular vectors that add to give the original, so the original is always the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form. Fundamental trigonometry gives them:

$$A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

and the reverse direction — components back to the resultant — uses the Pythagorean theorem:

$$A = \sqrt{A_x^{2} + A_y^{2}}$$

Resolving and recombining are the same relation read in opposite directions, which is why one method covers both.

## Adding vectors using components

The point of resolving is that components along the same axis are collinear, so they add as ordinary signed numbers. The steps:

1. **Resolve each vector into its $x$ and $y$ components.**
2. **Add the $x$ components of all the vectors.**
3. **Add the $y$ components of all the vectors.**
4. **Get the resultant using the Pythagorean theorem**, applied to the sum of each component:

$$R = \sqrt{\left(\sum A_x\right)^{2} + \left(\sum A_y\right)^{2}}$$

5. **Find the angle using arctan:**

$$\theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{\sum A_y}{\sum A_x}\right)$$

Note carefully what is being squared in step 4. The Pythagorean theorem is applied once, at the end, to the two *totals* — not to each vector individually.

## Practice

A GPS receiver indicates that your home is 15.0 km away and 40.0 degrees north of west, but the only path through the woods leads directly north. If you follow the path 5.0 km before it opens into a field, how far, and in what direction, would you have to walk to reach your home?

This is a vector subtraction handled by components: resolve the displacement to home, resolve the displacement already walked, and take the difference component by component before recombining.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Vector components** | The $x$ and $y$ parts into which a vector placed in a coordinate plane can be broken down |
| **Vector resolution** | The process of breaking a vector down into its components |

# 3.5-3.6 Projectile Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The concepts

A **projectile** is an object shot through the air. Its **trajectory** is the curved flight path that it follows.

**Ignoring air resistance, the net force on an object after it is launched is gravity.** Nothing pushes it forwards once it has left the hand or the boot; the only force is downwards. That single fact generates everything else in this section.

Projectile motion is a **combination of two independent motions**:

| Component | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal motion** | **Constant velocity** — there is no horizontal force, given no air resistance |
| **Vertical motion** | **Motion with constant acceleration** — free fall under gravity |

**The horizontal and vertical motions are independent.** They share only one quantity: the clock. **The time from launch to hitting the target is the same for both motions**, and time is therefore the bridge you use to pass from one to the other.

## Projectile launched horizontally

A projectile launched horizontally has **no initial vertical velocity**.

1. **Analyse the horizontal and vertical motion separately.** Horizontally, constant $v$, giving the range $x = v_x t$. Vertically, free fall, giving the height fallen $y = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^{2}$.
2. **The velocity vector at every instant is always tangent to the parabola.**
3. **The two motions are independent**, and the flight time is shared.
4. **What affects the range?** The **horizontal velocity** and the **flight time** — and the flight time is set by the height it falls from, not by how hard it was thrown.

Point 4 is the answer to the classic question of whether a bullet fired horizontally lands at the same time as one dropped: the vertical motion knows nothing about the horizontal velocity.

**How to solve:**

- **Given the $y$ values:** calculate how much time the free fall will take, then multiply the horizontal velocity by that time to obtain the range.
- **Given the $x$ values:** find the time from $t = d/v$, then substitute that time into the vertical equations to find the height or any other quantity.

## Projectile launched at an angle

Separate the initial velocity vector into its $x$ and $y$ components:

$$v_{0x} = v_0 \cos\theta \qquad v_{0y} = v_0 \sin\theta$$

Three quantities are usually asked for:

- **Maximum height** — the height of the projectile when its **vertical velocity is zero**. The horizontal velocity is not zero there; only the vertical component vanishes.
- **Level horizontal range ($R$)** — the horizontal distance the projectile travels before returning to its original height.
- **Flight time (hang time)** — how much time the projectile is in the air.

The solving method is the same as for horizontally launched projectiles, **except that there is now an initial vertical velocity in the equations**. In other words it is the same problem as throwing an object straight up or down, run alongside a constant-velocity horizontal motion.

## Practice

A player kicks a football at an angle of 45° above the horizontal. The football has an initial velocity of 10.0 m/s. Find:

1. the flight time;
2. the maximum height;
3. the range of the football;
4. the velocity and the acceleration of the ball at the maximum height;
5. the velocity of the ball 0.5 seconds after it is launched.

Part 4 is the conceptual test in the set: use the definition of maximum height and the statement that the net force after launch is gravity.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Projectile** | An object shot through the air |
| **Trajectory** | The curved flight path followed by a moving object |
| **Maximum height** | The height of a projectile at the moment its vertical velocity is zero |
| **Level horizontal range** | The horizontal distance a projectile travels before returning to its original height |
| **Flight time (hang time)** | How much time the projectile is in the air |

markdown:
# 3.8 Relative Velocity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

**Relative velocity** is the velocity of one body relative to another. A velocity is never simply "the" velocity — it is always measured with respect to some frame, and when two frames are themselves moving, the velocities add as vectors:

$$\vec{v}_{AC} = \vec{v}_{AB} + \vec{v}_{BC}$$

The velocity of $A$ with respect to $C$ is the velocity of $A$ with respect to $B$ plus the velocity of $B$ with respect to $C$. Because these are vectors, they combine by the tail-to-tip or component methods, not by ordinary addition.

## Wind

Wind is the everyday case of a moving frame, and its effect depends on the direction it comes from:

| Wind | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Tailwind** | Comes from behind, **increasing** the velocity |
| **Headwind** | Comes from the front, **decreasing** the velocity |
| **Crosswind** | Comes from the side, and can influence **both** the horizontal and the vertical components |

A tailwind and a headwind are collinear with the motion, so they add and subtract as signed numbers. A crosswind is not, which is why it must be resolved into components before it can be combined.

## Worked example: crossing a river

A boat travels at 30 m/s due east across a river that is 120 m wide, and the current is 12 m/s south.

1. **What is the velocity of the boat relative to the shore?** Add the boat's velocity through the water and the current's velocity as vectors. They are perpendicular, so the magnitude follows from the Pythagorean theorem and the direction from arctan.
2. **How long does it take the boat to cross the river?** The crossing time depends only on the eastward velocity and the width of the river. The current pushes the boat south, not backwards, so it does not slow the crossing — this is the same independence of perpendicular components that governs projectile motion.
3. **How far downstream will the boat land?** Multiply the current's speed by the crossing time found in part 2.

The structure of the answer is the point: solve for the time using the component across the river, then use that time in the component along the river.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Relative velocity** | The velocity of one body relative to another |
| **Tailwind** | A wind coming from behind, increasing velocity |
| **Headwind** | A wind coming from the front, decreasing velocity |
| **Crosswind** | A wind coming from the side, which can influence both the horizontal and vertical components |

markdown:
# 4.1 Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The basic idea

A **force** is a push or a pull exerted by one object on another. It is a **vector**.

The phrase "by one object on another" is doing real work in that definition: a force is always an **interaction between two objects**, and both must be named.

- The **system** is the object to whom the force is exerted.
- The **agent** is the object by whom the force is exerted.

If you cannot name the agent, you have not found a force.

## What a force does

A force produces one or both of the following effects:

- **A deformation** — a change in the dimension or shape of the object.
- **A change in the state of motion** — a change in velocity.

The unit of force is the **newton (N)**, defined so that

$$1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^{2}$$

Force is measured with a **spring scale**.

## The three factors of a force

Because a force is a vector applied at a place, three things must be specified before it is fully described:

| Factor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Magnitude** | The strength of the force vector |
| **Direction** | The direction in which the force vector acts |
| **Point of application** | The location at which the force is exerted |

Graphically a force is represented by a vector — an arrow whose length gives the magnitude and whose direction gives the direction, drawn from the point of application.

## Types of force

There are **four fundamental forces**:

- **Gravity**
- **Electromagnetic force**
- **Strong force**
- **Weak force**

For mechanics, a more useful division is by whether contact is required.

| | **Contact forces** | **Field forces** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | A force exerted through contact | A force exerted without contact |
| Examples | Friction ($F_{fr}$), drag force (air resistance or fluid resistance), tension ($F_T$), normal force ($F_N$), spring force ($F_{sp}$), applied force ($F_A$) | Gravity, and the other field interactions |

## The spring force and Hooke's law

**Hooke's law:** the magnitude of the force is **directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression**, within the limit of a spring.

$$F = kx$$

- $F$ is the force exerted by the spring on the attached object, in N
- $x$ is the displacement of the spring's end from its equilibrium position, in cm
- $k$ is the **spring constant**, in N/cm

The qualifier "within the limit" is the exception to keep: **a spring becomes deformed if it is stretched beyond its limit**, and past that point the proportionality no longer holds.

## Friction

Friction is classified by the kind of relative motion involved.

| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Sliding friction** | Friction arising from sliding. Divides into **static friction ($F_s$)**, caused by the tendency of no relative motion, and **kinetic friction ($F_k$)**, caused by relative motion |
| **Rolling friction** | Friction arising from rolling |
| **Fluid friction** | Friction acting when an object moves through a fluid |

**Magnitude of static friction.** Static friction is **the same as the force causing the tendency to relative motion** — it takes whatever value is needed to prevent sliding. It therefore has a **range**, with an upper limit:

$$F_s \le \mu_s F_N$$

where $\mu_s$ is the **static friction coefficient**.

**Magnitude of kinetic friction.** Once sliding has begun the friction takes a single definite value:

$$F_k = \mu_k F_N$$

where $\mu_k$ is the **kinetic friction coefficient**.

The structural difference is the thing to remember. Static friction is an inequality because it adjusts itself; kinetic friction is an equation because it does not.

**Air resistance** depends on:

- **Shape** — a streamlined shape reduces friction
- **Size** — friction increases as surface area increases
- **Speed** — friction increases with speed
- **Fluid type** — its viscosity

## Combining forces

Forces on an object combine by **vector addition**.

**Balanced forces.** Two different forces acting on the same object are balanced when they act at the **same point of application**, have the **same magnitude**, act in **opposite directions**, and act **along the same line**. A force that balances another in this way is an **equilibrant**.

**Equilibrium** is the state of an object experiencing balanced forces. Its defining condition is

$$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$

and it takes two forms: the object is **at rest**, or the object is in **uniform motion**. Both count as equilibrium, because in neither case is the velocity changing.

**Unbalanced forces** give a net force that is not zero, and an unbalanced force changes the object's motion — the object **starts moving**, **stops moving**, or **changes direction**.

## Free-body diagrams

A **free body diagram** is a physical model that represents all the forces on the system. To draw one:

- Draw **the system**;
- Draw **all the forces**, each **labelled**.

Because a free-body diagram isolates the system, it makes the vector sum in the equilibrium condition something you can actually carry out.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Force** | A push or pull exerted by one object on another; a vector |
| **System** | The object to whom a force is exerted |
| **Agent** | The object by whom a force is exerted |
| **Newton (N)** | The unit of force; $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2$ |
| **Contact force** | A force exerted through contact |
| **Field force** | A force exerted without contact |
| **Hooke's law** | The magnitude of the spring force is directly proportional to the amount of stretch or compression, within the limit of a spring |
| **Spring constant ($k$)** | The constant of proportionality in Hooke's law, in N/cm |
| **Static friction** | Friction caused by the tendency of no relative motion; ranges up to $\mu_s F_N$ |
| **Kinetic friction** | Friction caused by relative motion; equal to $\mu_k F_N$ |
| **Rolling friction** | Friction arising from rolling |
| **Fluid friction** | Friction acting when an object moves through a fluid |
| **Balanced forces** | Two forces on the same object with the same magnitude, opposite directions, the same line of action and the same point of application |
| **Equilibrant** | The force that balances another force |
| **Equilibrium** | The state of an object experiencing balanced forces: at rest or in uniform motion, with net force zero |
| **Unbalanced forces** | Forces whose net sum is not zero, changing the object's motion |
| **Free body diagram** | A physical model representing all the forces on the system |

markdown:
# 4.2-4.3 Newton's First Law of Motion and Mass

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Newton's first law

Also known as the **law of inertia**:

> Every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it.

Read carefully, the law says that rest and uniform motion are the same state as far as physics is concerned. Neither requires a force to maintain it; a force is needed only to change from one to the other.

## Inertia

**Inertia** is the tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line.

Two points about it are examined repeatedly:

- **Inertia is not a force.** It does not appear on a free-body diagram, and it has no agent. It is a property of the object.
- **The larger the mass, the larger the inertia.**

## Inertial reference frames

Newton's first law does not hold in every frame of reference, and this is why the frame has to be specified.

- **Inertial reference frames** are reference frames in which Newton's first law does hold.
- **Non-inertial reference frames** are reference frames in which Newton's first law does not hold.

## Mass

Newton said that **mass is a quantity of matter**. Two more precise definitions are used, and they arrive at mass from completely different directions.

**Inertial mass** is defined by the response of an object to a force: mass is equal to the **ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration**.

$$m = \frac{F_{net}}{a}$$

On this definition, **mass is a measure of the inertia of an object** — the larger the mass, the smaller the acceleration a given force produces.

**Gravitational mass** is mass as used in the law of universal gravitation: it **determines the size of the gravitational force between two objects**.

## The principle of equivalence

There is no obvious reason why a quantity measuring resistance to acceleration should be the same as a quantity measuring gravitational attraction. **Newton said that inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude** — the **principle of equivalence**.

This is what permits a single number, "the mass", to be used in both $m = F_{net}/a$ and in the gravitational force law.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's first law (law of inertia)** | Every object continues in its state of rest, or of uniform velocity in a straight line, as long as no net force acts on it |
| **Inertia** | The tendency of an object to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line |
| **Inertial reference frame** | A reference frame in which Newton's first law does hold |
| **Non-inertial reference frame** | A reference frame in which Newton's first law does not hold |
| **Mass** | A quantity of matter |
| **Inertial mass** | Mass defined as the ratio of the net force exerted on an object to its acceleration; a measure of inertia |
| **Gravitational mass** | Mass as used in the law of universal gravitation; it determines the size of the gravitational force between two objects |
| **Principle of equivalence** | Inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude |
