markdown:
# 3.2 Addition of Vectors — Graphical Methods

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **resultant**, or net vector, is the sum of two or more vectors. Two drawings produce it, and one theorem shortcuts the drawing when the vectors happen to be perpendicular.

## The tip-to-tail method

To find the resultant of $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$:

1. Move the tail of one vector to the head of the other, **without changing the magnitude or direction** of the vector being moved. Sliding a vector about the page is allowed; turning or stretching it is not, because those are the two things that define it.
2. The resultant points from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second — or, if there are more than two, to the head of the last.

Vector addition is **commutative**:

$$\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$$

so it makes no difference which vector you move.

### Vectors in one straight line

When the vectors lie along the same straight line the construction still applies, and it produces the familiar result that vectors in the same direction add and vectors in opposite directions subtract.

That case is worth dwelling on, because it is the counterexample to the commonest wrong instinct about vector sums: **the magnitude of a vector sum is not always greater than the magnitude of either contributing vector**. Adding two vectors can produce a resultant smaller than both.

There is, however, a ceiling: **the magnitude of the resultant of two vectors is never greater than the sum of the magnitudes of the two individual vectors**. The extreme case is the two vectors pointing the same way; every other arrangement gives less.

### More than two vectors

The same rule extends to any number of vectors: chain them head to tail in any order, and the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last.

This gives a useful test. **If three or more vectors form a closed polygon, there is no resultant** — the head of the last vector lands back on the tail of the first, so the arrow representing the sum has zero length.

## The parallelogram method

An alternative construction for two vectors:

1. Place the component vectors **tail-to-tail**.
2. Use the two vectors as adjacent sides and construct a parallelogram.
3. The **diagonal drawn from the common origin** is the resultant.

It gives the same answer as the tip-to-tail method; the choice between them is a matter of which is tidier to draw.

## The Pythagorean theorem

When the two vectors being added are at right angles, the tip-to-tail triangle is a right-angled triangle, and the resultant is its hypotenuse. Its magnitude then needs no measurement:

$$R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Resultant (net vector)** | The sum of two or more vectors |
| **Tip-to-tail method** | Moving the tail of one vector to the head of another without changing its magnitude or direction; the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last |
| **Commutative** | $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{B} + \vec{A}$: the order of addition does not affect the resultant |
| **Parallelogram method** | Placing vectors tail-to-tail, constructing a parallelogram on them, and taking the diagonal from the common origin as the resultant |

markdown:
# 3.3 Subtraction of Vectors, and Multiplication of a Vector by a Scalar

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Negative vectors

Two vectors are **negative** — that is, each is the negative of the other — if they have the **same magnitude but are 180° apart**, pointing in opposite directions. Writing $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ says exactly that about a pair of arrows: same length, reversed direction.

## Subtracting vectors

There is no separate rule for subtraction. Subtracting $\vec{B}$ from $\vec{A}$ *is* adding the negative of $\vec{B}$ to $\vec{A}$:

$$\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$$

So the procedure is: reverse the vector being subtracted, then add it by the tip-to-tail or parallelogram method exactly as in the previous section. Every rule about resultants carries over unchanged, because the operation being carried out is an addition.

## Multiplying a vector by a scalar

A vector $\vec{A}$ can be multiplied by a scalar $c$. The result $c\vec{A}$ has magnitude $cA$, and its direction depends on the sign of $c$:

| Sign of $c$ | Magnitude of $c\vec{A}$ | Direction of $c\vec{A}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ positive | $cA$ | The same as $\vec{A}$ |
| $c$ negative | $cA$ | Opposite to $\vec{A}$ |

The magnitude is $cA$ either way — a magnitude is a size and cannot be negative. All the sign of $c$ does is decide whether the arrow is stretched along its own direction or flipped and then stretched. Multiplying by $-1$ is therefore the same operation as forming the negative vector above, which is what makes subtraction a special case of scalar multiplication followed by addition.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Negative vectors** | Two vectors with the same magnitude but 180° apart, in opposite directions; $\vec{A} = -\vec{B}$ |
| **Vector subtraction** | $\vec{A} - \vec{B} = \vec{A} + (-\vec{B})$: adding the negative of the second vector |
| **Scalar multiplication of a vector** | $c\vec{A}$ has magnitude $cA$; its direction is the same as $\vec{A}$ if $c$ is positive and opposite if $c$ is negative |

# 3.4 Adding Vectors by Components

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Graphical addition is limited by the accuracy of the drawing. The component method replaces the drawing with trigonometry and gives an exact answer.

## Vector components

Once a vector is placed in a coordinate plane it can be broken down into **components** — the pair of perpendicular vectors, one along each axis, that add to give it. The process is called **vector resolution**.

The components come from the trigonometric functions of the angle $\theta$ the vector makes with the $x$-axis. Since the vector is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose legs are the components,

$$A_x = A\cos\theta \qquad A_y = A\sin\theta$$

Resolution is the reverse of the addition in the previous section: instead of combining two vectors into one, it splits one vector into two that are guaranteed to be at right angles, which is the arrangement that makes the arithmetic easy.

## Adding vectors using components

1. **Resolve each vector** into its $x$- and $y$-components.
2. **Add the $x$-components of all the vectors.** Their sum is the $x$-component of the resultant. Do the same for the $y$-components to get the $y$-component of the resultant.
3. **Get the resultant** from its two components.

$$R_x = \sum A_x \qquad R_y = \sum A_y$$

$$R = \sqrt{R_x^{\,2} + R_y^{\,2}} \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_y}{R_x}\right)$$

Step 2 is where the method earns its keep. Components along the same axis lie along the same straight line, so they add as ordinary signed numbers — no geometry, no protractor. The only vector work left is the final step, and because $R_x$ and $R_y$ are perpendicular that step is Pythagoras plus one inverse tangent.

Keep the signs of the components: a component pointing along the negative $x$-direction enters the sum as a negative number, and dropping that sign is the standard way this calculation goes wrong.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Components** | The perpendicular vectors, one along each axis, into which a vector placed in a coordinate plane can be broken down |
| **Vector resolution** | The process of breaking a vector down into its components |

markdown:
# 3.5 Projectile Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Concepts

A **projectile** is an object shot through the air. The curved flight path it follows is its **trajectory**.

After a projectile is launched, gravity is the net force on it. Nothing else acts once it has left the hand or the barrel, which is why the analysis is so clean.

The central idea is that **projectile motion is a combination of two independent motions**:

| Component | Character of the motion |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal** | Motion with constant velocity, when there is no air resistance |
| **Vertical** | Motion with constant acceleration |

The split follows directly from the fact that gravity is the only force: gravity acts vertically, so it changes only the vertical velocity, and leaves the horizontal velocity untouched.

## Projectile launched horizontally

A projectile launched horizontally has **no initial vertical velocity**. Horizontal and vertical motion are then analysed separately:

- **Horizontal motion** — the range. Constant velocity, so $x = v_x t$.
- **Vertical motion** — the height fallen. Free fall from rest, so $y = \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.

The velocity vector at each instant is always **tangent to the parabola**. Its horizontal part never changes while its vertical part grows, so the vector tips further and further from the horizontal as the flight goes on. The final velocity just before the projectile hits the ground is the resultant of those two components, found by the vector addition of the previous sections.

## Independence, and the time of flight

The horizontal and vertical motions are independent, and the link that ties the two separate calculations back together is the clock: **the time from launch to hitting the target is the same for both the horizontal and the vertical motion.**

The most striking consequence, and the one worth remembering, is that **an object projected horizontally will reach the ground in the same time as an object dropped vertically** from the same height. Giving a projectile a horizontal velocity does nothing to how fast it falls, because that horizontal velocity has no vertical component for gravity to act on.

## Factors affecting the range

How far a horizontally launched projectile travels before it lands depends on two things:

- the **horizontal velocity**, since range $= v_x t$;
- the **flight time**, which is set by the height it falls.

Height enters the range only through the time it buys. A projectile launched from higher up is in the air longer, so its unchanging horizontal velocity carries it further.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Projectile** | An object shot through the air |
| **Trajectory** | The curved flight path that is followed by a moving object |
| **Horizontal motion component** | Motion with constant velocity, when there is no air resistance |
| **Vertical motion component** | Motion with constant acceleration — free fall |

# 4.7 Solving Problems with Newton's Laws: Free-Body Diagrams

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three-step method

Every problem in this section and the next is worked the same way, and it is worth learning the shape of the method before any particular problem.

1. **Draw a free-body diagram**, resolved into the components of the motion. Every force acting on the object appears on it, drawn along or broken into the chosen axes.
2. **Analyse the relationship between the given data and the target data** using the condition that applies — equilibrium if the object is not accelerating, Newton's second law if it is.
3. **Bring in the given data** and get the result.

Step 1 is not a formality. The equations in step 2 are read off the diagram, so a force left off the diagram is a term missing from the equation, and the answer is wrong before any arithmetic starts.

## Translational equilibrium

An object is in **translational equilibrium** if the net force on it is zero.

There are two types of translational equilibrium, and the second is the one students forget:

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Static | The object is at rest |
| Dynamic | The object is moving at constant velocity |

Both count as equilibrium because in both the velocity is not changing, and it is a *change* of velocity that requires a net force. "In equilibrium" does not mean "not moving".

The condition $\sum \vec{F} = 0$ is a vector equation, so it holds in each direction separately:

$$\sum F_x = 0 \qquad \sum F_y = 0$$

That is what makes the free-body diagram useful: resolving the forces into components turns one vector equation into two ordinary ones.

## Worked example: an object hanging from strings

*A 20.0 N object hangs at rest from strings as shown. Find the tension force in each string.*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram of the point where the strings meet, showing the weight pulling down and the tension in each string pulling along its own direction, and resolve each tension into horizontal and vertical components.

**Step 2.** The object hangs *at rest*, so it is in translational equilibrium and both component equations apply. Horizontally, the horizontal components of the two tensions must cancel one another, since nothing else acts sideways. Vertically, the vertical components of the two tensions must together add to the weight the strings are supporting.

**Step 3.** Substitute the given weight, $20\ \text{N}$, into the two equations and solve them together for the two unknown tensions.

The structure is worth noting: two unknowns, and exactly two equations, one from each direction. That is the usual arithmetic of an equilibrium problem, and it is why resolving into components is the step that makes the problem solvable at all.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free-body diagram** | A diagram of a single object showing every force acting on it, resolved into the components of the motion |
| **Translational equilibrium** | The condition in which the net force on an object is zero; the object is either at rest or moving at constant velocity |

markdown:
# 4.8 Problems Involving Friction, Inclines

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Friction

**Friction** is a force that resists the relative motion, or the tendency of such motion, of two surfaces in contact. Because it resists motion, **the direction of friction is always opposite to the motion** — you never have to guess which way it points, you read it off the motion.

Two types have been met so far:

| Type | When it acts | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Static friction** | On objects at rest | Prevents them from starting to move; must be overcome by an applied force to initiate motion |
| **Kinetic friction** (dynamic friction) | On objects already in motion | Opposes the movement; generally weaker than static friction |

The magnitudes are set by the normal force $N$ pressing the surfaces together, through a coefficient for each case:

$$f_s \le \mu_s N \qquad f_k = \mu_k N$$

Static friction gets an inequality because it takes only the value needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum of $\mu_s N$; kinetic friction has a definite value once sliding has begun. That kinetic friction is generally weaker than static friction is why a stuck object often lurches forward once it finally breaks free: the resisting force drops the instant it starts to slide.

### Worked example: maximum acceleration of a car

*What is the maximum acceleration a car can undergo if the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the ground is 0.80?*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram, with weight down, normal force up, and friction horizontal — friction from the road is the only forward force a car has.

**Step 2.** The car does not move vertically, so the vertical forces balance and $N = mg$. Horizontally it accelerates, so $f = ma$. The largest possible acceleration comes from the largest possible friction, which is the maximum static value $f = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$. Then

$$ma_{\max} = \mu_s mg \quad \Rightarrow \quad a_{\max} = \mu_s g$$

The mass cancels: the answer does not depend on how heavy the car is.

**Step 3.** $a_{\max} = 0.8 \times 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2 = 7.84\ \text{m/s}^2$.

## Inclined planes

*A 5.0 kg box rests on a rough inclined plane which makes a 30° angle with the floor. Find the normal force and the friction force on the box.*

**Step 1.** Draw the free-body diagram with axes along and perpendicular to the *slope*, not horizontal and vertical, and resolve the weight into those two directions: $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope.

**Step 2.** The box *rests*, so it is in equilibrium in both directions. Perpendicular to the slope the normal force balances the perpendicular component of the weight, $N = mg\cos\theta$. Along the slope, static friction balances the component pulling the box down the slope, $f = mg\sin\theta$.

**Step 3.** Substituting $m = 5.0\ \text{kg}$, $g = 9.8\ \text{N/kg}$ and $\theta = 30°$:

$$f = mg\sin 30° = 24.5\ \text{N} \qquad N = mg\cos 30° = 42.4\ \text{N}$$

Choosing the axes along the slope is what keeps this short. With horizontal and vertical axes, both the normal force and the friction would have to be resolved and the box would be accelerating in neither direction but along neither axis either.

> The guide's worked line for this example writes the mass as 3.0 kg while quoting the results 24.5 N and 42.4 N, which are the values for the 5.0 kg box stated in the question. Use 5.0 kg.

## Connected objects

*Two boxes are connected by a cord running over a pulley, box A resting on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.20 between it and the table. The mass of the cord and pulley and any friction in the pulley are ignored. Find (a) the acceleration $a$ of the system, assuming the cord does not stretch, and (b) the tension in the cord.*

The solution of connected objects divides into two approaches: **the calculation of each object separately**, and **the calculation of the whole object**. Both give the same answers here, $a = 1.4\ \text{m/s}^2$ and $T = 16.8\ \text{N}$.

**First solution — divided.** Draw a free-body diagram for each box in turn and write Newton's second law for each. Box A on the table is driven by the tension and held back by kinetic friction; the hanging box is pulled down by its weight and up by the same tension. Because the cord does not stretch, both boxes have the same acceleration, and because the cord and pulley are massless and frictionless the tension is the same throughout. That gives two equations in the two unknowns $a$ and $T$, which are solved together.

**Second solution — whole.** Treat the two boxes and the cord as a single object. The tension is now internal to that object and disappears from the equation entirely, leaving the driving weight and the retarding friction acting on the total mass, which gives $a$ in one line. The tension is then recovered by returning to one of the individual boxes.

The trade-off between the methods is the point of doing both. The whole-system method gets the acceleration fastest precisely because it hides the tension; when the tension is what you were asked for, you still have to look inside the system to find it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Friction** | A force that resists the relative motion, or the tendency of such motion, of two surfaces in contact; always directed opposite to the motion |
| **Static friction** | Friction acting on objects at rest, preventing them from starting to move; must be overcome by an applied force to initiate motion |
| **Kinetic friction (dynamic friction)** | Friction acting on objects already in motion, opposing the movement; generally weaker than static friction |

title: Kinematics of Uniform Circular Motion
summary: An object moving in a circular path at constant speed experiences uniform circular motion. The velocity vector is always tangent to the circle. This is the reason the motion cannot be described as una
markdown:
# 5.1 Kinematics of Uniform Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Uniform circular motion

An object moving in a circular path at constant speed experiences **uniform circular motion**.

The **velocity vector is always tangent to the circle**. This is the reason the motion cannot be described as unaccelerated even though the speed never changes: a tangent to a circle points in a different direction at every point, so the velocity vector is being turned continuously, and since velocity is a vector, turning it *is* changing it.

## Centripetal acceleration

**Centripetal acceleration** is acceleration that points toward the centre of a circular path, causing a change in direction.

$$a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}$$

where $a_c$ is the centripetal acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$, $v$ is the speed of the object in $\text{m/s}$ and $r$ is the radius of the circular path in metres.

The motion can equally be described by how long each lap takes. Writing $T$ for the **period**, the time to complete one full revolution, the object covers one circumference in one period, so

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} \qquad a_c = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$$

and the **frequency** $f$, in hertz, is the number of revolutions per unit time — the reciprocal of the period:

$$f = \frac{1}{T}$$

Note the $v^2$ in the centripetal acceleration. Doubling the speed does not double the acceleration required to keep the object on the same circle; it quadruples it. That single fact is behind most of the results in the sections that follow.

## Check your understanding

**A satellite orbits Earth with a period of 90 minutes at a radius of 7000 km. Find its orbital speed.**

The period is $90 \times 60 = 5400\ \text{s}$ and the radius $7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$, so

$$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = \frac{2\pi (7.0 \times 10^{6})}{5400} \approx 8.1 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$$

**Two wheels are connected by a belt, with one wheel twice the radius of the other. How do their speeds compare?**

The belt does not stretch or slip, so it moves at one speed, and that is the speed of the rim of each wheel: the two wheels have the *same linear speed at the rim*. They do not turn at the same rate, though — the larger wheel has twice as far to go round, so it completes a revolution in twice the time.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Uniform circular motion** | Motion of an object along a circular path at constant speed |
| **Centripetal acceleration** | Acceleration that points toward the centre of a circular path, causing a change in direction; $a_c = v^2/r$ |
| **Period ($T$)** | The time to complete one full revolution |
| **Frequency ($f$)** | The number of revolutions per unit time, measured in hertz (Hz); $f = 1/T$ |

title: Dynamics of Uniform Circular Motion
summary: Centripetal force is the net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion. It is Newton's second law applied to the centripetal accelerati
markdown:
# 5.2 Dynamics of Uniform Circular Motion

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Centripetal force

**Centripetal force** is the net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion. It is Newton's second law applied to the centripetal acceleration of the previous section:

$$F_c = m a_c = \frac{m v^2}{r}$$

with $F_c$ in newtons.

## Identifying the source of the centripetal force

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is a *role*, filled by whichever real force happens to point toward the centre in the situation at hand, and it is provided by different forces in different situations — the tension in a string for an object whirled on the end of one, static friction for a car rounding a flat curve, gravity for a satellite in orbit.

The first move in any circular-motion problem is therefore to ask which real force is supplying the centripetal force. Only then does $F_c = mv^2/r$ have anything to be set equal to.

## Effects of centripetal force on motion

What the object does depends on how the available force compares with the $mv^2/r$ that the circle demands:

| Available force | Result |
|---|---|
| Equal to $mv^2/r$ | Uniform circular motion occurs |
| Less than $mv^2/r$ | The object moves outward — the curve it follows is wider |
| Greater than $mv^2/r$ | The object moves inward — the curve it follows is tighter |

The middle row is the case that matters practically: too little force does not send the object flying off sideways, it simply means the object cannot turn as sharply as the intended circle, and it takes a wider path.

## Centripetal and centrifugal force

Centripetal force is a **real force** that keeps an object moving in a circle. That is the contrast being drawn: the inward force is the one that exists and can be identified with a rope, a road or a planet, and it is the one that belongs in your equations.

## Motion in vertical circles

A vertical circle is not uniform circular motion, because gravity helps the motion on the way down and hinders it on the way up, and the analysis at the two extreme points is different.

**At the top of a loop**, gravity points toward the centre of the circle, so gravity itself can supply some or all of the centripetal force. The limiting case is when it supplies *all* of it and the string or track contributes nothing. That defines the minimum speed for staying on a circular path:

$$mg = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$$

Below that speed the required centripetal force would be less than the object's own weight, and there is no way to reduce gravity, so the object leaves the circular path.

**At the bottom of a loop**, tension is greatest. There gravity points *away* from the centre, so the tension has to supply the whole centripetal force and hold up the weight as well.

## Check your understanding

**A car makes a turn on an icy road and starts sliding outward. Explain why this happens in terms of centripetal force.**

The centripetal force for a turn on a flat road comes from friction between the tyres and the road. Ice greatly reduces the friction available, so the inward force falls short of the $mv^2/r$ the turn requires. As the table above says, a force less than the required one means the car cannot follow the intended circle and instead takes a wider path — which is what "sliding outward" is.

**A 5.0 kg object is swung in a 1.5 m radius vertical circle. Find the minimum speed needed at the top to maintain circular motion.**

$$v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 1.5} \approx 3.8\ \text{m/s}$$

The mass cancels out of $mg = mv^2/r$, so the 5.0 kg is not needed.

**A satellite is in orbit around Earth. If its speed doubles while maintaining the same radius, by what factor does the required centripetal force change?**

$F_c = mv^2/r$ depends on the square of the speed, so doubling $v$ multiplies the required force by four.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Centripetal force** | The net force directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in uniform circular motion; $F_c = mv^2/r$ |
| **Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle** | $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$, the speed at which gravity alone supplies the centripetal force |

title: Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked
summary: On a flat curve the centripetal force — the force that keeps a car moving in a circle — is provided by static friction if there is no other force. Nothing else on a flat road points toward the centre
markdown:
# 5.3 Highway Curves, Banked and Unbanked

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Unbanked curves

On a flat curve the centripetal force — the force that keeps a car moving in a circle — **is provided by static friction if there is no other force**. Nothing else on a flat road points toward the centre of the turn, so friction has the job on its own.

$$f_s = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

For a car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ moving at $14\ \text{m/s}$ on a flat curve of radius $50\ \text{m}$, the centripetal force needed is

$$F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{1000 \times 14^2}{50} = 3.9 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$$

and friction must be able to supply that much, or the car does not make the turn.

Since the friction available is at most $\mu_s N = \mu_s mg$, setting that against the requirement gives the maximum speed:

$$\frac{mv_{\max}^2}{r} = \mu_s m g \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$$

The mass cancels, so **the maximum speed on an unbanked curve is determined by the friction coefficient** and the radius, not by how heavy the vehicle is.

## Banked curves

**Banked curves** are curves that are tilted to help vehicles turn without relying on friction. Tilting the road tilts the normal force with it, and the normal force then has a horizontal component pointing toward the centre of the turn — a source of centripetal force that does not depend on the state of the tyres or the road surface.

For a given bank angle $\theta$ there is one speed at which that component is exactly the centripetal force required, and no friction is needed at all:

$$\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$$

For a curve of radius $100\ \text{m}$ banked at $15.0°$, the ideal speed is

$$v = \sqrt{100 \times 9.8 \times \tan 15.0°} \approx 16.2\ \text{m/s}$$

## When the speed is not the ideal speed

The ideal speed is a single value, and real traffic does not travel at exactly one speed, so friction returns as a correction rather than as the main effect:

| Speed | What friction does |
|---|---|
| Too fast | Friction increases to help keep the car from sliding **outward** |
| Too slow | Friction is needed to keep the car from sliding toward the **inside** of the curve |

The second case is the one that surprises people. Below the ideal speed the horizontal component of the normal force is *more* than the turn requires, so the surplus pushes the car down the bank toward the inside, and friction has to act up the slope to hold it on course.

## Check your understanding

**What happens if a car takes a turn on an unbanked curve with insufficient friction?**

Friction is the only source of centripetal force on a flat curve, so if it cannot supply the $mv^2/r$ the turn requires, the net inward force is too small and the car cannot turn as sharply as the curve demands. It slides outward, following a wider path than the road.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Unbanked (flat) curve** | A curve on which the centripetal force is provided by static friction alone |
| **Banked curve** | A curve that is tilted to help vehicles turn without relying on friction |
| **Ideal (design) speed** | The speed $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$ at which a banked curve can be taken with no friction needed |

# 5.6 Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The law

Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This force acts along the line joining the two particles.

$$F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $F$ | The gravitational force |
| $G$ | The universal gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| $m_1,\ m_2$ | The masses of the two objects |
| $r$ | The distance between the **centres** of the two objects |

The word *universal* is the claim being made: the same law and the same constant govern the attraction between any two masses anywhere, which is why one formula covers a falling apple, the Moon's orbit and the Earth's orbit alike.

Two features of the algebra are worth reading off directly. The force depends on the **product** of the masses, so if the mass of one planet doubles, the gravitational force doubles. The distance appears as an **inverse square**, so the force falls away far faster with separation than it grows with mass: doubling $r$ cuts the force to a quarter.

Note also that $r$ is measured between the centres of the objects, not between their surfaces.

## The Cavendish experiment

The law can be written down without knowing $G$, but nothing can be calculated from it until $G$ has a number. In 1798 **Henry Cavendish** used a **torsion balance** to measure the gravitational force between two objects in the laboratory, which allowed the universal gravitational constant $G$ to be calculated.

The measurement is difficult because gravitational attraction between laboratory-sized masses is extremely weak — which is the physical meaning of $G$ being so small a number.

## Important constants

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| Universal gravitational constant, $G$ | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| Mass of Earth | $5.972 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ |
| Radius of Earth | $6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ |

The guide tabulates several further constants for problems on this scale: the mass of the Moon and the Earth–Moon distance, the mass of the Sun and the Earth–Sun distance (one **astronomical unit**, 1 AU), the speed of light, and the **light year**, the distance light travels in a year.

## Worked example

*Find the gravitational force between the Sun and the Earth.*

Substitute the mass of the Sun for $m_1$, the mass of the Earth for $m_2$, and the Earth–Sun distance of 1 AU for $r$ into $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$. The answer is in newtons.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Newton's law of universal gravitation** | Every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them |
| **Universal gravitational constant ($G$)** | The constant of proportionality in the law of universal gravitation, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ |
| **Cavendish experiment** | Henry Cavendish's 1798 measurement, using a torsion balance, of the gravitational force between two objects, which allowed $G$ to be calculated |
| **Astronomical unit (AU)** | The distance between the Earth and the Sun |
| **Light year** | The distance light travels in one year |

# 5.7 Gravity Near the Earth's Surface: Geophysical Applications

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where $g$ comes from

The acceleration due to gravity is not an independent fact about the world. It follows from the law of universal gravitation applied to one particular pair of objects: an object of mass $m$ and the Earth.

For an object on the Earth's surface, the weight $mg$ *is* the gravitational attraction of the Earth, so

$$mg = G\frac{m M_E}{r_E^{2}}$$

The object's own mass appears on both sides and cancels, which is the algebraic reason all objects fall with the same acceleration. Solving for $g$ gives

$$g = \frac{G M_E}{r_E^{2}}$$

Substituting $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $M_E = 5.972 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and $r_E = 6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$ returns $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$: the familiar figure is a consequence of the Earth's mass and radius, not a separate constant of nature.

## Far from the Earth's surface

As the distance from the Earth's centre increases, the gravitational force decreases, and so does the acceleration it produces. The same formula applies with the distance from the centre in place of the Earth's radius:

$$g_r = \frac{G M_E}{r^{2}}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $g_r$ | The acceleration due to gravity at distance $r$ |
| $r_E$ | The radius of the Earth |
| $r$ | The distance from the Earth's centre |

Since the dependence is an inverse square in $r$, and $r$ is measured from the *centre*, climbing a few kilometres above the surface changes $r$ only very slightly from $r_E$ and so changes $g$ only very slightly. Gravity weakens with height, but not quickly — which is exactly why orbiting spacecraft, only a few hundred kilometres up, are still firmly held by the Earth.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Acceleration due to gravity at the surface** | $g = GM_E/r_E^2$, obtained by equating an object's weight to the Earth's gravitational attraction |
| **Acceleration due to gravity at a distance $r$** | $g_r = GM_E/r^2$, where $r$ is measured from the Earth's centre |

# 5.8 Satellites and "Weightlessness"

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Free fall and apparent weight

**Free fall** is the condition of an object falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance.

**Weightlessness** occurs when an astronaut in orbit feels weightless because both the shuttle and the astronaut are in free fall together. The quotation marks in the section title are doing real work: **the gravitational force is not zero**. There is no apparent weight only because there is no support force — the floor is falling away at exactly the rate the astronaut is falling, so it never pushes back.

What you feel as your weight is in fact the support force from whatever is holding you up. Remove the support while leaving gravity untouched, and the sensation of weight vanishes although the force has not.

## Orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit is held there by gravity, and gravity is therefore the source of the centripetal force. Equating the two,

$$\frac{G M m}{r^{2}} = \frac{m v^{2}}{r}$$

gives the **orbital speed**, in which the satellite's own mass has cancelled:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$

where $M$ is the mass of the central object and $r$ the radius of the orbit measured from its centre. The **orbital period** follows from the fact that one lap covers a circumference:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v}$$

Because the satellite's mass cancels, a heavy satellite and a light one at the same altitude travel at the same speed with the same period — the same cancellation, and the same reason, as for objects in free fall at the surface.

## Worked example

*A satellite orbits Earth 225 km above its surface. The Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}$ and its radius $6.38 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$. What are the satellite's orbital speed and period?*

The orbital radius is measured from the centre of the Earth, so the altitude must be added to the Earth's radius:

$$r = 6.38 \times 10^{6} + 2.25 \times 10^{5} = 6.605 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}$$

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(5.97 \times 10^{24})}{6.605 \times 10^{6}}} \approx 7.77 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m/s}$$

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi (6.605 \times 10^{6})}{7.77 \times 10^{3}} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{3}\ \text{s}$$

which is about 89 minutes. Forgetting to add the altitude to the Earth's radius is the standard error in this calculation, and it gives an answer that looks plausible, so it is worth checking deliberately.

## Check your understanding

**What causes an object to stay in orbit around Earth?**

Gravity. It supplies the centripetal force that continuously turns the satellite's velocity toward the Earth, so the satellite keeps falling toward the Earth without ever getting closer to it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Free fall** | When an object is falling with only gravity acting on it, without air resistance |
| **Weightlessness** | The sensation experienced when an astronaut and the craft are in free fall together; the gravitational force is not zero, but there is no apparent weight because there is no support force |
| **Orbital speed** | $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, where $M$ is the mass of the central object |
| **Orbital period** | $T = 2\pi r / v$, the time for one complete orbit |

# 5.9 Kepler's Laws and Newton's Synthesis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kepler's laws

Kepler's laws describe how planets actually move, and they were established from observation before there was any theory to explain them.

**First law.** Planets orbit the Sun in **elliptical** paths, with the Sun at one **focus**. Not at the centre — at a focus, which means a planet's distance from the Sun changes over the course of its year.

**Second law.** A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal time intervals**. Since the line is shorter when the planet is nearer the Sun, the planet must travel further along its orbit in a given time to sweep the same area, and so **planets move faster when they are closer to the Sun**. The law is a statement about speed disguised as a statement about area.

## Newton's synthesis

The orbital period and the orbital distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and **Kepler's third law can be derived using Newton's law** of universal gravitation.

The derivation is the same equation used for satellites in the previous section. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for a planet of mass $m$ in a circular orbit of radius $r$ about a central object of mass $M$:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

Substituting $v = 2\pi r/T$ and rearranging gives

$$T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM}\,r^{3}$$

so $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$, with a constant of proportionality that depends only on the mass of the central object — exactly the two dependencies stated above. Comparing two bodies orbiting the same central object, the constant cancels:

$$\frac{T_1^{2}}{T_2^{2}} = \frac{r_1^{3}}{r_2^{3}}$$

This is the synthesis: a law obtained from astronomical observation is shown to be a consequence of the same force that governs falling objects on Earth. The planets were not obeying a special rule of their own.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following best explains why astronauts on the International Space Station feel weightless?**

Because the station and the astronauts are in free fall together, so nothing supports the astronauts and they have no apparent weight. It is not because gravity is absent at that altitude — gravity is what holds the station in orbit.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kepler's first law** | Planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun at one focus |
| **Kepler's second law** | A line drawn from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals; planets move faster when closer to the Sun |
| **Kepler's third law** | $T^2 \propto r^3$; the orbital period and distance depend on the mass of the central object and the radius of the orbit, and the relation is derivable from Newton's law of universal gravitation |

markdown:
# 6.1 Work Done by a Constant Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What work is

**Work** is a scalar: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement.

$$W = F d \cos\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Its unit is the **joule** (J).

The definition has two halves, and both matter. There must be a displacement, and the force must have a component along it. A force at right angles to the motion contributes nothing at all, because $\cos 90° = 0$ — the parallel component it needs to supply is zero.

Work is **positive** when the force and the displacement are in the same direction.

## Worked example

*A sailor pulls a boat a distance of 0.30 m along a dock using a rope that makes a 25.0° angle with the horizontal. How much work does the sailor do on the boat if he exerts a force of 255 N on the rope?*

The boat moves horizontally, but the rope pulls at 25.0° to the horizontal, so only the horizontal component of the 255 N does work:

$$W = Fd\cos\theta = 255 \times 0.30 \times \cos 25.0° \approx 69\ \text{J}$$

The same pattern — pulling a crate with a rope at an angle — recurs throughout the chapter.

## Lifting an object

Lifting an object vertically is the other standard case. Here the force is along the displacement, and the work done equals the change in gravitational potential energy of the object. This is the first sign of the connection developed in the rest of the chapter: work is the mechanism by which energy is transferred and stored.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following results in zero work?**

A. Pushing a box across the floor
B. Holding a book without moving it
C. Pulling a sled in the snow
D. Dropping an object from a height

**Answer: B.** Holding a book takes force, but the book does not move, so the displacement is zero and $W = Fd\cos\theta = 0$. Effort is not work in the physics sense; work requires the point of application to move.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work** | A scalar quantity: the product of the magnitude of the displacement times the component of the force parallel to the displacement, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| **Joule (J)** | The unit of work |
| **Positive work** | Work done when force and displacement are in the same direction |

markdown:
# 6.2 Work Done by a Varying Force

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Work as an area

$W = Fd\cos\theta$ assumes a single value of $F$ for the whole displacement. When the force changes with position, there is no single $F$ to put in the formula, and work must be found another way: **from the area under the force versus displacement curve.**

The work done is the area between the graph of $F$ and the $x$-axis, between the starting and finishing positions.

This is not a new definition of work but the same one applied piecewise. Over a displacement small enough that the force barely changes, the work is $F$ times that small displacement — the area of a thin strip under the curve. Adding the strips across the whole journey adds their areas, and the total is the area under the curve. The constant-force case is the special one where the graph is a horizontal line and the area is a rectangle, $F$ times $d$.

## Integration

In the limit of infinitely thin strips, that sum is an integral:

$$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$$

## Check your understanding

**What does the area under a Force versus Position graph represent?**

A. Velocity
B. Acceleration
C. Work
D. Power

**Answer: C.**

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Work done by a varying force** | The area between the force–displacement curve and the $x$-axis, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F\,dx$ |

markdown:
# 6.3 Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Principle

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Kinetic energy

**Kinetic energy** is the energy of motion:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$$

Like work, it is measured in joules, and like work it is a scalar — it carries no direction, so the sign of the velocity is irrelevant. An object moving left at $5\ \text{m/s}$ and one moving right at $5\ \text{m/s}$ have the same kinetic energy.

The dependence on $v^2$ means kinetic energy grows far faster than speed: doubling the speed of an object quadruples its kinetic energy.

## The work-energy principle

The **work-energy principle** states that the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^{2}$$

This is what makes work worth defining. It converts a question about forces and displacements into a question about speeds, without any of the intermediate detail about how the force varied along the way.

## Worked example

*A 145 g baseball is thrown so that it acquires a speed of 25 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?*

Convert the mass to kilograms first — $145\ \text{g} = 0.145\ \text{kg}$ — since the joule is built on kilograms, metres and seconds:

$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.145)(25)^{2} \approx 45\ \text{J}$$

## Check your understanding

**If net work on an object is positive, what happens to its kinetic energy?**

A. It decreases
B. It stays the same
C. It becomes zero
D. It increases

**Answer: D.** By the work-energy principle $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$, so positive net work means a positive change in kinetic energy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Kinetic energy (KE)** | The energy of motion, $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ |
| **Work-energy principle** | The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy |

markdown:
# 6.4 Potential Energy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Stored energy

**Potential energy (PE)** is stored energy due to position. Two forms appear in this chapter:

| Form | Formula | Stored by |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$ | Raising a mass to a height $y$ |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$ | Stretching or compressing a spring by $x$ from its natural length |

Here $k$ is the spring stiffness constant, in newtons per metre.

## The reference point

Potential energy is **relative to a chosen zero level**. There is no absolute height and therefore no absolute gravitational potential energy: you choose where $y = 0$, and every value of $PE$ in the problem is quoted with respect to that choice.

The choice is free, and different choices give different numbers for the *same* physical situation. What they never change is a **difference** in potential energy between two points, and it is always a difference that appears in physical predictions. So choose whatever zero makes the arithmetic easiest — usually the lowest point of the motion, or the starting point — and then use it consistently.

## Worked example: a roller-coaster car

*A 1000 kg roller-coaster car moves from point 1 to point 2 and then to point 3.*

**(a) Taking $y = 0$ at point 1**, the gravitational potential energy at points 2 and 3 is $mgy$ with each height measured from point 1. A point below the chosen zero has a negative height, and therefore a negative potential energy — which is perfectly acceptable, since only differences are physical.

**(b) The change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3** is the difference of the two values found in (a).

**(c) Repeating with $y = 0$ at point 3** gives $PE = 0$ at point 3 by definition, and different numbers at points 1 and 2. But the change in potential energy from point 2 to point 3 comes out the same as in (b). That is the lesson of the example: the reference point moves all the individual values up or down together, and cancels out of every difference.

## Worked example: a spring

*A spring has a spring stiffness constant of 440 N/m. How much must this spring be stretched to store 25 J of potential energy?*

Rearranging $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ for $x$:

$$x = \sqrt{\frac{2\,PE}{k}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 25}{440}} \approx 0.34\ \text{m}$$

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following increases an object's gravitational potential energy?**

A. Lowering it to the ground
B. Compressing a spring
C. Raising it to a higher shelf
D. Sliding it on a level surface

**Answer: C.** Gravitational potential energy is $mgy$, so it increases only when $y$ increases. Compressing a spring stores energy, but elastic potential energy, not gravitational.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Potential energy (PE)** | Stored energy due to position |
| **Gravitational potential energy** | $PE = mgy$, the energy stored by raising a mass to a height |
| **Elastic (spring) potential energy** | $PE = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, the energy stored by stretching or compressing a spring |
| **Spring stiffness constant ($k$)** | The constant, in N/m, measuring how stiff a spring is |
| **Reference point** | The chosen zero level with respect to which potential energy is measured |

markdown:
# 6.5 Conservative and Nonconservative Forces

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The distinction

A **conservative force** is one for which the work done is **path-independent**: it depends only on the starting and finishing points, not on the route taken between them. Gravity is the standard example.

A **nonconservative force** is one for which the work done **depends on the path**. Friction is the standard example — the longer the route, the more work friction does against the motion, even if the object ends up in the same place.

| | Conservative | Nonconservative |
|---|---|---|
| Work done | Path-independent | Depends on the path |
| Example | Gravity | Friction |
| Potential energy | Can be defined | Cannot be defined |

## Identifying which type a force is

The test is the last row of that table: **if a potential energy can be defined for a force, the force is conservative.**

The reason follows from the previous section. Potential energy is a function of *position* alone — $mgy$ depends on where the object is and nothing else. For such a quantity to describe the work a force does, that work must itself depend only on the positions at the two ends of the journey. A force whose work depends on the route taken cannot be summarised by any function of position, so no potential energy exists for it.

## Mechanical energy and friction

*A box sliding down a ramp with friction loses mechanical energy due to friction.*

This is what the distinction costs in practice. Gravity does work on the box that can be fully accounted for as a change in gravitational potential energy, and recovered if the box goes back up. The work done against friction cannot be recovered: it is not stored anywhere as potential energy, and the mechanical energy of the box is reduced by it.

## Check your understanding

**Which of the following is a conservative force?**

A. Friction
B. Tension
C. Gravity
D. Air resistance

**Answer: C.** Gravity has a potential energy, $mgy$, defined for it; friction and air resistance both do path-dependent work.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Conservative force** | A force whose work is path-independent, such as gravity |
| **Nonconservative force** | A force whose work depends on the path taken, such as friction |

markdown:
# 8.1 Angular Quantities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Rotation needs its own set of quantities, because every point of a rotating body travels a different distance at a different speed while the body as a whole turns by one definite amount. The angular quantities describe the turning itself.

## Angular position and displacement

**Angular position** $\theta$ is the angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line. Its unit is the **radian** (rad), defined by

$$\theta = \frac{s}{r}$$

where $s$ is the arc length in metres and $r$ the radius in metres. A radian is thus the angle for which the arc length equals the radius; being a ratio of two lengths, it is a pure number, which is why radians can be multiplied into linear quantities without carrying a unit along.

Rotation has a sign convention, as straight-line motion does:

| Direction | Sign |
|---|---|
| Counterclockwise | Positive |
| Clockwise | Negative |

## Converting between degrees and radians

A full turn is $360°$ and also $2\pi$ radians, so the two units are related by $180° = \pi\ \text{rad}$:

$$\text{degrees} \to \text{radians:}\quad \theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\deg} \times \frac{\pi}{180}$$

$$\text{radians} \to \text{degrees:}\quad \theta_{\deg} = \theta_{\text{rad}} \times \frac{180}{\pi}$$

## Angular velocity

**Angular velocity** $\omega$ is the rate of change of angular displacement over time:

$$\omega = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$$

measured in radians per second (rad/s). It takes the same sign convention: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative.

Its properties are read off a graph of angular position against time, exactly as velocity is read off a position–time graph in straight-line motion:

- **Constant $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ against time is a straight line.
- **Changing $\omega$**: the graph of $\theta$ is curved, and the slope of the tangent at a point gives the instantaneous $\omega$ at that moment.

## Relationship between linear and angular quantities

A point at distance $r$ from the axis moves along an arc of length $s = r\theta$, so dividing by the time taken gives its linear speed:

$$v = r\omega$$

This single relation is the bridge between the two descriptions, and it says something that is easy to get wrong: the angular velocity belongs to the *whole rotating body*, while the linear speed belongs to a *particular point on it* and grows with distance from the axis.

## Check your understanding

**Two points, A and B, are on a rotating disk, with B farther from the centre. Which point has a greater angular velocity? Which has a greater linear velocity? Why?**

The disk is rigid, so both points sweep through the same angle in the same time: their **angular velocities are equal**. But $v = r\omega$, and B has the larger $r$, so **B has the greater linear velocity** — it has a longer circle to travel in the same time.

**Convert 2.5 radians into degrees.**

$$2.5 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \approx 143°$$

**Convert 135° into radians.**

$$135 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 2.36\ \text{rad}$$

**The Earth completes one full rotation in 24 hours. What is its angular velocity in rad/s?**

One full rotation is $2\pi$ rad and 24 hours is $86\,400\ \text{s}$, so

$$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{86\,400} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{rad/s}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Angular position ($\theta$)** | The angle an object has rotated relative to a reference line, $\theta = s/r$ |
| **Radian (rad)** | The unit of angular position, defined as the arc length divided by the radius |
| **Arc length ($s$)** | The distance measured along the circular path, in metres |
| **Angular velocity ($\omega$)** | The rate of change of angular displacement over time, $\omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t$, in rad/s |

# 1 Line and Texture

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Line

A **line** is a mark or stroke made with pen, pencil, paint or similar, to show
movement, an object's placement, or to communicate a visual feeling.

Depending on how line is used in a composition, the artist can use it to
communicate a specific emotion. This is the practical point of the unit: the
direction of a line carries meaning before any subject is recognised.

| Line | Communicates |
|---|---|
| **Vertical** | Stability, structure, power |
| **Horizontal** | Rest, relaxation, calmness |
| **Curving** | Movement, sporadic, energy |
| **Diagonal** | Unbalanced, chaotic |

**Contour** is the outline — the edge or line that defines or bounds a shape or
object. Objects would not be visible to the human eye without a contour:

- In a **two-dimensional** drawing or painting, the contour lines can be
  considered the object's outline
- In a **real, three-dimensional** object, the contour is simply the line that
  defines its edges

An **implied line** is a line that does not physically exist but is implied to
exist.

## Texture

**Texture** is a visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an
object looks and the way it feels to touch. **Visual texture** is used in art to
communicate an idea or emotion.

## Composition and its devices

**Composition** is a visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an
object looks and feels.

**Overlap** is when an object covers or partially covers another object in a
composition, to convey the idea of space. Overlapping helps communicate **depth
and a sense of real space**.

**Repetition** is when something is repeated or occurs over and over again within
the same composition. Using repetition helps give a composition **unity and
consistency**.

## Artists

| Artist | Known for |
|---|---|
| **Edgar Degas** | A French artist famous for his paintings, sculptures, prints and drawings |
| **Andy Warhol** | An American artist, director and producer; a leading figure in the visual art movement known as **pop art** |
| **Henri Matisse** | A French artist known for his use of colour and his fluid, original draughtsmanship. A draughtsman, printmaker and sculptor, but known primarily as a painter |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Line** | A mark or stroke made to show movement, an object's placement, or a visual feeling |
| **Contour** | The outline; the edge or line that defines or bounds a shape or object |
| **Implied line** | A line that does not physically exist but is implied to exist |
| **Texture** | The visual characteristic of the relationship between how an object looks and how it feels |
| **Composition** | The visual characteristic of the relationship between the way an object looks and feels |
| **Overlap** | When an object covers or partially covers another to convey space, communicating depth |
| **Repetition** | When something recurs in a composition, giving it unity and consistency |
| **Pop art** | The visual art movement in which Andy Warhol was a leading figure |

# 2 Colour and Value

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Colour (hue)

**Colour**, or **hue**, is the amount of light reflected on an object. The only
way an object's colour can be seen depends on the amount of light reflected from
its surface.

1. **Primary colours** — natural or basic colours that cannot be created by
   combining other colours
2. **Secondary colours** — the combination of two primary colours
3. **Tertiary colours** — the combination of a primary colour and a secondary
   colour

The three build on one another in order, which is why the wheel has the structure
the schemes below depend on.

## Value (tint, tone and shade)

**Value** is the degree of lightness or darkness within a given colour, shade,
tone or tint. Changing a colour's value usually makes the colour seem **less
intense or subtle**.

| Term | Added | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Shade** | Black | The value becomes darker with the degree of shade used |
| **Tone** | Grey | The value becomes greyer with the degree of tone used |
| **Tint** | White | The value becomes lighter with the degree of tint used |

## Colour schemes

| Scheme | Definition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Monochromatic** (单色模式) | A wide range of tints and shades of a single colour | Harmonious and subtle |
| **Complementary** (互补色模式) | Opposite colours on the colour wheel | Very vibrant |
| **Analogous** (相似色模式) | A set of colours adjacent to each other on the colour wheel | Harmonious and subtle |
| **Split complementary** (补色分割模式) | A combination of complementary and analogous schemes, allowing intensity but not as strong as pure complementary | Vibrant and harmonious |
| **Triadic** (三等分配色模式) | Three colours equally spaced around the colour wheel | Vibrant and harmonious |

## Balance

**Balance** is arranging elements in a composition so that no one part of a work
overpowers or seems heavier than any other part. It is a **principle of design**
dealing with the **visual weight** within a composition.

- **Symmetrical** — a balance showing stability, usually centred in the composition
- **Vertical** — a type of symmetrical balance with a vertical orientation
- **Horizontal** — a type of symmetrical balance with a horizontal orientation
- **Asymmetrical** — a balance that is neither centred nor symmetrical
- **Radial** — a balance where all the elements expand or spiral out from a
  central point

## Focal point, contrast and intensity

The **focal point** is the focus, or most important visual part, within a
composition. The basic elements and principles help determine it — for example
the way implied line is used, colour and value intensity, and contrast.

**Contrast** is the difference or opposition between two objects or elements. It
is a principle of design: the arrangement of opposite elements — light against
dark colours, rough against smooth textures, large against small shapes — to
create visual interest.

**Intensity** is the strength or sharpness of a colour, due to its degree of
freedom from mixture with its complement. A colour's intensity is seen at its
**purest form**, when not mixed with any other colour, shade, tone or tint. Other
factors also affect it, such as a change of value around a specific colour, or
the texture around a given colour.

Note how the three connect: contrast and intensity are both ways of directing the
eye, and both are among the means of establishing a focal point.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Colour (hue)** | The amount of light reflected on an object |
| **Primary colours** | Basic colours that cannot be created by combining others |
| **Secondary colours** | The combination of two primary colours |
| **Tertiary colours** | The combination of a primary and a secondary colour |
| **Value** | The degree of lightness or darkness within a colour, shade, tone or tint |
| **Shade** | Black added to a colour, darkening its value |
| **Tone** | Grey added to a colour, making its value greyer |
| **Tint** | White added to a colour, lightening its value |
| **Monochromatic** | A wide range of tints and shades of a single colour |
| **Complementary** | Opposite colours on the colour wheel |
| **Analogous** | Colours adjacent to each other on the colour wheel |
| **Split complementary** | Complementary and analogous schemes combined |
| **Triadic** | Three colours equally spaced around the colour wheel |
| **Balance** | Arranging elements so no part overpowers or seems heavier than another |
| **Symmetrical** | Balance showing stability, usually centred |
| **Asymmetrical** | Balance that is neither centred nor symmetrical |
| **Radial** | Balance in which elements expand or spiral out from a central point |
| **Focal point** | The most important visual part within a composition |
| **Contrast** | The arrangement of opposite elements to create visual interest |
| **Intensity** | The strength or sharpness of a colour, from its freedom from mixture with its complement |

# 3 Elements and Principles

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Shape

A **shape** is a two-dimensional area created when a line or contour is closed,
when there is a change in value, or through some other form of contrast.

Shapes help create complex drawings and paintings, affect composition, and
contribute to the balance within a work. **All shapes are two-dimensional**,
meaning they have only length and width — which is exactly what distinguishes
shape from form below.

- **Geometric shapes** are usually recognisable by name, and mathematics can be
  used to find information about them: circle, square, trapezoid
- **Organic shapes** seem to follow no rules
- **Tessellation** is an arrangement of shapes closely fitted together,
  especially polygons in a repeated pattern without gaps or overlapping

## Form

**Form** is an element of art similar to shape but with the added dimension of
**depth**.

## Movement and pattern

**Movement** is a principle of design that uses any element to show energy, flow,
or a feeling that objects within a composition are in motion.

**Pattern** is showing consistency with colours, lines, values and textures
throughout a composition.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Shape** | A two-dimensional area created when a line or contour closes, when value changes, or through contrast |
| **Geometric shape** | A shape usually recognisable by name, about which mathematics can give information |
| **Organic shape** | A shape that seems to follow no rules |
| **Tessellation** | Shapes closely fitted together in a repeated pattern without gaps or overlapping |
| **Form** | An element of art like shape, but with the added dimension of depth |
| **Movement** | A principle of design using any element to show energy, flow, or objects in motion |
| **Pattern** | Consistency of colours, lines, values and textures throughout a composition |

# 4 Inner Space and Perspective

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Space

**Space** is the visual element referring to the area between, around, above,
below and within objects. It gives artwork its dimension and helps communicate
**dynamic composition**. Sometimes the space is not actually within a piece — only
the **illusion** of it is.

**Negative space** is the space surrounding shapes or forms in two- and
three-dimensional art. It acts as a balance to positive space, is often
overlooked, and gives the eye **a place to rest**, increasing a composition's
appeal through subtle means.

**Positive space** is the area or part of a composition that the subject occupies
— the composition's actual **subject matter**, the main focus of a work. Its
specific elements render detail to catch the viewer's eye, and it should work
**equally with negative space**.

That last point is why negative space is treated as an element at all rather than
as leftover background.

## Proportion and foreshortening

**Proportion** is a principle of art describing the **size, location or amount of
one element in relation to another**, or to the whole — the relationship between
the sizes of figures and objects within a composition. For example the size of an
arm in relation to the rest of the body, or the size of a person in relation to
the size of a house.

**Foreshortening** is a method of rendering a specific object or figure in depth.
The artist records the **distortion seen by the eye** when an object or figure is
viewed at a distance or at an unusual angle.

## Perspective

**Perspective** was developed in the **15th century** by the architects **Leon
Battista Alberti (1404–72)** and **Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446)**. It remained
one of the basic principles of Western art until it was challenged by the ideas of
the **Cubists** at the start of the 20th century.

Two kinds are distinguished:

- **Linear perspective** deals with the organisation of shapes in space
- **Atmospheric or aerial perspective** deals with atmospheric effects on tones
  and colours

### One-point perspective

The perspective of a rectangle or box. It uses a **single vanishing point** to
draw an object, and is the **simplest** form of perspective drawing.

- The **front and back transversal planes always remain parallel to the picture
  plane**
- Only their **scale changes** as an object recedes into the distance
- Only the **receding orthogonal lines change angles**

There are **two types of construction line** used in perspective drawing.

### Two-point perspective

Used in illustrations of objects that have been **rotated at an angle to the
picture plane**. It uses **two sets of orthogonal lines and two vanishing points**
to draw each object, and there are **no longer any planes parallel to the picture
plane**.

The difference between the two follows from that last line: rotating the object
removes the parallel plane, and a second vanishing point is needed to place the
edges that are now receding.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Space** | The visual element referring to the area between, around, above, below and within objects |
| **Negative space** | The space surrounding shapes or forms, balancing positive space and giving the eye a place to rest |
| **Positive space** | The area a composition's subject occupies; its actual subject matter |
| **Proportion** | The size, location or amount of one element in relation to another or to the whole |
| **Foreshortening** | Rendering an object in depth by recording the distortion the eye sees at a distance or unusual angle |
| **Perspective** | The 15th-century principle developed by Alberti and Brunelleschi, challenged by the Cubists |
| **Linear perspective** | Perspective dealing with the organisation of shapes in space |
| **Atmospheric perspective** | Perspective dealing with atmospheric effects on tones and colours |
| **One-point perspective** | The simplest form, using a single vanishing point, with front and back planes parallel to the picture plane |
| **Two-point perspective** | Perspective for objects rotated to the picture plane, using two vanishing points and no parallel planes |
| **Vanishing point** | The point to which receding lines converge |
| **Orthogonal lines** | The receding lines that change angle as an object recedes |

# 5 Vocabulary of Art and Architecture

This unit is a vocabulary list. The terms are grouped here by what they describe,

## Techniques and materials

|---|---|
| **Fresco** | Plaster wall paintings |
| **Tempera** | A water-based pigment mixed with egg yolk |
| **Mosaics** | The use of small coloured objects to form a larger image |
| **Illumination** | Coloured illustrations containing gold and silver |
| **Printmaking** | The art of using different techniques to make prints |
| **Camera obscura** | A dark box or room with a small opening to let light in |

## Handling of light and detail

|---|---|
| **Chiaroscuro** | Extreme contrast of dark and light values |
| **Tenebrism** | Exaggerated contrast of darks and lights |
| **Realism** | Attention to extreme detail |
| **Symbolism** | The use of an object to represent a meaning other than its own outward appearance |

# 7 Movements from Neoclassicism to Primitivism

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The movements run in rough sequence, and several are defined by what they reject
in the one before.

## Neoclassicism

**Neoclassicism** literally means *the New Classic Period*. **Napoleon's interest
in the Classical Greek and Roman periods** resulted in his idea to **relive** those
periods.

**Allegorical** means symbols that tell a story — a symbolic narrative. Most of
**David's** works both told a story, mostly historical, and carried some symbolic
meaning or parallel to what was happening in modern-day France.

## Romanticism

**Romanticism** was a movement with a **revival of interest in Medieval stories and
the emotion of artistic elements**.

**Nonobjective** art is art that has **no recognisable subject matter, only the use
of raw elements**. Some artists in Romantic art used **non-representational subject
matter** to communicate the emotion of an idea.

## Realism

A **Realist** is an artist who painted in the Realist movement. The Realists
emphasised the **depiction of the common, everyday world** — a direct turn away from
Romanticism's medieval subjects.

## Photography

**Photography** is the art of producing images on **photosensitive**, or
light-sensitive, paper. The technology came from the idea of **printmaking** and how
an image can be made by first creating a mould or stencil.

## Impressionism and Pointillism

**Impressionism** is a style of painting emphasising **momentary effects of light on
colour**. Artists sought to create an **instant impression, not a detailed
analysis** — which is the direct opposite of Realism's attention to extreme detail.

**Pointillism** is colours **systematically applied to canvas with small dots**.
The guide notes we see a similar technique today in TV screens, computers and
colour printing.

## Expressionism

**Expressionism** is the **communication of strong personal and emotional feelings**
in artwork. **Van Gogh** was considered the artist who began this movement.

## Primitivism

**Primitivism** is the **less sophisticated native art of any culture**. **Gauguin**
moved to **Tahiti** because he became interested in a much more primitive lifestyle.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Neoclassicism** | Literally the New Classic Period; Napoleon's interest in Classical Greece and Rome led to his idea of reliving those periods |
| **Allegorical** | Symbols that tell a story; a symbolic narrative |
| **Romanticism** | A movement reviving interest in Medieval stories and the emotion of artistic elements |
| **Nonobjective** | Art with no recognisable subject matter, using only raw elements |
| **Realist** | An artist painting in the Realist movement, emphasising the common, everyday world |
| **Photography** | The art of producing images on photosensitive paper |
| **Impressionism** | A style emphasising momentary effects of light on colour, seeking an instant impression rather than detailed analysis |
| **Pointillism** | Colours systematically applied to canvas with small dots |
| **Expressionism** | The communication of strong personal and emotional feelings in artwork, begun by Van Gogh |
| **Primitivism** | The less sophisticated native art of any culture |
